title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
description: Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 introduces native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling the MCP data plane to run directly within your own Kubernetes cluster. This architecture ensures that AI agent request traffic and tool execution remain entirely inside your infrastructure while pulling configuration updates from the control plane. Developers can expose OpenAPI 3.0.x specifications as discoverable MCP tools, leverage existing security policies and API products, and trace end-to-end requests using W3C trace context headers.

description:
The Overview tab in the dashboard now lets you choose which metric appears on each project card.

Project cards used to show a fixed Real Experience Score in the top right, but not everyone on your team watches the same signal. You can now swap that slot for whichever metric matters for that project. A security-sensitive project can show firewall activity, while a marketing site project shows traffic.

Available widgets

  • Firewall: allowed requests, denied requests

  • Observability: alerts, edge requests, function invocations, error rate

  • Speed Insights: Real Experience Score, LCP, CLS

  • Web Analytics: visitors online, visitors, page views

Pick per project

Open the switcher in the top right of any project card. The menu shows the current value for each available metric. When you select one, your choice is saved for that project and follows your account across refreshes and devices.

Enable features from the card

If a project does not have a feature enabled, you can start the enable flow from the widget menu without leaving the Overview tab. This is available for Speed Insights Plus, Web Analytics, and alerts.

Get started

Open your team’s Overview tab and use the switcher on any project card.

title: Node.js Text Classification: Implementing Structured Output with a GPT API
description:
Node.js Text Classification: Implementing Structured Output with a GPT API

TL;DR: For a Node.js implementation of text classification using a GPT API, the important design choice is not which text model sounds best. It is whether the classifier returns a contract that the review queue can validate, retry, and safely apply twice. Put the model behind a narrow adapter, require a small structured result, reject malformed output, and make the write path idempotent.

A report classifier should be treated like an unreliable dependency in a production queue. The useful result is a label, a confidence value with a defined meaning, and enough trace context to explain why a human reviewer received the item. Everything else is optional prose.

Retries are part of the design.

Make the write conditional.

How should Node.js implement text classification using a GPT API?

Start with the workflow, not the prompt. A media report might arrive with a report ID, the reported text, a policy category, and a review priority. The classifier should return a bounded object such as category, priority, needs_human_review, and reason_code. The consumer must know what each field means before a model is called. The same boundary applies when implementing the client in Node.js: the JavaScript adapter can call the GPT API, but the queue worker should own validation and state transitions.

A free-form answer is hard to operate. It can contain a plausible label with a misspelled key, a confidence score on an unknown scale, or an explanation that quietly changes the decision. A schema makes those failures visible at the boundary. It also gives the team a place to decide what happens when the model cannot classify the report: route it to human review, rather than inventing a fifth state in application code.

The word “confidence” deserves care. Unless the serving system defines and calibrates it, treat that number as a signal for triage, not as a probability that the label is correct. The decision rule belongs to the service owner.

I first thought the prompt was the main implementation detail. The queue contract turned out to matter more: a beautifully worded answer still needs a valid category before it can create review work.

The incident lesson: duplicate delivery is a classification problem too

I approach this path with the same concern I bring to cron and queue workers: a retry is normal, and a duplicate delivery is not an exceptional event. Suppose a worker classifies report rpt_157, times out while acknowledging the queue message, and receives the same message again. If classification and the state transition are coupled to an unguarded insert, the second attempt can create two review tasks. The label may be right and the system can still be wrong.

The invariant is simple: the report ID is the idempotency key for the business decision. Store the decision with a uniqueness constraint, or use a conditional update that only advances the report from its expected prior state. Record the model request separately from the applied decision if audit detail matters. Do not use a generated request ID as the only deduplication key; retries generate new requests.

Here is the preventative shape in Go. A Node.js service can use the same interface boundary with a typed function and a schema validator. The classifier is an interface, so tests can return malformed data, a transient error, or a valid decision without contacting a provider. The repository owns the conditional write. That ownership matters during the awkward interval after a model response has been received but before the queue acknowledgement is durable: a worker crash can replay the message, and only the business-key check can distinguish a new decision from a repeated application.

type ModerationReport struct {
    ID   string
    Text string
}

type Decision struct {
    Category         string `json:"category"`
    Priority         string `json:"priority"`
    NeedsHumanReview bool   `json:"needs_human_review"`
    ReasonCode       string `json:"reason_code"`
}

type Classifier interface {
    Classify(context.Context, ModerationReport) (Decision, error)
}

type DecisionStore interface {
    ApplyOnce(context.Context, string, Decision) (bool, error)
}

func Process(ctx context.Context, c Classifier, s DecisionStore, r ModerationReport) error {
    d, err := c.Classify(ctx, r)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := validate(d); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = s.ApplyOnce(ctx, r.ID, d)
    return err
}

ApplyOnce should report whether it applied a new decision or found an existing one. The worker usually does not need to call the model again merely because the queue redelivered the message. If the first attempt failed before a durable decision, a retry remains useful. That distinction is the point of keeping the idempotency check at the business boundary.

The trade-off is deliberate: validation and replay code add maintenance, but accepting arbitrary prose moves that cost into every downstream consumer. This pattern is a poor fit for one-off exploration where outputs are disposable; it is a better fit for moderation records that can trigger human work.

This advice does not apply unchanged to exploratory labeling, where every run is intentionally a new experiment. Use a run ID there, keep outputs immutable, and compare runs explicitly. Production review state has a different contract.

How should the model boundary be tested?

The prompt is one input to a larger protocol. Test the protocol with fixtures that represent the failures operators actually see: an unknown category, missing keys, extra prose around JSON, an empty report, a request timeout, and a valid response delivered twice. The expected result is not always “retry.” A schema violation can be a quarantine or human-review event; a transport timeout can be retried with a bounded policy.

Keep a small golden set of reports that has been reviewed by humans. It should contain ambiguous language and examples near category boundaries, not just easy cases. Measure disagreements by category and inspect the false positives that create review load. A single aggregate accuracy number hides the operational cost of sending too many benign reports to an urgent queue.

Use two separate budgets: a request deadline and a retry budget. A deadline prevents one stuck call from holding a worker forever. A retry budget prevents a bad dependency or malformed contract from multiplying queue pressure. Backoff should include jitter, and permanent validation failures should stop retrying until a person or a controlled replay fixes the input.

Where do observability and deployment fit?

Log a correlation ID, report ID, classifier version, schema version, latency, outcome class, and retry count. Do not put the complete report text or sensitive user content in ordinary logs by default. A reviewer needs to find the decision; an operator does not need a second copy of the report in every log line.

Dashboards should separate transport errors, schema failures, rejected inputs, human-review fallbacks, and successful applications. Alert on queue age and fallback rate, not just HTTP error rate. A service can return successful requests while the classification contract is drifting and the review queue is filling with manual work.

Roll out changes as data migrations, even when no database table changes. Version the output schema, preserve the old parser during a transition, and replay a fixed evaluation set before changing the application rule. If the category vocabulary changes, migrate stored decisions deliberately; do not let a prompt edit silently reinterpret historical moderation records.

Choosing an implementation without choosing a vendor

The decision criteria are concrete. Prefer an integration that can enforce structured output or make validation practical, expose bounded request controls, and return enough request metadata for tracing. A hosted API, a self-hosted model, and a library wrapper each move different responsibilities between your team and the serving layer. The wrapper may shorten initial code while leaving versioning, retries, and schema enforcement to your service. A direct client may expose more control while requiring more adapter code. A self-hosted path can change deployment and capacity work without removing the need for idempotent writes.

For a Node.js team, using a familiar SDK can reduce adapter code, while a direct HTTP client can make request and retry behavior easier to audit. Neither choice supplies the business idempotency rule for you.

The reference integration documentation for a popular chat abstraction is useful for understanding how a wrapper presents model calls, but it is not a substitute for your production contract. Keep the adapter narrow enough that changing the serving path does not change the queue semantics.

For this media workflow, I would accept a slightly slower path that produces a validated, auditable decision over a faster path that emits attractive prose. Human review is the fallback. The system should make that fallback explicit.

Sources

  • https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/chat/openai/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9333

title: MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB in 2026: Inserts, Lookups, Updates and Storage, Benchmarked
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Most "MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB" debates are fought with benchmarks from 2014 and opinions from Twitter. I run both in my day job and side projects, so I put the current versions, MongoDB 9.0.4 (released October 13, 2026) and PostgreSQL 18.6, on the same VM, loaded the same 200,000 order documents into each, and measured the things a real app does all day: inserts, lookups by an indexed field, containment filters, partial updates of nested fields, aggregations and disk usage.

The short version: neither one wins everywhere. Postgres answered B-tree indexed reads more than twice as fast through the Node.js drivers, but MongoDB loaded data almost 4x faster, updated nested fields about 50% faster and used 5.6x less disk. And one index choice that most JSONB tutorials recommend, a GIN index on the whole document, turned out to be the most expensive line in my Postgres schema.

TL;DR: MongoDB vs Postgres JSONB

If your app is relational with some flexible fields, keep it in Postgres and index the JSONB paths you query with B-tree expression indexes, not one big GIN index. If your data really is documents that get written and updated a lot, and disk or cache size matters, MongoDB did that work faster and far more compactly in my tests.

200,000 docs, 16 clients (median of 3) PostgreSQL 18.6 JSONB MongoDB 9.0.4
Bulk insert, 1,000 per batch 12,337 docs/s 46,448 docs/s
Single inserts 24,594 docs/s 18,506 docs/s
Point lookup by orderNo 44,701 ops/s (B-tree), 29,417 (GIN) 19,139 ops/s
Latest 10 orders of a customer 19,322 ops/s 8,855 ops/s
Containment filter, LIMIT 20 2,531 ops/s 4,605 ops/s
Count of 1,411 matching docs 2,094 ops/s 1,067 ops/s
Nested field update 16,786 ops/s 24,603 ops/s
Append to an array 16,542 ops/s 26,755 ops/s
Revenue by country (full scan) 182.8 ms 154.6 ms
Top 10 SKUs (unwind items) 161.3 ms 283.1 ms
Disk: data + indexes after load 308.4 MB 55.2 MB
Disk after 1.5 to 2.3 million updates 1,231.5 MB 138.8 MB

How I tested

Everything ran on one Linux VM: 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon, KVM), 16 GB of RAM, Debian 13. The databases and the Node.js client shared the machine and talked over loopback TCP, so there's no network latency in these numbers. The VM is shared with other workloads, so I logged the load average and free memory with every result and re-ran everything after one early run stalled (more in the limitations).

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 (PGDG build) in its own cluster with shared_buffers = 512MB, max_wal_size = 4GB and otherwise default settings, including fsync = on and synchronous_commit = on.
  • MongoDB 9.0.4 Community, the official Debian 12 tarball, as a standalone server with --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 0.5 so both databases got the same 512 MB of cache. Everything else default: snappy compression, journaling on, default write concern.
  • Node.js 22.20.0 with pg 8.23.1 and mongodb 7.7.0, the latest npm releases on October 29, 2026.
  • Data: 200,000 generated e-commerce orders from a seeded random generator, the same documents for both databases. Each order has a customer, status, total, tags, a nested shipping object, 1 to 5 line items and an events array. That's about 770 bytes as JSON, 979 bytes per row as JSONB and 806 bytes as BSON.
  • Method: 16 concurrent clients (a 16-connection pool on both sides) in a closed loop for 10 seconds per test, 3 runs per test, and I report the median. Aggregations ran 5 times per run.

Every query I timed returned the same answer on both databases: for example, both found exactly 1,411 orders that are shipped, going to the UAE and tagged gift, and both aggregations returned identical totals.

The schema and the indexes

Postgres gets one jsonb column plus an identity key. To compare the two ways people index JSONB, I created both: a GIN index over the whole document and B-tree expression indexes on the fields the app looks up.

```sql title="postgres.sql"
CREATE TABLE orders (
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
doc jsonb NOT NULL
);
-- one index for any containment query (@>)
CREATE INDEX orders_gin ON orders USING gin (doc jsonb_path_ops);
-- B-tree expression indexes for the hot lookups
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX orders_orderno ON orders ((doc->>'orderNo'));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders
(((doc->>'customerId')::int), (doc->>'createdAt') DESC);






```js title="mongo-indexes.js"
db.orders.createIndex({ orderNo: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1, "shipping.country": 1 });
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1 });

Two things to know about the Postgres side. The query has to match the index: doc->>'orderNo' = $1 uses the B-tree, doc @> '{"orderNo": "..."}' uses the GIN index, and neither one can use the other's index. And JSONB has no date type, so createdAt is an ISO 8601 string. It sorts correctly as text, but in MongoDB it's a real Date.

Insert throughput

Inserts (median of 3) PostgreSQL 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Bulk, 1,000 docs per call, all indexes 12,337 docs/s 46,448 docs/s
Bulk, without the GIN index 26,918 docs/s not applicable
Single inserts, 16 clients, defaults 24,594 docs/s (p50 0.485 ms) 18,506 docs/s (p50 0.571 ms)
Single inserts, synchronous_commit = off / { j: true } 31,459 docs/s 16,070 docs/s

For bulk loads MongoDB was 3.8x faster: 200,000 orders in 4.3 seconds against 16.2 seconds for Postgres with a multi-row INSERT ... SELECT unnest($1::jsonb[]). Half of the Postgres cost was the GIN index. Without it the same load ran at 26,918 docs/s, 2.2x faster.

Single inserts flipped the result. With 16 clients each inserting one document at a time, Postgres did 24,594 per second with every commit flushed to the WAL. Postgres groups concurrent commits into one flush, which is why durability cost it so little here. MongoDB's default write concern gave 18,506 inserts per second, and asking it to wait for the journal on every insert ({ j: true }) gave 16,070.

Point lookups: GIN vs B-tree expression index vs MongoDB index

Fetching one order by its unique orderNo is the most common query in most apps.

Lookup by orderNo (median of 3) 16 clients 1 client, p50 1 client, p99
Postgres, B-tree expression index (->>) 44,701 ops/s 0.057 ms 0.316 ms
Postgres, GIN jsonb_path_ops (@>) 29,417 ops/s 0.123 ms 0.506 ms
MongoDB, { orderNo: 1 } index 19,139 ops/s 0.076 ms 0.377 ms

The B-tree expression index was the fastest way to find one document in either database, and 52% faster than the GIN index on the same table. EXPLAIN shows why: the B-tree query is a plain index scan, while the GIN query is a bitmap index scan plus a bitmap heap scan with a recheck, and the planner guessed 20 matching rows for a unique value because it has no real statistics for containment. With GIN you also pay for an index that covers every key and value in the document.

MongoDB's own query planner used its fast EXPRESS_IXSCAN path, and with one client its p50 (0.076 ms) sat between the two Postgres indexes. With 16 clients it delivered less than half the throughput of the B-tree. I didn't profile the client side, but part of the gap is likely decoding: pg hands JSONB to V8's native JSON.parse, while the MongoDB driver decodes BSON in JavaScript.

Customer feed: the latest 10 orders

A compound index on customer and date, then ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10. Both databases read the index backwards from the newest entry and stopped after 10 rows.

Latest 10 orders for a random customer Ops/s p50 p99
Postgres, expression index on (customerId::int, createdAt DESC) 19,322 0.67 ms 2.40 ms
MongoDB, { customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 } 8,855 1.55 ms 4.50 ms

Postgres returned the 10 documents 2.2x faster. Same pattern as the point lookups: when the access path is a known B-tree, Postgres plus pg moved more rows per second.

Containment filters and counts

Now an ad-hoc filter: orders with a given status, shipping country and tag, such as shipped to the UAE with the gift tag. In Postgres that's one @> against the GIN index. In MongoDB it's a normal filter that used the { status, shipping.country } index and checked tags on the fetched documents.

SELECT doc FROM orders
WHERE doc @> '{"status": "shipped", "shipping": {"country": "AE"}, "tags": ["gift"]}'
LIMIT 20;

db.orders.find({ status: "shipped", "shipping.country": "AE", tags: "gift" }).limit(20);
Filter on 3 fields (4 rotating filters) Postgres GIN @> MongoDB
First 20 matches 2,531 ops/s (p50 5.76 ms) 4,605 ops/s (p50 2.86 ms)
Count all matches (1,411 for the UAE filter) 2,094 ops/s (p50 6.83 ms) 1,067 ops/s (p50 14.21 ms)

MongoDB was 1.8x faster at returning the first 20, because it can walk the compound index and stop as soon as it has 20 documents. Postgres builds a bitmap from the GIN index for all matches before it reads the first row, so LIMIT 20 saves less. For a full count Postgres was 2x faster: the GIN index matched all three conditions at once, while MongoDB had to fetch every shipped UAE order to check its tags. A tags field in MongoDB's compound index would change that, and so would a B-tree on the hot fields in Postgres. The point is that GIN gives you decent speed on any combination of fields without planning indexes, not the best speed on any one of them.

Partial nested updates

Updating one nested field is where the two storage engines differ the most. Here are three updates by orderNo: set shipping.status and updatedAt, push an event onto the events array, and increment a counter.

-- Postgres
UPDATE orders
SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{shipping,status}', to_jsonb($2::text))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1;

UPDATE orders
SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{events}',
  (doc->'events') || jsonb_build_array(jsonb_build_object('type', $2::text, 'at', now())))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1;

// MongoDB
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $set: { "shipping.status": status, updatedAt: new Date() } });
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $push: { events: { type: "note", at: new Date() } } });
db.orders.updateOne({ orderNo }, { $inc: { views: 1 } });
Updates by orderNo, 16 clients (median of 3) Postgres, all indexes Postgres, no GIN MongoDB
Set a nested field 16,786 ops/s 22,979 ops/s 24,603 ops/s
Append to an array 16,542 ops/s 22,154 ops/s 26,755 ops/s
Increment a counter 17,604 ops/s 23,298 ops/s 26,638 ops/s

MongoDB was about 50% faster than Postgres with the full set of indexes. jsonb_set reads like a partial update, but Postgres stores JSONB as one value, so every update writes a complete new copy of the row. Worse, it can't be a HOT (heap-only tuple) update once any index is built on an expression over doc, because Postgres only knows the indexed column changed. I checked this on a small table: 5,000 jsonb_set updates gave 0 HOT updates with a doc->>'orderNo' index and 2,215 without it. So every update also inserts new entries into every index, including the GIN index, which holds an entry for every value in the document. Dropping the GIN index made Postgres updates 32 to 37% faster and closed most of the gap.

Aggregations

Two reports over all 200,000 orders: revenue and order count per shipping country for shipped and delivered orders, and the 10 best-selling SKUs, which needs unwinding the items array.

SELECT doc->'shipping'->>'country' AS country, count(*) AS n,
       sum((doc->>'total')::numeric) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE doc->>'status' IN ('shipped', 'delivered')
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 3 DESC;

SELECT i->>'sku' AS sku, sum((i->>'qty')::int) AS qty
FROM orders, jsonb_array_elements(doc->'items') AS i
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1 LIMIT 10;

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: { $in: ["shipped", "delivered"] } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$shipping.country", n: { $sum: 1 }, revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
]);
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $unwind: "$items" },
  { $group: { _id: "$items.sku", qty: { $sum: "$items.qty" } } },
  { $sort: { qty: -1, _id: 1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
]);
Full-collection aggregation (median of 3 x 5 runs) Postgres 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Revenue by country (70% of orders match) 182.8 ms 154.6 ms
Top 10 SKUs (about 600,000 line items) 161.3 ms 283.1 ms

A split result. The grouped sum was close (MongoDB took 15% less time, which is inside the run-to-run noise for that Postgres query), and Postgres took 43% less time on the unwind. Postgres used parallel workers for these scans (2 per query by default) and still had to parse ->> paths and cast text to numeric for every row. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed the revenue query sorting on disk with the default work_mem of 4 MB, which I left untuned. If reports like this matter, move the summed fields into real columns, or raise work_mem for the reporting role.

Storage size

After loading 200,000 orders PostgreSQL 18.6 MongoDB 9.0.4
Table / collection data 212.6 MB 45.6 MB (161.2 MB before compression)
Indexes 95.7 MB (GIN 71.9 MB) 9.7 MB
Total 308.4 MB 55.2 MB
Total without the GIN index 236.5 MB not applicable

MongoDB used 5.6x less disk. WiredTiger compresses collections with snappy and indexes with prefix compression by default, so 161 MB of BSON became 46 MB. Postgres only compresses a JSONB value when it's bigger than about 2 KB (the TOAST threshold), and these documents averaged 979 bytes, so none were compressed. The GIN index alone was larger than MongoDB's collection and all five of its indexes together.

Then I ran the update tests from the previous section and measured again. Those runs also grew the documents (new events, a views counter, an updatedAt field), so average document size went up by about a fifth in both databases.

After the update tests PostgreSQL, all indexes PostgreSQL, no GIN MongoDB
Updates applied 1,461,709 2,128,223 2,308,992
Total size 1,231.5 MB 627.0 MB 138.8 MB
Of which indexes 512.2 MB (GIN 466.0 MB) 50.6 MB 9.7 MB

Postgres grew 4x with autovacuum running at default settings, and the GIN index grew 6.5x to 466 MB even though no indexed value changed. MongoDB's indexes stayed the same size, because updating fields that aren't indexed doesn't touch its indexes. Its collection grew to 129.1 MB, of which 67.4 MB was free space WiredTiger will reuse. Postgres will reuse its dead space too after vacuum, but a heavily updated JSONB table with a whole-document GIN index needs much more disk and cache than the same data in MongoDB.

The same operations in Node.js

This is the module I used to check that each query does the same thing in both databases. A test inserted 3 orders, ran every function against both and asserted identical results. It passed.

```ts title="orders.mjs"
import pg from "pg";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.PG_URL });
const mongo = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGO_URL);
const orders = mongo.db("shop").collection("orders");

// Insert
export const pgInsert = (doc) => pool.query("INSERT INTO orders (doc) VALUES ($1)", [doc]);
export const mgInsert = (doc) => orders.insertOne(doc);

// Point lookup: ->> matches the B-tree expression index; @> would go to GIN
export const pgByOrderNo = async (no) =>
(await pool.query("SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1", [no])).rows[0]?.doc;
export const mgByOrderNo = (no) => orders.findOne({ orderNo: no });

// Customer feed: latest 10 orders
export const pgFeed = async (customerId) => (await pool.query(
SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE (doc->>'customerId')::int = $1
ORDER BY doc->>'createdAt' DESC LIMIT 10, [customerId])).rows.map((r) => r.doc);
export const mgFeed = (customerId) =>
orders.find({ customerId }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(10).toArray();

// Containment filter
export const pgFilter = async (status, country, tag) => (await pool.query(
"SELECT doc FROM orders WHERE doc @> $1::jsonb LIMIT 20",
[JSON.stringify({ status, shipping: { country }, tags: [tag] })])).rows.map((r) => r.doc);
export const mgFilter = (status, country, tag) =>
orders.find({ status, "shipping.country": country, tags: tag }).limit(20).toArray();

// Partial nested update
export const pgShip = (no, status) => pool.query(
UPDATE orders SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{shipping,status}', to_jsonb($2::text))
WHERE doc->>'orderNo' = $1, [no, status]);
export const mgShip = (no, status) =>
orders.updateOne({ orderNo: no }, { $set: { "shipping.status": status } });




Two driver details that cost me time. `pg` serializes a plain object to JSON for a `jsonb` parameter, but a JavaScript `Date` inside it becomes an ISO string, and it comes back as a string. And `pg` returns `numeric` and `count(*)` as strings (`"361.5"`, `"3"`), while MongoDB returns numbers, so convert before you compare or add.

## Which should you choose?

- **Your data is relational and some of it is flexible: Postgres JSONB.** Joins, foreign keys, transactions across tables and SQL reporting still matter more than raw document speed for most apps. Use B-tree expression indexes (or generated columns) for the paths you query often. They were the fastest lookups in this whole test.
- **Add a GIN index only when you need ad-hoc containment queries.** It made any combination of fields queryable, but it halved bulk insert speed, slowed updates by about a quarter and was the biggest object on disk, and it grew fastest under updates. If you only filter on a few known keys, index just those paths, for example a GIN index on `(doc->'tags')` queried with `doc->'tags' @> '["gift"]'`. It should cost far less, though I didn't measure that variant.
- **Your data is documents that get written and updated all day: MongoDB.** It loaded 3.8x faster, updated nested fields about 50% faster and stored the same orders in 18% of the space, which also means more of your working set fits in RAM.
- **Updates are frequent and documents are large: avoid whole-document rewrites in Postgres.** Put fast-changing fields like status, counters and timestamps in normal columns next to the JSONB, so updates can be HOT and don't rewrite every index.

If you're also deciding what else Postgres can absorb, I measured [Postgres full-text search against Elasticsearch and Meilisearch](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/postgres-full-text-search-vs-elasticsearch) and [Postgres job queues against BullMQ on Redis](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/postgres-job-queue-pg-boss-vs-bullmq). For primary keys on big tables, see [UUIDv7 in Postgres](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/uuidv7-postgres), and for the ORM layer, [Drizzle vs Prisma](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/drizzle-vs-prisma).

## Limitations of this benchmark

- One VM, a single node of each database, everything on loopback. No replica set, so MongoDB's write concern never waited for a second node, and Postgres had no replica either. Real networks add a round trip to every call.
- 200,000 documents of under 1 KB each, which fits in RAM. With a working set larger than memory, MongoDB's 5.6x smaller footprint would likely matter even more, but I didn't test that.
- The VM is shared with other workloads. My first full run stalled for about a minute while the VM was almost out of free memory, so I discarded it and re-ran everything. Then MongoDB crashed mid-run because a snapshot agent on the VM dropped a temporary file into its journal folder, so I restarted it with log file removal turned off (`log=(remove=false)`) and re-ran all MongoDB tests from scratch. Most tests stayed within 10% of their median across the 3 runs, but a few varied by up to 47% (one Postgres aggregation run, the GIN lookups and some update runs). That's why I report medians, and why I'd treat any gap under about 20% as noise.
- Node.js drivers on both sides, so client-side decoding (JSON vs BSON) is part of every read number.
- I didn't tune `work_mem`, autovacuum or fillfactor in Postgres, or anything in MongoDB beyond the cache size. I also didn't test transactions, sharding, schema validation or change streams.


---

*Originally published on [fabwaseem.com](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/mongodb-vs-postgres-jsonb).*

title: What I Learned From Integrating 3rd Party APIs
description:
I've worked with a lot of third-party APIs: telecom and messaging services, social media platforms, and a few others. This post is what I learned about keeping those integrations from breaking, in the order I ran into the problems.

I'm still not a pro, and I won't cover everything. This is just how I know it. I split it into three stages: novice, a little knowledge, and intermediate. Each stage starts with a problem the last one couldn't handle.

The short version

  • Always set a timeout. Retry only errors that can go away on their own, with backoff and jitter. Know when to give up.
  • Respect rate limits and 429 responses. Put work the user doesn't wait for on a queue.
  • Make repeated operations safe. Then add circuit breakers, fallbacks and dead letter queues if you need them.
  • Track latency, error rate and retries for each provider.
  • Don't build all of it at once. I start with timeouts, rate limits, queues and retries.

Stage 1: novice

My first integrations were simple. I called the API over HTTP, wrapped it in a try/catch, and logged the error if it failed. Nothing much. My error handling was basically console.error and hope.

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.provider.example/v1/messages", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Provider returned ${res.status}`);
  return await res.json();
} catch (err) {
  console.error("provider call failed", err);
  throw err;
}

It all looked good at first. Then the first real problem showed up.

Stage 2: a little knowledge

Timeouts

The problem was my API waiting on the external API. If the provider is slow or never answers, the request just sits there. It holds a connection and memory. Enough of those and my service runs out of resources, even though the problem is on someone else's server.

That's how I learned about timeouts. You set one (30 seconds, or whatever fits your use case) and throw an error when it passes. If a user is waiting, use a shorter one. A background job can wait longer.

const res = await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000),
});

At first I thought a timed-out request meant the provider had done nothing. But a timeout only means I stopped waiting. The provider may have done the work and just answered too slowly. This causes trouble later, in stage 3.

Retries, and which errors deserve one

Next, my API felt unreliable. A user sent a request, the provider had a bad moment, and the user got an error. So I learned about retries. My first version retried every error.

That doesn't work either. Some errors go away on their own and some don't.

A transient error can go away: a timeout, a dropped connection, a 502 or 503. A non-transient error fails the same way every time: a 400 for a bad payload, a 401 for a wrong API key, a 404 for something that doesn't exist. Retrying those fixes nothing. A 401 doesn't turn into a 200 because you asked nicely five times. It just wastes calls and delays the real error.

Retry the first kind. Fail fast on the second.

A transient error doesn't always mean it's safe to retry. If a POST times out, the provider may have already done the work, and a retry could do it twice. I'll come back to this in stage 3.

Exponential backoff

I also found out that retrying too fast makes things worse. If the provider is struggling, hitting it again right away adds more load. So you wait between attempts, and you wait longer each time: 1 second, then 2, then 4, then 8. That's exponential backoff.

Jitter

Backoff caused its own problem. Say a thousand requests fail at the same moment. They all wait 1 second and retry together. They fail together, wait 2 seconds, and retry together again. It's like everyone redialing the same busy number at the exact same second. The provider gets hit in waves. This is called the thundering herd problem. With no quiet moment to recover, a small problem can get a lot worse.

The fix is jitter. Add some randomness to the wait so the retries spread out.

When to stop retrying

At first I didn't know you could drop a request. I thought I had to keep retrying until it worked, so my code was a loop with no exit.

Retrying forever is a bug of its own. The user is still waiting, your workers are busy, and the provider keeps getting hit. Drop the request when any of these is true:

  • The error is non-transient. A 400, 401 or 404 fails every time, so drop it right away.
  • You've tried enough times. Pick a number, like 4, and drop the request after that.
  • You've waited too long. Give the whole request a time limit, like 10 seconds, no matter how many tries it takes. A 30 second timeout with 4 tries can leave the user waiting about two minutes. Nobody waits that long.
  • The provider asks you to wait too long. If its Retry-After header says 5 minutes and you can only wait 10 seconds, drop it. Waiting won't help.

When you drop a request, still do something with it. If a user is waiting, tell them it failed and that they can try again. If it's background work, move the job to a dead letter queue (more on that below) so it isn't lost.

This code puts it all together: a timeout on every try, retries only for transient errors, backoff with jitter, the Retry-After header, and the rules for giving up.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public status: number,
    public retryAfterMs?: number,
  ) {
    super(`Provider returned ${status}`);
  }
}

// Timeouts, network failures, 408, 429 and some 5xx errors may be transient.
// Check your provider's docs. 400, 401, 404 and similar fail every time.
const TRANSIENT_STATUS = [408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504];

function isTransient(err: unknown): boolean {
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return TRANSIENT_STATUS.includes(err.status);
  // fetch throws a TypeError on network failures, but a bug in your code can too
  return err instanceof Error && (err.name === "TimeoutError" || err.name === "TypeError");
}

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function withRetry<T>(
  fn: (timeoutMs: number) => Promise<T>,
  maxAttempts = 4,
  budgetMs = 10_000,
): Promise<T> {
  const deadline = Date.now() + budgetMs;
  let lastErr: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const timeLeft = deadline - Date.now();
    if (timeLeft <= 0) throw lastErr ?? new Error("Out of time"); // don't start another try
    try {
      // each try gets at most 3 seconds, and never more than the time left
      return await fn(Math.min(3_000, timeLeft));
    } catch (err) {
      lastErr = err;
      const backoff = Math.random() * 1000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1); // backoff + jitter
      const asked = err instanceof HttpError ? err.retryAfterMs : undefined; // from Retry-After
      const wait = asked ?? backoff;
      const outOfTime = Date.now() + wait >= deadline;
      if (attempt >= maxAttempts || outOfTime || !isTransient(err)) throw err; // drop it
      await sleep(wait);
    }
  }
}

const result = await withRetry(async (timeoutMs) => {
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const seconds = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? NaN);
    throw new HttpError(res.status, Number.isNaN(seconds) ? undefined : seconds * 1000);
  }
  return res.json();
});

This is a simple example to learn from, not code to paste straight into production. Change the number of tries, the waits and the time limit to fit your provider. Check its docs to see which errors it wants you to retry. Real code needs more care. For example, not every TypeError is a network problem, because a bug in your own code can throw one too. And POST requests are not always safe to retry (see stage 3).

Rate limits and 429

After that I ran into 429 Too Many Requests. It means I had sent more requests than the provider allows. That limit is called a rate limit. I retried harder, and it only made things worse. The provider was saying "slow down", and I answered by going faster.

So I learned about throttling. It means slowing yourself down, so you never go over the provider's limit. Use a limiter that caps how many calls you make each second or each minute. If you run more than one server, make them all share the same limiter. Otherwise each server counts on its own, and together they still go over the limit.

If a 429 still gets through, wait before you try again. Many providers send a Retry-After header. It tells you how long to wait. Use it instead of guessing.

Queues

Then I learned when to use queues. A lot of work doesn't need to happen while the user waits: sending emails or SMS, generating reports, and similar jobs. The request returns right away, and a worker calls the provider in the background.

This is where everything above came together for me. The worker handles the timeout, the retries with backoff and jitter, and the rate limit. You decide how many workers call the provider at once, so a spike of user requests doesn't become a spike of provider calls. If a job fails, the worker can retry it in the background. The user's request doesn't have to stay open while that happens.

Stage 3: intermediate

Duplicate operations

Retries can cause a new problem: doing the same thing twice. Take the timeout from earlier. The provider may have already sent the SMS and just answered too slowly. If you retry, the user gets two SMS.

It can also happen without a timeout. Many queues promise to deliver a job at least once. That means the same job can run more than once. A worker sends the SMS, then crashes before it marks the job as done. The queue doesn't know the SMS went out, so it gives the job to another worker. That worker sends the same SMS again.

So the next thing I learned was how to make an operation safe to repeat. The word for this is idempotent: doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. Whenever you can, make queue jobs idempotent, especially jobs that call an outside service or change important data.

If the provider supports idempotency keys, use them. An idempotency key is a unique ID that you send with each request. When the provider sees the same ID again, it knows the request is a repeat and doesn't do the work twice. Not every provider supports this.

If yours doesn't, keep your own record of what you've already sent. Check that record before you retry. And if you don't know whether the first try worked, ask the provider for the status first.

I wrote more about this in my post on payment integrations, where a duplicate means a duplicate charge.

Circuit breakers and fallbacks

This is where I got more excited about system design. I'm still new to this part. I only know the basics, and I'm learning more in my free time. Even a basic understanding of circuit breakers and distributed systems helps, though.

Say a provider is down for ten minutes. Retrying every request against it wastes time and ties up your workers.

A circuit breaker counts recent failures. When they pass a threshold, it stops calling the provider and fails right away. After a cool-down, it lets a few test requests through. If they succeed, traffic starts flowing again.

A fallback decides what happens while the breaker is open. It could be a second provider, a cached answer, or a plain "try again later" message.

Dead letter queues

Some jobs still fail after every retry. Retrying forever is a waste, and dropping them loses data. So they go to a dead letter queue. It holds them while you find out why they failed. Then you fix the cause and replay them.

Observability

Then someone asked me how my system was performing, and I had no idea. My answer was basically a shrug. That's when I learned about observability. I started with three things: latency, error rates and retries.

Look at latency in percentiles like p95, not just the average. The average hides the slow requests. Rising latency often shows up before the timeouts do.

The error rate tells you when a provider has gone bad, and which errors it returns.

Retries hide failures from users. So a rising retry count is how you spot a struggling provider before anyone complains.

You don't need all of it at once

All of this took me a lot of time to learn, so I wouldn't build it all in one go. Pick what fits the integration and the tradeoffs you're willing to take. A small script that calls one API once a day probably doesn't need a circuit breaker.

I usually start with timeouts, rate-limit handling, queues and retries. I add the rest when the integration needs it.

I'm Nishant, a backend-focused full-stack developer from Nepal. The original of this post, and the products I build, are on my site.

If you don’t like to support Frontend Dogma, you can still follow Frontend Dogma’s individual topic feeds as well as Frontend Dogma’s social media accounts on Mastodon and Bluesky. These are less convenient and reliable but still workable options to stay up-to-date.

title: Git seance: I let deleted functions speak from beyond the grave (with local Gemma)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every repository is a graveyard. Functions get written, argued over, shipped, and then one day a commit quietly removes them, and nobody says a word.

git seance holds the funeral they never got. It walks your git history, finds functions that were deleted and never came back, and lets one of them speak through a local Gemma model: who wrote it, when it was born, and the commit that killed it.

python git_seance.py --list path/to/repo                                   # visit the graveyard
python git_seance.py --summon set_http_proxy --ask "do you forgive them?" path/to/repo

My personal favourite:

python git_seance.py path/to/repo                        # summon a random ghost

It's a single Python file with zero dependencies (standard library only), and it understands Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Go and Rust definitions.

Demo

That's a real run on psf/requests, with gemma3:4b on my laptop's CPU through Ollama (long pauses trimmed). Its last 400 commits hold seven ghosts. The most tragic is set_http_proxy: 85 lines of carefully documented proxy handling, added to Session on 27 November 2020 and reverted the same day by its own author.

Here is what it said when I asked if it forgives them (another real run, unedited):

It's… strange, this quiet. A lingering echo of code, a phantom limb of functionality. I was a helpful thing, really. I took messy proxy strings – URLs, schemes, hostnames, ports – and neatly slotted them into the requests.Session object. I was born on November 27th, 2020, courtesy of Sylvain Marie. Then, poof. November 27th, 2020 again. […]

My advice to the living: don't prematurely prune your tools.

Code

DrunkWiz / git-seance

Talk to the functions your repo deleted. A stdlib-only Python CLI that lets dead code speak through local Gemma.

git seance

Commune with the code your repository buried.

git seance walks a repo's git history, finds functions that were deleted and never came back, and lets one speak from beyond the grave through a local open-weight model (Gemma 3 via Ollama by default): who wrote it, when, and the commit that killed it. With no model reachable it falls back to an offline "planchette" mode that only arranges the real facts.

One file, Python standard library only, no runtime dependencies.

A real run on psf/requests with gemma3:4b on a laptop CPU, long pauses trimmed.

Why an open model

Your git history is your team's private diary: names, dates, half-finished ideas, the commit messages people wrote at 2am. git seance reads all of it, so it should not have to leave your machine. With an open-weight model like Gemma running locally through Ollama, the whole seance happens on your laptop…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

Finding the dead. git log -p -U0 --no-merges gives every removed line in history. I parse the removed hunks, start a body at any line that looks like a definition (def, function, func, fn), and end it at the next definition at the same or lower indentation. That last rule came from a bug: the first version merged neighbouring deleted methods into one long ghost. In requests, initialize_options, finalize_options and run_tests were deleted from a setup.py command class together, and they kept coming back as a single conjoined spirit.

Making sure they're really dead. A function that was moved isn't a ghost. Before summoning, git grep -w checks the current tree for a definition with the same name. If one exists, the function just moved house.

Finding the birth certificate. Git's pickaxe (git log -S"def set_http_proxy") finds the commit that first added the function. My favourite bug lived here: requests later moved requests/ to src/requests/, and git's default history simplification hid every commit on the old path behind a merge. Every ghost was "born: unknown", and Gemma happily made up a birth story to fill the gap. --full-history brought the real birthday back.

Speaking. The facts (name, file, length, birth, death, the killing commit's message, the final source) go into a prompt along with a system prompt that tells the model to speak as the function, to be wistful and darkly funny but never cruel, and not to invent facts. The reply streams token by token from Ollama's /api/chat with nothing but urllib, typed out like a planchette moving. An OpenAI-compatible provider is there too, for anyone who'd rather point it at a gateway.

When the spirits won't come. If no model is reachable, planchette mode arranges the real facts into an epitaph with no AI at all. That came in handy: Ollama's CUDA runner crashes on my RTX 2060, so I added SEANCE_NUM_GPU=0 to run Gemma on the CPU. At 4B parameters, that's still fast enough.

Tests. A unittest suite covers the diff parser on a synthetic log, the dead-or-moved check on a throwaway repo, and both streaming providers against a fake model server on 127.0.0.1, so the tests never touch the network.

A ghost is an unreliable narrator, and I'd rather say so. The header line comes straight from git. Everything after it is Gemma, and despite the instructions it sometimes embellishes (in one run it insisted it had been reverted "twice"). --offline gives you only the facts.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because a git history is a diary. It holds names, dates, abandoned ideas, and commit messages written at the worst moments of people's weeks. A tool that reads all of that should not have to send it anywhere.

With an open-weight model like Gemma running locally, the whole seance happens on your own machine: no API key, no account, no bill, and it works on a private company repo or with no internet at all. I learned this the practical way. I first tried a hosted gateway, and its free tier wouldn't serve API calls without a key. Gemma 3 4B on Ollama just worked, on a laptop CPU, offline.

Open models also make the medium yours. You can read how it was made, swap it for a different one, or fine-tune it on your own team's commit messages. And open source is what gives the ghosts something to haunt: I could only summon set_http_proxy because requests keeps its whole history in the open.

My Agent Session

I built this with an AI coding agent (Claude Code). It ran the real seances against requests, tracked down the history-simplification and GPU bugs above, wrote the offline test suite, recorded the demo and helped draft this post. Every transcript and number here comes from an actual run.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos isn't about fearing the dead. It's about remembering them by name. Every deleted function was somebody's afternoon. git seance puts the name, the date and the author back on the gravestone, and lets the code say goodbye.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: the medium is gemma3:4b, running locally through Ollama.

title: Why Your Controller Feels Different on PC vs Console (and How to Test Both)
description:
If you have ever plugged a controller you love on console into a PC and thought "this feels wrong," you are not imagining it. The same pad can behave differently across platforms, and most of the time it is not broken — it is being read differently.

The first difference is the driver layer. On console, the system knows exactly which controller you have and applies its own deadzones and curves. On PC, Windows usually exposes the pad through XInput or DirectInput, and each game then adds its own layer on top. A stick that rests at a tiny offset might be hidden by the console's deadzone but show up plainly on PC, or the other way round.

The second difference is calibration. Consoles rarely let you calibrate a stick; PCs do, through Steam Input, DS4Windows, or the manufacturer's app. That is useful, but it also means a bad calibration can follow you from game to game until you reset it. If a controller suddenly feels off after you changed software, check calibration before you blame hardware.

So how do you tell which layer is lying to you? Test the controller outside any game. Connect it to a PC, open a browser tester, and watch the raw inputs: leave both sticks untouched for ten seconds and see whether either one reports movement on its own. That is your drift baseline. Then move each stick slowly in a full circle and watch whether the motion is smooth or jumps. Press every button and pull both triggers fully, checking that each one reaches its full value and returns cleanly to zero.

You can test your controller online for free (https://www.gamepadtesterpro.com) — no install, just the browser reading what the operating system reports. Do the same test with the pad wired and then over Bluetooth if you use both; a stick that only drifts on Bluetooth is usually a connection or battery issue, not a worn sensor.

If the raw test is clean but a game still feels wrong, the problem is almost certainly in that game's deadzone or sensitivity settings, or in a calibration profile. Raise the game's deadzone a notch, or reset the calibration profile and retest. If the raw test shows drift while the stick sits untouched, cleaning around the stick base sometimes helps, but persistent drift on a worn pad usually means the sensor module is tired — cleaning buys time, it does not restore a worn track.

One more practical habit: test a controller the day you buy it, used or new, and again after any repair. A two-minute baseline makes every later "is this getting worse?" question answerable instead of guesswork. Controllers wear gradually, and noticing a small change early is what keeps a minor annoyance from becoming a ruined ranked match.

title: Database Migration Best Practices: How to Achieve Zero Downtime
description:
Changing a production database is rarely just a database operation. The application code running during the change may expect the old schema, while a newly deployed version may depend on a new one. Background workers, scheduled jobs, and older application instances can make the transition more complicated.

A migration that works perfectly in a development environment can still cause production errors if the application and database move to their new states at different times.

Zero-downtime database migration is about managing that transition so the service can continue handling requests while the schema and data evolve.

Why a single-step migration is risky

Imagine an application that stores a customer's name in a column called full_name. A team wants to replace it with separate first_name and last_name columns.

The simplest approach might be to rename the column, update the application code, and deploy everything together. But production systems often run multiple application instances. During a rolling deployment, old and new versions may operate simultaneously.

The old version expects full_name. The new version expects the two new columns. If the database changes before every old instance has stopped, some requests may fail.

A safer approach separates the change into smaller, backward-compatible steps.

Use the expand-and-contract pattern

The expand-and-contract pattern lets the database and application evolve over several releases.

  1. Expand the schema: Add the new columns without removing the existing column. The old application can continue using the old structure.
  2. Deploy compatible application code: Update the application to support the new schema. Depending on the change, it may temporarily read from the old column while writing to both old and new columns.
  3. Backfill existing data: Populate the new columns for existing records. For large tables, process data in batches rather than running one long operation that could create heavy locks or resource pressure.
  4. Verify consistency: Compare old and new values, check for missing data, and monitor errors. Do not assume the backfill succeeded simply because the job completed.
  5. Switch reads to the new structure: Once the new data is complete and verified, move application reads to the new columns. Keep compatibility for as long as older application instances or background jobs may still need the old schema.
  6. Contract the schema: Remove the old column only after the team has confirmed that no active code depends on it. This may happen in a later release.

The sequence matters. Each step should leave the system in a state that remains compatible with the application versions currently running.

Plan for data and locking risks

Schema changes can affect availability even when the application code is compatible.

Adding an index, changing a column type, or updating a large table may consume substantial resources or hold locks that delay normal queries. The impact depends on the database engine, table size, operation, and chosen migration method.

Before running a production migration, understand how the database handles the specific operation. Use online or concurrent operations where supported and appropriate. Test with realistic data volumes, monitor lock waits and query latency, and have a clear plan for stopping or resuming the migration safely.

For large data backfills, make the process restartable. Track progress, process bounded batches, and ensure rerunning a batch will not corrupt data or create duplicate side effects. These considerations also apply when modernizing the wider data architecture.

Rollback is more than reverting code

A common mistake is to assume that reverting the application version reverses the database change.

Once data has been written in a new format, the previous application may not be able to interpret it. A destructive schema change may also make recovery difficult if old data has already been discarded.

Before deployment, decide which steps can be reversed, which require a forward fix, and how data will be recovered if validation fails. Preserve the old schema until the new path is proven stable whenever practical.

A rollback plan should be tested, not just documented. For some migrations, restoring service safely may mean correcting the new schema rather than reversing it.

Make migration checks part of the delivery pipeline

Database migration best practices are easier to follow when the release process enforces them.

Use automated checks to verify migration scripts, test application compatibility with relevant schema versions, and confirm that deployment ordering is safe. Monitor application errors, query performance, replication lag where applicable, and data consistency during the rollout.

Not every database change can be completed without a brief interruption. The realistic goal is to choose a migration method that meets the service's availability requirements and makes any necessary maintenance window explicit.

A broader cloud transformation strategy can also account for infrastructure resilience and the operational requirements of evolving production systems. For teams working on data platforms, data engineering services provide further context on building and maintaining data solutions.

Treat schema changes as staged releases

A reliable zero-downtime database migration depends on compatibility, sequencing, data validation, and observability. The expand-and-contract pattern helps teams avoid forcing application code and database structure to change at exactly the same moment.

By treating schema evolution as a staged release rather than a single operation, teams can reduce deployment risk and keep production systems available while the underlying data model changes.

title: A Local-First VS Code Extension: No Git, No Telemetry, No Network, and It Works in Codespaces
description:
| SavePoint Diff runs entirely inside the extension host, so it works across local, SSH, WSL, containers, Codespaces, and vscode.dev.

Plenty of dev tools want an account, a network call, or a telemetry opt-out. I wanted the opposite for SavePoint Diff.

What "100% local" means here

  • Everything runs inside the VS Code extension host
  • No Git required
  • No telemetry
  • No network requests
  • No external services
  • The baseline is held in memory for the current window session and never touches disk

The only requirement is VS Code 1.60.0 or later.

Works where you work

Because there are no external dependencies, it behaves the same across:

  • Local folders
  • Remote-SSH
  • WSL
  • Dev Containers
  • GitHub Codespaces
  • Virtual filesystems like vscode.dev and github.dev

Make it yours

Everything is toggleable in settings:

{
  "savepointDiff.showAdded": true,
  "savepointDiff.showModified": true,
  "savepointDiff.showDeleted": true,
  "savepointDiff.showOverviewRuler": true,
  "savepointDiff.showBackgroundHighlight": false,
  "savepointDiff.enableRevertInHover": true
}

Prefer a subtle gutter only? Leave highlighting off. Want changed lines tinted too? Set showBackgroundHighlight to true. There's also a one-click status bar toggle (SavePoint: ON / OFF) if you want it out of the way temporarily.

Good to know

In Git repositories, VS Code's own editor-gutter "quick diff" colors are typically driven by Git's provider. SavePoint Diff's panel entry, badges, and diff view work independently alongside it, in Git and non-Git folders alike.

Try it 

ext install StayElite.StayElite-Savepoint-Diff

title: Empty Video Rooms in 2026: How to Debug Accumulating Cleanup
description:
TL;DR: When empty video rooms accumulate, make the disconnect handler list current participants and delete the room only when that list is empty. Run the same check from a scheduled sweep because leave events can be missed. Keep deletion idempotent, and report the open-room count so drift becomes visible before someone opens a debug console.

For a B2B SaaS product that uses video calls and pushes in-app status notifications, the clean boundary is occupancy, not the browser's last disconnect callback. The client can reconnect; the server must verify presence. A notification such as "call ended" should follow that verified transition, while missed notifications belong to a separate reconnect-and-backfill path. Mixing those two jobs makes cleanup fragile.

Infrai is a practical fit for a small team that wants this RTC cleanup boundary behind plain REST: there is no SDK to install or client-library version to maintain, and the same key can cover a broader backend surface. I recommend trying it for the occupancy check and room deletion when a language-neutral HTTP handoff matters more than adopting a specialist video SDK.

Infrai uses one API key and one bill across its backend capabilities. In this workflow, that means the RTC sweep and adjacent notification infrastructure do not add separate credentials and invoices to a small team's rotation; the platform documents 295 routes across 20 modules. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is available without a key, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages, so the integration can inspect the current schema before deployment.

Why doesn't the last-participant event close the room?

A disconnect signal is evidence that one connection ended. It is not proof that occupancy reached zero. The same user may reconnect, another participant may still be present, or the handler may never run. Handlers miss events; the sweep is not optional.

This distinction also keeps notification delivery honest. On a reconnect, backfill notification state from your application's durable cursor. Do not infer missed business events from whether an RTC room still exists. Cleanup owns room lifecycle; the notification stream owns delivery and backfill. Two boundaries.

The failure pattern is easy to spot: active calls finish, users disappear, yet the open-room gauge climbs. The correction is specific. Both the event path and the sweep call one reconciliation function, and neither path treats its trigger as authoritative.

This is the boundary.

Implement the occupancy gate first

The following TypeScript file is runnable on Node.js 20 or newer. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and ROOM_ID, then run it with your normal TypeScript runner. It uses only the participant-list and room-delete routes. The response extractor does not assume an undocumented envelope; it locates the named participant array and fails closed if the payload does not contain one.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const room = process.env.ROOM_ID;

if (!apiKey || !room) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and ROOM_ID");
}

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

async function waitForRetry(response: Response, attempt: number): Promise<void> {
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
  const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
    ? retryAfter * 1_000
    : Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 16_000);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
}

async function listParticipants(roomId: string): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/rtc/participant/list/${encodeURIComponent(roomId)}`,
      { method: "GET", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` } },
    );
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 5) {
      await waitForRetry(response, attempt);
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    return response;
  }
  throw new Error("Participant request retry limit reached");
}

async function deleteRoom(roomId: string): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/rtc/room/delete/${encodeURIComponent(roomId)}`,
      {
        method: "DELETE",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Idempotency-Key": `empty-room:${roomId}`,
        },
      },
    );
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 5) {
      await waitForRetry(response, attempt);
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    return;
  }
  throw new Error("Delete request retry limit reached");
}

function participantArray(value: unknown): unknown[] | undefined {
  if (!value || typeof value !== "object") return undefined;
  for (const [key, child] of Object.entries(value)) {
    if (key === "participants" && Array.isArray(child)) return child;
    const nested = participantArray(child);
    if (nested) return nested;
  }
  return undefined;
}

async function reconcileRoom(roomId: string): Promise<boolean> {
  const listResponse = await listParticipants(roomId);
  const participants = participantArray(await listResponse.json());
  if (!participants) throw new Error("Participant list missing from response");

  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    metric: "video_room_open",
    room: roomId,
    value: participants.length > 0 ? 1 : 0,
  }));

  if (participants.length > 0) return false;

  await deleteRoom(roomId);
  return true;
}

const deleted = await reconcileRoom(room);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ room, deleted }));

Use the same function in two callers. The disconnect handler invokes it after a participant leaves. A scheduled job enumerates room IDs from the application's own room registry and invokes it again. That registry is also where an aggregate open_room_count belongs; the sample emits a per-room value that a metrics collector can sum without inventing a second control plane.

Deletion has to tolerate both callers racing. The stable idempotency key makes repeated attempts converge on one cleanup intent, while checking occupancy immediately before deletion protects a room that still has participants. Do not send an end-of-call notification merely because deleted is true unless your application state also says the call ended.

Reconnect and backfill are a separate state machine

A browser can vanish long enough to trigger disconnect handling and then return. Give the returning client a durable notification cursor, fetch events after that cursor, and resume live delivery only after the backfill completes. The exact cursor store is application-owned; the RTC participant list cannot replace it.

This is the trade-off I would accept for a solo-operated product: one extra state boundary in exchange for deterministic recovery. Trying to make the room itself serve as notification history looks simpler on day one, but it leaves no trustworthy answer to "what did this user miss?" after a reconnect.

Keep the transition order explicit: verify current occupancy, reconcile the room, update the application's call state, then publish the corresponding in-app event. On reconnect, read from the last acknowledged application event before attaching the live stream. That sequence makes cleanup retryable without duplicating business notifications.

Choose the provider around the boundary

The useful comparison is operational fit, not a feature-count contest. Infrai exposes the two cleanup operations through HTTP and publishes a self-describing discovery surface; its documented capabilities include runnable TypeScript examples. That reduces integration upkeep when the rest of the product already speaks REST.

Pusher, Ably, and PubNub are real alternatives worth evaluating for the in-app notification side of this design. Socket.IO is another option when the team wants to operate the connection layer itself. These tools do not remove the need to verify RTC occupancy: they fit the live delivery and reconnect path, while the video provider still owns participant and room semantics. A specialist video service may be better when the video layer needs to own more of the architecture. Review each provider's presence and replay contract before translating the backfill flow; do not assume that a disconnect callback means the same thing everywhere. This split is deliberate: choose notification transport for cursor recovery and choose the RTC API for authoritative room occupancy, then join them in application state rather than forcing one product's connection signal to answer both questions.

Option Sensible fit Boundary to verify
Infrai A small backend that favors one plain REST surface Participant-list response and idempotent room deletion
Pusher Managed in-app event delivery Reconnect recovery and retained history
Ably Managed realtime notification transport Presence and replay contract
PubNub Managed publish/subscribe delivery Cursor and backfill behavior

There is no measured latency, uptime, or cost result here, so none should decide the selection. Run a reconnect test against the provider you intend to use: disconnect the final client, reconnect during cleanup, drop the event handler entirely, and confirm that the sweep reaches the same final state.

Operate the cleanup loop

Start with a sweep interval that matches how long an empty room may remain visible in your product, then observe rather than guess. Report the total open-room count on every sweep, alongside the number found empty and the number deleted. Alert on sustained divergence between your application registry and verified occupancy. A single leftover room is a debugging fact; a rising series is an operating signal.

Keep the checklist short in practice. The disconnect path calls reconciliation but does not own correctness. The sweep repeats it. Both paths use the same stable idempotency key, surface non-success response bodies, and back off on 429 responses. Reconnect tests must cover the gap between listing participants and deleting a room, while notification tests must prove cursor backfill independently of RTC cleanup.

If a provider offers lifecycle controls that better match your existing stack, use them. If this HTTP boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability schema before wiring production data.

  • Twilio Video documentation
  • Daily documentation
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Infrai official documentation

description:
API Gateway

Deprecated

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. Negative values there are deprecated and will be rejected in a future release; until then, creating an API config with one returns a warning in the operation metadata. OpenAPI 3.x backends already reject a negative deadline. To use the default, omit the field or set it to 0.
