title: Gemini 4 Argon now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini 4 Argon from Google is now available on AI Gateway.

Gemini 4 Argon is built for coding, agentic work, and complex reasoning. It has a 1M token context window, accepts text, image, PDF, and video input, and supports tool calling.

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. The model also reads dense diagrams, spreadsheets, layout-heavy documents, and video, which suits tasks like a financial analysis spread across several spreadsheet tabs. Beyond code, it handles work in finance, health, and law, and hard problems in math and science. Gemini 4 Argon uses thinking levels (low, medium, and high) instead of thinking budgets.

Call Gemini 4 Argon through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Set the thinking level with reasoning in the AI SDK or reasoning_effort in Chat Completions, and see reasoning for the other controls.

Use google/gemini-4-argon as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select google/gemini-4-argon in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Gemini 4 Argon in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Deleted deployments are permanently removed sooner
description:
Deployments deleted before they are 30 days old now have a shorter recovery period before permanent deletion. As developers deploy more frequently on Vercel, this reduces the buildup of old deployments on the Recently Deleted page.

For successfully built deployments, the recovery period is the time you have to restore them after deletion:

When the deployment is deleted

Time to restore after deletion

By retention policy before it reaches 30 days old

Same length as the policy. A 7-day policy gives you 7 more days.

Manually, less than 1 day after creation

1 more day

Manually, at least 1 day but less than 30 days after creation

Same as its age at deletion. Delete it 3 days after creation, and you have 3 more days.

Manually or by retention policy, 30 days or more after creation

30 more days, unchanged

After this time, deployments are permanently deleted and cannot be restored. Unsuccessful deployments may be permanently deleted sooner.

Learn more in the deployment retention documentation.

title: pgvector: Embedding Column on the Table or a Separate Embeddings Table?
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: Put the embedding where the row it describes is written least. A document that is chunked needs a chunks table anyway; an embedding that will be regenerated by a second model belongs in its own table keyed by chunk and model, with an untyped vector column. A vector column on a hot parent row costs a 6 KB HNSW entry on every non-HOT edit of any other column: 5,000 title edits took a 31 MB index to 67 MB.

An embedding belongs where the row it describes is written least, and for most RAG schemas that is not the parent table. A document that gets chunked needs a chunks table whatever you decide, and an embedding you expect to regenerate with a newer model belongs in its own table keyed by chunk and model. The one case for a vector column on the parent row is one vector per entity, on a row that nothing else updates.

The reason is what an HNSW index costs on a row that changes for other reasons. We measured it on PostgreSQL 17.11 with pgvector 0.8.7: a documents table with a vector(1536) column and an HNSW index, 5,000 rows loaded in one INSERT, then one UPDATE that appended a few words to every title and never touched the vector. PostgreSQL made zero HOT updates, the heap went from 2.8 MB to 5.7 MB, and the HNSW index went from 31 MB to 67 MB. VACUUM left it at 67 MB. The control was a chunk_embeddings table holding 20,000 vectors of the same size under an 81 MB HNSW index: the same title edit on its parent rows cannot touch it, and did not.

Why a vector column makes every update of the row expensive

Every non-HOT update of a row with an HNSW index adds a new, full-size entry to the index, and after a bulk load at the default fillfactor nothing is HOT.

The zero is not the vector's doing. A copy of the table with no vector column at all, loaded and updated the same way, also made 0 HOT updates out of 5,000: INSERT ... SELECT packs each page to the default fillfactor of 100, so there is no room on the page for a new row version, and a HOT update needs exactly that. The title column had no index either, so the only indexes in play were the primary key and the HNSW index. What the vector decides is the price of each non-HOT update. A vector(1536) value is 6,148 bytes (pg_column_size on the measured table), pgvector declares the type with external storage, so PostgreSQL keeps it out of line and uncompressed in the TOAST table (2.8 MB of heap against 39 MB of TOAST for the 5,000 rows), and the HNSW entry for the new row version carries the whole vector again. That is why one pass of title edits roughly doubled the index.

Lowering the fillfactor helps but does not fix it. A copy of the table created WITH (fillfactor = 90) made 834 of the 5,000 updates HOT: better, and still 4,166 new index entries for an edit that did not change a single vector.

After VACUUM the index stays at 67 MB: PostgreSQL never shrinks an index file, and pgvector reuses the freed slots for later inserts, so a second pass of title edits after the vacuum left it at 67 MB and a third took it to 72 MB. Until vacuum runs, pgvector's README warns that dead elements can cut the number of rows a search returns, and it says vacuuming an HNSW index "can take a while", recommending REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY first. A parent table that is edited every day carries an index that is always part dead and never smaller than its worst day.

Should pgvector embeddings be in a separate table?

Yes when the text is chunked or when you will ever re-embed; a column on the row only when there is exactly one vector per entity and nothing else on that row is updated.

Three layouts cover the real cases:

Vector column on the parent row chunks table with a vector column Separate chunk_embeddings (chunk_id, model)
One document, many vectors Impossible: one row holds one vector Natural: one row per chunk Natural
Second embedding model A second column, backfilled by an UPDATE of every row A second column per chunk, same backfill New rows under a new model value
Edits to the document's other columns New HNSW entry per non-HOT edit (measured above) Only when the chunk row itself changes Never
A model with a different dimension ALTER COLUMN TYPE refused once rows exist Same An untyped vector column and one cast partial index per model
Filter by tenant or document On the same table, where pgvector's remedies work Needs document_id on the chunk, or a join Needs the filter column copied onto this table, or a join
Extra joins on read None One, chunk to document Two, embedding to chunk to document

The middle column is the usual answer. A RAG pipeline splits a document into chunks sized for the model's context, so the chunk row already exists with its position and text, and the vector sits beside the text it encodes. The chunk row changes only when the text changes, which is when the vector must change anyway.

The right column earns its second join when models change. ALTER TABLE documents ALTER COLUMN embedding TYPE vector(768) fails the moment a row holds a 1,536-value vector: PostgreSQL answers ERROR: expected 768 dimensions, not 1536. A new column per model is the same ALTER TABLE on the table that holds the text, then a backfill UPDATE of every row, which by the measurement above adds a new entry to the existing HNSW index for every row it touches, then two indexes on one row and a cleanup migration later. A chunk_embeddings table keyed by (chunk_id, model) takes the new model as new rows and nothing in the tables that hold the text changes. To hold two sizes at once the column is declared as an untyped vector, which pgvector's README recommends for mixed dimensions, and each model gets its own partial index over a cast:

CREATE TABLE chunk_embeddings (
    chunk_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES chunks (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    model     text   NOT NULL,
    embedding vector NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (chunk_id, model)
);
CREATE INDEX chunk_embeddings_small ON chunk_embeddings
    USING hnsw ((embedding::vector(1536)) vector_cosine_ops)
    WHERE (model = 'text-embedding-3-small');
CREATE INDEX chunk_embeddings_nomic ON chunk_embeddings
    USING hnsw ((embedding::vector(768)) vector_cosine_ops)
    WHERE (model = 'nomic-embed-text');

Measured on the same server: 200 chunks stored under both models, 1,536 and 768 values side by side in one column, both indexes built. Queries use the same cast and the same WHERE model = ... so the planner picks the right partial index, and the old model's rows are deleted when the switch is done. A model over 2,000 dimensions needs a halfvec cast instead, which is pgvector's index limit for vector.

The left column is for entity embeddings: one vector per product, per user profile, per support ticket, that changes only when the entity's own text changes, on a row nothing else updates. If the table also carries a view_count or a last_seen_at, it is no longer that case, and the index growth above is what you get.

Where does the tenant filter go?

Keep the column you filter on in the same table as the HNSW index, because pgvector's remedies for a filtered search, a partial index per value or an exact B-tree search, only work when the column is on the indexed table.

pgvector's README is direct about what happens otherwise: with an approximate index, "filtering is applied after the index is scanned", and with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40 a condition that matches 10% of rows leaves about 4 candidates. A tenant filter that lives two joins away on documents is in that position with no index to help it. The README's own remedies are a partial index per filter value when there are few of them, a plain B-tree on the filter column for exact search when the condition is selective, and from pgvector 0.8 iterative index scans (SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order) that keep scanning until enough rows pass, which work with a join too.

For the chunk_embeddings layout that means copying tenant_id onto the embeddings row. A CHECK cannot see another table, so the honest way to keep the copy true is a composite foreign key: UNIQUE (id, tenant_id) on chunks, then FOREIGN KEY (chunk_id, tenant_id) REFERENCES chunks (id, tenant_id) ON UPDATE CASCADE on the embeddings table. For the chunks layout it usually means document_id is already there and tenant_id joins in from documents; put the filter on chunks too, the same way, if the tenant filter is on every query.

Designing the three tables in Schemity

Schemity draws a pgvector column with its dimension and an HNSW index with its operator class and options exactly as PostgreSQL stores them, and flags an index PostgreSQL will refuse before the migration runs.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. Connect it to a database with pgvector installed, or import the pg_dump of one, and the layout above is drawn with what pgvector actually stores: embedding VECTOR on chunk_embeddings with no dimension, VECTOR(1536) where one was declared, the composite primary key on (chunk_id, model), and each HNSW index with its cast expression, its WHERE condition, its operator class and its WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64) in the table's Indexes list, read from reloptions rather than typed in.

That matters when you design the next one on a schema you did not write. A vector column with no dimension looks fine on a canvas and builds no plain index: pgvector refuses CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw on it with column does not have dimensions, and refuses it again above 2,000 dimensions for vector and 4,000 for halfvec. Schema lint reports both as "HNSW index on a vector column PostgreSQL will refuse" before the migration runs.

The change preview is what shows the model-switch mistake: changing vector(1536) to vector(768) on a column that holds rows is drawn as an altered column, with the planned ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE statement for you to read before it runs, so the chunk_embeddings rows arrive as a design decision instead of a failed deploy.

Adding a plain vector index is one dialog: pick HNSW, the operator class pgvector needs (there is no default one, CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding) fails with data type vector has no default operator class for access method "hnsw"), and the options, and the written SQL is CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m=16, ef_construction=64). An agent working over MCP creates the same index with create_index, operator class included, and is declined if it leaves the class out.

The field editor labels the length of a VECTOR column as its dimensions, which is the number the whole decision above turns on.

The numbers above came from a 5,000-row table on one laptop. Scale them by your row count and your edit rate, and the choice usually makes itself: the same way an integer key that outgrows its type forces a rewrite you would rather have planned, an embedding on the wrong row forces an index rebuild you would rather never need.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

title: Ranking is a choice: what I built instead of a news feed algorithm
description:
Most news apps decide two things for you: what you see, and in what order. When I started building Hushread, an RSS and news reader, I decided it would decide neither. Ranking is a choice, and I chose not to make it.

That choice creates its own problems. A newest-first feed of 200 sources is noisy, repetitive and endless. This post is about what I built instead of an algorithm to fix that, and the parts any developer building a feed, an inbox or a dashboard can reuse.

What you see: only what you chose

The feed is built from the sources you follow and nothing else. A source can be:

  • an RSS or Atom feed, or a site with no feed at all (Hushread checks the page and turns new posts into items),
  • a subreddit, with the post's text rather than a bare link,
  • a YouTube channel or a public Facebook page,
  • a topic ("chip exports", your football club) that pulls new coverage from any outlet,
  • or one of 2,500+ curated sources.

Nothing is injected from outside that list, and there are no ads or ad tracking.

In what order: newest first, always

The feed is every article from your sources, newest first. Nothing is ranked, boosted or reordered. AI is used in a few places (summaries, linking articles about the same event, judging tone for rules), but never to choose or reorder what is in the feed.

A chronological feed only works if it is finishable, so the reader helps you get to the end: articles are marked read as you scroll past them, read articles are hidden the next time the feed loads, and the feed ends at "All caught up!".

The real fix for noise: group things

The biggest source of noise in a chronological feed isn't order, it's repetition. When thirty outlets cover one event, you get thirty cards. So Hushread groups:

Articles into stories. When several articles tell the same story, you see one card with an "Also mentioned in" strip listing the other outlets. Syndicated copies and follow-up rewrites fold under the newest version. When 8 or more publishers cover an event, a "See whole story" tile opens the full story: a summary of where things stand, then every outlet's report, day by day, each linking to the original.


One story, 66 sources: the summary so far, then every outlet's report in time order.

Sources into folders. Folders group sources, tags group articles, and a source can sit in more than one folder. Any folder can filter the feed or be the screen the app opens on, so "everything" stops being the only view.


Folders and sources in the menu, each with its own unread count, next to the feed.

Surging stories into Trending, on a separate screen. Trending ranks stories by how many different publishers are covering them over the last 48 hours, not by clicks, and it never touches the feed itself.

Rules you write, not rules learned about you

Instead of a model guessing what to hide, you write the rule: mute, mark read, or notify, by keyword or phrase, by source or folder, and optionally by an article's tone. "Mute anything with crypto" or "mark negative articles as read" does what it says, and you can pause or delete it any time.

What I'd take from this for any feed

  • Repetition is a bigger problem than order. Collapse duplicates before you reach for ranking.
  • Keep every original one tap away when you group. A group that hides its sources isn't trusted.
  • Make the end of the feed reachable. "All caught up" is a feature.
  • Put ranked views on their own screen, so the main view stays predictable.

You can try it in the browser with no sign-up: https://app.hushread.com/demo?utm_source=devto

title: One editor, three runtimes: Bun, Browser, and the one in between
description:
Here are five lines of JavaScript:

"document" in globalThis;
"Bun" in globalThis;
globalThis.process?.versions?.bun ?? "not Bun";

import { readdir } from "node:fs/promises";
(await readdir(".")).length;

What do they print?

It depends on where they run. Run them in Bun and there's no document, there is a Bun, and readdir counts your files. Run them in a browser and document is there, Bun isn't, and that node:fs import doesn't make it past the build.

Most of us switch between those worlds all day. This post is about turning that into one switch per tab, in JSLab. It's our own tool, so discount the praise accordingly. The snippet above comes straight from the runtime docs.

Three runtimes, one menu

Each JSLab tab runs its code in one of three runtimes. You pick one from the runtime menu in the status bar, from Actions → Runtime, or from the command palette.

Runtime What your code gets Web View
Bun (default) Bun and Node globals and the full Node API surface, with no DOM No
Browser & Node APIs A real page, with the DOM and web APIs, plus a Node compatibility layer Yes
Browser A real page only, with no Node APIs at all Yes

Your code is bundled before it runs, so importing an installed package works in all three.

Bun: the default

New tabs open in Bun. Your code runs in a separate Bun process, using the Bun that ships inside JSLab. You get fs, path, child_process, http and the rest, and no DOM.

This is where scripts, data wrangling and algorithm sketches go. Because it's a separate process, an infinite loop or a crash doesn't take the editor down with it.

Browser: a real page, nothing else

The Browser runtime is a real WebKit page with no Node at all: a blank HTML page with your bundled code running in it.

document.body.innerHTML = "<p>Plain browser page</p>";
navigator.userAgent.includes("AppleWebKit");

fetch is the page's own, and CORS applies exactly as it would on a website. That's the point: if you want to know what a site would actually see, this is the honest runtime. Import a Node module and the build fails with a code frame pointing at the import.

Browser & Node APIs: the one in between

The surprising one. It's a real page with document, canvas and requestAnimationFrame, plus a Node compatibility layer bridged out to JSLab:

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import os from "node:os";

document.body.innerHTML = `<h1>Hello from ${os.platform()}</h1>`;
createHash("sha256").update("JSLab").digest("hex");
document.querySelector("h1");

A page that renders a heading and hashes a string with Node's crypto, in one file, with no server.

You get fs/promises and the callback-style fs functions, child_process.exec, execFile and spawn, plus os, path, crypto, buffer, events and friends. And fetch goes through JSLab, so it reaches any URL without CORS getting in the way:

const response = await fetch("https://api.github.com/zen");
response.status;
await response.text();

It's not all of Node. Synchronous fs, http, net, tls, dgram, worker_threads and vm aren't available. Call one and the message offers to switch the tab to Bun. For a synchronous fs call, it also names the async alternative.

The Web View

Both browser runtimes render into a Web View tile beside the console. Bun has no page, so it has no Web View. Toggle it with ⌥⌘W.

Every run reloads the page, so the DOM starts clean each time. Nothing from the last run hangs around. The page starts with a single <div id="root">.

Now the fun part: React. You can mount a component the usual way, with createRoot, and it renders in the Web View like it would on any page:

But you don't have to. Default-export a component and JSLab renders it for you:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function App() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello from React</h1>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Clicked {count} times</button>
    </div>
  );
}

No createRoot, no index.html, no dev server. Auto Run fires a moment after you stop typing, so you change the JSX and the component rerenders in the tile.

JSLab works out the framework from your imports: React, Vue, Solid or Angular. The Framework menu in the status bar shows what it found, and you can override it. You need the framework's renderer package installed (react-dom for React); if it's missing, the console tells you which one. The quickest start is the + button in the tab bar. Pick a framework and JSLab sets the tab's language, runtime and framework, installs the packages and opens starter code.

It isn't only components. Canvas, Three.js and Web Audio run in the Web View as they would in a browser.

The rule of thumb

You can use this even if you never touch JSLab. Choose a runtime by asking what your code needs to reach:

  • Only data and the file system? Use a Node-style runtime. No DOM means no accidental browser assumptions.
  • Only a page? Use a plain browser with real CORS, so what works is what will ship.
  • A page and a file or an API? That's the in-between case, the one we usually solve with a dev server, a proxy and a script.

Try it

JSLab is a JavaScript and TypeScript scratchpad for Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 14 or later, with a 14-day free trial. It launches on November 15. Until then, read Choosing a runtime and The Web View. Then guess what those five lines print in each runtime, before you can check.

title: Adding an AI Chatbot to a Website: 7 Things Developers Should Get Right
description:
Installing a chatbot is straightforward. Making it helpful, trustworthy, and maintainable is where the interesting work begins.

AI chatbots are becoming increasingly common on business websites.

But a successful chatbot needs more than a language model connected to a text box.

It needs useful knowledge, careful configuration, a good interface, and a fallback when automation cannot handle the request.

Here are seven important considerations when implementing an AI chatbot for a real business.

  1. Define What the Chatbot Should Answer

Begin by understanding the customer's requirements.

A retail website may need product and shipping answers.

An educational website may require course descriptions and admission information.

A service business might need to answer questions about pricing, availability, and operating hours.

Define these use cases before choosing a solution.

  1. Build Around Business Knowledge

An AI chatbot should use accurate business information.

Useful sources may include:

Product catalogs.

Website content.

Frequently asked questions.

Uploaded reference documents.

Company policies.

Without relevant information, a chatbot may produce responses that sound correct but aren't.

The objective is to ground answers in trustworthy material.

  1. Plan for Missing Information

What should happen when the assistant doesn't know the answer?

A useful solution should avoid inventing unsupported facts.

Instead, it can explain that the information isn't available and guide the visitor toward human assistance.

This is particularly important for pricing, inventory, service guarantees, and other business-specific claims.

  1. Keep Installation Simple

Many business owners don't want to build a custom frontend integration just to add chat support.

An embed snippet or a supported website plugin can simplify deployment.

MySampark, for example, provides a website chat widget that can be installed using a script snippet.

It also offers a WordPress integration.

The widget can be customized with brand colors, logo, and welcome messages.

  1. Design for Mobile Users

Website chat interfaces must work well across screen sizes.

A widget shouldn't obstruct important buttons, hide product information, or make navigation difficult.

Before deployment, test the chatbot on mobile and desktop layouts.

Check scrolling, message readability, input behavior, and the visibility of close controls.

  1. Provide Human Escalation

Even a well-configured assistant will encounter requests outside its knowledge.

Customers may need assistance with complex requests, sensitive complaints, or questions requiring judgment.

MySampark includes human takeover, allowing a team member to handle a conversation while AI responses are temporarily paused.

This is an important feature for real-world support workflows.

  1. Test Before Launch

Create a test set covering:

Common product questions.

Questions with missing information.

Similar or ambiguous product names.

Requests for human support.

Incorrect or outdated knowledge.

Mobile interface usability.

Repeated and unusual inputs.

Also review security, permissions, privacy notices, retention settings, and operational costs for any platform you integrate.

A chatbot isn't production-ready simply because it responds to "Hello."

Example: A Product-Aware Website Assistant

Consider an online clothing store.

A visitor asks:

"Does this jacket come in medium?"

A business-aware assistant can reference catalog information to answer if the necessary data exists.

If availability isn't known, the assistant should avoid guessing.

That distinction matters because a fluent answer isn't necessarily an accurate answer.

Using an Existing AI Chatbot Platform

Not every company needs to develop a complete chatbot infrastructure from scratch.

A hosted solution can be practical for teams that want to focus on their website or business rather than maintaining AI support systems.

MySampark combines a customizable website chat widget with business knowledge sources, human takeover, and a browser-based management interface.

It is one option for teams exploring this approach.

Conclusion

A useful AI chatbot isn't defined by how quickly it can generate messages.

It is defined by whether customers can trust the information and reach a person when required.

Start with accurate knowledge, keep the interface simple, and test real customer scenarios.

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2

Introduction
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model where in the core infrastructure of IT is hosted and managed by a third party provider. These services are delivered to the customers over the internet.
The providers usually offer management consoles and API for self service provisioning which gives the IT team direct control over the virtual infrastructure without owning a physical hardware, this prevents organizations form buying and maintaining physical servers, allowing them to rent virtualized resources when needed.
The lack or limited use of physical hardware reduces capital expenditure (CapEx) and enables rapid scalability.

**

Key features of Iaas

**
It is important to consider the core components of IaaS in order to understand how such a model works, each of its components work together in order to provide a comprehensive, scalable, and secure computing environment.
Some of these core components include;
a. Management and Automation tools
Tools such as API’s and web portals are provided through IaaS. These tools allow users to manage resources, automate tasks and configure networking. These lead to the automation of tasks such as scaling, backup and improving operational efficiency
b. Networking
IaaS provides virtual networks, subnets, VPNs, IP addresses and firewalls that support a complex architecture, and are used between the internet and virtual machines to ensure secure and efficient data transfer
c. Security
IaaS security components include identity and access management (IAM), encryption, intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDPS), and data protection mechanisms. These protect data, applications, and infrastructure from threats and help organizations adhere to data security and privacy regulations.
d. Storage
A variety of storage options are available through IaaS, such as block storage, file storage, and object storage. IaaS providers offer scalable and flexible storage solutions that can be easily dialed up or down to meet changing needs. Storage solutions offered by IaaS providers support everything from website content to enterprise databases.
e. Virtualization
Virtualization technology enables the pooling of physical resources and their allocation to VMs as needed. It allows multiple VMs to run on a single physical server, efficiently utilizing the underlying hardware.

Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS)

Though AWS does not offer a set of IaaS services, AWS is the world’s most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers, including the fastest-growing start-ups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies, are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.
This makes it faster, easier, and more cost effective to move your existing applications to the cloud and build nearly anything you can imagine.

How Amazon EC2 works
Amazon EC2 (Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud) offers on-demand, scalable computing power in the AWS Cloud. Using Amazon EC2 reduces hardware costs so you can develop and deploy applications faster. Launch as many or as few virtual servers as you need, with the ability to configure security, networking, and manage storage efficiently. Scale up to handle compute-intensive tasks or traffic spikes, and scale down when demand decreases, ensuring optimal flexibility and cost-efficiency.
EC2 is not just one service. It’s composed of many things at a high level.

  1. You can rent virtual machines on EC2, they’re called EC2 instances.
  2. You can store data on virtual drives or EBS volumes.
  3. You can distribute load across machines, Elastic Load Balancer (ELB).
  4. You can scale services using an auto-scaling group (ASG).

So, how does Amazon EC2 actually work?
EC2 instances are virtual servers running on Amazon’s physical hardware in their data centers. This virtualization technology allows Amazon to efficiently utilize hardware, providing customers with flexible and scalable computing capacity. Multiple instances can run on the same physical server through virtualization, offering a cost-effective solution for various computing needs.
Amazon EC2 instances are virtual servers that run on physical servers. Amazon uses a hypervisor to manage these virtual resources. Each physical server can support multiple virtual servers, known as instances. This virtualization technology enables Amazon to efficiently use the hardware, offering flexible and scalable computing resources to customers.

Challenges when using IaaS

  1. Unpatched vulnerabilities in guest operating systems create entry points for exploitation. You control OS maintenance in infrastructure as a service, making timely patching critical for stopping known exploits.
  2. Shadow IT and sprawl happen when teams provision resources without security oversight. Untracked instances lack proper monitoring, compliance controls, and protection against attacks.
  3. Insider threats and credential theft give attackers legitimate access through stolen API keys, access tokens, or employee credentials. Once inside, attackers blend in with normal cloud API activity.
  4. Inadequate IAM (Identify And Management) policies grant excessive permissions that let attackers escalate privileges or move laterally. Overly permissive roles enable ransomware operators to encrypt entire cloud estates after compromising a single service account.
  5. Misconfigured cloud storage remains the leading cause of cloud data breaches. Misconfigured public Amazon S3 buckets have exposed hundreds of millions of records across multiple incidents, including high-profile cases such as those affecting Facebook and Capital One, where default or improperly configured access controls favored accessibility over security, leading to large-scale data exposure.

Conclusion

IaaS has reshaped how organizations build and scale IT infrastructure. It replaces hardware ownership with on-demand access, delivering the agility and efficiency today’s businesses require. The most successful strategies, however, don’t rely on IaaS alone. They blend it with colocation, private cloud, and edge computing to balance flexibility with control

title: The Connect Page Is the Revenue Page
description:
Every SaaS has a page where money actually changes hands, and it is rarely the pricing page. For a recovery tool it is the connect page: the unglamorous screen where a merchant grants access to their payment platform. Until that click, the trial is a promise; after it, recoveries can start. Everything upstream — ads, articles, trials — exists to deliver a merchant to that one screen in a state of mind to finish it.

That status changes how you write it. Instructions in simple words. Exact clicks, named in the order they happen. One action per step, because two actions per step is where people quietly close the tab. Our own rule for this surface is absolute: nothing on it changes without a deliberate review, because a confusing sentence here costs more than a confusing sentence anywhere else in the product combined.

Swipe Again treats connect completion within twenty-four hours of signup as the funnel's pulse for exactly this reason. When the number dips, we do not rewrite the homepage — we re-read the connect page as a stranger would, at midnight, mid-task, on a phone. The recovery flow cannot recover anything for a merchant who never connected. Revenue pages deserve revenue-grade attention, wherever in the product they happen to sit.

title: Stop Using cat for Everything: 9 Better Ways to Read Linux Files
description:
Practical tools to inspect, page, slice, and debug files without freezing your terminal

Running cat /var/log/nginx/access.log on an active server is an unforced error that most engineers make once before watching their shell lock up.

The utility name is short, muscle memory takes over, and the binary exists on every Unix host in existence. But cat stands for concatenate. Its original Unix design was to join multiple input streams together and ship the output down a pipeline. It was never built as an interactive file viewer.

When you use cat to inspect files interactively, you offload stream buffering directly to your terminal emulator. If that file happens to be a multi-gigabyte JSON log or an active audit trail, your terminal tries to process, parse, and render millions of lines into its local scrollback window. Your terminal emulator consumes gigabytes of memory, remote SSH sessions drop keystrokes, stray escape sequences scramble font settings, and you have zero ability to pause, scroll, or search inline.

Linux comes with specialized utilities built to inspect, page, slice, reformat, and navigate files without wasting system resources or locking your session.

Here are nine better ways to read files on Linux, along with the exact flags to use in production.

1. bat: Syntax Highlighting, Git Awareness, and Smart Paging

If you want to view a configuration file, shell script, or source code file directly on stdout without opening an interactive viewer, bat is the modern replacement for cat.

On Debian and Ubuntu distributions, the package is installed as batcat to prevent name clashes with another system binary:

sudo apt-get install bat
alias bat="batcat"

Unlike raw cat, bat inspects file extensions and shebang lines to apply high-contrast syntax highlighting across hundreds of languages. It renders line numbers automatically and integrates directly with Git to show added, modified, and removed lines directly in the left gutter.

To view an Nginx configuration with line numbers and syntax highlighting:

bat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

One of the best features in bat is automatic smart paging. If the target file fits within the height of your terminal screen, bat writes the output straight to stdout and drops you back at your shell prompt. If the output exceeds your terminal height, it routes the stream through an interactive pager automatically.

You can also use bat to expose non-printable control characters, trailing spaces, and hidden carriage returns:

bat -A /etc/environment

The -A flag displays tab stops as arrows, spaces as subtle dots, and newlines as explicit symbols, making syntax debugging straightforward.

2. less with -FXRS: Zero-Memory Paging and Instant Regex Search

When a file exceeds a few megabytes, printing it straight to stdout is risky. The less pager remains the industry benchmark for high-performance file viewing because it does not load the entire file into RAM before displaying it.

less uses memory mapping (mmap) to read only the small slice of bytes needed to fill your current terminal dimensions. You can open a 50GB database dump or a massive systemd log instantaneously without causing memory pressure or disk thrashing on the host:

less -FXRS /var/log/syslog

The four flags combined here make less behave cleanly for system administration:

  • -F tells less to exit immediately if the entire file fits on a single terminal screen.
  • -X stops less from sending the terminal initialization strings that clear the screen on exit, leaving the inspected lines visible in your terminal scrollback.
  • -R processes raw ANSI color escape codes properly, ensuring colored log output from modern CLI tools renders correctly instead of displaying garbled control sequences.
  • -S disables line wrapping. Long log lines are truncated horizontally instead of wrapping into messy multi-line blocks. You can pan horizontally using the left and right arrow keys to inspect wide timestamps and JSON structures.

Inside less, you navigate quickly using single keystrokes:

  • Press G to jump straight to the end of the file.
  • Press g to return to the first line.
  • Type / followed by a search pattern to search forward using regular expressions.
  • Type ? followed by a search pattern to search backward through previous entries.
  • Press n to jump to the next search match, or N to jump to the previous match.
  • Press +F to enter follow mode, which updates the view in real time as new lines append to the file, identical to tail -f. Pressing Ctrl+C drops you back into scrollable, searchable mode without closing the file.

You can set these flags permanently by adding this export to your shell configuration (~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc):

export LESS="-FXRS"
export PAGER="less"

3. tail -F and head: Slicing Boundaries and Tracking Rotated Logs

Most operational debugging tasks focus on either the beginning of a configuration file or the very latest events recorded by an application. Reading the entire file to find those lines wastes I/O bandwidth.

head and tail let you slice specific boundaries with minimal overhead:

# Print the first 25 lines of a configuration file
head -n 25 /etc/redis/redis.conf

# Print the last 40 lines of an audit log
tail -n 40 /var/log/audit/audit.log

A common operational trap occurs when tracking active server logs using tail -f. Standard tail -f hooks into the underlying file descriptor of the target file. When background services like logrotate compress and rotate logs, the active file is renamed or moved, and a brand-new file is created with the original filename.

Because standard tail -f follows the inode rather than the filename, it remains attached to the old, unlinked file descriptor and stops displaying new lines.

To avoid missing critical production events, use -F (capitalized):

tail -F /var/log/nginx/access.log

The -F flag instructs tail to track the file by its filename rather than its file descriptor. If the underlying inode changes or the file is temporarily unavailable during log rotation, tail re-establishes its handle on the new file as soon as the service recreates it.

You can also use tail to slice from a specific line number to the end of a file using the plus notation:

# Display output starting from line 150 through the end of the file
tail -n +150 /var/log/messages

4. tac: Bottom-Up Reverse Reading for Fast Crash Diagnostics

Troubleshooting is chronologically inverted. When an alert fires or a container crashes, you want to inspect the failure event that occurred five seconds ago, not the initialization messages recorded when the system booted three weeks ago.

The standard core utility tac prints lines in reverse order, starting from the final line and working backward to the first.

tac /var/log/dpkg.log | head -n 30

This command surfaces the thirty most recent package installations or upgrades without piping through sort -r or forcing the shell to buffer thousands of lines.

When paired with sed, tac provides an efficient way to pull the most recent stack trace from an application log:

tac /var/log/app/error.log | sed '/TRACEBACK_START/q' | tac

The inner tac reverses the log so the latest crash appears first. The sed statement reads until it matches the start marker of the traceback, prints it, and quits immediately. The second tac restores normal chronological order. You get the exact crash context without reading hundreds of megabytes of older events.

5. zless, zcat, and zstdcat: In-Place Compressed Log Inspection

On production machines, log rotation policies quickly compress historical logs using gzip (.gz), xz (.xz), or zstandard (.zst) to save disk space.

Extracting these files to disk with gunzip or unxz simply to check an error message consumes disk storage, adds write cycles to your drive, and creates leftover files that require cleanup.

Linux provides compression-aware utilities that decompress data directly into memory streams:

# Read a gzipped log file using full less keybindings
zless /var/log/nginx/access.log.2.gz

# Stream an xz-compressed archive directly into grep
xzcat /var/log/syslog.3.xz | grep -i "oom-killer"

# Inspect modern zstandard compressed logs
zstdcat /var/log/journal.zst | head -n 25

zless works with all standard less navigation commands, including forward search (/), backward search (?), and horizontal scrolling (-S). You inspect multi-gigabyte compressed files without writing a single uncompressed byte to disk.

6. view: Read-Only Structural Navigation Without Edit Accidents

Opening production configuration files inside an active text editor like vim or nano is dangerous. An accidental key press, stray paste buffer, or an unthinking write command (:wq) can modify critical runtime configurations without leaving a clear trace in your command history.

Using view (which opens Vim in read-only mode, equivalent to vim -R) gives you complete structural navigation tools while protecting the file from accidental writes:

view /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

Inside view, the buffer modification flag is disabled. You get the full power of Vim syntax parsing and movement commands:

  • Press % while your cursor is over an opening parenthesis, bracket, or curly brace to jump directly to its matching closing counterpart.
  • Press * to find the next occurrence of the word currently under your cursor.
  • Use zo and zc to open and close code folds, collapsing long YAML blocks or nested structures.
  • Type :set number to turn on contextual line numbering.

If you accidentally strike an edit key, the editor displays an explicit warning and prevents saving changes to disk.

7. nl: Structured Line Numbering with Logical Page Boundaries

When people want line numbers, they often run cat -n. While cat -n works, it numbers every single line indiscriminately, including empty whitespace, trailing breaks, and formatting separators.

The dedicated nl (number lines) utility gives you fine-grained control over how lines are counted, formatted, and displayed:

nl /etc/pam.d/common-auth

By default, nl only assigns numbers to non-empty lines, keeping the output clean and visually tied to functional configuration directives.

You can modify its numbering logic to suit specific file structures:

# Number all lines including blank ones, right-aligned with 4 digits and zero padding
nl -b a -n rz -w 4 /etc/hosts

# Number only lines matching a specific regex pattern
nl -b p'^[[:space:]]*server' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

nl also understands logical page delimiters (\:\:\:, \:\:, and \: for headers, body, and footers), allowing you to restart line numbering automatically across distinct sections of generated source files or technical reports.

8. column -t: Formatting Jagged Delimited Files into Clean Tables

Reading delimited text files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/fstab, or CSV exports with cat produces jagged, misaligned output because fields have different lengths.

The column utility parses delimited input and aligns it into neat, human-readable vertical tables:

# Format /etc/passwd using the colon delimiter
column -t -s ":" /etc/passwd | head -n 15

The -t flag instructs column to determine the number of columns dynamically, and -s sets the delimiter character.

For whitespace-delimited files like storage mount configurations:

grep -v '^#' /etc/fstab | column -t

Instead of struggling to see where mount points end and filesystem options begin, every field aligns neatly under its respective column.

9. od, hexdump, and xxd: Exposing Invisible Bytes and Encoding Traps

A frustrating shell issue happens when a bash script exits with cryptic syntax errors, yet opening the script with cat shows clean, correct code.

cat does not reveal invisible characters, including:

  • Windows carriage returns (\r\n or CRLF) inserted by editors on non-Linux systems.
  • Zero-width non-breaking spaces copied from online documentation.
  • UTF-8 Byte Order Marks (BOM) added at the beginning of text files.
  • Embedded null bytes or escape codes from corrupted data transfers.

When text files behave unexpectedly, inspect their underlying bytes directly:

# Inspect the first 128 bytes with hex and ASCII side by side using xxd
xxd -l 128 /etc/environment

# Use hexdump in canonical format to check character offsets
hexdump -C /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh | head -n 10

# Inspect character representations with od
od -c /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh | head -n 15

Running od -c exposes line endings immediately. A proper Linux newline appears as \n. A file containing Windows line endings displays explicit \r \n character pairs. Catching this with od in five seconds saves hours of debugging broken shell loops.

Quick Reference: Choosing the Right Tool

Syntax highlighting & code files:
Use bat. It provides language-aware colorization, git status in the left gutter, and automatic pager fallback when output overflows your screen.

Multi-gigabyte logs & large dumps:
Use less -FXRS. It memory-maps files with zero RAM overhead, provides forward and backward regex search, and avoids terminal lockups.

Live log monitoring:
Use tail -F. It tracks files across rotation and inode updates rather than losing track of the file descriptor.

Recent errors & stack traces:
Use tac. It traverses files bottom-up so recent events appear first without needing sorting pipelines.

Compressed archives (.gz, .xz, .zst):
Use zless, xzcat, or zstdcat. They stream and inspect compressed files directly in RAM without extracting data to disk.

Safe configuration inspection:
Use view. It provides full Vim movement and syntax folding while preventing accidental modifications.

Readable line numbers:
Use nl. It numbers non-blank lines by default and supports custom regex patterns and padding styles.

Jagged delimited files (CSV, /etc/passwd):
Use column -t -s ":". It aligns delimiter-separated text into structured vertical columns.

Invisible characters & encoding errors:
Use od -c or hexdump -C. It reveals carriage returns, zero-width spaces, and binary corruption instantly.

An Interesting Fact About cat

The cat command was written in 1971 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie for the First Edition of Unix. Its sole intended purpose was concatenating files: reading contents from multiple sources and combining them into a single stream.

By 1995, engineers overusing cat as a file viewer had become so widespread that the Usenet community created the Useless Use of cat Award (UUOC). The award called out shell pipelines that ran cat file | command instead of using direct shell redirection (command < file) or passing the file as an argument (command file), which eliminates an unnecessary subshell, process fork, and context switch.

Practical Takeaways for Your Daily Workflow

Habits are hard to change, but defaulting to cat for file inspection creates unnecessary friction and risks shell lockups on busy production nodes.

A simple step is adding an alias to your interactive shell profile:

alias cat="bat 2>/dev/null || less"

Save cat for its original purpose: gluing multiple files together into a pipe (cat chunk.* > full_archive.tar). For reviewing configurations, debugging errors, and inspecting logs, pick the tool designed for that specific data format.

What command or alias do you reach for when a multi-gigabyte log file is filling up disk space on a production server?

title: When Strict Mode reruns Effects: inspect subscription setup and cleanup
description:
When Strict Mode logs an Effect setup twice, check whether cleanup ran between the setups and how many subscriptions remain. Reducing the setup count to one does not establish that cleanup works.

A small subscription was compared in React 19.3.0 development and production builds. Initial behavior also differed between wrapping the root in Strict Mode and wrapping only part of the tree.

Count registration and removal without external communication

The test subscription target is a Set. Setup registers a handler, and a local button invokes all registered handlers. There are no network connections or notification services.

function Subscription({ room, cleanup }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const handler = () => trace.events.push(`message:${room}`);
    trace.active.add(handler);
    trace.events.push(`setup:${room}`);
    if (cleanup) {
      return () => {
        trace.active.delete(handler);
        trace.events.push(`cleanup:${room}`);
      };
    }
  }, [room, cleanup]);
  return <output id="room">{room}</output>;
}

trace.active contains registered handlers, and trace.events records their order. The normal version uses cleanup: true; the deliberately incomplete comparison uses false. The room can change from A to B, and the root is unmounted at the end.

Separate bundles were built with development and production values for process.env.NODE_ENV. In the root-wide condition, <StrictMode> wraps the element rendered by createRoot. In the partial condition, it wraps only Subscription beneath a parent outside Strict Mode.

Placement changed initial setup and cleanup

Build and placement Initial setups Initial cleanups Handlers remaining after initial processing
Development, root Strict Mode, with cleanup 2 1 1
Development, no Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Development, child-only Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Production, root Strict Mode, with cleanup 1 0 1
Development, root Strict Mode, without cleanup 2 0 2

The normal development root logged setup:A → cleanup:A → setup:A during initial processing. It removed the earlier subscription before setting it up again.

The official Strict Mode documentation distinguishes the extra development setup/cleanup cycle from the condition where initial Effects are not rerun because Strict Mode does not wrap the root. Check where Strict Mode is placed before interpreting repeated Effect logs.

The table counts Effect work. It does not establish component-function invocation counts or DOM painting counts.

Omitting cleanup accumulated handlers

Pressing the local notification button once after initial setup logged one message:A with cleanup and 2 without it. The next step changed the room to B.

Development root condition After initial registration After changing room After unmount
With cleanup 1 1 0
Without cleanup 2 3 3

The normal version logged cleanup:A → setup:B on the room change and cleanup:B on unmount. Without cleanup, the A handlers remained while a B handler was added. They stayed in the Set after unmount too.

The comparison shows what remains when the implementation omits its removal step. Each case discards its Set; the incomplete version was not integrated into an application.

Check the matching teardown before limiting calls

For this example, the fix is to remove the same handler that setup registered. A room change removes the old room's subscription before registering the new one. The useEffect reference describes cleanup with previous values followed by setup with the new values when dependencies change.

This experiment does not apply the extra-execution scenario to API writes, payments, or email delivery. Its scope is a subscription with matching registration and removal. If real logs differ, investigate actual unmounts and remounts or development-tool updates as well as Strict Mode placement.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152 and no React Compiler. The fixture code and results for the 5 conditions include room changes and unmounts as well as initial processing.
