title: Automating tax calculation from Amazon VAT reports: a system design for VAT service providers
description:
For firms that provide cross-border VAT services, the most labor-intensive step usually isn't registration. It's calculating tax every filing period. Sellers send over their Amazon VAT Transactions Report, and accountants sort it in Excel by country, rate and deductible item, then copy the numbers into each country's return. With more countries and more sellers, both the error rate and the turnaround time go up.

We built an online platform for a cross-border tax compliance provider covering VAT registration and agent transfer, tax calculation, filing and payment, EPR and authorized representative services. This article covers only the tax calculation part: how the system turns an Amazon report into numbers ready to file. It should be useful for VAT service providers and tax agents who want to turn their service into a product.

The input: how the Amazon report is structured

The Amazon VAT Transactions Report has one row per transaction. Each row includes the transaction type, who collects the tax (Amazon or the seller), whether the buyer gave a valid VAT number, the ship-from and ship-to countries, the tax rate, gross and net amounts, currency and other fields.

Calculating tax comes down to deciding, for each row, "in which country, as what kind of supply and at what rate is this sale reported", then totaling by country and filing period.

Core design: classify first, then calculate

Instead of writing rules country by country, we first put every transaction into one of 7 sales categories. The classification combines three fields:

  • Tax collector: Amazon collects (as the deemed supplier) or the seller self-reports
  • Buyer VAT number: whether the buyer is a business with a valid VAT number
  • Ship-from / ship-to country: domestic sale, intra-EU cross-border sale or export outside the EU

Combined, these put each transaction into a category such as domestic sale, intra-EU distance sale, supply to a VAT-registered business, export or marketplace-collected. Each category has a fixed treatment: some are charged output tax at the local rate, some are reported at zero rate and listed separately, and for marketplace-collected sales the seller pays no further tax but still has to report them.

The benefit is that country differences collapse into one table of "how each country treats each category", instead of being scattered across hundreds of if-else branches. Adding a country means filling in that table.

The system has built-in cross-border rules for all 27 EU member states. Tax calculation is live for the UK and 8 EU countries: Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and Austria.

Input tax: C79, C88 and PVA

UK import VAT is the part most often missed, so the system handles three kinds of documents separately:

  • C79: the import VAT certificate issued by HMRC, which is the basis for reclaiming import VAT. The system collects C79 amounts per filing period and counts them as input tax
  • C88: the import declaration, used to reconcile import value and tax, and part of the supporting evidence
  • PVA (Postponed VAT Accounting): the seller pays no VAT at import and instead reports the same amount as both output and input tax on the return. The system puts PVA amounts in both boxes; the net effect is zero, but it must be reported

None of these are in the Amazon report, so sellers upload them separately. In the filing workspace they are separate items with reminders when something is missing.

The output: UK VAT Return boxes

The UK VAT Return has fixed boxes (Box 1 to Box 9) for output tax, EU acquisitions tax, input tax, net tax, total sales and purchases, and intra-EU supplies and acquisitions. Once transactions are sorted into the 7 categories and C79 / C88 / PVA are processed, every box can be derived directly, without an accountant reconciling spreadsheets by hand.

For the 8 EU countries, the system outputs totals that match the structure of each country's return.

Currencies and exchange rates

The currency of a transaction in the Amazon report isn't always the filing currency. The system fetches exchange rates daily and converts each transaction at the rate for its date. The rate source and conversion date are stored with each calculation so reviewers can trace them.

Workflow: tax calculation inside the filing workspace

Tax calculation isn't a standalone tool; it's one step in the filing workflow. The workspace moves through these states: awaiting report upload → awaiting tax confirmation → awaiting submission → being filed by the accounting firm → awaiting payment → filed.

  • Seller side: upload the Amazon report and deduction documents, see the calculated tax, confirm and submit
  • Operations side: review calculations and filings, manage payment proofs and receipts, with role permissions and audit logs

With tax calculation inside the workflow, sellers see "how much is due this period and why" instead of an Excel file they have to interpret themselves.

Engineering safeguards

Mistakes in tax data are expensive, so we put several safeguards in place:

  • 20 end-to-end automated tests covering the main calculation paths
  • A database schema comparison before each release so migrations don't drop fields
  • Calculation results keep the mapping from original rows to totals, so a reviewer can trace any total back to individual transactions

The platform went through 300+ iterations in about 4 months, with about 44 business pages, 77 API endpoints and 19 data models. The stack is React 19 + TypeScript + Koa + MySQL, with Alibaba Cloud for OCR and object storage.

Advice for VAT service providers

If you're thinking about turning manual tax calculation into a system, start here:

  1. Write your tax rules as a "category × country" table first. It takes no code, but it exposes the gray areas in your rules
  2. Model deduction documents separately from marketplace reports; they come from different sources on different cycles
  3. Make every result traceable to individual rows, so reviewers are willing to sign off
  4. Start with the UK and one or two EU countries, get the workflow running, then add countries

FXTech is an e-commerce technology agency and Shopify Partner based in Shenzhen, China. We build VAT compliance systems for VAT service providers, tax agents and cross-border e-commerce teams (we don't file taxes ourselves), and also build Shopify stores and headless DTC storefronts and optimize web performance. Case study: https://fxweb.dev/cases/#vat-compliance-saas . VAT solutions: https://fxweb.dev/vat/ .

title: Local SEO Guide: How Businesses Can Improve Their Visibility in Local Search
description:
Local SEO Guide: How Businesses Can Improve Their Visibility in Local Search
Local SEO is an important strategy for businesses that want to attract customers from nearby areas. Whether you run a training institute, restaurant, retail store, or service-based company, appearing in local search results can help people discover your business. For digital marketing enthusiasts exploring a Digital Marketing Course in Thane West, understanding local SEO is also a valuable skill for building practical marketing knowledge.
What Is Local SEO and Why Does It Matter?
Local SEO is the process of optimizing a website and online presence to improve visibility in location-based search results. For example, when someone searches for "digital marketing institute near me" or "best training institute in Thane," Google displays relevant businesses based on location, relevance, and other ranking factors.

Unlike traditional SEO, local SEO focuses on attracting customers from specific geographical areas. It helps businesses connect with people who are actively looking for nearby products or services.
5 Effective Local SEO Strategies for Better Visibility

  1. Optimize Your Google Business Profile Google Business Profile is one of the most important tools for local SEO. It allows businesses to display essential information such as their address, phone number, website, business hours, photos, and customer reviews.

To improve your profile:

  • Add accurate business information.
  • Select relevant primary and secondary categories.
  • Upload genuine business photos regularly.
  • Update working hours and contact details.
  • Respond professionally to customer reviews.
  • Share relevant business updates. A complete and regularly maintained profile helps customers understand your business and makes it easier to discover.
  • Target Location-Based Keywords Keyword research plays an important role in local SEO. Businesses should identify search terms that include their services and target locations.

For example, a training institute can target phrases such as "digital marketing classes in Thane West" and "SEO training near me."

Include relevant keywords naturally in website titles, headings, service pages, and descriptions. Someone looking for a Digital Marketing Course in Thane West should be able to find relevant information without navigating through unrelated pages.

  1. Create Location-Specific Website Pages Creating dedicated location pages can improve your website's relevance for different service areas.

For example, a business serving Thane, Mumbra, Airoli, and Bhiwandi can create separate pages explaining its services in these locations.

Each page should contain unique information, relevant keywords, customer benefits, contact details, and useful content. Avoid creating multiple pages with nearly identical descriptions just to target different locations.

  1. Build Local Citations and Quality Backlinks Local citations are online mentions of your business name, address, and phone number. These listings can appear on business directories, industry websites, and local platforms.

Maintain consistent business information across relevant platforms. Additionally, build quality backlinks through guest articles, industry publications, and local business websites.

Focus on relevance and credibility instead of creating hundreds of low-quality backlinks. A few useful links from relevant websites can provide more value than spammy directory submissions.

  1. Collect and Manage Customer Reviews Online reviews influence how potential customers perceive a business. Encourage genuine customers to share their experiences after using your products or services.

Respond to both positive and negative reviews politely. Thank customers for positive feedback and address complaints with helpful solutions.

Never purchase fake reviews or offer incentives in exchange for positive ratings. Authentic customer experiences help build long-term trust.
Common Local SEO Mistakes to Avoid
Many businesses struggle with local search visibility because they overlook basic optimization practices.

Some common mistakes include:

  • Using incorrect business contact information.
  • Ignoring Google Business Profile updates.
  • Stuffing location keywords into website content.
  • Publishing duplicate location pages.
  • Building irrelevant or spammy backlinks.
  • Ignoring customer reviews.
  • Forgetting to optimize websites for mobile users. Regular monitoring and improvement can help businesses avoid these issues. Learn Local SEO and Build Practical Digital Marketing Skills Local SEO requires continuous learning, keyword research, content optimization, Google Business Profile management, and performance tracking. Understanding these concepts can help beginners develop useful digital marketing skills.

If you want to explore SEO, Google Ads, social media marketing, and other essential marketing concepts, consider learning through a structured Digital Marketing Course in Thane West.

You can explore

to learn more about digital marketing training and practical learning opportunities.
Conclusion
Local SEO is not just about ranking higher on Google; it is about helping the right customers discover your business at the right time. By optimizing your Google Business Profile, targeting location-based keywords, creating useful website pages, earning relevant backlinks, and managing customer reviews, you can build a stronger local online presence.

For anyone interested in pursuing a Digital Marketing Course in Thane West, learning local SEO is a valuable starting point for understanding how businesses attract customers through search engines.

title: Building a Behavior-Based Email Welcome Flow Without Complex Automation
description:
Most welcome email systems follow a predictable pattern: subscribe, receive three generic emails, then join a newsletter.

I think we can build something more useful without introducing an expensive automation platform.

Consider an application with 400 newsletter subscribers. Some are beginners, while others already understand your product. Sending identical onboarding messages to both groups wastes an opportunity to personalize communication.

Here's how I would design a lightweight, event-driven welcome sequence with three branches, five possible emails, and a few simple tags.

1. Model Subscribers With Minimal State

I would start with three tags:

  • beginner
  • experienced
  • unengaged

Each subscriber also needs signup time, email preferences, and consent information.

const subscriber = {
  id: "user_123",
  email: "user@example.com",
  tags: [],
  subscribedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  consent: true,
  unsubscribed: false
};

For production, I would persist this information in a database rather than storing it in memory.

2. Email 1: Capture Intent Immediately

My first email delivers whatever someone requested during signup.

Below download link, I would include two options:

  • I'm just starting out.
  • I've been doing this a while.

Each link points to an authenticated preference endpoint.

For example:

GET /preferences?choice=beginner&token=...
GET /preferences?choice=experienced&token=...

One important detail: email security scanners sometimes follow links automatically.

I would therefore show a confirmation page before permanently updating preferences. Tokens must be signed, scoped, and expire after a reasonable period.

Actual preference changes should use a validated POST request.

3. Implement Three Branches

Once preference selection is confirmed, subscriber state determines upcoming emails.

function getWelcomeSchedule(segment) {
  const common = [
    { day: 0, template: "welcome" },
    { day: 8, template: "expectations" },
    { day: 12, template: "next-step" }
  ];

  const branches = {
    beginner: [
      { day: 2, template: "beginner-mistakes" },
      { day: 5, template: "beginner-checklist" }
    ],
    experienced: [
      { day: 2, template: "advanced-tactics" },
      { day: 5, template: "campaign-teardown" }
    ],
    unengaged: [
      { day: 3, template: "preference-reminder" },
      { day: 5, template: "general-example" }
    ]
  };

  return [...common, ...branches[segment]]
    .sort((a, b) => a.day - b.day);
}

This function returns five scheduled messages for any supported segment.

I would initially classify subscribers without a preference as unselected, using unengaged only after a defined inactivity period.

4. Schedule Emails Reliably

For a small application, a queue worker or scheduled job is sufficient.

Every scheduled message should have a unique key:

const jobKey =
  `${subscriber.id}:${templateId}`;

Before sending, I would check:

  1. Has this message already been sent?
  2. Is subscriber consent still valid?
  3. Has someone unsubscribed or reduced frequency?
  4. Has their preferred segment changed?

A database-backed uniqueness constraint and transactional job claiming can prevent duplicate sends across workers.

I would also suppress outdated branch messages whenever preferences change.

5. Measure Actual Engagement

Open tracking is increasingly unreliable because of privacy protections and automated activity.

I prefer measuring confirmed preference selections, meaningful clicks, replies, and unsubscribes.

Consider a hypothetical 400-subscriber cohort:

Segment Subscribers
Beginner 120
Experienced 80
No selection 200

Initial preference selection:

(120 + 80) / 400 * 100 = 50%

If another 20 subscribers choose a preference after receiving a reminder:

220 / 400 * 100 = 55%

That's a five-percentage-point increase in known preferences, not proof of improved revenue or retention.

For accurate reporting, I would exclude detected bot activity and track each cohort separately.

6. Avoid Overengineering

Small mailing lists rarely need complex customer-data infrastructure.

Before selecting an email service provider, I would evaluate automation support, API limits, webhook reliability, and pricing.

For additional platform context, Sprout24 maintains an independent email marketing software comparison directory.

I would also implement unsubscribe handling, bounce processing, retry limits, suppression lists, and relevant email authentication requirements before going live.

Final Thoughts

My preferred architecture is straightforward:

Signup → Welcome Email → Preference Selection → Branch Scheduling → Engagement Measurement

No complicated scoring engine is necessary.

I'd start with explicit user preferences, add behavior-based segmentation only when useful, and improve implementation using real subscriber feedback.

How would you handle preference changes while multiple email jobs are already queued?

Id be interested in comparing approaches using database jobs, queue workers, or serverless functions.

title: How we bundled Java 8 into a one-click Windows zip for our game
description:
Disclosure: I'm Snow, and I run SnowRSPS, a free custom 317 game server online since 2012.

Our game client is a Java 8 jar. For years the #1 support question was "it won't open." Players had no Java, the wrong Java, or a 32-bit PC. Here's what we shipped instead.

The layout 

SnowRSPS/
  Play SnowRSPS.bat   <- the only thing players click
  SnowRSPS.jar
  java64/             <- Java 8 runtime for 64-bit Windows 7/8/10/11
  java32/             <- Java 8 runtime for old 32-bit Windows
  README-EN.txt
  README-CN.txt

What the launcher does

  1. Picks the right runtime. It checks whether Windows is 64-bit and uses java64, otherwise java32. No system Java needed, no PATH changes.
  2. Survives odd folder names. Many of our players unzip to folders with spaces or Chinese characters, so every path is quoted and the script works from its own directory.
  3. Retries with less memory. If the JVM can't reserve the heap on a weak PC, it relaunches with a smaller -Xmx instead of failing silently.

Why a zip and not an exe

Unsigned .exe downloads get blocked more often by browsers. A zip with a .bat inside goes through more easily. Players still see Windows "protected your PC"; the README says: More info → Run anyway.

Build notes

  • Compile with compliance 1.8 so the bundled runtime can run it.
  • Eclipse → Export → Runnable JAR → "Package required libraries into generated JAR".
  • Ship two READMEs (English + Simplified Chinese). It cut down our support questions a lot.

Takeaways

Bundle the runtime, make the first click obvious, and add a fallback for weak machines.

If you want to see it in action: download the SnowRSPS client.

title: Why did my birthday move? A date-only bug across time zones
description:
Someone enters their birthday as 12 June. After travelling, they open the app and see 11 June.

They haven't changed it. One possible cause is that the app turned a calendar date into a moment in time, then displayed that moment in a different time zone.

Here's a small example of how that can happen, and what to test in an app that stores birthdays.

Watch the short video: Why did my birthday move?

From 12 June to 11 June

Suppose a birthday is 1994-06-12. An app saves it as midnight UTC:

1994-06-12T00:00:00Z

That timestamp identifies a moment. At that moment in Los Angeles, the local date and time are 11 June 1994, 17:00. If the app converts the timestamp to the device's time zone and takes the date, it will show 11 June.

The time-zone conversion is doing what it was asked to do. The problem is that a birthday was represented as a moment in the first place. Travelling doesn't change a correctly stored birthday.

Here's the conversion in Kotlin:

import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

val savedMoment = Instant.parse("1994-06-12T00:00:00Z")
val displayedDate = savedMoment
    .atZone(ZoneId.of("America/Los_Angeles"))
    .toLocalDate()

println(displayedDate) // 1994-06-11

The offset depends on the zone's rules for the date in question. Using a named zone such as America/Los_Angeles lets the time API apply those rules, including daylight saving time.

Keep a birthday as a date

For a birthday, the value we need is a year, month and day. In Java or Kotlin, LocalDate represents that without a time or time zone:

import java.time.LocalDate

val birthday = LocalDate.parse("1994-06-12")
val apiValue = birthday.toString() // "1994-06-12"
val loadedBirthday = LocalDate.parse(apiValue)

check(loadedBirthday == birthday)

The important part is what happens between those two operations. Agree on a date-only value in the API, for example:

{ "birthday": "1994-06-12" }

Then preserve it as a date through the server and database. For example, PostgreSQL's DATE type stores a calendar date without a time of day. On the way back, parse the value as a date and format it for the person's locale—without converting it through an instant.

On Android, java.time.LocalDate is available from API level 26. If you support older Android versions, check your project's Java API desugaring configuration and supported APIs.

Test the full round trip

A parsing test alone can't catch a conversion hidden in the API, database mapping or UI. Try a test that exercises the actual save and reload path:

  1. In UTC, enter and save 1994-06-12.
  2. Reload it and check that the API returns 1994-06-12 and the screen displays 12 June.
  3. Change the device or test environment to America/Los_Angeles, reload the same record and check both values again.
  4. Repeat with a zone east of UTC, such as Asia/Tokyo, and include dates near year boundaries and a leap day.

For an automated integration test, run the save and reload through your real serialization and persistence layers in each relevant test environment. Inspect what travels over the API as well as what appears on screen; a date-only string can still be converted incorrectly by a client.

Existing timestamp data needs care. Before migrating, establish what the stored timestamps meant and which time zone was used when the original dates were converted. A timestamp alone may not reliably reveal the intended birthday; don't apply a blanket conversion without checking the data and assumptions.

A birthday isn't the only date-only value: a due date or anniversary may be one too. Scheduled meetings and payment events, on the other hand, represent moments and need appropriate time-zone handling. Choose the representation based on what the value means.

References

  • Java LocalDate
  • Java Instant
  • PostgreSQL date and time types
  • Android Java API desugaring

Disclosure: AI assisted with drafting this article. The example is illustrative.

title: Node.js Audio Transcriptions 503 — Portable Fallback Boundaries for Marketplace Moderation
description:
Short answer: treat 503 Service Unavailable and model available: false as two different facts, then make the fallback decision from a capability registry rather than from the HTTP status alone. In a marketplace moderation pipeline, the durable boundary is a provider-neutral transcription request and a stored result envelope; the provider adapter owns readiness checks, timeout policy, and translation of errors.

This is a boundary problem before it is a client-library problem.

That separation matters because an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/transcriptions route can be reachable while the selected transcription model is not ready for that request. Retrying the same route blindly turns a temporary readiness signal into queue pressure. A fallback that changes providers without recording why also makes moderation audits difficult.

The decision rule I would put in the architecture record is narrow: retry a request only when the adapter can identify a transient condition and the operation is safe to repeat; use another provider only when its capability, region, audio constraints, and data policy have already been verified; otherwise keep the report pending for human review. No silent downgrade.

What does “model available: false” actually mean?

It is a readiness result, not a diagnosis of the whole service. The route may accept authentication and parse the multipart request while the model pool, deployment, or capacity allocation behind it cannot serve the requested operation. A 503 is likewise a service-availability response, not proof that the audio is malformed. RFC 9110 defines 503 as a temporary inability to handle the request and permits a Retry-After indication, but the client still has to decide whether repeating the operation is appropriate.

For moderation, I separate four states in storage: accepted, transcribing, waiting, and failed_permanently. waiting carries a reason such as provider_model_unavailable; it does not pretend that the transcript is empty. The distinction is operationally small and legally useful. An empty transcript can look like a user submitted no speech, while a waiting record says the system has not reached a conclusion.

The same request can fail at several boundaries:

Boundary Observable signal Correct interpretation Next action
Client validation 4xx before provider work File, auth, or request contract needs correction Do not retry unchanged
Route availability 503 or timeout before a result Provider may be temporarily unable to serve Apply bounded retry policy
Model readiness available: false, unavailable deployment, or capacity response This model cannot serve now Consult capability registry, then fallback or wait
Content result Successful response with low confidence or empty text A transcription exists but may need review Store provenance and use moderation policy

The table is deliberately boring. Boring boundaries survive incidents.

That is intentional.

How should a Node.js-compatible audio transcription client handle a 503 fallback?

The adapter should return a normalized outcome, not leak one provider's error vocabulary into the moderation service. The example below keeps the critical path explicit. It uses Python because the policy is easier to inspect as a small decision function; the same state transitions can sit behind a Node.js client.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Outcome = Literal["transcript", "retry", "fallback", "wait", "reject"]

@dataclass
class Attempt:
    http_status: int | None
    model_available: bool | None
    retry_after_seconds: int | None
    request_replayable: bool
    audio_validated: bool

def decide(attempt: Attempt, attempts_used: int, fallback_ready: bool) -> Outcome:
    if not attempt.audio_validated:
        return "reject"
    if attempt.http_status == 200 and attempt.model_available is not False:
        return "transcript"
    if attempt.http_status == 503 and attempt.request_replayable and attempts_used < 2:
        return "retry"
    if attempt.model_available is False and fallback_ready:
        return "fallback"
    if attempt.http_status == 503 or attempt.model_available is False:
        return "wait"
    return "reject"

The limit of two attempts here is a policy example, not a universal number. It makes the boundary visible so it can be reviewed against queue depth, audio length, and the moderation service-level objective. A real worker should honor a valid Retry-After, add jitter, and cap total elapsed time. It should also persist an idempotency key or a stable report-attempt identifier before sending audio, because a timeout leaves the client uncertain about whether the provider completed the work.

There is a real trade-off here: a shorter deadline protects the queue but increases pending reviews, while a longer deadline improves completion probability but holds worker capacity behind one unavailable model. The right value depends on the moderation service-level objective and the cost of delaying a human decision; it is not a property of a compatibility route. Keep it explicit.

The long tail matters more than the happy path in this workflow. A report can arrive with an audio object that is valid, a provider route that is reachable, a readiness probe that passed 90 seconds ago, and a model that becomes unavailable while the worker is sending bytes. The worker therefore needs a durable transition for uncertainty, a retry budget tied to elapsed time rather than only attempt count, and a policy check before it sends the same object to a second destination. Those details are less attractive in a demo than a one-line fallback chain, but they are the difference between a recoverable delay and an untraceable moderation decision.

A Node.js implementation should use an AbortSignal for the request deadline, classify the response body without assuming every provider emits the same JSON fields, and record the adapter name separately from the model identifier. Do not turn an arbitrary fetch exception into a fallback. DNS failure, local cancellation, invalid credentials, and a provider-side 503 have different owners and different recovery paths.

Which fallback preserves provider portability?

Portability is not the ability to swap one URL for another. It is the ability to preserve the moderation contract while changing the speech engine. That contract should include the source object reference, content hash, language hint, duration if known, transcript text, segment timing when available, provider-neutral status, adapter identity, model identifier, attempt count, and timestamps. Provider-specific response fields can be retained as opaque metadata, but they should not be required to decide whether a report enters human review.

The capability registry needs more than a boolean. For each configured adapter, record whether transcription is enabled, accepted audio formats, maximum duration, supported languages, geographic or data-residency constraints, and current readiness with an expiry time. A stale true is not readiness; it is only the last observation. The registry should be advisory, with the live request remaining authoritative.

Option Portability boundary Failure surface Valid use case
Self-hosted Whisper-compatible worker Stable internal adapter and object-storage contract Capacity, model loading, accelerator scheduling Predictable traffic and controlled data handling
Amazon Transcribe adapter Normalized transcript envelope over a managed API Region, quotas, job lifecycle, and service availability Teams accepting asynchronous managed processing
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text adapter Same envelope, with provider-specific feature mapping Supported encoding, quotas, and feature differences Workloads already governed in that cloud
OpenAI audio transcription adapter Same envelope behind an isolated client Provider availability and request contract A separately approved external processing path

These are not interchangeable feature lists. Amazon Transcribe documents batch and streaming workflows; Google documents encoding and recognition configuration; OpenAI documents an audio transcription endpoint. The useful comparison is the boundary each adapter has to absorb, not which row appears most capable. A managed API can reduce local operations work while increasing dependence on its job model, region rules, and data-processing terms. A self-hosted worker can improve control while making capacity and model loading your responsibility.

The rejected option is a single global fallback chain embedded in the moderation handler: call provider A, then B, then C until any text comes back. It looks portable in a diagram and is dangerous in production. It can duplicate billable work, violate residency policy, reorder reports, and conceal a systematic language or audio-format gap. It is valid only for an explicitly non-authoritative enrichment path where duplicates are acceptable, policy permits every destination, and the result is labeled as enrichment rather than evidence.

The limitation is important: this adapter design does not make providers feature-equivalent. It is a poor fit when moderation depends on a provider-specific diarization, vocabulary, or streaming behavior that cannot be represented in the neutral envelope. In that case, keep the specialized path separate and document why portability is being traded away.

Portability has a boundary.

How do we test readiness without making it the product contract?

A readiness probe should be cheap, bounded, and separate from user audio. It can verify credentials, route reachability, a known-small fixture, and the adapter's ability to map a response into the normalized envelope. It cannot prove that a later report will have capacity, the same language coverage, or identical latency. I would expire the probe result quickly and treat a failed probe as a reason to stop sending new work, not as permission to erase queued work.

The test matrix should include a reachable route with model_available: false, a 503 with Retry-After, a timeout after the request was sent, malformed audio, a successful empty transcript, and a provider response that contains fields the adapter does not recognize. For each case, assert the stored state, retry count, audit event, and whether the fallback was allowed. Test the policy, not just the HTTP client.

Observability needs three correlated identifiers: the marketplace report ID, the transcription attempt ID, and the provider request ID when one exists. Metrics should distinguish waiting_provider, fallback_selected, permanent_rejection, and transcript_completed. Log hashes and metadata needed for correlation, not raw user audio or uncontrolled transcript content. A queue dashboard that reports only 503s cannot tell capacity trouble from invalid files; that is a poor dashboard and an even poorer incident signal.

My storage rule is strict: never overwrite the prior attempt when changing providers. Append an attempt record, link the resulting transcript to the successful attempt, and keep the policy decision that allowed the transition. This costs rows. It buys an explanation when a moderator asks why a report was delayed or why two engines produced different text.

The architecture decision

For marketplace moderation, choose an adapter layer with a provider-neutral result envelope, an expiring capability registry, bounded retries, and an explicit waiting state. Keep the audio object immutable and the attempt history append-only. A 503 may justify a short retry; model available: false should trigger a capability decision; neither should silently become a blank transcript.

That architecture leaves room for three provider adapters, a self-hosted worker, or a later engine change without moving provider assumptions into moderation policy. It also accepts an uncomfortable truth: sometimes the correct fallback is no transcription yet. Human review is a controlled state. Pretending otherwise creates a more expensive data-quality problem than the original outage.

References

  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • MDN, 503 Service Unavailable: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/503
  • OpenAI, Audio API reference: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/audio
  • Amazon Transcribe Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/what-is-transcribe.html
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation: https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text/docs

title: Low-Latency LLM Chat Streaming — First-Token Tradeoffs for Healthtech Catalog Enrichment
description:
A catalog chatbot should optimize for the first useful token, but the platform decision should optimize for the next provider migration. For the stated comparison, GPT-4o-mini is the leading interactive choice at roughly 200 ms time to first token, with streaming enabled; Claude Haiku is a credible alternative at roughly 300 ms when its speed-and-quality balance fits the evaluation better. Put either behind an adapter, count the prompt before dispatch, and keep the chat event format independent of the provider.

Short answer: use a small streaming model for the user-facing turn, make prompt length visible, and treat provider portability as an operational contract. The answer changes if the SLO is about completed answers, tool calls, or clinical review instead of perceived responsiveness.

The incident lesson is a boundary, not a model ranking

The bounded production scenario is a product-catalog enrichment chat: a merchandiser pastes a supplier description such as "sterile polymer tubing, 3/8 in, non-DEHP", and the assistant proposes normalized attributes for search and review. A slow blank screen makes the workflow feel broken even when the final answer is accurate, so the first SLO should cover streaming TTFT, followed by completion latency and an explicit human-review path for uncertain fields.

The decision is not a permanent ranking. It is a boundary choice. A smaller model generally streams faster, but prompt size, network distance, and output length still affect the result. Measure TTFT with the same region and prompt shape before changing the model, then keep a fallback whose output can be rendered by the same chat UI.

The invariant is simple: the UI may depend on a stream, but the rest of the system must depend on an adapter. If a provider changes its request format, the catalog workflow should not.

Measure the seam.

How should an LLM streaming chat handle low latency?

The comparison needs a clear boundary. GPT-4o-mini is the leading choice for this narrow goal: the supplied comparison puts it near 200 ms TTFT and identifies it as the fastest streaming option for chat interfaces. Claude Haiku is around 300 ms TTFT, a reasonable trade when speed and answer quality need a different balance. Cohere Rerank is useful for ordering retrieved catalog candidates, but it is not a replacement for a conversational generation model; putting it in the same latency race would be a category error.

Option What it contributes here Boundary to keep visible
GPT-4o-mini Fastest stated streaming path, about 200 ms TTFT Validate extraction quality on the catalog vocabulary
Claude Haiku About 300 ms TTFT with a speed-and-quality balance A slower first token may be acceptable under a quality-first SLO
Cohere Rerank Candidate ordering after retrieval Reranking does not generate the chat response

The practical choice is therefore not “which vendor wins forever?” It is “which adapter meets the interactive SLO while preserving an exit path?” A provider-neutral service can run GPT-4o-mini today, expose the same internal event stream for Haiku tomorrow, and use reranking only where retrieval needs it. That is portability with a testable interface, not a claim that all models are interchangeable.

What does the preventative path look like in Go?

The request below uses the OpenAI-compatible chat surface, sends an explicit method, streams the response, and honors Retry-After on rate limits. The model and base URL are supplied through environment variables so the adapter can switch models or providers without changing the request path. The credential is also read from the environment.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type chatEvent struct {
    Choices []struct {
        Delta struct {
            Content string `json:"content"`
        } `json:"delta"`
    } `json:"choices"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    model := os.Getenv("MODEL_ID")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if key == "" || model == "" || baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, and MODEL_ID are required")
    }

    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "model":  model,
        "stream": true,
        "messages": []map[string]string{{
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Normalize attributes from: sterile polymer tubing, 3/8 in, non-DEHP",
        }},
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    resp, err := request(context.Background(), key, baseURL, body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    scanner := bufio.NewScanner(resp.Body)
    for scanner.Scan() {
        line := scanner.Text()
        if !strings.HasPrefix(line, "data: ") || line == "data: [DONE]" {
            continue
        }
        var event chatEvent
        if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "data: ")), &event); err != nil {
            continue
        }
        if len(event.Choices) > 0 {
            fmt.Print(event.Choices[0].Delta.Content)
        }
    }
    if err := scanner.Err(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

func request(ctx context.Context, key, baseURL string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")+"/chat/completions", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            responseBody, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
        }
        return resp, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

This example is intentionally small. A production adapter should finish consuming the stream, associate each emitted event with an internal request record, and record TTFT separately from total completion time. The token-count capability can check prompt length before inference; trimming duplicated supplier text is often a better latency intervention than chasing a different model. That check is especially useful when descriptions contain repeated regulatory or packaging text.

The retry loop is appropriate for the read-like inference request shown here because it does not create a catalog record. If a surrounding workflow writes enrichment results, give that write a client-supplied idempotency key and make the consumer tolerate duplicate delivery; a 24-hour default deduplication window is useful only when the key is stable. I don't treat a chat stream as a substitute for those storage semantics.

Is one backend surface worth the coupling?

For this workflow, the one-key REST shape is a real portability advantage. A service that can send HTTP can call it, so a Go adapter does not acquire an SDK version as a second dependency. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples across 10 languages; that helps a platform team replace a provider without rewriting every application. The second advantage is operational breadth: 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key, so catalog inference and adjacent backend capabilities do not require a new credential for every integration. That reduces the specific friction of rotating secrets, teaching each service a different request convention, and reconciling separate bills. Infrai is a reasonable fit when that unified REST boundary and single credential matter more than choosing specialized services independently.

The alternative stack is concrete: OpenAI for inference, Sentry for error capture, and Datadog for metrics and logs means three legitimate products, three credential sets, and glue code for request correlation, retry semantics, dashboards, and retention. A team may prefer those specialized controls. The combined surface has a cost that should be said plainly: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Portability improves only if the adapter and data export story are tested before an incident.

There are hard boundaries here. Audio transcription is present in the catalog but currently unavailable, voice sessions are pending and limited to the western region, there is no dedicated moderation endpoint, and image upscale is limited to Lanczos. That limitation makes the combined surface a poor fit if the project is primarily voice or audio transcription; use a specialized provider there. For text moderation, the stated fallback is a chat model with json_schema; for this catalog assistant, human review remains the right boundary for consequential normalization.

The decision rule

Choose GPT-4o-mini when the user is waiting for the first token and the roughly 200 ms TTFT target is the dominant SLO. Choose Claude Haiku when its roughly 300 ms first-token profile is acceptable and the speed-quality balance better matches evaluation results. Add Cohere Rerank for retrieval ordering, not generation. Keep all three behind an adapter, count prompts before dispatch, and make telemetry part of the same request path.

That is the useful outcome of the comparison: faster streaming improves the chat experience, but a provider boundary protects the catalog workflow from becoming a model-specific product. The first token gets attention; the evidence trail keeps the decision reversible.

Sources

  • OpenAI, Chat Completions API: https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat
  • Anthropic, Claude models overview: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models
  • Cohere, Rerank overview: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank-overview
  • OpenTelemetry, HTTP semantic conventions: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in Singapore

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

When you set up a connection, self-service modeling will now be available only if a role that grants create_self_service_from_table also selects it through that role's model set.

Fixed

The opacity for the comparison bar in short KPI visualizations has been reduced to increase legibility.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

To help protect your data and provide a baseline level of persistence, RDB snapshots are enabled by default when you create an instance using the Google Cloud console. This feature is generally available.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

General availability support for the following integration:

  • Cloud Storage for Firebase

Feature

VPC Service Controls feature (Status: Preview): Support for automated remediation suggestions is available in the VPC Service Controls violation analyzer.

Remediation suggestions analyze access denial events and generate actionable, narrowly scoped configuration changes to resolve perimeter denials and adhere to the principle of least privilege. The remediation engine can automatically propose ingress rules, egress rules, VPC accessible services updates, and existing or new context-aware access levels.

For more information, see Resolve access denials with remediation suggestions.

Attach Outbound Endpoints to forwarding zones or server policies to enable direct DNS query forwarding from VPC networks to external and on-premises DNS resolvers using private IP addresses. For more information, see Outbound Endpoints overview.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Regular expression matchers in host and route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA).

You can now use regular expressions (regex) matchers to configure more flexible and precise traffic routing rules within URL maps for Application Load Balancers. This feature allows you to leverage the power of RE2 syntax for matching on:

  • URL Paths: Using the regexMatch field within routeRules.
  • HTTP Headers: Using the regexMatch field within headerMatches in routeRules.
  • HTTP Query Parameters: Using the regexMatch field within queryParameterMatches in routeRules.

This feature is available in:

  • Global external Application Load Balancers
  • Regional internal Application Load Balancers
  • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers
  • Regional external Application Load Balancers

For more information, see URL map concepts: Regular expressions matchers in host and route rules.

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

title: Prefetch on intent, not on sight: a <Link> wrapper for Next.js
description:
My portfolio is a 3D map with six destinations. On the home page they sit in a
rail under the scene. On every other page they sit in the header. In both
places they are plain Next.js <Link>s, so the HTML works without JavaScript.

And <Link> prefetches every route as soon as it enters the viewport. Six
links that are always visible means six routes prefetched on every page,
always.

The symptom

I measured it on next start, on the home page. 2.1 seconds after opening it,
the browser had asked for the RSC payload of all six pages: 565 KB. That
payload carries whatever those pages declare with preload: the sky and eight
photos of the About page, the Projects room, the Experiments window, plus four
stylesheets from other pages. In total, 1.3 MB of other pages, requested
before the 872 KB three.js chunk that draws the scene the visitor is actually
looking at.

The console was the second symptom. Chrome prints "preloaded but not used" for
every preload nobody consumes. I counted 1,830 of those warnings across 174 page
loads.

Why the obvious fix didn't work

The obvious fix is "prefetch later". Wait until the scene is drawing, or six
seconds after the browser goes idle, then prefetch the six routes in the
background. The bandwidth fight goes away.

The warnings didn't. React applies the preload hints from the RSC payload as
soon as it receives it, and Chrome warns about every preload that isn't used,
no matter when it was requested. With the deferred prefetch I still got 14
warnings on the home page and 19 on the Education page.

So the question changed. Not when to prefetch six routes, but which route
the visitor is about to open. A preload is only "used" if a navigation follows.

What I did

Every <Link> on the site goes through one wrapper, IntentLink. It turns off
viewport prefetch and prefetches when you point at the link, focus it or touch
it. Every file imports it under the old name, so call sites didn't change:

import { IntentLink as Link } from "@/components/intent-link";

pointerenter also fires on touch screens, before click, so phones go
through the same path. And it stays progressive enhancement: the <a href>
navigates the same without JavaScript.

The code

The wrapper, trimmed from components/intent-link.tsx:

export function IntentLink({ href, onPointerEnter, onFocus, children, ...rest }: ComponentProps<typeof Link>) {
  const prefetch = usePrefetchOnIntent();
  const target = typeof href === "string" ? href : null;
  return (
    <Link
      href={href}
      prefetch={false}
      onPointerEnter={(event) => {
        if (target) prefetch(target);
        onPointerEnter?.(event);
      }}
      onFocus={(event) => {
        if (target) prefetch(target);
        onFocus?.(event);
      }}
      {...rest}
    >
      {children}
      <RoutePending />
    </Link>
  );
}

And the hook, from lib/world-prefetch.ts:

const INTENT_DWELL_MS = 160;

function stillIntended(href: string): boolean {
  for (const link of document.querySelectorAll("a:hover, a:focus")) {
    if (link.getAttribute("href") === href) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

export function usePrefetchOnIntent() {
  const router = useRouter();
  return useCallback(
    (href: string) => {
      window.setTimeout(() => {
        if (stillIntended(href)) router.prefetch(href);
      }, INTENT_DWELL_MS);
    },
    [router],
  );
}

There is no timer to cancel on pointerleave. After 160 ms the hook just asks
the DOM whether that link is still hovered or focused. If the cursor already
left, nothing happens.

My own mistake: hovering is not intent

The first version prefetched on the first pointerenter. It looked right on a
fast connection. On a slow one it made things worse.

The black hole sits in the center of the home page. A cursor crossing the map
toward another planet almost always passes over it. Each pass prefetched the
About page with its preloads: the sky and seven photos, about 390 KB. Then the
visitor clicked Contact, and Contact had to share the network with photos
nobody wanted. With DevTools' "Slow 4G" applied, Contact arrived 2.9 seconds
after the transition's flash had already faded.

That's why the 160 ms dwell exists. Intent is staying, not passing over. The
unit test says it in one line:

it("pasar por encima de camino a otro sitio no precarga", () => {
  render(<IntentLink href="/es/sobre-mi">Sobre mí</IntentLink>);
  fireEvent.pointerEnter(screen.getByRole("link"));
  act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTime(500));
  expect(useRouter().prefetch).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});

(The test names are in Spanish; it reads "passing over on the way somewhere
else doesn't prefetch".)

The click doesn't depend on any of this. A <Link> requests its route when you
press it, and on the map the 2.6-second transition prefetches the route at
takeoff.

The trap: a click that changes nothing

Turning prefetch off has a cost you only see on a slow network. A header click
to a page that wasn't prefetched changed nothing on screen for one to three
seconds. It read as a frozen site.

That's the <RoutePending /> in the wrapper. It uses useLinkStatus from
next/link and publishes a flag on <html> while the clicked page is pending:

function RoutePending() {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!pending) return;
    const root = document.documentElement;
    root.dataset.routePending = "true";
    return () => {
      delete root.dataset.routePending;
    };
  }, [pending]);
  return null;
}

CSS turns that flag into a thin progress line at the top, with a 250 ms delay,
so a fast navigation never shows it. The component renders nothing inside the
link: no text, no box. A test checks that the link has zero child elements.

What isn't solved

  • A tap navigates before 160 ms, so on phones the prefetch almost never fires. The route is requested on click. It's correct, but touch doesn't get the head start a mouse gets.
  • stillIntended compares the href attribute as a string. A link built from a UrlObject gets target = null and simply never prefetches.
  • The first trip from the home page still downloads the client chunk of the six worlds (about 50 KB compressed) only when you navigate, because the RSC prefetch doesn't request it. I left it on purpose. It's a candidate.

Over to you

160 ms is a number I picked to separate "passing over" from "staying", and it
fixed the slow-network case I measured. I haven't tested it against real
visitors' cursors. How do you decide when a hover means a click is coming? A
fixed dwell, cursor velocity, something else?

You can try the map, and watch the network tab while you move over the
planets, at jonasjavier.dev.

I'm Jonás Javier Encarnación, a full-stack developer in Santo Domingo,
Dominican Republic. I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant; the code,
the bug and the decisions are from my project.
