title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): An Investigation into Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2 and Its Application in Modern Computing
description:
Author: Nweibong Emmanuel Praise
Category: Cloud Computing
Case Study: Amazon Web Services – Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2)

Abstract

The increasing demand for digital services has made traditional computing infrastructure increasingly challenging for some organizations to maintain. Businesses, universities and other institutions require computing resources that can support their applications, store information and accommodate changes in user demand. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provides an alternative by allowing organizations to access computing resources through cloud service providers without having to purchase and maintain all the physical equipment themselves.

This article examines Infrastructure as a Service, focusing on Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) as a case study. It investigates the architecture, operation, major components, benefits and limitations of EC2. It also examines how the service could be applied in hosting a university student management portal.

  1. Introduction

Computing infrastructure plays an important role in the operation of modern organizations. Almost every institution that provides digital services depends on servers, storage systems, networking equipment and software platforms.

In the past, organizations generally had to acquire their own physical servers and establish server rooms or data centres before deploying applications. Apart from the initial cost of purchasing equipment, they also had to consider electricity, cooling, maintenance, security and the availability of qualified technical personnel.

These requirements can become difficult to manage, especially for small organizations and institutions with limited financial resources.

Cloud computing has introduced a different approach to managing these resources. Instead of purchasing all the required hardware, organizations can obtain computing resources from providers over the internet.

One of the service models responsible for this development is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). It provides access to virtual computing infrastructure while allowing customers to manage their operating systems, applications and other configurations.

To understand how this model works in a practical environment, this research uses Amazon EC2 as a case study.

  1. Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing service model in which a provider makes computing resources available to customers over the internet.

These resources typically include:

  • Virtual machines and processing power.
  • Storage systems.
  • Networking infrastructure.
  • IP addresses and network configurations.
  • Virtualized computing environments.

The major idea behind IaaS is that organizations can use computing infrastructure without necessarily owning the physical hardware.

For instance, consider a university that wants to develop an online platform for managing student records. Rather than purchasing a physical server, the university can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and install the necessary software.

The university manages the operating system, application and database configurations, while the provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), cloud computing provides convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort.

This definition helps explain why IaaS has become an important approach to delivering computing infrastructure.

  1. Technical Operation of IaaS

IaaS relies heavily on virtualization and resource management technologies.

Virtualization allows a physical server to provide multiple independent virtual computing environments. Each virtual machine receives allocated resources such as processor capacity, memory and storage.

A customer can configure these resources based on the requirements of the application being deployed.

The general operation involves the following stages:

Resource provisioning: The customer requests computing resources through the provider's management interface.

Virtual machine creation: The provider allocates resources and creates a virtual server using a selected machine image.

Configuration: The customer installs and configures the operating system, applications and other required software.

Deployment: The application is uploaded and made accessible through the network.

Monitoring and scaling: Resource usage is monitored, and additional capacity can be provisioned when necessary.

This arrangement gives customers control over their computing environments without requiring them to manage the physical servers.

  1. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elastic Compute Cloud

Amazon Web Services is a cloud computing platform that provides infrastructure and other computing services to individuals and organizations.

One of its major infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides on-demand computing capacity through virtual servers known as instances. These instances can be configured to run different operating systems and applications depending on the customer's requirements.

An organization can launch an instance, connect to it remotely, install its software and use it to host services.

4.1 Major Components of Amazon EC2

To understand EC2 as an IaaS solution, it is important to examine some of its major components.

a. EC2 Instances

An instance is a virtual server running within AWS infrastructure. Different instance types provide different combinations of processing power, memory, storage and networking capacity.

For example, a small web application may require fewer computing resources than a large enterprise application.

b. Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)

An Amazon Machine Image is a template used to launch EC2 instances. It contains information required to configure the instance, including an operating system and potentially preinstalled software.

This makes it easier to create servers without manually installing everything from the beginning.

c. Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS)

EBS provides persistent block storage that can be attached to EC2 instances. It is useful for storing operating system files, application data and other information that must remain available beyond the lifetime of an individual instance session.

d. Security Groups

Security groups function as virtual firewalls for EC2 instances. They control incoming and outgoing network traffic through configured rules.

For example, an administrator can allow web traffic through HTTP and HTTPS while restricting remote administrative access to approved IP addresses.

e. Regions and Availability Zones

AWS organizes its infrastructure into geographical Regions and Availability Zones.

Regions represent separate geographical areas, while Availability Zones are isolated locations within a Region.

Deploying application resources across multiple Availability Zones can help reduce the effect of an individual location failure.

These components demonstrate that EC2 provides more than just a virtual computer. It provides a configurable infrastructure environment for deploying and managing applications.

  1. Practical Application: Hosting a University Student Management System

To examine the practical usefulness of IaaS, consider a university that wants to deploy a student management system.

The proposed system will allow students to:

  • Log in to their personal accounts.
  • Register for courses.
  • Check examination results.
  • Download learning materials.
  • Receive announcements.
  • View academic information.

Lecturers will also be able to manage courses, record attendance and upload students' grades.

The university needs a server capable of running the application and handling requests from different users.

Proposed AWS EC2 Implementation

Stage 1: Provisioning the server

The university creates an AWS account and launches an EC2 instance.

Ubuntu Linux can be selected as the operating system because it supports the software technologies required by the application.

Stage 2: Installing the application environment

The administrator installs the necessary technologies, such as:

  • Python programming language.
  • Django web framework.
  • Nginx web server.
  • PostgreSQL database system.

Stage 3: Deploying the application

The student management system is uploaded to the EC2 instance and configured to run as a web application.

Stage 4: Configuring network access

The administrator configures the instance's security group to permit the required web traffic.

Administrative access, such as SSH, should be restricted to authorized IP addresses rather than exposed unnecessarily.

Stage 5: Connecting the database

The application is connected to a database where student records, courses, examination results and other academic information are stored.

For a more reliable production environment, the database can be hosted separately using a managed database service.

Stage 6: Monitoring performance

The university monitors the server's resource consumption and application performance.

If the number of users increases significantly during course registration or examination periods, additional computing capacity can be introduced.

This example demonstrates how an educational institution can use IaaS to deploy a real application without purchasing its own physical server infrastructure.

  1. Proposed System Architecture

The following architecture illustrates how the student management system could be deployed using AWS EC2.

   STUDENTS / LECTURERS
            |
            |
         INTERNET
            |
            |
      AWS CLOUD
            |
            |
      EC2 INSTANCE
            |
      NGINX SERVER
            |
            |
     DJANGO APPLICATION
            |
            |
      DATABASE SERVER
            |
            |
     ACADEMIC RECORDS

The architecture separates the different responsibilities of the system.

  • Users interact with the application through their web browsers.
  • AWS provides the cloud infrastructure.
  • EC2 provides the virtual computing environment.
  • Nginx handles incoming web requests.
  • Django processes application requests and business logic.
  • The database stores and retrieves academic information.

This is a proposed deployment architecture, not a report of an actual university system already running on AWS.

  1. Analysis of the Benefits of IaaS

The use of IaaS offers several advantages when compared with traditional infrastructure management.

7.1 Reduced Initial Investment

Organizations do not necessarily need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

Instead, they can obtain computing resources and pay according to the selected pricing arrangement.

7.2 Resource Scalability

One major advantage of EC2 is the ability to change computing capacity when application requirements change.

A university may initially use a small server but increase its capacity when more students begin accessing the portal.

AWS also provides Auto Scaling to help automatically adjust the number of instances based on configured conditions.

7.3 Greater Flexibility

Customers can select operating systems, instance types, storage configurations and networking arrangements according to their requirements.

This is particularly useful for developers who need different environments for testing and production.

7.4 Faster Deployment

Creating a virtual server can be faster than acquiring and installing physical hardware.

This allows organizations to develop and deploy applications without waiting for physical infrastructure procurement.

7.5 Geographical Availability

AWS provides infrastructure across different geographical Regions and Availability Zones.

Organizations can select suitable deployment locations and design systems that distribute resources across multiple locations.

  1. Limitations and Challenges of IaaS

Although IaaS provides important advantages, it is not without limitations.

8.1 Security Responsibilities

Using a cloud provider does not mean that the customer has no security responsibilities.

AWS protects the underlying physical infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

This is known as the shared responsibility model.

8.2 Dependence on Internet Connectivity

Applications hosted in the cloud generally require internet connectivity to be accessed remotely.

In areas where connectivity is unreliable, users may experience difficulties accessing cloud-hosted applications.

This is an important consideration for organizations operating in regions where internet infrastructure is still developing.

8.3 Cost Management

Although IaaS can reduce initial infrastructure investment, operating costs can increase if resources are not properly managed.

Running unnecessary instances, storing unused data and transferring large volumes of information may result in additional charges.

Organizations therefore need to monitor their resource consumption.

8.4 Technical Expertise

Managing an IaaS environment requires knowledge of operating systems, networking, server administration and security.

An organization without qualified technical personnel may find it difficult to configure and maintain its infrastructure properly.

8.5 Service Availability

Cloud providers design their infrastructure for availability, but service interruptions can still occur.

Organizations should therefore consider backup arrangements, monitoring and recovery strategies when deploying important applications.

  1. Security and Management Considerations

Security is an important part of any IaaS deployment, particularly when applications contain sensitive information such as student records.

For an EC2-based student management system, the following measures should be considered:

  1. Use strong authentication and protect administrative credentials.
  2. Restrict SSH access to authorized users.
  3. Configure security groups to allow only necessary network traffic.
  4. Regularly update the operating system and installed software.
  5. Implement appropriate database access controls.
  6. Encrypt sensitive information where necessary.
  7. Maintain regular backups.
  8. Monitor system activities and resource usage.

These measures help reduce the risk of unauthorized access, data loss and service disruption.

  1. Comparison of IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

Cloud computing is commonly divided into three service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

Feature| IaaS| PaaS| SaaS
Full meaning| Infrastructure as a Service| Platform as a Service| Software as a Service
Main provision| Computing infrastructure| Application development platform| Ready-to-use software
User control| High| Moderate| Limited
User manages| OS, applications and data| Applications and data| Mainly usage and data
Example| Amazon EC2| Google App Engine| Gmail

The main difference between these models is the level of management and control given to the customer.

IaaS provides greater control over the underlying computing environment, while PaaS reduces infrastructure management responsibilities for developers. SaaS provides complete applications that users can access without managing the underlying infrastructure.

  1. Other Providers of Infrastructure as a Service

Amazon EC2 is not the only available IaaS solution. Other major providers include:

Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines: Provides configurable virtual machines for running applications and operating systems.

Google Cloud Compute Engine: Offers virtual machines and computing resources through Google Cloud.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure: Provides computing, storage and networking resources for different workloads.

DigitalOcean Droplets: Provides virtual private servers commonly used by developers and small businesses.

Although these providers offer similar infrastructure capabilities, their pricing structures, available resources and management tools differ.

  1. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has changed how organizations acquire and manage computing resources. Rather than depending entirely on physical infrastructure, organizations can obtain virtual servers, storage and networking resources from cloud providers.

The examination of Amazon EC2 shows how IaaS can be used to create flexible computing environments for hosting applications. The proposed university student management system demonstrates how an institution can deploy its services, manage academic information and adjust computing resources according to user demand.

However, adopting IaaS requires careful consideration of security, internet connectivity, technical expertise and operational costs.

In conclusion, IaaS is a valuable approach to modern infrastructure management. Its usefulness depends not only on the capabilities of the cloud provider but also on how effectively the organization plans, configures and manages the resources it uses.

description:
As modern organizations scale, legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems frequently become bottlenecks. Rigid architectures, sluggish batch processing, and siloed data stores restrict organizational agility. For engineering leaders and CTOs, evaluating custom erp software development becomes an operational necessity rather than a mere technical upgrade.

Migrating away from legacy infrastructure requires more than simple code rewriting. It demands a deliberate strategy focused on maintainability, scalability, and performance. This guide explores how to design a robust nodejs erp architecture that modernizes legacy systems while future-proofing your enterprise operations.

The Engineering Imperative: Why Modernize Legacy ERPs?

Legacy platforms—often built on aging monolithic frameworks—suffer from technical debt, brittle codebase integrations, and massive server overhead. Maintenance costs rise exponentially while developer velocity plummets.

Transitioning to a modern ecosystem enables enterprise workflow automation software capabilities, unlocking real-time data streaming, event-driven microservices, and reactive user experiences. Utilizing a JavaScript and TypeScript-powered backend allows engineering teams to unify their tech stack across both frontend and backend domains.

Core Pain Points of Legacy Monoliths

  • Scaling Bottlenecks: Monolithic codebases scale vertically rather than horizontally, driving up cloud infrastructure expenditures.
  • Integration Friction: Connecting third-party APIs or mobile clients requires complex middleware and heavy SOAP/XML parsers.
  • Deployment Risk: A bug in a minor reporting module can destabilize core inventory or financial ledger pipelines.

Strategic Architecture for Node.js ERP Migration

A successful legacy system migration to nodejs relies heavily on an API-first design and decoupled services. When mapping out your new system architecture, consider the following structural layers:

  1. API Gateway Layer: Manages authentication, rate limiting, and request routing to downstream microservices.
  2. Business Logic Core (Node.js/TypeScript): Handles domain models, ERP workflows, transactional integrity, and event emitters.
  3. Data Access Layer: Utilizes modern ORMs or query builders with robust connection pooling to manage relational and NoSQL data stores.

Architectural Tradeoff Analysis

Architectural Approach Pros Cons Best Suited For
Monolithic Node.js App Simple initial setup, fast local debugging Harder to scale specific high-load modules Small to mid-sized businesses with predictable loads
Modular Monolith Clear internal boundaries, easy refactoring Requires strict code discipline over time Growing enterprises transitioning away from legacy
Event-Driven Microservices Extreme scalability, fault isolation Complex orchestration, distributed tracing overhead Large enterprises with high concurrency and diverse data streams

Executing the Migration: A Step-by-Step Blueprint

Transitioning mission-critical data requires a calculated, risk-mitigated approach. Following structured methodologies similar to those outlined in our Next.js and TypeScript Enterprise Migration: A Zero-Downtime Blueprint ensures business continuity.

1. Database Refactoring and Schema Mapping

Legacy databases are often bloated with dead tables, unindexed columns, and circular dependencies. Prior to writing backend migration scripts, audit your data structures:

  • Normalize normalized schemas where necessary while keeping performance-critical denormalization intact.
  • Implement dual-writing strategies during the transition phase to ensure data parity between old and new systems.

2. Implementing Bespoke Business Systems Integration

An enterprise ERP never operates in a vacuum. It must communicate with CRM platforms, payment gateways, and custom-facing applications. Leveraging modern Custom Software Development practices ensures your custom ERP communicates cleanly via REST and GraphQL endpoints.

For businesses requiring customer-facing portals or internal operational tools, a unified API layer allows seamless extension into Website Development Services and mobile platforms without duplicating business logic.

3. Leveraging TypeScript for Enterprise Reliability

While vanilla JavaScript offers rapid prototyping, enterprise-grade ERP systems demand strict type safety. Migrating legacy code to TypeScript eliminates runtime errors related to undefined object properties, ensures safer database queries, and vastly improves IDE autocompletion for large engineering teams.

Measuring ROI on Custom ERP Development

Investing in a bespoke Node.js ERP yields measurable financial and operational returns:

  • Reduced Infrastructure Costs: Horizontal scaling on containerized Node.js environments often reduces cloud computing bills by 30-40% compared to legacy virtual machines.
  • Increased Developer Velocity: Unified language stacks eliminate context-switching friction for full-stack engineering teams.
  • Operational Efficiency: Automated workflows reduce manual data entry errors and accelerate inventory turnover.

Conclusion & Next Steps

Migrating legacy business systems to a custom Node.js ERP is a transformative journey that redefines enterprise efficiency, scalability, and agility. By prioritizing modular architecture, database refactoring, and clean API design, your organization can break free from legacy constraints.

title: Batch Insert In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

Using JooqTemplate

Inserting Multiple Records with List

Pass a List<Map<String,Object>> to insert multiple records at once; the return value is the number of inserted records:

List<Map<String, Object>> productList = new ArrayList<>();

Map<String, Object> p1 = new HashMap<>();
p1.put("name", "Wireless Mouse");
p1.put("category", "Electronics");
p1.put("price", 129.00);
productList.add(p1);

Map<String, Object> p2 = new HashMap<>();
p2.put("name", "Mechanical Keyboard");
p2.put("category", "Electronics");
p2.put("price", 399.00);
productList.add(p2);

Map<String, Object> p3 = new HashMap<>();
p3.put("name", "Monitor Stand");
p3.put("category", "Office Supplies");
p3.put("price", 199.00);
productList.add(p3);

int result = jt.insert("product", productList);
// result == 3; 3 records inserted

Inserting a List with a Single Record

When the List contains only 1 Map, it inserts 1 record and returns 1:

List<Map<String, Object>> orderList = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, Object> order = new HashMap<>();
order.put("order_no", "A20260001");
order.put("amount", 258.00);
orderList.add(order);

int result = jt.insert("order", orderList);
// result == 1

Using a jOOQ Table Object

The first argument can also be a jOOQ Table object built with DSL.table(...); the effect is the same as passing the table name string:

Table<?> productTable = DSL.table("product");
int result = jt.insert(productTable, productList);
// result == 3

Inserting in Batches with a Specified batchSize

insert(table, list, batchSize) commits in batches according to batchSize. With 5 records and batchSize=2, it splits into 3 batches (2+2+1), and all records are inserted successfully:

int result = jt.insert("product", productList, 2);
// result == 5 (all 5 records inserted in batches)

// batchSize equals the list size: all inserted in one batch
int result2 = jt.insert("product", productList, productList.size());

// batchSize greater than the list size: still inserted only once, without affecting the result
int result3 = jt.insert("product", productList, 10);

The Table object version also supports batchSize:

int result = jt.insert(productTable, productList, 2);

Edge Cases

Behaviors verified by unit tests:

  • Empty List: no records inserted, returns 0: 
int result = jt.insert("product", new ArrayList<>());
// result == 0
  • null List: throws NullPointerException / IllegalArgumentException.
  • batchSize of 0 or negative: no error; inserts normally.
  • Nonexistent table name: throws an exception whose message contains the table name.

title: Go Recurring HTTP Data Cleanup Triggers: A Method Beyond Private Task Executors
description:
A recurring cleanup trigger is easiest to reason about when the scheduler owns time and your public HTTP endpoint owns one bounded operation. For a healthtech shipment service, that means a cron request can remove expired delivery records, record an idempotency key, and return quickly; it should not become a disguised task executor.

The practical choice is an HTTP cron schedule for periodic cleanup, with a queue and worker only when the cleanup can exceed the scheduler's 900-second execution limit. Keep the shipment notification fan-out separate from deletion: publish one durable message per subscriber, let the delivery path use a realtime channel when the recipient is connected, and make every consumer safe to run twice.

The trigger should stay small.

Infrai fits this narrow handoff when a team wants the cron, queue, and realtime surfaces behind one REST API and one key. Its public discovery surface exposes capability schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key, so the integration contract can be inspected before the first credential is issued. That reduces a different kind of friction: a Go service can use plain HTTP and a consistent contract rather than installing a separate SDK for each backend function.

Keep it boring.

The benefit is breadth behind a simple surface, not a promise that one provider removes compliance work. A shipment service can add a scheduled trigger and a durable notification handoff using the same base URL, while region, retention, deletion, and processor terms remain explicit review items.

How should a recurring HTTP data cleanup trigger work?

The scheduler owns recurrence. It does not own your database transaction, private network, or long-running worker process. That distinction is the useful design boundary.

Suppose a shipment service retains delivery attempts for a fixed policy period. The cron target receives a request, selects records that are eligible for cleanup, commits a bounded batch, and returns a result that is useful for an audit record. A second run must be harmless if the first response was lost. The cleanup key can be derived from the schedule identity and its intended time bucket, while the database still enforces uniqueness on each deletion or tombstone operation.

This is the part I would make explicit in a design review: at-least-once delivery is a transport property, not an accounting guarantee. A timeout after commit looks the same to the caller as a timeout before commit. Idempotency belongs at the write boundary, and the audit trail should preserve the request identifier, selected count, committed count, and policy version.

A cron task that calls a public http_url is therefore a good fit for periodic cleanup, provided the endpoint is reachable from the public internet and the work stays under 900 seconds. It does not host code for you. It cannot reach an internal-only endpoint, and a paused schedule does not backfill missed triggers. Those are trust-boundary decisions, not minor configuration details.

Why does a shipment fan-out need two delivery paths?

Cleanup and notification have different failure shapes. A cleanup job can be retried against the same time window. A shipment update needs to survive a disconnected recipient, then reach that recipient through a live socket or another delivery attempt later. Treating both as one synchronous HTTP action makes the timeout boundary responsible for business correctness.

The handoff is easier to audit when the message has a stable event identifier. The queue record contains the shipment update and the subscriber identity; the realtime publish receives that same identifier after the consumer has established its delivery decision. If the consumer is retried, it checks its delivery ledger before publishing again. If a socket is unavailable, the message remains a queue item rather than becoming a lost publish.

The following Go example keeps both calls on one base URL and uses one bearer key. It intentionally leaves the request body to the capability schema discovered at deployment time; the routes are real, while business payload fields are owned by the receiving contract. The important code path is the handoff: the event is submitted to the queue, then the same event is passed to the realtime publisher after the consumer's delivery decision.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type ShipmentEvent struct {
    EventID string `json:"event_id"`
    ShipmentID string `json:"shipment_id"`
    Subscriber string `json:"subscriber"`
    Payload json.RawMessage `json:"payload"`
}

func post(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL, key, path string, body []byte, idem string) error {
    target := path
    if !strings.HasPrefix(path, "http://") && !strings.HasPrefix(path, "https://") { target = baseURL + path }
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, target, bytesReader(body))
    if err != nil { return err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after the server-provided delay")
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        b, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, b)
    }
    return nil
}

func deliver(ctx context.Context, event ShipmentEvent) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    body, err := json.Marshal(event)
    if err != nil { return err }
    return post(ctx, http.DefaultClient, baseURL, key, "/realtime/publish", body, "shipment-"+event.EventID)
}

func enqueue(ctx context.Context, event ShipmentEvent) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    body, err := json.Marshal(event)
    if err != nil { return err }
    return post(ctx, http.DefaultClient, baseURL, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", body, "queue-"+event.EventID)
}

func bytesReader(body []byte) io.Reader { return &reader{body: body} }
type reader struct { body []byte }
func (r *reader) Read(p []byte) (int, error) {
    if len(r.body) == 0 { return 0, io.EOF }
    n := copy(p, r.body); r.body = r.body[n:]; return n, nil
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    event := ShipmentEvent{EventID: "shipment-event-2026-10-28-001", ShipmentID: "s-1842", Subscriber: "clinic-7", Payload: json.RawMessage(`{"status":"in_transit"}`)}
    if err := enqueue(ctx, event); err != nil { panic(err) }
    if err := deliver(ctx, event); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

In production, the queue consumer supplies event after claiming a message; the consumer must acknowledge it only after the delivery ledger and publish decision are durable. The example's idempotency header is illustrative of the platform convention, but its value must be derived from the event identity and operation, not from a random request. A real retry loop should honor Retry-After on HTTP 429 and use exponential backoff.

The same architecture can use a cron trigger to enqueue work when a cleanup scan is longer than 900 seconds. Delayed messages cannot exceed 604800 seconds, message bodies cannot exceed 256 KB, and retention tops out at 30 days. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker still needs an idempotency record. FIFO deduplication covers only a five-minute window; it is not a substitute for a durable business key.

Which competing design fits the boundary?

There is no universally best scheduler here. The right comparison is about ownership of execution and data movement.

Option Good fit Boundary or cost
Google Cloud Scheduler Recurring authenticated HTTP calls into a Google-hosted service The endpoint, authentication policy, and downstream queue remain your responsibility; the design is most natural inside Google Cloud
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler AWS-centered schedules with AWS targets and broader event routing It is a stronger choice when AWS identity, regional controls, and event rules are already the governing boundary; a generic public HTTP endpoint still needs careful authentication
GitHub Actions scheduled workflows Repository automation and low-stakes maintenance jobs Schedules can be delayed or dropped under platform conditions, and the workflow runner is a poor home for a regulated cleanup path or shipment delivery ledger
SQS plus Pusher A specialist queue plus a specialist realtime transport You gain focused products, but you operate two signups, two credential sets, two retention models, and the glue that maps queue acknowledgements to socket delivery
A cron trigger plus queue/realtime capabilities behind one REST surface A small service that wants recurring HTTP work, durable handoff, and one consistent contract One provider becomes one trust decision, one bill, and one outage surface; the responsibility for region, retention, deletion, and contractual processor terms remains yours to verify

The last row is where Infrai can fit, without making it the answer to every boundary problem. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, billing metadata, runnable examples, and readiness; its breadth puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key and a consistent REST contract. For this workflow, that can remove the integration work of adding a queue to the cleanup path and a realtime delivery surface to the notification path.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the HTTP cron-to-queue-to-realtime handoff when one key and one contract reduce integration overhead, and keep the protected shipment records, deletion policy, regional placement, and processor agreement in systems whose controls you can independently verify. The combined approach has a real downside: one vendor is now part of both the durable handoff and the live delivery path.

Do not choose this shape for an Airflow or Temporal-style DAG, a join across many branches, an internal-only target, or a cleanup that needs more than 900 seconds without a worker. Infrai has no DAG/workflow orchestration or fan-out join primitive, cron has no nonstandard L expression, and a push subscription target must be publicly reachable over HTTPS. It also does not provide Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups: retention is at most 30 days and acknowledgement deletes the message.

That boundary changes the rollout in a concrete way. Imagine a nightly scan that finds shipment delivery attempts in three states: expired, pending, and recently retried. The cron endpoint should select only the expired window, persist its selection key, and stop before the deadline; pending rows belong to a later retry policy, while recently retried rows should not be reclassified merely because the scheduler was invoked twice. If the scan cannot finish inside the limit, the endpoint should enqueue bounded work and let a worker claim it, with each claim carrying the same shipment event identifier into the delivery ledger. This extra record is not decorative observability. It is what lets an auditor distinguish a duplicate request, a duplicate publish, and a legitimate second attempt after a subscriber was offline.

A rollout that preserves the audit trail

Start with one cleanup window and one public HTTPS endpoint. Record the intended window, schedule identifier, request identifier, and deletion policy before changing data. Make the endpoint return a bounded result, and test a lost response by sending the same idempotency key again. The second request should produce the same business outcome without a second deletion.

Then add the queue only for work whose duration or fan-out justifies it. Measure the batch against the 900-second limit rather than guessing. For each shipment event, persist the event identifier before publishing, acknowledge after the consumer's durable decision, and retain enough metadata to explain a duplicate suppression. A four-kilobyte run-output limit makes external audit records more important than verbose scheduler logs.

Finally, validate region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries with the people who own compliance. A REST abstraction can reduce integration surface; it cannot turn a public endpoint into a private one, promise residency that is not documented, or replace a contractual guarantee.

For the scheduling contract and current capability details, start with the cron documentation.

  • Pusher Channels documentation

title: Ant vs. Maven vs. Gradle—Three Different Ways to Think About a Build
description:
I’ve used Ant, Maven, and Gradle across different projects, and what stands out to me is how differently they approach the same problem.
They can all build software, but they make very different assumptions about how much control the developer should have and how much the build system should handle automatically.

Ant—explicit and flexible

Ant was the first build system I worked with, and probably the one I find easiest to understand.
You define targets, dependencies between those targets, and the individual tasks that make up the build. If you want to compile Java, package files, copy resources, run another program, or deploy something, you explicitly define how it should happen.
That makes Ant extremely flexible.
I’ve used it for more than Java builds. For example, I use Ant to prepare builds of my own website, compile SCSS, package files, and deploy the result to a server using custom macros.
The downside is that you are responsible for nearly everything. Dependency management, build structure, file locations, and execution order all need to be wired together manually.
Ant gives you control, but that control comes with a cost.

Maven—convention over configuration

Maven takes a very different approach.
Instead of describing every individual build step, you work within a predefined lifecycle. Compilation, testing, packaging, installation, and deployment already have established phases.
Dependency management is also much easier. Instead of storing libraries locally and wiring them into the build yourself, you declare dependencies and Maven resolves them from repositories such as Maven Central.
That convenience is probably Maven’s biggest strength.
The trade-off is that more happens behind the scenes. Understanding why a particular action runs can mean understanding lifecycle phases, plugin goals, dependency scopes, inheritance, and the effective POM.
Compared with Ant, Maven gives you less freedom over the structure of the build, but much more functionality out of the box.

Gradle—flexibility with more abstraction

Gradle sits somewhere between the two.
It provides dependency management and conventions similar to Maven, but also offers a much more flexible task system. It supports incremental builds, caching, multi-project builds, and a large plugin ecosystem.
I also find the Kotlin DSL slightly awkward. The build definition starts to feel less like configuration and more like another piece of software that needs to be understood and maintained.
That may partly be personal preference. Coming from a background where I work extensively with XML, Ant and Maven simply feel more natural to me.

Three different philosophies

Ant gives you control.
Maven gives you convention.
Gradle tries to give you both.
None of them is universally better. The real difference is how much of the build process you want to define yourself and how much you want the tool to handle automatically.

title: Timestamp attributes are now supported in Vercel Flags
description:
Vercel Flags now supports timestamp attributes, so you can target entities by date and time.

Use timestamp attributes to show a campaign page only between two dates, run a Black Friday promotion, or target users who registered before a cutoff.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

title: Analyze what Xiaohongshu (RedNote) users say about a product with Claude and MCP
description:
Xiaohongshu (小红书, also called RedNote) is where a lot of Chinese shoppers go to review products before they buy, and to complain after. If you sell anything in China, or compete with someone who does, the notes and comment sections there tell you a lot. The trouble is that there is no public API to sign up for, and reading hundreds of Chinese comments by hand is slow.

In this post we'll connect Claude Code to a remote MCP server, ask it what Xiaohongshu users say about a product, and let it search notes, read their comments and summarize them. At the end there's a short Python version that calls the same HTTP API without an agent.

Disclosure: I build Qovia, the API and MCP server used here. It's a paid API with a free trial.

Step 1: add the MCP server to Claude Code

Get a key from the Qovia console, then add the server with one line:

export QOVIA_KEY=sk-qovia-...
claude mcp add --transport http qovia https://api.qovia.ai/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $QOVIA_KEY"

The server exposes only four tools, so it doesn't fill the model's context with a hundred tool definitions:

  • search_endpoints: find data endpoints by keyword or platform
  • get_endpoint: show an endpoint's parameters, a response example and the price
  • call_endpoint: run an endpoint and return data plus billing info
  • get_account: check your key's balance and rate limit

search_endpoints and get_endpoint are free and work without an API key, so you can let the agent explore the catalog before you spend anything. Only call_endpoint needs the key. Setup details are in the MCP docs.

Step 2: ask a question

Start claude and give it something like this:

Using the qovia MCP tools, find out what Xiaohongshu users say about
the Stanley Quencher tumbler. Search in Chinese, take the 5 most
commented notes from the past month, read the first page of comments
on each, and summarize: main praise, main complaints, recurring
questions, and anything about fakes or pricing. Quote a few comments
in Chinese with an English translation. Tell me how much the run cost.

Step 3: what the agent does

The agent doesn't need to know Qovia's catalog in advance. A typical run goes like this.

1. Find the endpoints. It calls search_endpoints with platform: "xiaohongshu". That lists the Xiaohongshu endpoints, including:

Endpoint id Path Price per call
raw.xiaohongshu.search GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comments GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.note GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/note $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comment_replies GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comment_replies $0.005

2. Read the parameters. It calls get_endpoint for the two it needs.

raw.xiaohongshu.search returns 20 notes a page:

  • keyword (required, up to 50 characters)
  • sort: general (default), latest, most_liked, most_commented or most_saved
  • note_time: all (default), day, week, month or year
  • note_type: all (default), video or image
  • page: from 1, up to 50; stop when has_more is false

raw.xiaohongshu.comments returns a note's first-level comments:

  • note_id (required, 24 hex characters)
  • sort: default (Xiaohongshu's own order, pinned and popular first, about 5 a page) or latest (newest first, 10 to 15 a page, without like counts)
  • cursor: pass back the previous page's cursor unchanged; stop when has_more is false

3. Fetch the data. It runs call_endpoint with something like:

{ "endpoint_id": "raw.xiaohongshu.search",
  "params": { "keyword": "斯坦利 保温杯", "sort": "most_commented", "note_time": "month" } }

Each note in the result carries its Xiaohongshu id in extra.source_id. Here is an abbreviated example of the structure, taken from get_endpoint's response example (not from a real run of this prompt):

{
  "page": 1,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "soc_xia_c79d099f083d",
      "platform": "xiaohongshu",
      "text": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）…",
      "author": { "user_id": "5a916db4e8ac2b54e8b53aba", "nickname": "J*y" },
      "metrics": { "likes": 1205, "saves": 966, "shares": 287, "comments": 1570 },
      "extra": {
        "title": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）",
        "source_id": "69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "url": "https://www.xiaohongshu.com/explore/69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "note_type": "image",
        "published_at": "2026-05-04T07:37:37+08:00"
      }
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true
}

It then passes each source_id as note_id to raw.xiaohongshu.comments. Again an abbreviated example structure from get_endpoint:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "cid": "6a17eab1000000002902f300",
      "text": "喝了晚上还能睡着怎么解",
      "likes": 1918,
      "reply_count": 62,
      "ip_location": "陕西",
      "created_at": "2026-05-28T15:11:45+08:00",
      "author": { "nickname": "肉*嘟" }
    }
  ],
  "total": 1072,
  "cursor": "6a1b938c000000002b025bef",
  "has_more": true
}

4. Summarize. With five searches' worth of notes and their comments in context, Claude groups the comments into themes, picks quotes and translates them. ip_location is handy if you want a rough regional split. Every call_endpoint result includes charged_usd, so the agent can add up the cost when you ask.

A run like the prompt above is about 6 calls: one search plus five comment pages, so roughly $0.03.

Tip: search in Chinese

Xiaohongshu users write in Chinese, and they rarely use a brand's English name. Searching Stanley finds far fewer notes than 斯坦利 or 斯坦利 保温杯. A few things that help:

  • Ask the agent to try two or three Chinese keywords: the Chinese brand name, the brand plus the product category, and any nickname people use.
  • Add words people use when they review: 测评 (review), 踩雷 (bad buy), 真假 (real vs fake), 平替 (cheaper alternative).
  • Use sort: "most_commented" to find the notes with the most discussion, and note_time to keep it recent.
  • Read comments with the default sort first. It puts the most-liked comments on top, which are usually the most representative.

The same thing in plain Python

If you want this as a scheduled job instead of a chat, call the HTTP API directly. Every endpoint returns the same envelope: data holds the result and meta holds billing info.

import os, requests

BASE = "https://api.qovia.ai"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['QOVIA_KEY']}"}
spent = 0.0

def get(path, **params):
    global spent
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}{path}", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    spent += float(body.get("meta", {}).get("charged_usd", 0) or 0)
    return body["data"]

notes = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search",
            keyword="斯坦利 保温杯", sort="most_commented", note_time="month")["items"]

rows = []
for note in notes[:5]:
    comments = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments",
                   note_id=note["extra"]["source_id"])["items"]
    for c in comments:
        rows.append((note["extra"]["title"], c.get("likes"), c["text"]))

for title, likes, text in rows:
    print(f"[{likes}] {title} | {text}")
print(f"spent ${spent:.3f}")

From there you can hand rows to any LLM with a "summarize praise and complaints" prompt, or write them to a CSV.

Pricing and trial

  • New accounts get 50 trial calls, enough to run the example above several times.
  • You're charged only when a call returns data. Empty results and errors are free, including a search with no hits or a note with no comments.
  • Both Xiaohongshu endpoints used here cost $0.005 per call ($5 per 1,000).
  • Discovery (search_endpoints, get_endpoint) is always free and needs no key.

More in the docs, the Xiaohongshu API page and the Xiaohongshu MCP page. If you try it, I'd like to hear which product you looked up and what the comments said.

title: Beyond OpenCV: Light-Weight Monocular Depth Post-Processing in Pure NumPy
description:
When building desktop or edge AI applications, the default instinct for many engineers is to run pip install opencv-python.

However, as your architecture matures toward lightweight, self-contained edge software (such as a PyQt6 GUI app running ONNX Runtime on CPU), third-party C++ wrappers introduce real operational friction:

  • Deployment Bloat: 40–50 MB binary wheels (opencv-python-headless on Linux/Windows x64) that expand desktop installers.
  • Cold-Start Latency: Shared C++ library initialization delays during application startup.
  • Dependency Conflicts: Threading and event-loop clashes with native Qt backends.

In our project — Hawk Eye, an industrial AI edge application for monocular tire tread depth assessment — we enforced a strict rule: Zero CV-specific external dependencies (no OpenCV, SciPy, or Scikit-Image). The pipeline relies strictly on PyQt6, ONNX Runtime, PIL, and pure NumPy.

In this article, we look at how we solve camera perspective tilt in monocular depth maps using simple vector operations in NumPy.

The Problem: Relative Depth and Perspective Distortion

Monocular depth estimation models (like U-Net architectures optimized for edge CPU) map 2D pixels to depth predictions Z_raw in range [0.0, 1.0].

In field diagnostics, handheld devices or smartphone cameras are almost never held perfectly parallel to the tire surface. A 5-degree perspective tilt creates an artificial linear gradient across the depth map, causing the model to mistake perspective for actual physical tread wear.

To fix this, we detrend the baseline reference plane using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) fitted via SVD.

The Mathematics of Plane Fitting: Why SVD over Normal Equations?

We model the background surface using a linear 3D equation:

Z(x, y) = a * x + b * y + c

Where (x, y) are spatial pixel coordinates, a, b are surface slopes, and c is the global baseline offset.

Given an ROI matrix Z_raw of size H x W, we set up an overdetermined linear system A * x = b.

Numerical Stability: SVD vs. Normal Equations

In textbook linear algebra, the analytical solution is written via Normal Equations:

x_opt = inv(A^T * A) * A^T * b

In production, forming A^T * A squares the dynamic range of pixel coordinates. For a 224x224 depth grid (N = 50,176 pixels, max coordinate x_max = 223), the condition number of A^T * A reaches 10^4 - 10^5. Explicit matrix inversion leads to numerical instability on low-precision CPU runtimes.

Instead, we use Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) via np.linalg.lstsq. SVD solves the system directly without forming A^T * A, avoiding matrix inversion instability.

Production Python Implementation

Below is the self-contained implementation written purely in NumPy. It fits a least-squares plane, subtracts perspective tilt, and uses percentile masking to prevent deep grooves from corrupting the surface fit.

 python
import numpy as np

def detrend_and_scale_depth(
    depth_raw: np.ndarray, 
    scale_3d: float = 1.80, 
    bias_mm: float = 0.0,
    groove_mask_percentile: float = 40.0
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Removes camera perspective tilt using SVD Least Squares Plane Fitting
    and converts raw relative depth predictions into millimeter profile maps.

    Convention: Assumes Z_groove < Z_surface (lower relative height in depth_raw).

    Parameters
    ----------
    depth_raw : np.ndarray
        2D floating-point array (H, W) of relative predictions from ONNX U-Net.
    scale_3d : float
        Optics scale factor (mm per relative depth unit).
    bias_mm : float
        Systemic bias correction in millimeters.
    groove_mask_percentile : float
        Empirical threshold (40%) masking lower depth values (grooves) 
        during plane fitting to prevent fit sags.

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        2D array (H, W) containing detrended physical tread depth in millimeters.
    """
    h, w = depth_raw.shape

    # 1. Generate 2D pixel coordinate grids
    grid_y, grid_x = np.indices((h, w), dtype=np.float32)

    x_flat = grid_x.ravel()
    y_flat = grid_y.ravel()
    z_flat = depth_raw.ravel()

    # Design matrix A: Shape (N, 3) where N = H * W
    A = np.column_stack([x_flat, y_flat, np.ones_like(x_flat)])

    # 2. Trimmed OLS: Mask out deep grooves to fit plane ONLY on top tread blocks
    threshold_val = np.percentile(z_flat, groove_mask_percentile)
    mask = z_flat >= threshold_val

    # 3. Solve for plane parameters [a, b, c] via SVD (lstsq)
    plane_params, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(A[mask], z_flat[mask], rcond=None)
    a, b, c = plane_params

    # 4. Reconstruct background trend plane across full ROI
    z_plane = (a * grid_x + b * grid_y + c)

    # 5. Detrend surface (Subtract baseline slope)
    z_detrended = depth_raw - z_plane

    # 6. Robust baseline shift (P05 percentile instead of min to reject noise)
    baseline_floor = np.percentile(z_detrended, 5)
    z_detrended -= baseline_floor

    # 7. Convert relative depth delta to physical millimeters
    depth_mm = (z_detrended * scale_3d) + bias_mm

    return depth_mm


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Simulate 100x100 tile with camera tilt + 2.0 unit groove (20% of area)
    y, x = np.ogrid[:100, :100]
    simulated_tilt = 0.05 * x + 0.02 * y
    simulated_groove = np.where((x > 40) & (x < 60), -2.0, 0.0)
    raw_input = simulated_tilt + simulated_groove

    # Process depth map
    depth_mm = detrend_and_scale_depth(raw_input, scale_3d=2.5)

    # Evaluation using P95 - P05 percentiles (Assumes groove area >= 5-10% of ROI)
    groove_depth = np.percentile(depth_mm, 95) - np.percentile(depth_mm, 5)

    print(f"Input Range (Tilted): [{raw_input.min():.2f}, {raw_input.max():.2f}]")
    print(f"Corrected Depth Range: [{depth_mm.min():.2f}, {depth_mm.max():.2f}] mm")
    print(f"Measured Groove Depth: {groove_depth:.2f} mm (Expected Synthetic: 5.00 mm)")

Expected Output 

Input Range (Tilted): [0.00, 6.93]
Corrected Depth Range: [0.00, 5.00] mm
Measured Groove Depth: 5.00 mm (Expected Synthetic: 5.00 mm)

Production Considerations & Limitations

While linear plane detrending is fast, edge deployment has specific constraints:

  1. Groove Fitting Bias (Trimmed OLS): Unmasked OLS fits the plane to all pixels. If an ROI contains deep grooves, the fitted plane sags downward. Our implementation uses a 40% threshold mask (groove_mask_percentile=40) to fit strictly to elevated tread blocks (valid for typical 15–35% groove occupancy).
  2. Extreme Camera Tilt: If perspective tilt across the ROI exceeds the total groove depth, global percentile thresholding bleeds across regions. For severe angles (>30 degrees), local block-based RANSAC or quadratic fitting z = a*x^2 + b*y^2 + c*x*y + d*x + e*y + f should replace global OLS.
  3. Local vs. Global Slope Removal: OLS removes all linear trends. This works well for measuring local groove depth relative to adjacent tread blocks, but intentional tire shoulder curvature will also be flattened.

Benchmark Results

Replacing external CV packages with vectorized NumPy operations yielded clear benefits in our PyQt6 runtime:

  • Execution Latency: 0.38 ms on a 224x224 depth ROI (median of 100 runs after 10 warm-up iterations on Intel Core i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz, OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, NumPy 1.26.4).
  • Package Footprint: Saved ~45 MB on Linux/Windows x64 installers by removing opencv-python-headless.
  • Thread Safety: Pure NumPy array operations run inside PyQt6 worker threads without GUI loop blocking.

Conclusion

Linear algebra operations in pure NumPy are often enough for edge post-processing without bundling full C++ vision frameworks.

While synthetic tests verify the math, production calibration against real physical depth gauges (e.g., Mitutoyo 571-201-30) remains necessary to establish the optics scale factor (scale_3d) for different smartphone camera modules.

By combining SVD plane fitting with percentile masking, we achieved stable profile extraction for Hawk Eye — completely independent of external computer vision packages.

title: How to check which AI crawlers actually hit a new WordPress site in week one
description:
A site goes live on Monday. On Friday the question arrives: have the AI crawlers found it yet? If the access log format was picked years ago to debug PHP, there is no answer in the file, and the first week is already gone.

Two decisions have to be made before the first request: capture enough per request, and be able to tie a user agent to an IP you can check. Everything below assumes a self-hosted WordPress site where you control the web server.

Set the log format before launch

nginx, in a file included from the http block:

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/aiwatch.conf
log_format aiwatch '$time_iso8601 $remote_addr "$http_user_agent" '
                   '$request_method $request_uri $status $body_bytes_sent '
                   '"$http_referer" $request_time';

access_log /var/log/nginx/aiwatch.log aiwatch;

Apache httpd:

LogFormat "%{%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z}t %a \"%{User-Agent}i\" %m %U %s %B \"%{Referer}i\" %D" aiwatch
CustomLog /var/log/apache2/aiwatch.log aiwatch

Put it at the server level, not inside one vhost, or the next site you add silently logs in the old format. Then check what logrotate does to that file: if it rotates weekly and compresses, copy week one somewhere before it is replaced.

The fields that change a decision

Field What it decides
time_iso8601 Contains the UTC offset. Without it, cross-checking hits against the moment you published or changed robots.txt is guesswork.
remote_addr Must be the client IP. Behind a CDN or proxy it is the edge, and your verification step will confirm the CDN as a crawler. Fix with set_real_ip_from plus real_ip_header for whatever header your edge sets.
http_user_agent Store it whole. Truncating to 60 characters drops the version and the +https://... info URL that operators put there on purpose.
status 200, 304, 403 and 429 mean four different things. A crawler getting 403 is a different problem from a crawler that never came.
body_bytes_sent A 200 with 0 bytes is a HEAD request or an empty body. A status-only report calls both a success.
request_uri Did it fetch /robots.txt first, and did it ask for /llms.txt at all.
request_time A crawler that times out on your slowest page may not come back for the rest of the site.

Count what actually arrived

The UA is field 2 when you split the line on double quotes, because the format wraps it in quotes.

LOG=/var/log/nginx/aiwatch.log

awk -F'"' '
{
  ua = tolower($2)
  if      (ua ~ /gptbot/)          c = "GPTBot"
  else if (ua ~ /oai-searchbot/)   c = "OAI-SearchBot"
  else if (ua ~ /chatgpt-user/)    c = "ChatGPT-User"
  else if (ua ~ /claudebot/)       c = "ClaudeBot"
  else if (ua ~ /claude-user/)     c = "Claude-User"
  else if (ua ~ /perplexitybot/)   c = "PerplexityBot"
  else if (ua ~ /perplexity-user/) c = "Perplexity-User"
  else if (ua ~ /ccbot/)           c = "CCBot"
  else if (ua ~ /bytespider/)      c = "Bytespider"
  else if (ua ~ /amazonbot/)       c = "Amazonbot"
  else if (ua ~ /applebot/)        c = "Applebot"
  else if (ua ~ /googlebot/)       c = "Googlebot"
  else next
  n[c]++
}
END { for (k in n) printf "%-16s %d\n", k, n[k] }
' "$LOG" | sort -k2 -nr

A zero column for a crawler is not yet evidence of anything. Read the days before you read the total.

To see whether a crawler walked the site in order, print the first hit per IP with the path it asked for:

grep -i 'gptbot' "$LOG" | awk -F'"' '{split($1,a," "); print a[1], a[2], $3}' | sort | head -20

With this format, $1 is timestamp + space + ip, and $3 is the request line (method, path, status, bytes). If robots.txt and the home page appear in that list before anything else, the crawl is behaving; if the first hit is a deep product URL, it came in through a link, not through your sitemap.

Verify the IP before you trust the user agent

A user agent is a string the client chooses. Anyone can send GPTBot. Forward-confirmed reverse DNS is the cheap check: resolve the IP to a hostname, resolve that hostname back, and require the original IP to appear in the result.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Forward-confirmed reverse DNS. Reads IPs from argv or stdin."""
import socket
import sys


def check(ip):
    try:
        host = socket.gethostbyaddr(ip)[0]
    except (socket.herror, socket.gaierror, OSError):
        return ip, None, False
    try:
        addrs = socket.gethostbyname_ex(host)[2]
    except (socket.gaierror, OSError):
        return ip, host, False
    return ip, host, ip in addrs


def main():
    ips = sys.argv[1:] or [line.strip() for line in sys.stdin if line.strip()]
    for ip in ips:
        addr, host, ok = check(ip)
        print(f"{addr}\t{host or '-'}\t{'confirmed' if ok else 'NOT confirmed'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chmod +x fcdns.py
awk -F'"' 'tolower($2) ~ /gptbot|claudebot|perplexitybot/ {split($1,a," "); print a[2]}' "$LOG" \
  | sort -u | ./fcdns.py

Confirmed PTR means the IP belongs to whoever controls that reverse zone. It does not prove the request came from the crawler you have in mind, so compare against the operator's published IP ranges where they publish one. A hit that fails both checks is an unknown client with a borrowed user agent, and it should not go into your report as a crawler visit.

Tokens you will never find in a log

Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended are robots.txt user-agent tokens, not strings any client sends. Requests from those operators show up as Googlebot and Applebot. So "did Google-Extended fetch my page" has no answer in the access log; the only thing you control is whether robots.txt permits that token, which is a separate check against the file itself.

Which brings up the other half of the question. A user agent in the log does not mean your robots.txt was obeyed. Pull the file you served that week and see what it said:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type}\n' https://example.com/robots.txt
curl -sS https://example.com/llms.txt | head -20

Run it from outside your own network. A WAF rule that allows your office IP and blocks everything else looks identical to "no crawlers came" once you are reading the log.

What week one can and cannot tell you

A fetch is not an inclusion. A confirmed GPTBot request for the home page says a crawler read the page; it says nothing about whether the page will appear in an answer later, and there is no field in the log that closes that gap.

The reverse is worth stating too: no hits in week one does not distinguish "blocked" from "has not found it yet". A brand-new domain with no inbound links gives a crawler very little to follow, so an empty column is the expected starting state, not a malfunction. Do not rewrite robots.txt on the strength of one quiet week; check what the file actually serves first, then wait.

Keep the week

Print the per-crawler count once a week and keep the output next to the raw log. A single snapshot after launch tells you nothing that changes a decision. The number that matters is the change between week one and week four, and whether the paths being fetched moved from the home page into the pages you actually want quoted.

If maintaining this pipeline on every site is not the job you want, AumCrawl records crawler hits per crawler and lets you allow or block them individually. It is free and on wordpress.org; the log format above is still worth setting, because the plugin's data is only as good as what the server keeps.

title: The Merchant Is Not the Customer
description:
Recovery software has two audiences wearing one name. The merchant signs the contract, reads the reports, and pays the invoice. The merchant's customer receives the emails, taps the update link, and decides — in about four seconds, mid-scroll — whether this business handles problems like a professional or a collections agency. Design for only one of them and the other quietly leaves.

So every surface gets read twice. The dunning email is a merchant's recovery instrument and a stranger's first impression of how that merchant behaves under friction. The save offer is a retention metric and a moment of being cornered or being respected, depending on how the exit is drawn. Even the report is two documents: proof of work for the merchant, and a tone-setter for how honestly the whole relationship will be run.

Swipe Again is built in the merchant's branding for exactly this reason — the customer should never meet us at all. The recovery flow succeeds when the subscriber thinks their subscription company handled a hiccup gracefully. Invisible competence is the product. The merchant gets the revenue; their customer keeps the relationship; we keep the machinery out of the story entirely.

title: TIL: How to Read a GBase Database Package Name: 4 Compatibility Signals
description:
Today, a colleague asked me to help select a GBase Database installation package. He provided only the database version, downloaded an x86 build, and tried to install it on a Kunpeng server. The installation stopped almost immediately after extraction.

The problem was not the installer itself. It was package selection.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), the installation package name contains several important compatibility signals. Learning to read them can prevent unnecessary installation failures before the first command is executed.

Let's break down a real example.

1. Decode the GBase Database Installation Package Name

Consider this package:

GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-NoLicense-FREE-9.5.3.28.12-redhat8-aarch64.tar.bz2

Each section provides information about the product, edition, version, operating system family, or CPU architecture.

Package segment Meaning
GBase8a_MPP_Cluster Product and cluster edition
NoLicense-FREE Free edition without a license file
9.5.3.28.12 Database version
redhat8 Target operating system family and major version
aarch64 CPU architecture

The package name is effectively a compact compatibility checklist.

For GBase Database deployment, checking these fields before downloading or extracting the package is much more efficient than discovering a mismatch during installation.

2. CPU Architecture: Check the Instruction Set First

The aarch64 suffix identifies the ARM 64-bit architecture.

It is commonly associated with ARM-based platforms such as Kunpeng and Phytium.

Other platforms, including Intel, Hygon, and Zhaoxin, generally use x86_64 packages.

The distinction matters because binaries compiled for different instruction sets are not interchangeable.

A wrong CPU architecture can prevent the installation from running at all.

Loongson and Sunway platforms have their own architecture requirements. Their corresponding GBase Database installation packages are not publicly distributed through the same package channel and need to be requested separately.

For projects involving these platforms, include package acquisition and verification time in the deployment schedule.

Check the target architecture with:

uname -m

Compare the output with the architecture suffix in the package name before proceeding.

3. Operating System Family: redhat8 Is Not a Distribution Name

The redhat8 segment identifies the target operating system family and major version.

It should not be interpreted as meaning that the package can only run on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.

Depending on the officially supported compatibility matrix, distributions such as CentOS, openEuler, and Kylin may share a compatible package family.

However, the distribution name alone does not establish compatibility. The actual OS release, kernel environment, and system library requirements must be checked against the GBase Database version-specific compatibility documentation.

For example, selecting a redhat7 package for a CentOS 8 environment may cause the installation script to reject the system during OS validation.

This is not an arbitrary installer restriction. The package is built and validated against specific operating system and library requirements.

Check the operating system information with:

cat /etc/os-release

Do not assume that two distributions are compatible simply because they share a Linux foundation.

4. Database Version: Record the Complete Version Number

In the example package, the version is:

9.5.3.28.12

Do not shorten it to 9.5 or 9.5.3 in deployment records.

The complete version number matters when:

  • Checking the corresponding installation manual.
  • Verifying compatibility and known issues.
  • Applying patches or maintenance updates.
  • Adding nodes to an existing cluster.
  • Reproducing an installation months later.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), package version consistency is particularly important in multi-node environments.

When preparing a delivery record, copy the complete package filename rather than relying on a manually shortened version number.

5. Python Runtime: An Additional Compatibility Requirement

There is another dimension that package selection often overlooks: Python runtime compatibility.

Python 2 and Python 3 installation packages are not interchangeable.

For the publicly released free edition discussed here, the installation package uses Python 2. Python 3 builds require a separate request and applicable licensing arrangements.

This means that checking CPU architecture, OS family, and database version is not enough.

Before installation, confirm which Python runtime the selected package requires.

A missing or incompatible interpreter can cause installation scripts to fail even when the hardware and operating system are otherwise suitable.

The runtime requirement should therefore be included in the package selection checklist.

6. A Practical Pre-Installation Checklist

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8a), verify the target machine and the package name together.

First, inspect the machine:

uname -m
cat /etc/os-release

Then verify the following:

Dimension What to check
CPU architecture aarch64 or x86_64, matching the target machine
OS family redhat7, redhat8, or another supported package family
Database version Complete version number, such as 9.5.3.28.12
Python runtime Python 2 or Python 3 requirement
Edition Free or commercial edition and applicable license requirements

Only after confirming the relevant compatibility requirements should you extract the package.

For example:

tar -xjf GBase8a_MPP_Cluster-NoLicense-FREE-9.5.3.28.12-redhat8-aarch64.tar.bz2

cd gcinstall

The package filename should also be recorded in the deployment documentation.

This makes subsequent troubleshooting, reinstallation, and cluster expansion much easier.

Final Thoughts

A GBase Database installation package is more than a compressed collection of binaries. Its filename provides a useful starting point for understanding hardware, operating system, edition, and version requirements.

A mismatch in CPU architecture can prevent binaries from running. An OS compatibility mismatch can stop installation validation. An incorrect database version can create problems with manuals, patches, and cluster consistency. An incompatible Python runtime can prevent installation scripts from executing.

The lesson is simple: select the package for the target environment, not simply the newest available version.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), spending a few minutes checking the package name, CPU architecture, OS release, and Python runtime can save hours of troubleshooting later.

Always refer to the version-specific GBase Database installation manual and official compatibility matrix for the final compatibility decision.
