title: crustc ports rustc to C and builds it with GCC
description:
The crustc repository is C code that you compile with GCC and GNU make into a working Rust compiler. Point make at a matching LLVM build and the binary it produces reports rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c712ea946 2026-06-16), then goes on to build core, alloc and std. The author built it on ARM64 Linux with GCC 13.3.0 and the LLD 18.1.3 linker. An unoptimized build takes about 78 seconds of wall time (937 seconds of user time with make -j20). It still needs LLVM at runtime, because rustc uses LLVM, so the repo asks you to supply libLLVM.so.22.1-rust-1.98.0-nightly from the matching nightly toolchain rather than shipping a binary.

That is rustc itself, translated to C and built by a C compiler. The repo is a demo for cilly, the author's Rust-to-C toolchain and, by their count, the 14th attempt at the problem over three years (rustc_codegen_clr was an earlier public one). cilly is a Rust library that generates C plus a rustc backend plugin. Instead of handing MIR to LLVM for machine code, it emits C and passes that to whatever C compiler you nominate for the target. Compiling rustc with itself through that path is the flashiest thing to show, so that is what the repo does.

The useful engineering is that cilly does not assume a fixed C dialect. It emits "witness" programs and compiles them to learn what the target compiler and platform actually support: a file containing _Thread_local int KEYWORD_TLS_SUPPORTED; only compiles if the compiler has _Thread_local, so that tells cilly whether it can use the keyword. It queries type layouts, sizes, alignments, character encoding (ASCII) and integer representation (two's complement), with fallbacks where it can. The author aims to assume nothing outside ANSI C, works around newer-standard hazards like strict aliasing, and documents the few unavoidable assumptions ((void*)(uintptr_t)(ptr) round-trips, CHAR_BIT == 8) with runtime asserts where possible. The cost is that output is target-specific. C generated for Arm64 will not run on riscv32; you regenerate per target.

cilly can also talk to a C compiler over TCP, with UART floated as a possibility. You run rustc on an ordinary Linux box and let cilly drive a small C server on the target, which covers platforms that have no C cross-compiler at all. The author used this to build small Rust programs for x86 Plan 9 VMs from an Arm64 Linux host; the binary printed Hello, world! and carried a rust_begin_unwind symbol. cilly can embed markers in its object files, cache its IR, and emit a directory of makefiles, so the end product is a tree you build with a C compiler and make.

Compiling Rust through C does not undo Rust's safety guarantees. The borrow checker and type system run in rustc's frontend, which cilly does not touch; crustc is rustc, so those checks still happen before any C is emitted. The change is in the codegen trust base: you are now relying on cilly's translation and a C compiler to be correct, on top of the documented assumptions above. The author is candid that the demo is rough. They are chasing optimization-related bugs and recommend building without optimizations, both because enabling them "may break stuff" and because they choke on larger Rust files. Generated code is mostly ABI-compatible with normal rustc output, with a known exception on Arm64, where rustc picks an sret convention that C cannot express for small structs under 16 bytes.

The target user is anyone who maintains Rust that people keep asking to run on old or obscure hardware, the recurring "Rust doesn't support Plan 9" objection whenever a project moves off C. The stated goal is targets that have a C compiler but no LLVM or GCC Rust backend. It is not there yet. The author says cilly is not ready for public consumption and that real use waits on the full toolchain. crustc is the evidence it works: a Rust compiler that builds from C with stock GCC and make, self-hosting included.

title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Understanding Cloud Computing Through Amazon EC2
description:
** INTRODUCTION**

Cloud computing is a modern technology that provides flexible and reliable computing resources whenever they are needed. It allows users to access different services and resources through the internet from anywhere and at any time. These resources can also be easily managed and adjusted based on the user's needs.

Cloud computing resources can be easily managed and adjusted to meet users' needs. It is a technology that allows people to access different computing resources over the internet whenever they need them. These resources include networks, servers, storage, applications, and other services.

There are different types of cloud deployment models, including private cloud, public cloud, hybrid cloud, and community cloud. Cloud computing also provides three main service models: Software as a Service (SaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article focuses on Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), which is the most basic cloud computing service model. IaaS provides users with virtual computing resources such as servers, storage, and networks through a cloud service provider. With these resources, users can install and run their own operating systems, software, and applications. The cloud provider manages the physical hardware, while users can choose and manage the virtual resources according to their needs.

What is Infrastructure as a Service(IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is the delivery of
hardware (server, storage and network), and associated
software (operating systems virtualization technology,
file system), as a service.
Examples: AWS, Microsoft Azure, IBM Cloud.

** How does IaaS work?**

IaaS works through a technology called virtualization. This means that a cloud service provider uses powerful physical computers to create virtual computers, servers, storage, and networks that users can access through the internet.

The cloud provider allows users to choose the type and amount of resources they need, such as storage space, memory, and processing power. These virtual resources work almost like normal physical computers, allowing users to install operating systems, run applications, and store data without owning the actual hardware.

IaaS providers also offer additional tools that help users manage their resources. These tools allow users to:

  • Monitor performance: Check how well their servers and applications are working.
  • Manage security: Protect their virtual servers and data from unauthorized access.
  • Manage backups: Save copies of important data to prevent data loss.
  • Control resources: Increase or decrease computing resources when needed.
  • Manage networks: Control how their virtual servers connect and communicate. Example: Amazon EC2 is a good example of how IaaS works. A user can rent a virtual server from AWS, install Ubuntu Linux, set up a website, and make it available on the internet without purchasing a physical server.

IaaS simply works by allowing people and businesses to rent computing resources over the internet instead of buying and maintaining physical computer equipment.

Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2

Introduction:
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a cloud computing service that provides resizable, secure compute capacity as virtual servers. It offers over 1,000 instance types across Intel, AMD, and Arm processors and serves developers, enterprises, and teams running web apps, HPC, machine learning, and Windows workloads.
**
Features of Amazon EC2**
Amazon EC2 provides the following high-level features:
S
Instances
Virtual servers.

Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
Preconfigured templates for your instances that package the components you need for your server (including the operating system and additional software).

Instance types
Various configurations of CPU, memory, storage, networking capacity, and graphics hardware for your instances.

Amazon EBS volumes
Persistent storage volumes for your data using Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS).
**
Instance store volumes**
Storage volumes for temporary data that is deleted when you stop, hibernate, or terminate your instance.

Key pairs
Secure login information for your instances. AWS stores the public key and you store the private key in a secure place.

*Security groups
**A virtual firewall that allows you to specify the protocols, ports, and source IP ranges that can reach your instances, and the destination IP ranges to which your instances can connect.
*

How does Amazon EC2 work?
**

1.Choose an instance type
Choose an instance type and Amazon Machine Image in the console, CLI, or API. EC2 matches your workload to the right processor, storage, and networking configuration.

2.Launch your instance
Launch the instance and configure security groups, storage, and networking. EC2 provisions secure compute capacity in minutes on the AWS Nitro System.

3.Select a purchase model
Select a purchase model such as On-Demand, Spot, or Savings Plans. EC2 aligns cost to your usage pattern for steady or variable demand.

4.Scale capacity with demand
Scale capacity up or down as demand changes. EC2 adds or removes instances within minutes under a 99.99% availability SLA.

Conclusion

In conclusion, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is an important part of cloud computing because it allows individuals and businesses to access computing resources such as servers, storage, and networks over the internet without having to purchase physical equipment. It makes it easier, faster, and more affordable to manage IT resources. With services like Amazon EC2, users can create virtual servers, run applications, host websites, and increase or decrease their resources whenever needed. Although IaaS has some challenges, such as security risks, internet dependency, and management costs, its benefits make it a useful solution for modern businesses and individuals. As technology continues to develop, IaaS will remain an important part of cloud computing.

https://www.academia.edu/download/7299777/cloud%20computing%20a%20study%20of.pdf

**
Author: GIFT HYCINTH LECHI**

title: My sidebar footer is the whole auth UI: an initial, a role badge, and a logout button
description:
I didn't set out to design an auth UI. I set out to stop answering the same three questions every time I opened the app: who am I signed in as, what can I do, and how do I get out? All three answers ended up in the same place — the footer of the sidebar, in my starter kit's Layout component.

Here's what sits down there: a circle with the first letter of the user's name, uppercased, falling back to "U" if there's no name yet. Under it, the user's name, and a small badge showing user role exactly as the API returned it — "admin" or "user". And a Logout button.

The initial needs no avatar upload, no image pipeline, no broken-image icon when a profile photo is missing. It's a circle with a letter in it, and it works on day one for every user, including the seeded demo admin.

The role badge is the honest part. It shows the role right under the name. There's no separate "account type" page to visit, no settings screen to dig through. If you're wondering why you can't see the Users link, the badge tells you: you're not an admin. That same isAdmin check (user role === 'admin') is what hides the Users nav link above, so the badge and the navigation can never disagree.

And the logout button does the full job, not half of it. Its handler awaits logout() from AuthContext and then navigates to /login. The logout posts to /auth/logout — which revokes the current token on the server — and removes saas_token from localStorage. Only then does the sidebar navigate to /login. Logging out is not "clear the token and hope"; it's revoke server-side, clear client-side, then move. If the API call fails, the client still clears the token, so a dead session can't linger — but the normal path revokes properly.

The same initial shows up again in the top header, top-right. Same letter, same user, two places. That's not decoration; it's a cheap consistency check. If the header and the footer ever disagreed, something would be wrong with the auth state, and you'd spot it instantly.

None of this is clever. That's the point. A starter kit's auth UI shouldn't need a design system or a profile service. It needs to answer three questions at a glance, in one place you always see. An initial, a role badge, and a logout button that actually logs you out — that's the whole thing, and it's enough.

The full Layout, AuthContext, and token handling ship in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig — a $19 one-time boilerplate, so your next project starts with this already working instead of half-built.

title: The Polite Machine
description:
Automation has a bedside manner whether its builders chose one or not. A system that retries at 3 a.m., emails in all caps urgency, and cancels without a closing word has a manner — a rude one, executed at scale, in the merchant's name, while the merchant sleeps. The machine's politeness is not a soft feature layered over the real work. At volume, the manner is the product's public behavior.

Politeness, engineered, is a set of refusals: never attempt while a fix is in progress, never send a message that cannot change the outcome, never let a deadline pass without the closing courtesy of saying so. Plus a set of habits: confirm what worked, thank without groveling, state the next step in the customer's language. None of it is expensive. All of it is load-bearing, because the customer cannot separate the machine's manners from the merchant's character.

Swipe Again is built as a polite machine on purpose — the recovery flow treats every automated touch as a representative sent into someone's day. Scale does not excuse rudeness. It compounds it, or compounds the opposite.

title: Node.js-Friendly Production Logging API Explained — User Activity in Logistics
description:
Short answer: for a small logistics application that mainly needs to ingest structured user-activity and pipeline events, a REST log-ingest API is usually the least disruptive starting point. The expensive decision is not the first POST. It is what you retain, how quickly you can reconstruct a failed nightly run, and which deletion or alerting operations you will need later.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate when the team wants one key and a self-describing REST surface, with the schema and runnable examples discoverable before an SDK is installed. It is not a complete incident platform: there is no alert or notification route, no span-tree query, no user-specific log deletion, and no batch export or subscription interface in the stated boundary. A specialist wins when those omissions are part of the first release, not a future nice-to-have.

What does the bill actually follow?

For a nightly data pipeline, retained event volume is the first number I would estimate. Suppose a shipment-ingestion job processes 80,000 records and writes one structured event for each record, plus a small number of run-level events. The dominant term is the per-record event stream, not the handful of messages that say the scheduler started or stopped. The exact storage bill depends on the selected service and its retention policy, but the engineering choice is stable: avoid logging payloads that cannot help reconstruct a decision.

I would keep identifiers, stage names, outcome codes, timestamps, and the pipeline run identifier. I would avoid copying an entire customer profile or shipment document into every event. That is a retention decision, not a logging-library trick. It reduces the material that must be protected and keeps a later reconstruction focused on joins between events.

The trade-off is uncomfortable and real. If I discard the input snapshot, a failed run may tell me which record failed without preserving the exact data that produced the failure. If I retain it forever, a user-activity log becomes a second data warehouse with a larger compliance surface. For a small app, short-lived structured logs plus durable domain records can be a sensible boundary, provided the team has a documented replay source.

Do not mistake free offerings for free operations. The facts for this option explicitly limit the free path to offerings without alert-based integrations, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed as a complete control surface. The cost question therefore includes the cost of polling, triage, exports, and eventual migration.

Which Node.js-friendly API fits production logging for user activity?

My first useful result for a nightly logistics pipeline is not a colorful dashboard. It is an answer to this question: which run, stage, and record explains the missing shipment update? That answer needs structured events that can be related by a run identifier and a record identifier. It also needs a predictable ingest path from the application that already emits the event.

The integration friction is usually spread across four places: credentials, client libraries, request schemas, and the time between sending the first event and seeing a useful result. A Node.js service can produce JSON easily, but every additional vendor SDK brings its own initialization, transport settings, retry behavior, and secret-management convention. The friction is small in a demo and surprisingly persistent in a production worker.

That is the part teams underestimate.

The public discovery manifest lists 295 routes across 20 modules, while this decision only needs one verified logs-ingest route. That breadth is useful when the same application later needs another backend capability, but it is not a reason to accept a weak log search or data-lifecycle contract. I would still test the incident question with a small, representative nightly run before expanding the integration.

A self-describing API changes the first step. The public discovery surface can describe capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That means an engineer can inspect the contract before adding a dependency. The practical benefit is modest but valuable: fewer guesses in the adapter, fewer credentials scattered across local tools, and a shorter path from a pipeline event to a verified request shape.

Here is a minimal discovery check. It does not invent an ingest payload; it asks the service for its current public description instead.

import os
from json import load
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

request = Request(
    'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery',
    method='GET',
    headers={
        'Accept': 'application/json',
        'Authorization': f\"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}\",
    },
)

with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
    discovery = load(response)

print(discovery['version'])
print(len(discovery['capabilities']))

For a real ingest adapter, use the returned schema for the logs capability and keep the application-side event model narrow. The verified route is POST /v1/logs/ingest; the important point here is that the discovery document, rather than an article or memory, should supply the request fields. That discipline matters because the search and metrics filter parameters are not declared in discovery, so I would not design a client around guessed filters.

How do the practical alternatives differ?

Datadog is the more natural choice when a team wants a mature hosted observability product with logs, dashboards, monitors, and a broad integration catalog in one operational workspace. Its advantage is depth around day-two operations. The cost is a larger product surface and a stronger commitment to its agent, conventions, and account model than a tiny app may need for one nightly pipeline.

OpenSearch with the Elastic-style ecosystem is a better fit when query control, self-hosting, and ownership of the storage layer are primary requirements. It gives an experienced platform team room to shape indexing and retention. That freedom comes with operational work: cluster capacity, upgrades, access control, backups, and the ingestion path become the team's responsibility. It is a poor first choice when nobody owns that work.

Better Stack is attractive for a smaller team that values a hosted log workflow and a quick path to searching and alerting. Its managed experience can remove infrastructure tasks that come with running OpenSearch. The boundary is product fit: a team with unusual retention, export, deletion, or cross-system query requirements should validate those workflows before committing, rather than assuming that a polished search page implies every data-lifecycle operation.

Option Integration shape First useful result Boundary to test
Infrai REST discovery plus one key Inspect the contract before adding an SDK No alerting, user-specific deletion, or batch export
Datadog Hosted platform with integrations and agents Search, dashboards, and operational monitors Larger product and account surface
OpenSearch / ELK Self-managed or managed search stack Query control over owned indexes Capacity, upgrades, backups, and access control
Better Stack Hosted logging workflow Quick hosted search and alerting Validate unusual retention and export needs

The table is a decision aid, not a feature-count contest.

Infrai sits in a different part of this comparison. Its useful distinction is not that it replaces every observability product. It offers one REST surface across backend capabilities, and its discovery endpoint is public and self-describing. The same discovery system documents runnable examples across ten languages. That can remove SDK installation and reduce credential sprawl for a small application that is already composing several backend calls.

The recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the ingestion leg of a small Node.js logistics application when the priority is discovering a request contract quickly and keeping backend integration behind one key. Do not choose it as the sole incident-response system when alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, or governed data export is a launch requirement.

What retention boundary will hurt later?

The missing features matter most during the incident after the incident. There is no alerting or notification route, so threshold rules and SMS, phone, or webhook delivery need a separate system or polling loop. There is no distributed tracing query or span tree; trace and span identifiers can relate records, but the log surface does not become a trace backend. There is no source-map or crash-symbolization workflow, session replay, or health-check monitor for the silent case where a scheduled job never runs.

The data-lifecycle boundary is sharper. The stated capability does not provide a user-specific log deletion interface, batch export, or subscription interface. Deletion has no recycle bin, and retention or cold-storage error codes do not amount to a configuration control. For user activity, that should be reviewed with the person responsible for privacy requirements before production launch. A log that records account identifiers is still personal data even when its purpose is debugging.

I would also keep a local run ledger or another durable domain record for the facts required to reconcile a shipment update. Logs are excellent evidence of what the service observed; they should not be the only source of business truth. When the pipeline fails, the ledger answers what was expected, while the log answers what the worker attempted. That separation is more useful than adding another dashboard.

A decision rule for the first release

Choose the smallest system that can answer the first incident question and survive the first deletion request. For the scenario here, that means:

  1. Define a compact event contract around run, stage, record, outcome, and timestamp identifiers.
  2. Discover the ingest schema before writing the Node.js adapter, and keep secrets in the runtime environment rather than source code.
  3. Retain enough event context to reconstruct a run, but keep the source document in the system of record.
  4. Add a separate alerting or health-check tool if a missing run is more dangerous than a failed event.
  5. Test deletion, export, and incident reconstruction before calling the design production-ready.

Infrai is a good fit inside that boundary when integration friction is the problem being solved. Datadog is the stronger answer when hosted operational depth is the priority. OpenSearch is the stronger answer when storage ownership and query control justify platform work. Better Stack is a practical hosted option when a small team wants search and alerting without operating a cluster.

The right choice is the one whose missing operation you can tolerate.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js structured logging guide and verify the current discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry signals and metrics concepts
  • Datadog log collection
  • OpenSearch documentation
  • Better Stack uptime and observability documentation

title: Failed Payments, Grace Periods and Automatic Access Revocation in Telegram Communities
description:
Suppose a subscriber's renewal payment fails at 10:00 UTC. Your bot removes them at 10:01. Two hours later, a payment retry succeeds, but the subscriber is still banned.

The payment retry succeeded, but the access workflow never restored the subscriber's ability to rejoin.

This walkthrough shows how to keep paid time separate from grace, set a fixed recovery deadline, and recover when removal conflicts with a later payment.

The scope is a custom bot managing access to a private Telegram community. The timeline is illustrative, and the Python function covers the access decision only. A working integration still needs billing, event processing, and Telegram delivery checks.

Give grace its own deadline

Keep payment status, entitlement, and observed membership separate. In particular, use different fields for paid time and temporary access:

Application field Meaning
paid_through End of the period granted by confirmed payment
grace_until End of a separately authorized recovery window
renewal_enabled Whether future automatic renewal is enabled
desired_membership Whether the access policy currently permits membership
observed_membership Last known membership state in Telegram

These are application fields, not a provider's universal schema. Preserve the payment and subscription references that explain each grant.

A failed renewal does not erase a period already purchased. Grace does not turn an unpaid period into a paid one.

Keep the evidence behind each deadline. Support should be able to distinguish purchased time, a recovery allowance, and a delayed removal without reconstructing them from one status flag.

Define one policy before writing handlers

Suppose Maya's paid period ends on December 1, 2026, at 10:00 UTC. Her renewal fails at that boundary.

The example community gives existing subscribers a 72-hour recovery window. This duration is an illustrative policy choice, not a Telegram default or a recommended duration for every community.

The policy is:

  • Grace applies to an eligible renewal after a previously paid period, not to an unpaid first purchase.
  • Its deadline is the previous paid-period end plus 72 hours.
  • A repeated failure or notification does not restart the clock.
  • Canceling renewal before the due date preserves paid time but does not create a recovery window for a renewal that was never due.
  • If grace has already been promised, turning renewal off does not silently shorten that promise.
  • Refunds, disputes, and moderation restrictions have their own explicit rules.

Record the grace decision against a stable renewal identifier, such as a provider invoice ID, with a uniqueness constraint and policy version. Schedule reconciliation at the renewal boundary even if no failure webhook has arrived: retrieve the billing state and evaluate the eligible renewal before removing access.

Do not calculate grace_until = webhook_received_at + 72 hours. Anchor it to the previous paid-period end. In this example, that same preauthorized window covers eligible renewals awaiting verification. Keep paid_through unchanged and distinguish unknown billing state from confirmed failure. Repeated events cannot restart the window. If verification remains unavailable, alert operators before the deadline; any outage exception needs separate authorization and a recorded end time. Never create new grace from an old invoice after a newer renewal has settled.

Two possible outcomes

Time, UTC Successful recovery No recovery
Dec 1, 10:00 Renewal fails; grace ends Dec 4, 10:00 Same
Dec 2, 10:00 Another failure; original deadline remains Same
Dec 3, 09:00 Payment settles the Dec 1–Jan 1 renewal period; grant is recorded once Still unpaid
Dec 4, 10:00 New paid period permits access; old removal task is obsolete Temporary entitlement ends; removal is due

This timeline uses calendar-month website billing with an unchanged billing anchor. Map the actual period covered by the settled invoice item to the access grant. Do not award a full new month from the retry time. Plan changes and prorations need their own mapping.

Separate collection retries from access grace

There are three independent retry mechanisms:

  1. Collection retry: the payment system tries to collect money again.
  2. Webhook retry: the sender attempts to deliver a notification again.
  3. Access-task retry: your worker attempts the Telegram operation again.

Only the first can result in a new payment. The other two must not charge the customer or grant duplicate paid time.

Stripe's retry documentation describes configurable collection behavior. Some failures require customer action or a new payment method. Do not promise another automatic attempt merely because the account is overdue.

Collection can continue after grace ends. Define the late-payment outcome before launch. Record the period a late payment settles, and restore current access only if that period or another valid grant covers the present time. A payment on January 5 for December 1–January 1 is historical settlement, not a reason to unban the subscriber. Compensation for interrupted access is a separate policy.

Explain that possibility to subscribers. If your offer instead promises no further collection after access ends, align the billing configuration with that promise.

Translate provider signals into access decisions

For an independent website subscription using Stripe, a compact mapping is:

Signal Application action
invoice.payment_failed Identify the affected renewal; evaluate grace eligibility
invoice.payment_action_required Direct the customer to complete the required payment action
invoice.paid Validate the applicable invoice and subscription state; record the corresponding grant once
Subscription update or termination Reconcile billing and cancellation policy; recompute entitlement

Stripe's subscription webhook guide explains these events and statuses. past_due does not guarantee another collection attempt. An active subscription alone is not proof that every outstanding invoice was paid. Avoid treating either status as your complete access model.

Cancellation also needs interpretation: period-end cancellation differs from immediate termination. Preserve your paid-grant history rather than replacing it with one cancellation flag.

For digital purchases inside Telegram bots or Mini Apps, Telegram requires Stars, using XTR. An external provider integration is not a substitute for that in-app requirement.

For bot subscriptions, use subscription_expiration_date from a confirmed SuccessfulPayment to map the paid deadline. Recurring Stars periods currently use 30 days, so do not copy the calendar dates above. BotSubscriptionUpdated includes states such as failed and canceled; a failure signal does not grant paid time.

Native paid channel subscription links are a separate mechanism. This custom grace policy does not configure Telegram's native subscription behavior.

Make the access decision testable

This Python 3.10+ function evaluates approved deadlines for one subscription. The caller must validate payment evidence and authorize grace first; this function makes no provider or Telegram requests.

from datetime import datetime

def access_state(
    *,
    now: datetime,
    paid_through: datetime | None,
    grace_until: datetime | None,
    blocked: bool = False,
) -> str:
    for value in (now, paid_through, grace_until):
        if value is not None and value.utcoffset() is None:
            raise ValueError("Use timezone-aware timestamps")

    if blocked:
        return "blocked"
    if paid_through is not None and now < paid_through:
        return "paid"
    if grace_until is not None and now < grace_until:
        return "grace"
    return "expired"

The caller supplies only grace that the policy has already authorized. For a subscriber with multiple subscriptions or other grants to the same community, evaluate all valid grants before removing access. An expired subscription must not override another current grant. Apply a community-wide moderation block separately.

At exactly grace_until, this function returns expired, unless paid time or a block produces a different result. Store timestamps as instants, use UTC in logs, and show the customer an unambiguous deadline with a timezone.

The policy deadline is not a guarantee of second-precise removal. Scheduler frequency, queues, and API failures introduce enforcement delay. Record that delay rather than quietly extending the entitlement date to match it.

Treat revocation as durable work

Track removal as pending, confirmed, or failed. Mark it confirmed only after checking the Telegram result.

When the deadline passes, recompute eligibility and write a removal task durably. Commit the decision and task together—for example, through a transactional outbox—so a crash cannot lose the action between them.

Use authenticated webhook input, durable event storage, and atomic uniqueness checks. Stripe documents duplicate events and unordered delivery. A late failure must not undo a later settled renewal. Deduplicating event IDs also does not replace deduplicating the business grant.

A removal task should carry a membership key, entitlement revision, reason, and decision time. The worker loads the latest state before acting and skips obsolete work.

That check reduces errors but does not close the whole race: payment can arrive between the database read and the Telegram request. Coordinate grant and removal operations for each user–community pair. After uncertain or concurrent results, reconcile actual membership against the latest entitlement. A database transaction cannot include Telegram in the same atomic commit.

banChatMember requires bot administrator rights. In supergroups and channels, re-entry requires unbanning, and the documented revoke_messages value is always true. Test its message-deletion behavior against your discussion archive. On recovery, unbanChatMember with only_if_banned=true avoids removing an existing member. Unbanning does not automatically rejoin someone.

Lift only a ban your billing workflow owns. A new payment must not reverse an independent moderation decision. Then offer re-entry through your controlled admission flow, checking current entitlement again.

If removal fails, retain the original deadline and mark enforcement as pending or failed. Retry transient failures with backoff; escalate missing permissions. After a timeout, check the result before assuming the action never happened.

Tell the subscriber what to do

A recovery notice should identify the failed renewal, the exact access deadline, and the required action. For Maya, it could say:

Your renewal payment was unsuccessful. Access remains available until December 4, 2026, at 10:00 UTC while you resolve it. Open billing settings to update your payment method or complete authentication. We will confirm when payment succeeds.

Do not promise a scheduled charge unless the billing system confirms one. Use the appropriate secure billing flow rather than collecting card details in chat.

Send notices for meaningful transitions: entering grace, approaching its deadline, confirmed recovery, and actual removal. Deduplicate them so repeated webhooks do not produce repeated warnings. Cancel obsolete reminders after recovery, and keep payment support reachable after community access ends.

Removal stops future membership under this workflow; it cannot recall copies of content already saved by a subscriber.

Test the failure paths

Use a payment test environment and a private test community with ordinary member accounts. These are proposed integration checks, not claimed deployment results.

Scenario Expected outcome
First purchase fails No paid grant or renewal grace
Renewal fails before paid time ends Existing paid access remains; grace uses the original period boundary
Same renewal fails again One grace decision; unchanged deadline
Failure notification is delayed or verification is unavailable Scheduled reconciliation evaluates the preauthorized window; no deadline is reset from delivery time, and unresolved verification is escalated
Paid renewal is followed by an older failure Paid grant remains; no new grace or removal
Grace deadline is reached without recovery Entitlement expires; a durable removal task is created
Payment arrives while removal is pending Obsolete task is skipped, or the membership error is repaired
Payment settles after removal Re-entry is offered only if a valid grant covers now and no independent moderation block applies; settling an ended period alone does not restore access
Another valid grant exists No removal solely because this subscription expired
Bot loses removal permissions Entitlement remains expired; failed enforcement is visible to operators

Monitor expired-but-present memberships and entitled-but-banned accounts. For confirmed removals, measure enforcement lag from the applicable access deadline to confirmed removal, recording any authorized exception separately. Investigate task failures and distinguish voluntary departures from admission errors. Keep event and grant references in logs, excluding payment credentials and bot tokens.

Conclusion

An unsuccessful renewal starts a recovery workflow. Whether access continues depends on existing paid time and an explicit grace policy.

Keep the deadline fixed, record successful renewal once, and treat removal and re-entry as operations that can fail. That makes the system easier to explain to subscribers and easier to repair when billing and Telegram disagree.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

Read more

title: Model Payment Statuses as a State Machine
description:
Turning scattered payment updates into explicit, enforceable lifecycle rules.

A payment status is not an arbitrary label. It represents a position in a controlled financial lifecycle.

Real transactions can be pending, processing, completed, failed, expired, reversed, or refunded. Problems appear when API handlers, background workers, webhooks, and staff tools can assign these values independently.

Define the valid transitions instead:

TRANSITIONS = {
    "pending": {"processing", "failed", "expired"},
    "processing": {"completed", "failed"},
    "failed": {"refunded"},
    "completed": set(),
    "refunded": set(),
}

Route every change through one domain service. Inside a database transaction, lock the payment row, validate the transition, save the provider evidence, and apply any ledger effect exactly once. Emit notifications only after the database commit succeeds.

Terminal states need special protection. A delayed processing event must never move a completed payment backward. Likewise, two simultaneous success signals must not produce two credits.

State machines make those rules explicit, testable, and shared by every entry point. In payment infrastructure, that is far safer than treating status as a writable string.

Centralize transitions instead of centralizing status writes

A common first improvement is to create a helper that updates the status field. That reduces duplication, but it does not yet protect the lifecycle. The service must understand the meaning of each transition and the work attached to it.

Moving from processing to completed may release a hold, post a ledger entry, update a linked order, and schedule a notification. Moving from processing to failed may refund the sender. These are domain operations, not model assignments.

The transition service should accept evidence, not trust callers to supply a final state blindly. A provider adapter can normalize its response into a small internal event containing the provider reference, normalized status, event time, and sanitized payload. The transition layer then decides whether that evidence is newer, valid, and financially actionable.

Protect transitions from concurrency

Imagine a polling worker and webhook handler receiving success at nearly the same time. Both read processing; both decide to complete; both attempt to credit the recipient. A state-machine table alone does not prevent this race.

Use a database transaction and row-level lock. After acquiring the lock, re-read the current state and check whether the financial effect already exists. Back the ledger reference with a unique database constraint. Application checks explain intent; database constraints provide the final concurrency guarantee.

Keep transition history

The current state answers where the payment is now. It does not explain how it got there. Record transition history with the previous state, next state, source, actor, provider evidence, and timestamp.

This history makes support and reconciliation substantially easier. It also reveals operational patterns such as transactions repeatedly moving into manual review or providers producing late events.

Test the lifecycle as a graph

Useful tests cover more than successful examples. Verify every permitted edge, every rejected edge, terminal-state protection, duplicate success signals, late failure events, and concurrent completion attempts.

The strongest invariant is simple: regardless of event order or retry count, the transaction reaches one valid state and every financial effect occurs at most once.

Implementation checklist

Before shipping a lifecycle, document every state and transition, identify the service responsible for each edge, define terminal states, and specify the ledger effect attached to every financial transition. Add database constraints for unique effects and structured transition logs for investigation. Review all writers of the status field; ideally, none should remain outside the transition service.

Monitor invalid transition attempts as well. They often reveal late provider events, duplicate jobs, or an endpoint bypassing the domain layer. A state machine is valuable not only because it permits valid movement, but because it makes invalid movement visible.

The result is a payment lifecycle that remains understandable under retries, concurrency, and operational intervention.

title: Why Flat-Text PDF Parsing Breaks RAG (And How Spatial 2D Grounding Fixes It)
description:
When building Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, the standard ingestion step usually looks like this:

  1. Read a PDF file.
  2. Dump all text content into a single flat string.
  3. Split the string into 500-token chunks with some overlap.
  4. Generate vector embeddings and store them in a vector database.

While this works for simple blog posts or single-column articles, it breaks down completely when applied to production documents like financial reports, scientific papers, and legal contracts.

The Three Hidden Failures of Flat-Text Ingestion

1. Table Flattening

PDF files do not store tables as HTML table elements or markdown grids. They store independent text strings positioned at absolute coordinates, combined with vector stroke lines.

When a standard parser strips away positioning, rows and columns collapse into a single stream. A table comparing quarterly revenues across three divisions becomes a scrambled sequence of numbers. By the time your chunk reaches an LLM, the relational context is destroyed.

2. Multi-Column Reading Order

Dense academic papers and annual reports frequently use two-column or three-column layouts. A naive parser reads across horizontal bands, interweaving sentences from the left column with sentences from the right column. The resulting embeddings represent garbled nonsense.

3. The Lack of Visual Provenance

When an LLM produces a critical answer, such as an interest rate or an EBITDA figure, users need to verify it. If your RAG system only stores raw text chunks, the best you can show the user is a quoted string. You cannot point to the exact page, line, or table cell where the
fact originated.

The Current Trade-off: Fast and Blind vs. Accurate and Slow

Right now, developers face two extremes:

• Legacy C-based Parsers (PyMuPDF, Poppler, PDFium): Extremely fast, but originally designed for rendering pixels onto desktop screens rather than feeding structured spatial trees into AI pipelines. They also introduce heavy C/C++ compilation toolchains, breaking in
lightweight container environments.
• Vision-Language Models and OCR (Marker, Docling, Nougat): These rasterize pages into images and run deep learning models to predict layout. While accurate, they require GPUs, cost significant compute per page, and introduce seconds of latency per document.

The Alternative: Spatial RAG with Native 2D Grounding

The coordinate geometry needed to reconstruct document structure already exists inside the PDF content streams, you do not need a GPU to rediscover it.

This is why I built RasgaPDF (https://github.com/MartinsMessias/rasgapdf): a lightweight, pure Rust PDF engine built specifically for Spatial RAG.

Instead of outputting an unstructured string, the engine reconstructs the document as a spatial 2D hierarchy with exact coordinates:

{
  "page_number": 1,
  "width": 612.0,
  "height": 792.0,
  "rotation": 0,
  "text_blocks": [
    {
      "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 70.6, "x1": 384.6, "y1": 82.7 },
      "lines": [
        {
          "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 70.6, "x1": 384.6, "y1": 82.7 },
          "text": "Revenue increased by 14% year-over-year..."
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "tables": [
    {
      "bbox": { "x0": 60.0, "y0": 121.0, "x1": 540.0, "y1": 245.0 },
      "markdown": "| Metric | 2025 | 2026 |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n..."
    }
  ]
}

Visual Citation in User Interfaces

Because every chunk retained its physical bounding box ([x0, y0, x1, y1]), your frontend can render the original PDF page and draw an exact translucent highlight over the source passage. The user gets instant, trustworthy verification without hunting through a 50-page
document.

Pure Rust: Zero C/C++ Toolchains

By implementing the ISO 32000-1 specification natively in safe Rust:

• cargo build and pip install work without MSBuild or C compiler installations.
• Memory safety is enforced at compile time.
• A dense 12-page academic paper parses in approximately 15 ms on a single CPU core.

Native Integration with LangChain and LlamaIndex

You do not need to write custom spatial wrappers. RasgaPDF integrates directly into standard AI orchestrators:

    from rasgapdf import RasgaPDFLoader

    # Load with physical 2D metadata preserved in every Document chunk
    loader = RasgaPDFLoader("financial_report.pdf", mode="elements")
    docs = loader.load()

    first_chunk = docs[0]
    print(first_chunk.page_content)
    print(first_chunk.metadata["bbox"])
   # {'x0': 60.0, 'y0': 70.6, 'x1': 384.6, 'y1': 82.7}

Conclusion

If your RAG system is hallucinating data or failing on complex documents, the problem is often not your embedding model or prompt, it is flat-text ingestion destroying spatial context before the model ever sees it.

Preserving 2D physical coordinates gives you reliable tables, accurate reading order, and verifiable visual citations at native speed.

• GitHub: https://github.com/MartinsMessias/rasgapdf
• Interactive Playground: https://martinsmessias.github.io/rasgapdf/

How are you currently handling table extraction and citation verification in your RAG pipelines? Let us discuss in the comments below.

title: Onboarding Is a Funnel, Not a Form
description:
Most SaaS onboarding is designed as paperwork: collect the fields, show the dashboard, send the welcome email, wonder about activation later. But activation is a funnel with conversion rates at every step, and each step's drop-off is a design decision whether anyone made it or not. Our order is deliberate: signup, then card, then connect — because a merchant who has put a card down has made a commitment that makes the connect step worth finishing, and a merchant asked to connect first stalls on permissions for a trial they have not yet decided to want.

The metric that falls out of that order is the one we watch: the share of trials connected within twenty-four hours. It is the business's pulse. When it dips, the problem is rarely the product — it is a step that asked for trust before giving a reason, or instructions written for the person who built the page instead of the person reading it at midnight.

Swipe Again writes onboarding like the funnel it is: one action per step, exact clicks, plain words for what success looks like, and no step that exists to satisfy us rather than the merchant. The recovery flow starts earning only after connect — so connect is where the design budget lives. Forms collect data. Funnels create customers. The difference is whether someone counted the drop-offs and felt responsible for them.

title: BioSmart: Construí un motor de IA en Go con pipeline cognitivo de 15 fases para agricultura urbana
description:
BioSmart es una plataforma inteligente para agricultura urbana, trazabilidad de donaciones y e-commerce ecológico. No es un proyecto de clase — está desplegado y funcionando.

👉 Demo en vivo 👉 Código fuente

│ pgx/v5 │
└──────────────┘
🧠 GopherMind AI: el motor en Go
Esta es la parte que más me enorgullece. Construí un pipeline cognitivo de 15 fases en Go puro:

Sanitización CUSUM — detección de cambios en las series temporales de sensores
Filtro Hampel — eliminación de outliers sin perder señal real
Predicción multi-motor — múltiples modelos generan predicciones independientes
Fusión Bayesiana — combina las predicciones con pesos probabilísticos
Detección de drift Page-Hinkley — identifica cuando el modelo se desactualiza
Calibración de confianza — cada insight tiene un score de fiabilidad
¿Por qué Go y no Python?
Goroutines + Channels: análisis simultáneo de múltiples racks hidropónicos sin bloquear
Zero-Copy: el pipeline procesa datos sin copias innecesarias en memoria
Compilado: latencia mínima en las respuestas de la API de IA
HMAC-SHA256: cada insight lleva firma de integridad para auditoría IEEE
// Ejemplo simplificado del pipeline
func (gm *GopherMind) Analyze(rack RackData) Insight {
sanitized := gm.cusumSanitize(rack.Readings)
filtered := gm.hampelFilter(sanitized)
preds := gm.multiPredict(filtered) // goroutines
fused := gm.bayesianFuse(preds)
drift := gm.pageHinkley(fused)
insight := gm.calibrate(fused, drift)
insight.Signature = gm.hmacSign(insight)
return insight
}
🌍 Globo 3D con Three.js
La landing tiene un globo terráqueo interactivo que visualiza las donaciones globales en tiempo real. Implementé una transición fluida de vista 3D (Three.js) a vista 2D satelital (Leaflet.js) según el nivel de zoom.

title: Churn prediction where the simple model wins: logistic regression against five rivals
description:
This was my final project for IBM's Supervised Machine Learning: Classification course: predict which telecom customers will leave, using the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 customers, 26.5% of whom churned). The modelling was the easy part. The interesting decision came at the end, when the best three models turned out to be indistinguishable.

A fair comparison first

Every model family was grid-searched on the same five stratified folds of the same 80/20 split, scored by ROC AUC, and then evaluated once on the held-out test set with a 95% confidence interval.

Model CV AUC Test AUC 95% CI
Gradient boosting 0.849 0.846 0.825–0.868
Random forest 0.849 0.843 0.821–0.865
Logistic regression (L2, C = 0.1) 0.844 0.843 0.821–0.865
SVM, RBF kernel 0.844 0.843 0.819–0.865
k-nearest neighbours 0.838 0.832 0.808–0.854
Decision tree (pruned) 0.839 0.831 0.807–0.854

Gradient boosting has the highest number, but its lead over logistic regression is 0.003 AUC, well inside overlapping confidence intervals. When the accuracy is a tie, I pick on the things that matter after deployment: can the business read the model, and is its ranking stable?

Why logistic regression got the job

Logistic regression gives odds ratios that a retention team can act on directly:

Feature Odds ratio What it means
Two-year contract 0.33 a third of the churn odds of month-to-month
Fibre-optic internet 2.43 2.4 times the odds of DSL
Tenure (per ~24 months) 0.45 churn risk halves with every two years
Tech support add-on 0.68 support customers stay more often

I checked whether the simple model was leaving signal on the table: permutation importance on the gradient-boosting model ranks the same drivers (tenure, contract, fibre) at the top. The model is also stable: eight variations (L1 or L2, C from 0.1 to 10, with and without class weights) all land within 0.001 AUC of each other.

Two details that are easy to miss

Collinearity. MonthlyCharges is almost entirely determined by the service flags (R² = 0.999), and TotalCharges is essentially tenure times monthly charges (r = 0.9996). Keeping them makes coefficients unreadable without adding information, so both were dropped, leaving 22 model features.

The threshold. The default 0.5 threshold is rarely the right one for an imbalanced problem. I set it at the point on the precision–recall curve that maximises F1 (0.35 for logistic regression), which gives precision 0.58 and recall 0.70. Class weighting does something similar: class_weight="balanced" lifts recall from 0.52 to 0.79 at the default threshold, at a cost in precision.

What it means for a retention campaign

A churn model is only useful if it changes who gets a call. Ranking customers by predicted probability:

  • contacting the top 20% reaches 50% of the churners and 56% of the revenue at risk;
  • the top 30% reaches 66% of the churners and 71% of that revenue.

Limits

The dataset is a single snapshot with no time dimension, so the model predicts who has churned rather than who will churn next quarter. The threshold ignores the cost of contacting a customer, which a real campaign would put in.

  • Code, notebook and the 10-page report: github.com/engomaressam/telco-churn-classification
  • Kaggle notebook: Telco churn: 6 models compared
  • Model: omaressamrme/telco-churn-logistic-regression

Omar Essam El Sherbiny. Head of Data at WalaPlus. Data platforms on Google Cloud, data governance, applied ML. More at omaressam.web.app.

title: 6 Problems with Traditional Video Surveillance and How AI Can Solve Them
description:
Author: Burak Kekeç

Published: October 14, 2026

Updated: October 22, 2026

Reading time: 11 min

Source: Ant Media

IP cameras have become a fundamental part of modern video surveillance systems. They are used almost everywhere: construction sites, factories, warehouses, retail stores, campuses, transportation systems, smart cities, and traditional security installations.

Deploying cameras, however, is no longer the hardest part.

A modern surveillance system may have tens, hundreds, or even thousands of cameras continuously producing video. The real challenge is turning all that video into useful information. A camera can capture an event. But who is going to notice it?

Traditional video surveillance systems are designed primarily to capture, display, and record video. While these capabilities remain essential, they are no longer sufficient for environments that require proactive monitoring, rapid incident detection, and intelligent analysis.

AI video surveillance is used across many industries, including construction, manufacturing, warehouses, retail, and security. It helps organizations detect safety risks, monitor equipment, identify unusual activities, and improve operational efficiency through intelligent video analysis.

Let’s explore six major problems with traditional video surveillance and how Ant Media Server and AIVision can help solve them.

Table of contents

  1. Human Operators Cannot Monitor Every Camera
  2. Too Much Video, Too Little Useful Information
  3. Traditional Video Analytics Are Difficult to Customize
  4. Limited Control Over AI Processing and Data Privacy
  5. Continuous AI Analysis Can Be Expensive and Resource-Intensive
  6. Adding AI to Existing Video Surveillance Infrastructure Is Complex
  7. Bonus: Real-World Example – Detecting Workers Without Safety Helmets

1. Human Operators Cannot Monitor Every Camera

The Problem

Traditional surveillance systems generally follow a simple model:

Camera → Video Management System → Monitor / Recording → Human Operator

This works well for viewing and recording video, but it creates several problems as the number of cameras grows.

Imagine a construction site with 50 cameras.

An operator may need to detect something that happens for only a few seconds:

  • A worker entering a restricted area.
  • Someone working without a safety helmet.
  • Smoke appearing in a corner of the site.
  • A person falling or experiencing an accident.

Even if every camera is working perfectly, expecting someone to continuously monitor dozens of video feeds and notice every important event is unrealistic.

The problem becomes even larger when hundreds or thousands of cameras are involved.

The Solution: AI-Assisted Monitoring

Instead of relying entirely on human attention, AI can analyze camera feeds and identify potentially important situations.

Ant Media Server manages incoming IP camera streams, while AIVision connects those streams to Vision Language Models (VLMs) capable of understanding visual content.

For example, AIVision can periodically analyze camera frames using questions such as:

  • Is anyone not wearing a safety helmet?
  • Is there smoke or fire visible?
  • Has anyone entered a restricted area?
  • Is anyone lying on the ground?

When a potential problem is identified, the system can generate an event or alert for further action.

2. Too Much Video, Too Little Useful Information

The Problem

Surveillance cameras generate enormous amounts of video. But most of that video does not require anyone’s attention.

A camera monitoring a warehouse entrance, for example, may record for 24 hours while only a handful of events actually matter.

Traditional surveillance systems often require operators to:

  • Continuously watch live camera feeds.
  • Manually review recordings after an incident.
  • Search through hours of video to identify relevant moments.
  • Determine whether an event requires further investigation.

The challenge is not capturing video. It is finding the few important moments hidden inside thousands of hours of recordings.

The Solution: Turn Video into Actionable Events

AIVision changes the workflow from passively recording everything to actively identifying relevant events.

Live Stream → Sample Frame → Vision Model → Analysis → Result

AIVision can periodically extract frames from live streams and submit them to a vision model for analysis.

The resulting information can be associated with the stream and timestamp, stored, and retrieved through APIs.

For example, rather than searching through hours of construction-site recordings, an application can use AI-generated results to identify when a potential safety violation occurred.

This enables applications to:

  • Identify important events automatically.
  • Associate analysis results with specific cameras and timestamps.
  • Retrieve relevant detections through APIs.
  • Build notification systems and monitoring dashboards.
  • Help operators focus on events instead of continuously watching video.

The result is a shift from passive video recording toward actionable video intelligence.

3. Traditional Video Analytics Are Difficult to Customize

The Problem

Traditional computer vision systems are often built around specialized models designed for specific detection tasks.

For example:

  • Helmet detection may require a dedicated PPE detection model.
  • Fire detection may require a separate fire and smoke detection model.
  • Fall detection may require a distinct pose estimation and fall detection pipeline.
  • Equipment monitoring may require another specialized solution.

Each new requirement can introduce additional model development, integration, deployment, and maintenance work.

This becomes particularly challenging when surveillance requirements change frequently or when different industries need different types of analysis.

The Solution: Use Vision Language Models and Natural Language Prompts

Vision Language Models introduce a more flexible approach. Instead of building a separate detection pipeline for every question, applications can describe what they want to know about an image using natural language.

For example, the same camera stream could be analyzed using different prompts:

  • “Is anyone not wearing a safety helmet?”
  • “Is there smoke or fire visible?”
  • “Has anyone entered the restricted area?”
  • “Describe any potentially unsafe activity in this image.”
  • “What objects are visible in the scene?”

AIVision provides the integration layer between live video streams and these vision models.

In suitable use cases, introducing a new surveillance rule may become a matter of defining a new prompt rather than developing an entirely new computer vision pipeline.

This approach also enables capabilities beyond traditional object detection, including:

  • Scene description.
  • Optical Character Recognition (OCR).
  • Visual question answering.
  • Context-aware scene analysis.

Specialized models may still be preferable for tasks requiring high accuracy, precise localization, or continuous motion analysis. However, VLMs offer a flexible alternative for many visual monitoring scenarios.

4. Limited Control Over AI Processing and Data Privacy

The Problem

One approach to AI video analytics is continuously sending video or extracted images to external cloud services.

However, this may not be acceptable for every organization.

Factories, construction sites, corporate campuses, critical infrastructure, and other private environments may contain sensitive visual information.

Cloud-based processing can introduce several concerns:

  • Sensitive video data leaving the organization’s infrastructure.
  • Dependency on external AI service providers.
  • Additional data transfer and inference costs.
  • Security and compliance requirements.
  • Limited control over how video data is processed.

For many organizations, keeping video recordings on-premise is not enough. AI inference and analysis results may also need to remain within their own infrastructure.

The Solution: On-Premise AI Video Analytics

AIVision provides the flexibility to use both cloud-based and locally hosted AI models, allowing organizations to choose the deployment approach that best fits their requirements.

  • Cloud AI Models: Leverage cloud-based vision-language models without maintaining dedicated AI infrastructure.
  • On-Premise AI Models: Process video data within your own infrastructure to meet privacy, security, or compliance requirements.
  • Model Flexibility: Use different compatible vision-language models without redesigning the entire video surveillance system.
  • Infrastructure Independence: Deploy Ant Media Server on-premise or in the cloud, depending on your operational needs.

With Ant Media Server and AIVision, organizations can build AI-powered video surveillance solutions without being locked into a single AI provider or deployment environment.

For the use cases which requires data privacy, it offers such an architecture.

IP Cameras → Local Ant Media Server → AIVision → Local Vision Model

In this architecture:

  • IP camera streams are received by a locally deployed Ant Media Server.
  • AIVision extracts frames within the organization’s infrastructure.
  • Frames are analyzed by a locally running vision model.
  • Analysis results can be stored and accessed locally.
  • External cloud AI APIs are not required.

This provides several advantages:

  • Data ownership: Greater control over sensitive video information.
  • Security: Support for private and isolated network deployments.
  • Independence: Reduced dependency on external AI providers.
  • Cost control: Avoidance of per-request cloud inference fees.
  • Flexibility: Greater control over the selection and deployment of vision models.

Organizations can therefore introduce AI capabilities without necessarily transferring their surveillance data to external services.

5. Continuous AI Analysis Can Be Expensive and Resource-Intensive

The Problem

Analyzing every frame from every surveillance camera can require significant computing resources.

Consider a surveillance system with 100 cameras operating at 30 frames per second.

That produces:

100 cameras × 30 FPS = 3,000 frames per second

Running AI inference on every frame may require substantial GPU capacity.

However, not every surveillance application needs frame-by-frame analysis.

For example:

  • Checking whether workers are wearing safety helmets may only require periodic inspection.
  • Monitoring warehouse occupancy may not require continuous inference.
  • Checking whether an area is obstructed may be possible at longer intervals.

Processing every frame can therefore be unnecessary for certain use cases.

The Solution: Configurable Frame Sampling

AIVision can periodically extract frames from live streams instead of continuously sending every frame to an AI model.

For example:

  • Sample a frame every few seconds for workplace safety checks.
  • Sample a frame every minute for periodic environmental inspection.
  • Use longer intervals for low-priority monitoring tasks.

The sampling interval can be configured according to the application’s requirements.

This approach reduces the number of AI inference operations and can significantly lower the computing resources required. It also allows organizations to allocate processing capacity according to the importance of each monitoring task.

For fast-moving events, however, longer sampling intervals can miss short incidents. Sampling frequency should therefore match the detection requirements of each application.

6. Adding AI to Existing Video Surveillance Infrastructure Is Complex

The Problem

Building an AI-powered surveillance system from scratch often requires integrating several independent components.

A typical implementation may need to:

  • Receive streams from IP cameras.
  • Decode incoming video.
  • Extract individual frames.
  • Convert frames into formats supported by AI models.
  • Communicate with inference services.
  • Process and store analysis results.
  • Expose APIs for other applications.
  • Deliver video streams to monitoring interfaces.

Managing these components separately increases development complexity and maintenance effort.

Organizations may already have a working surveillance infrastructure but lack a straightforward way to add AI analysis to their existing video streams.

The Solution: Integrate AI Directly into Ant Media Server

Ant Media Server provides the video infrastructure required to ingest, manage, process, record, and deliver live streams.

IP cameras and other video sources can be connected to Ant Media Server, which supports streaming technologies including WebRTC, HLS, and LL-HLS for video delivery. AIVision Plugin extends this infrastructure by connecting live video streams to AI vision models.

IP Camera → Ant Media Server → AIVision → Vision Model → Analysis Result

Rather than developing an entirely separate AI video processing infrastructure, developers can build on the existing Ant Media Server ecosystem.

AIVision provides capabilities for:

  • Sampling frames from live streams.
  • Sending images and natural-language prompts to vision models.
  • Receiving AI-generated analysis results.
  • Storing results and alerts.
  • Accessing information through REST APIs.
  • Building custom monitoring applications.

This makes it easier to add AI-powered video intelligence to existing streaming workflows.

Bonus: Real-World Example – Detecting Workers Without Safety Helmets

Consider a construction site with 20 IP cameras monitoring different working areas.

Traditionally, someone would need to monitor those cameras continuously or review recordings after an incident.

With Ant Media Server and AIVision, the workflow changes:

  1. Stream Ingestion: The IP cameras publish their streams directly to Ant Media Server.
  2. Sampling & Prompting: AIVision periodically extracts frames from selected streams and sends them to a vision model with the prompt: “Is there any person in this image who is not wearing a safety helmet?”
  3. Analysis: The vision model analyzes the frame. If no violation is visible, no action is taken.
  4. Event Trigger: If a worker without a helmet is detected, the result is attached to the stream with a precise timestamp.
  5. Action: An application built on the AIVision API generates a notification, highlights the relevant camera feed, and alerts safety personnel. 
Camera → AMS → AIVision → VLM → Safety Violation → Event / Alert

Instead of requiring someone to continuously watch all 20 cameras, the system helps direct human attention toward situations that may require action.

We will present how AIVision works in the next blogpost for this example. The screenshot above is just a teaser.

Conclusion: From Traditional Surveillance to Video Intelligence

Traditional video surveillance systems are effective at recording and monitoring environments, but they still rely heavily on human attention and manual processes. AI-powered surveillance goes a step further by automatically analyzing video streams, detecting potential risks, and providing actionable insights in real time.

By combining Ant Media Server’s video streaming capabilities with AIVision’s AI-powered analysis, organizations can build smarter surveillance solutions without replacing their existing camera infrastructure. This makes it easier to improve safety, reduce manual monitoring, and scale surveillance operations across different environments.

Ready to make your cameras smarter? Try AIVision and start building your own AI-powered surveillance solution.
