title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2.
description:
1. Introduction

Cloud computing has transformed the way businesses, institutions, and individuals access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, organizations had to purchase physical servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and other IT infrastructure to operate their applications and services. However, maintaining these resources could be expensive and time-consuming.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, including Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS).

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is one of the most important cloud computing models because it provides users with virtualized computing resources over the internet.

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its characteristics, benefits, and challenges, using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) as a practical case study.

  1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized IT resources such as servers, storage, networking, and computing power over the internet.

Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware, users rent computing infrastructure from a cloud service provider and pay according to their usage.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including servers, data centres, and networking hardware, while customers manage their operating systems, applications, and data.

Key Characteristics of IaaS

Some major characteristics of IaaS include:

  • Virtualization: Physical computing resources are converted into virtual machines that multiple users can access.
  • Scalability: Users can increase or decrease computing resources depending on demand.
  • Pay-as-you-go pricing: Customers pay for the resources they consume.
  • Resource management: Users have control over operating systems, applications, and configurations.
  • Internet accessibility: Infrastructure can be accessed and managed remotely.
  • Flexibility: Users can select computing resources according to their specific requirements.
  1. Case Study: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2)

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a cloud computing service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS).

It is a practical example of Infrastructure as a Service because it allows users to rent virtual servers instead of purchasing physical computers and server equipment.

With Amazon EC2, developers and organizations can launch virtual machines, install operating systems, deploy applications, configure networks, and manage storage.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Amazon EC2 operates through virtualization technology.

Users access the AWS management console and select the computing resources they need. They can choose an operating system, processor capacity, memory, storage, and networking configurations.

Once configured, AWS provisions a virtual server known as an EC2 instance.

The user can then:

  1. Launch a virtual server.
  2. Select an operating system such as Linux or Windows.
  3. Install the required software and applications.
  4. Configure security and network settings.
  5. Store and manage application data.
  6. Increase or decrease computing resources when necessary.

This allows organizations to operate applications without owning physical server infrastructure.

  1. Major Features of Amazon EC2

Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for businesses and developers.

  1. Virtual Servers

EC2 provides virtual machines that users can configure according to their computing requirements.

  1. Flexible Computing Resources

Users can select different combinations of processing power, memory, storage, and networking capabilities.

  1. Storage Integration

EC2 supports integration with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent storage for virtual servers.

  1. Security Management

Users can configure security groups, which function as virtual firewalls to control network traffic entering and leaving their instances.

  1. Scalability

Computing capacity can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

  1. Multiple Availability Locations

AWS provides different geographical regions and Availability Zones, allowing organizations to deploy applications across separate locations to improve resilience.

  1. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

Amazon EC2 offers several advantages.

Cost Reduction

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers or maintain large server rooms. They can rent resources and pay according to their usage.

Scalability and Flexibility

Businesses can increase their computing resources during periods of high demand and reduce them when demand decreases.

Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be created within minutes, allowing developers to deploy applications without waiting for physical hardware installation.

Reliability

Applications can be deployed across multiple Availability Zones to reduce dependence on a single location.

Remote Accessibility

Users can manage their cloud infrastructure from different geographical locations through the internet.

  1. Challenges and Limitations of Amazon EC2

Despite its advantages, Amazon EC2 has some limitations.

  1. Security Responsibilities: Although AWS protects its physical infrastructure, customers must secure their operating systems, applications, access permissions, and data.

  2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud resources requires a reliable internet connection.

  3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused instances continue running.

  4. Technical Complexity: Managing virtual servers, networking, operating systems, and security configurations requires technical knowledge.

  5. Vendor Dependency: Organizations may become dependent on AWS services, making migration to another provider complicated.

  6. Practical Application of Amazon EC2

Consider a university that wants to develop an online student registration system.

Traditionally, the university would need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networks, and employ technical personnel to maintain the infrastructure.

Using Amazon EC2, the university can:

  • Launch a virtual server to host its registration application.
  • Install the required operating system and web server.
  • Deploy the student registration application.
  • Connect the application to a database service.
  • Configure security to protect student information.
  • Increase computing capacity during registration periods when many students access the platform.

This demonstrates how IaaS can help educational institutions reduce infrastructure costs, improve flexibility, and manage changing computing demands.

  1. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has become an important component of modern cloud computing because it provides flexible, scalable, and cost-effective computing resources.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how organizations can access virtual servers, storage, and networking resources without purchasing and maintaining physical infrastructure.

Although IaaS introduces challenges such as security responsibilities, internet dependency, and cost management, its benefits make it a valuable solution for businesses, educational institutions, developers, and other organizations.

As technology continues to evolve, IaaS will remain an important foundation for digital transformation and modern application development.

  1. References

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)? https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html

  4. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation. https://aws.amazon.com/documentation-overview/ec2/

  5. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). AWS Shared Responsibility Model. https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox

A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

title: Cohere Rerank v5 Pro and Fast for C# Developers
description:
Most retrieval-augmented apps follow the same path. A vector search returns 30 or 50 passages, and the chat model reads all of them. Some of those passages are close but wrong. Some are right but buried. The model spends tokens on the noise and sometimes answers from the wrong paragraph.

A reranker sits between the search and the chat model. It reads the query and the candidate passages together, scores each one, and returns them in order of relevance. Your code decides how many to keep and where to cut.

Cohere Rerank v5 is now in Microsoft Foundry in two versions, Pro and Fast, and both add a feature called Context Focus. This post covers when each one fits, a table of the trade-offs, and a C# console app that calls both.

If you missed it, I covered the Cohere family in Foundry earlier in Cohere Command A+ Lands in Microsoft Foundry. Command A+ is the chat model that pairs well with a reranker like this one.

Sources for the model details below: the Foundry announcement (October 21, 2026), the Cohere Rerank 5 post, and the Cohere Rerank v5 changelog. I've used only one figure from Cohere's evaluations, the calibration error, because it changes how you set thresholds. Your own queries and documents will tell you more.

What you get

Three things from the Rerank 5 release matter for .NET apps:

  • Two tiers. Pro is tuned for ranking quality, especially reasoning-heavy queries and long or specialized documents. Fast is tuned for low latency and high throughput.
  • Calibrated scores. The relevance_score is meant to behave the same way across queries and domains. Cohere suggests a cut-off of 0.50 for Pro and 0.45 for Fast, so one number can filter results before they reach the model.
  • Context Focus. An optional setting that returns the most relevant character spans inside each document, so you can pass a few sentences to the chat model instead of whole pages. It is off by default.

The Foundry model cards list both models as text classification, in preview, for over 100 languages, with text and image input.

The numbers that matter for design

Rerank v5 Pro Rerank v5 Fast
Foundry model name Cohere-rerank-v5-pro Cohere-rerank-v5-fast
API model ID rerank-v5.0-pro rerank-v5.0-fast
Languages Over 100 Over 100
Score cut-off suggested by Cohere 0.50 0.45
Expected Calibration Error (lower is better) ~0.06 (Rerank 4 Pro: ~0.38) ~0.06
Cohere API price $0.05 per 1M tokens $0.02 per 1M tokens
Status on Foundry Preview Preview

Calibration is what makes one cut-off work across queries. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures how far a score sits from the real chance that a passage is useful. Cohere reports about 0.06 for both Rerank 5 models, against 0.38 for Rerank 4 Pro on human judgments (0.31 on NIST judgments). In practice, a Rerank 5 score of 0.7 is much closer to a real 70% chance of being useful, so a fixed threshold filters the same way on every query. These are Cohere's own figures from the Rerank 5 post.

⚠️ Uncertain: Foundry price. Cohere's own price is listed above. The Foundry model cards link to a pricing page, which is in-correct; thus rather than showing a rate, confirm the Foundry rate before you try out the samples.

Where each one fits

These are the situations where reranking earns its place. Each one has a clear reason to rerank.

1. Grounding a RAG answer

Your vector search returns 40 passages. Rerank them, keep the top 3 that clear the threshold, and send only those to the chat model. The answer is grounded in fewer, better passages, and the prompt stays small.

Use Pro here. A wrong passage in the final three is expensive, because the chat model will quote it confidently.

2. Agents that search many times per task

An agent might run 5 to 10 searches before it answers. Each search returns a candidate list that needs ordering. The latency adds up across those calls.

Use Fast here. The quality gap matters less than the time per call, and the agent can run more searches inside the same budget.

3. Help-desk article matching

A customer writes "I was charged twice this month". Your help center has a few hundred articles. Vector search finds the likely ones, and the reranker decides which article to show first.

Use Fast for high volume, and check a sample of matches with Pro during setup.

4. Multilingual support content

Support articles are often written in one language and asked about in another. Both models cover over 100 languages, so the same reranker can order English, Spanish, German, and Japanese passages against one query.

Test both on your own languages. Cohere's language claims are general, and your articles may behave differently.

5. Semi-structured records

Product catalogs, incident logs, and CRM entries are often JSON or tables. Cohere's guidance is to pass each record as a YAML string so the field names stay with the values. That gives the reranker more to match on. Plain JSON may also work, so test both formats on your own records before you settle on one.

Use Pro when records are long or specialized, such as contracts or clinical notes.

6. Answer or abstain

This is the use case I'd build first. When no candidate clears the threshold, the app says "I do not know" and does not call the chat model at all. The calibrated score makes that cut-off possible without guessing.

Either model works. Set the threshold, then test it against queries you know have no answer in your data.

Pros and cons

Model Good for Pros Cons Pick it when
Pro RAG grounding, long or specialized documents, reasoning-heavy queries Ranks complex queries better, stronger on long documents Slower and more expensive per call than Fast The top few results must be right, and a wrong pick costs more than the extra latency
Fast Agents with many searches, high-volume help-desk matching Low latency, high throughput, lower price Less accurate on hard or long documents Volume and speed matter more than the last few points of quality
Neither Tiny candidate lists you can scan in code No extra call, no extra cost Does not scale to large lists or fuzzy queries You have fewer than about five candidates

Two things a reranker does not do:

  • It does not search. You pass it the candidates. Keep your vector or keyword search for finding them.
  • It does not write. Summaries, rewrites, and answers still belong to the chat model. The reranker decides what the chat model reads.

Calling Rerank v5 from C

The complete project is on GitHub at taswar/Cohere-Rerank-V5-Pro-Fast-Csharp-Sample. Clone it if you want to run the code without copying it from this post.

The sample reads an endpoint for Pro and one for Fast. When both models are deployed in the same Foundry resource, the two endpoints are the same URL. Each one takes an API key if you set one. If you leave the key out, the app signs in with Entra ID through DefaultAzureCredential, so run az login first. The sample sends the same query to both and prints each result with a keep or drop decision based on that model's cut-off.

The request goes to {endpoint}/providers/cohere/v2/rerank, the Foundry route for Cohere models, with a bearer token in the Authorization header. The token is your API key if you set one, or an Entra ID token if you don't. The model field takes the Foundry model name, Cohere-rerank-v5-pro or Cohere-rerank-v5-fast. If your deployment expects a different header or path, the code is the only part to change.

Create the project on .NET 10 and add the configuration packages:

dotnet new console -n Cohere-Rerank-v5-CSharp-Sample
cd Cohere-Rerank-v5-CSharp-Sample
dotnet add package Azure.Identity
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.UserSecrets
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.EnvironmentVariables
dotnet user-secrets init

Store the endpoints with user secrets. Use the base URL of your Foundry resource, with no path. The two API key lines are optional, so leave them out to use Entra ID:

dotnet user-secrets set "COHERE_RERANK_PRO_ENDPOINT" "https://YOUR-RESOURCE.services.ai.azure.com"
dotnet user-secrets set "COHERE_RERANK_PRO_API_KEY" "your-pro-key"
dotnet user-secrets set "COHERE_RERANK_FAST_ENDPOINT" "https://YOUR-RESOURCE.services.ai.azure.com"
dotnet user-secrets set "COHERE_RERANK_FAST_API_KEY" "your-fast-key"

To check what the app will read, run:

dotnet user-secrets list

The project file is Cohere-Rerank-v5-CSharp-Sample.csproj. The UserSecretsId is the one dotnet user-secrets init writes:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <UserSecretsId>b9934625-9fc9-4364-ae1e-0107ce65b680</UserSecretsId>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Azure.Identity" Version="1.21.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.EnvironmentVariables" Version="10.0.12" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.UserSecrets" Version="10.0.12" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Then Program.cs:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Net.Http.Headers;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Nodes;
using Azure.Core;
using Azure.Identity;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;

var config = new ConfigurationBuilder()
    .AddUserSecrets<Program>()
    .AddEnvironmentVariables()
    .Build();

var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();

var pro = ReadModel(config, "Pro", "Cohere-rerank-v5-pro", 0.50);
var fast = ReadModel(config, "Fast", "Cohere-rerank-v5-fast", 0.45);

var query = "What is the refund window for annual plans?";
var documents = new[]
{
    "Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time. The change takes effect at the end of the billing period.",
    "Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, the remaining months are prorated.",
    "Refund requests are submitted from the billing page under Invoices.",
    "Our offices are closed on public holidays in Ottawa and Toronto.",
    "Enterprise contracts follow the terms in the signed order form, not this page.",
    "Gift cards cannot be refunded but can be transferred to another account."
};

using var http = new HttpClient { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60) };

foreach (var model in new[] { pro, fast })
{
    var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    var results = await RerankAsync(http, credential, model, query, documents, topN: 3);
    stopwatch.Stop();

    Console.WriteLine($"{model.Name} ({stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms, threshold {model.Threshold:0.00})");
    foreach (var result in results)
    {
        var decision = result.Score >= model.Threshold ? "keep" : "drop";
        Console.WriteLine($"  {result.Score:0.00}  {decision}  {documents[result.Index]}");
    }

    var kept = results.Count(r => r.Score >= model.Threshold);
    Console.WriteLine(kept == 0
        ? "  No passage cleared the threshold. Answer 'I do not know' instead of guessing."
        : $"  {kept} passage(s) passed to the chat model.");
    Console.WriteLine();
}

static RerankModel ReadModel(IConfiguration config, string name, string modelId, double threshold)
{
    var key = name.ToUpperInvariant();
    var endpoint = config[$"COHERE_RERANK_{key}_ENDPOINT"]
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException($"Set COHERE_RERANK_{key}_ENDPOINT with dotnet user-secrets.");
    // The API key is optional. Without one, the app signs in with Entra ID through az login.
    var apiKey = config[$"COHERE_RERANK_{key}_API_KEY"];

    return new RerankModel(name, modelId, endpoint.TrimEnd('/'), apiKey, threshold);
}

static async Task<List<RerankResult>> RerankAsync(
    HttpClient http, TokenCredential credential, RerankModel model, string query,
    IReadOnlyList<string> documents, int topN)
{
    var body = new JsonObject
    {
        ["model"] = model.ModelId,
        ["query"] = query,
        ["top_n"] = topN,
        ["documents"] = new JsonArray(documents.Select(d => (JsonNode)d).ToArray())
    };

    using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, $"{model.Endpoint}/providers/cohere/v2/rerank");
    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(model.ApiKey))
    {
        request.Headers.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", model.ApiKey);
    }
    else
    {
        var token = await credential.GetTokenAsync(
            new TokenRequestContext(["https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default"]),
            CancellationToken.None);
        request.Headers.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token.Token);
    }

    // StringContent sets a fixed Content-Length; JsonContent uses chunked encoding.
    request.Content = new StringContent(body.ToJsonString(), Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");

    using var response = await http.SendAsync(request);
    var text = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
    if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
    {
        throw new InvalidOperationException($"{model.Name} returned {(int)response.StatusCode}: {text}");
    }

    using var doc = JsonDocument.Parse(text);
    var results = new List<RerankResult>();
    foreach (var item in doc.RootElement.GetProperty("results").EnumerateArray())
    {
        results.Add(new RerankResult(
            item.GetProperty("index").GetInt32(),
            item.GetProperty("relevance_score").GetDouble()));
    }

    return results;
}

record RerankModel(string Name, string ModelId, string Endpoint, string? ApiKey, double Threshold);

record RerankResult(int Index, double Score);

Run it:

dotnet run

Run it on your own query and documents before you copy the thresholds. The output shows each passage with its score, the keep or drop decision, and the time per call. Your timings and scores will differ from anyone else's, so record them alongside your data.

Output 

Pro (2512 ms, threshold 0.50)
  0.81  keep  Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, the remaining months are prorated.
  0.13  drop  Refund requests are submitted from the billing page under Invoices.
  0.06  drop  Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time. The change takes effect at the end of the billing period.
  1 passage(s) passed to the chat model.

Fast (2138 ms, threshold 0.45)
  0.81  keep  Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, the remaining months are prorated.
  0.06  drop  Refund requests are submitted from the billing page under Invoices.
  0.05  drop  Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time. The change takes effect at the end of the billing period.
  1 passage(s) passed to the chat model.

The sample doesn't use Context Focus yet. To try it, add a relevant_spans object to the request body, with mode set to enabled and a threshold and max_spans. Cohere's changelog shows the shape, and the spans come back in each result.

Final thoughts

The reranker is the cheapest quality step in a RAG pipeline. It doesn't write anything, and it doesn't need your whole index. You pass it the candidates your search already found, and it tells you which ones matter.

Start with Fast if you run many searches, and Pro for answers where the top passage has to be right. Whichever you pick, set the threshold on your own data, and build the "I do not know" path before you tune anything else. 🙂

Resources

  • Cohere-Rerank-V5-Pro-Fast-Csharp-Sample on GitHub
  • Cohere Rerank V5 is now available in Microsoft Foundry
  • Cohere Rerank 5 (Cohere blog)
  • Cohere Rerank v5 changelog
  • Cohere on Azure: reranking
  • Cohere-rerank-v5-pro in the Foundry catalog
  • Cohere-rerank-v5-fast in the Foundry catalog
  • Cohere Command A+ in Microsoft Foundry (previous post)

title: Break it before you merge it: introducing litmus-lite
description:
Several years ago, we started LitmusChaos with a simple belief: chaos engineering is not just for Ops. Litmus has since grown into a CNCF incubating project, and many SRE and platform teams use it to put chaos to work on Kubernetes.

But one moment kept nagging us. You are about to open a pull request. You added a retry, a timeout, maybe a fallback. You think it works. The honest way to find out is to make the dependency slow or flaky and watch, but that usually means a cluster, a platform team, or a throwaway script nobody will ever run again. So most of us skip it, and production runs the test for us.

So we built the other end of the loop, at the developer's desk.

litmus-lite is chaos testing for developers and their agents.

It is one static binary. You describe a failure and what must stay true, it injects the failure, watches your service, and tells you which of your statements held. No cluster, no control plane, no account.

From a sentence to a verdict

In Cursor (or any MCP client), you just ask:

Add 800 ms of latency to the checkout API for 12 seconds and tell me whether it copes and how fast it recovers.

The agent writes a *.chaos.yaml next to your service, validates it, runs it, and answers in terms of the hypotheses it wrote. The important part: the test is the file. Commit it, review it, change a number, and run it again without the agent. Every MCP tool is just a CLI command you could have typed.

It fits how developers already work

  • Tests live in your repo. A scenario sits beside the service it tests and goes through code review like any other test.
  • It runs where your tests run. In a terminal or in CI, with -junit for your test reporter. The exit code is the verdict: 0 every hypothesis held, 3 the run finished and one did not. That is a finding about your service, not a tool error.
  • CI setup is one command. litmus-lite ci github writes a workflow that validates every scenario on every push.
  • It can reach into your code. For Go services, a small failpoint package lets you put hooks in your own code. They stay dark until a scenario arms them, so you can fail "the charge step" and not just "the network".
  • You stay in control. An agent cannot grant itself destructive permissions. Loopback targets only, PIDs you name, -yes for anything irreversible, and every fault is rolled back on exit or Ctrl-C.

A verdict you can trust

There is no "resilience: 73" here. You state what must hold, such as error_rate < 15% or recovery <= 5s, and the run reports which statements held. No data counts as a failure, and a service that never came back fails as "not recovered".

Every run also writes one self-contained HTML report that puts the fault next to its impact, so you can see the failure land and the service recover (or not):

A real red run: the sample service has no fallback, and the report says so.

Under the hood there is plenty to break: HTTP latency, errors and timeouts through a built-in proxy, failpoints, process pause and kill, docker pause, CPU and memory pressure, and disk fill. Add a load generator (VegaLoad, k6 or your own command) when you want to see what real traffic felt during the fault. And there is no telemetry: by default, nothing leaves your machine.

Try it in five minutes 

# Grab a release: https://github.com/litmuschaos/litmus-lite/releases
litmus-lite init     # connects Cursor (MCP server + rules); other MCP clients work too

Then ask your agent for a failure. The quick start walks you through one green run and one red run against a sample service. The red one ends with a line I like a lot:

Hypothesis charge survives its own outage failed: error_rate < 5% (observed 100.00%).

A test that can fail, and tells you why in plain words, is the whole point.

Where this goes next

This is a start, not a finish. Directions we are excited about (ideas, not promises):

  • Richer probes: request headers and bodies, JSON assertions, TCP probes.
  • Per-probe hypotheses and breakdowns in the report.
  • A published container image, so a scenario can also run as an in-cluster Job.
  • More faults, driven by what you ask for, including reaching apps running in VMs and path to the bigger experiments on your Kubernetes clusters via the OG LitmusChaos!

Come build it with us

litmus-lite is Apache-2.0 and developed in the open, and the best time to shape it is now:

  • Try it on your own service and tell us what broke, what confused you, and what you wished it did. Open an issue.
  • Add a fault or a hub template. Faults are plugins, so adding one barely touches the engine. See CONTRIBUTING.
  • Improve the docs, or share the prompt that made your agent do something clever.
  • Say hi in #litmus on Kubernetes Slack.

Start here:

  • Overview: litmuschaos.io/litmus-lite
  • Docs: litmuschaos.github.io/litmus-lite
  • Code and releases: github.com/litmuschaos/litmus-lite

Chaos engineering began as a way for teams to build confidence in production. We would love litmus-lite to help it start a little earlier, at the developer's desk, with a sentence and a file. Pip is waiting.

Uma Mukkara and Karthik Satchitanand, co-creators of LitmusChaos

title: React vs Angular: Which Should Beginners Learn?
description:
Imagine a student three weeks into JavaScript. A friend says "learn React." A YouTube video says "Angular gets you hired in big companies." A college senior says "just pick one." The student closes the laptop and learns nothing that day.

If that sounds familiar, this guide is for you. It covers react vs angular for beginners, with real code, current data, and a clear rule for choosing.

Why this choice matters

Both tools build the part of a website that users see and click, called the frontend. Both are mature and used in real products, so neither is a "dead" option.

Still, the choice shapes your first six months. It decides what you read, which jobs you can apply for, and how fast you build your first project.

In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, React was used by 44.7% of respondents and Angular by 18.2%. The State of JavaScript 2025 survey reports that the front-end ranking stayed stable, and that React tops the list of developer pain points, partly because it is the most used tool.

Usage favors React, and complaints exist for both. The real question is which one fits you.

What React and Angular actually are

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. A library gives you tools for one job, and you choose the rest yourself, such as routing, forms, and data fetching.

Angular is a full framework from Google. A framework makes more decisions for you. Routing, forms, HTTP calls, and testing tools come in the box, and it uses TypeScript by default.

TypeScript is JavaScript with types. A type tells the code what kind of value to expect, like a number or a string. It catches many mistakes before you run the app.

React Angular
Type Library Full framework
Language JavaScript or TypeScript TypeScript
Built-in routing and forms No, you pick packages Yes
Setup choices Many Few
Template style JSX (HTML inside JavaScript) HTML templates with Angular syntax
Maintained by Meta and community Google

The learning curve for students with no experience

Is React easier than Angular? React is easier to start. Angular is easier to keep organized.

React has a small core: components, props, state, and hooks. You can build a working page in a day. The hard part comes later, when you must choose a router, a state tool, and a folder structure. Nobody tells you what is "correct," so beginners often feel lost.

Angular asks for more upfront. You meet components, services, dependency injection, TypeScript, and RxJS (a tool for handling streams of data) early. The first week feels heavy. After that, every Angular project looks similar, so you rarely wonder where things go.

Think of cooking. React hands you a knife and a pan. Angular hands you a full kitchen with a manual.

The same feature in both

Let's build one small feature twice: a course list with a search box. It shows how each tool handles state, which is data that changes while the app runs.

React version 

import { useState } from "react";

const courses = [
  { id: 1, title: "HTML Basics" },
  { id: 2, title: "JavaScript Basics" },
  { id: 3, title: "React Basics" },
];

export default function CourseList() {
  // "search" holds what the user typed. setSearch updates it.
  const [search, setSearch] = useState("");

  // Keep only courses whose title matches the search text.
  const visibleCourses = courses.filter((course) =>
    course.title.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase())
  );

  return (
    <section>
      <input
        value={search}
        onChange={(event) => setSearch(event.target.value)}
        placeholder="Search courses"
      />
      <ul>
        {visibleCourses.map((course) => (
          <li key={course.id}>{course.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}

useState stores the search text. When it changes, React runs the component again and redraws the list. The key helps React track each list item.

Angular version 

import { Component, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-list',
  template: `
    <input #box (input)="search.set(box.value)" placeholder="Search courses" />
    <ul>
      @for (course of visibleCourses(); track course.id) {
        <li>{{ course.title }}</li>
      } @empty {
        <li>No courses found</li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CourseList {
  courses = [
    { id: 1, title: 'HTML Basics' },
    { id: 2, title: 'JavaScript Basics' },
    { id: 3, title: 'Angular Basics' },
  ];

  // A signal holds a value and tells Angular when it changes.
  search = signal('');

  // A computed signal recalculates only when its inputs change.
  visibleCourses = computed(() =>
    this.courses.filter((course) =>
      course.title.toLowerCase().includes(this.search().toLowerCase())
    )
  );
}

This uses current Angular features. The Angular signals guide explains signals, and the built-in @for and @if blocks replace the older *ngFor and *ngIf. Tutorials may still show the old syntax, so check the date of any course you follow.

Both versions do the same thing. React puts HTML inside JavaScript. Angular keeps the template separate and adds its own syntax. If JSX feels strange, Angular may feel safer. If decorators and extra structure feel heavy, React will feel lighter.

Starting a project today

The React team deprecated Create React App in February 2025 and now suggests starting new apps with a framework such as Next.js or React Router. For a first learning project, a simple Vite setup also works well:

npm create vite@latest my-first-app -- --template react
cd my-first-app
npm install
npm run dev

If a tutorial starts with npx create-react-app, skip it or expect differences.

Angular setup is shorter because the CLI makes the choices:

npm install -g @angular/cli
ng new my-first-app
cd my-first-app
ng serve

Angular wins on simplicity here. React gives you more freedom but asks for more decisions.

What each one teaches you

React teaches core JavaScript well. Components are mostly functions, and you use array methods like map and filter all the time. These skills transfer to almost any JavaScript job.

Angular teaches structure. You learn services, dependency injection, typed code, and testing patterns early. These habits help in large codebases and carry over to backend frameworks like Spring or .NET.

Neither choice wastes your time. Many developers learn the second tool in a few weeks once the first one clicks.

Which has more jobs in 2026, React or Angular?

Usage data points to more React openings. A tool used by 44.7% of surveyed developers will appear in more job posts than one used by 18.2%. I could not find a reliable public count of open roles for either tool, so I will not invent one.

Angular still has real demand. It is common in large companies, banks, and enterprise teams that want strict structure. Those jobs often face less competition from self-taught beginners.

You can check the market in ten minutes. Search "React developer" and "Angular developer" on LinkedIn, Naukri, and Indeed with your city and "fresher" as filters. Note the counts and the common skills listed. Live data beats any article.

React or Angular for a first job as a fresher in India

Freshers in India usually apply to two kinds of employers: product and startup teams, and large service companies.

Startups and product teams often lean toward React, since it pairs with Next.js and fits small teams. Large service companies and enterprise clients often run Angular for long projects, since its structure suits big teams.

So the best fit depends on where you want to apply. Look at 15 companies you would actually apply to. If most list React, learn React. If many list Angular, learn Angular.

Either way, job posts also ask for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Git, and REST APIs. A student who knows these well and has one real project beats a student who half-knows two frameworks.

A simple decision guide

Your situation Start with
You are new to programming and want quick wins React
You like clear rules and a fixed structure Angular
You want startup or freelance work React
You target enterprise or service company roles Angular
You already know TypeScript or Java Angular
You still cannot decide React

The last row is not a cop-out. When two options fit equally, pick the one with more tutorials and community help.

A four-week plan that works for either

  1. Week 1: JavaScript functions, arrays, objects, and fetch.
  2. Week 2: Core ideas of your chosen tool. For React: components, props, and useState. For Angular: components, signals, and templates.
  3. Week 3: Build the course list above, then add a form and fetch data from a free public API.
  4. Week 4: Add routing, deploy the project to a free host, and write a short README.

Avoid three common traps. Do not switch tools after ten days. Do not follow outdated tutorials. Do not skip JavaScript, because most "React is hard" stories are really "JavaScript is hard" stories.

The bottom line

For most beginners, React is the easier door to walk through. Its small core, large community, and wide job reach make the first months smoother. Angular is the better pick if you like structure, want enterprise roles, or already know TypeScript.

Both are safe, and both can get you hired if you build real projects. The framework you finish learning beats the framework you keep researching.

FAQ

Q1. Should I learn React or Angular first?

Ans. Most beginners should start with React because it has a smaller core and more learning material. Choose Angular first if you prefer strict structure or aim for enterprise jobs.

Q2. Is React easier than Angular for beginners?

Ans. React is easier to start. Angular takes longer at the beginning but gives you clear structure once you pass that hump.

Q3. Which has more jobs in 2026, React or Angular?

Ans. React has wider usage, so it likely appears in more job posts. Angular remains in steady demand at larger companies. Search job sites in your city to see real numbers.

Q4. Do I need TypeScript for React or Angular?

Ans. Angular requires it. React works with plain JavaScript, though many teams use TypeScript. Learn JavaScript first, then add TypeScript.

title: A Java IDE in Your Browser, With Your Files in Your Browser
description:
If you're used to opening a page and immediately changing an app, installing a Java development environment is a substantial detour. I want your first encounter with Codename One to be the app running.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Our new browser IDE is a highly experimental, very early preview. Open it, press Run and start changing the Java. It has a project tree, multiple files and an application preview. Think of the Playground growing into a proper IDE workspace.

I'm calling it Not a Cloud IDE because the editing, compilation for preview and application execution happen in your browser. Your project files stay in that browser's storage. The ordinary build server enters the workflow when you request a cloud build.

Start with an app on the screen

The first visit opens a GettingStarted project. Press Run in the top toolbar. The editor compiles Java and shows the application beside its source. This screenshot shows that starter running in the public preview:

You can start with a small edit. Inside the starter's runApp() method, this replaces its initial screen with a counter:

Form hi = new Form("First app", BoxLayout.y());
Label count = new Label("Trips: 0");
Button add = new Button("Add a trip");
int[] trips = {0};
add.addActionListener(event -> count.setText("Trips: " + (++trips[0])));
hi.addAll(count, add);
hi.show();

The starter already imports the UI and layout classes. Run it, click the button and change the label. The point of this first exercise is to shorten the distance between an idea and a visible result.

Compiler errors appear against the source. Completion, hover information and source navigation help you explore the API. They don't amount to a full Java language server or IntelliJ's refactoring model, and I don't want to present them that way.

What runs where

The site delivers the editor and toolchain. Dependencies may need downloading too. That doesn't make the editing session a remote machine: there is no server-side workspace running your development loop.

A cloud build is an explicit handoff of build inputs to the existing Codename One service. It is separate from local preview and doesn't back up your editable workspace. Opening the IDE also doesn't make the whole workflow available offline.

Browser storage is local storage

The toolbar says Saved only in this browser · No cloud backup. Take that literally. Signing in on a second computer or switching browser profiles won't bring your project along.

Use Download ZIP to keep a backup and take the project to your desktop. Clearing the site's browser data or using private browsing can erase your local work. The export gives you a project you can continue building with the usual Maven or Gradle tools.

This is also why I like the approach for getting started. You can try the framework in a page, then keep the code when you're ready to set up a local environment.

Where the experiment ends today

This will not replace IntelliJ. We can't reproduce the full Java ecosystem, every desktop tool and every build plugin inside JavaScript. Browser preview supports a defined subset of dependency and build behavior; projects outside that subset need a local build.

Backend projects can be created, edited and exported, but there is no backend runtime in the browser. Full stack preview currently runs the client only. Don't expect Wayline's backend to start inside the editor tab.

The IDE exposes settings, GUI Builder and cloud-build actions, but this is early software. A successful browser preview is also not proof that every device API will behave identically on a phone. Check your real targets as the project grows.

Make the first experiment small

Last week's Playground compiler showed real Java compilation in a page. The IDE gives that loop a workspace you can grow beyond one snippet.

Try the counter, change its layout and download the project. That is the experience I want to make ordinary: a person curious about Java can see their own change running before spending the afternoon configuring tools.

This closes our weekly release series. Between a full-stack ride-hailing application and a browser workspace, we're working on both ends of the same problem: getting you to the part of an application that is yours.

Discussion

What is the first small app you would try if opening a page were all the setup it needed?

title: SQL Pattern Matching Without the Pain: LIKE, Wildcards, and the Gotchas Nobody Warns You About
description:
A practical guide to searching text in SQL using LIKE, wildcards, SUBSTRING and LOWER, with real examples and the mistakes that cost you hours.

Every app I've worked on eventually hits the same moment: someone types a few letters into a search box and expects the right row to show up.

Behind that tiny feature sits one of the oldest tools in SQL: pattern matching. It looks simple, but it has quirks that silently return wrong results, or make a fast query crawl.

In this post I'll walk through pattern matching using a small Employees table, then cover the gotchas I wish someone had told me earlier.

The setup 

CREATE TABLE Employees (
  EmpID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name VARCHAR(50),
  Department VARCHAR(50),
  Email VARCHAR(50)
);

INSERT INTO Employees (EmpID, Name, Department, Email) VALUES
  (1, 'Alice Johnson', 'HR',      'alice.johnson@example.com'),
  (2, 'Bob Smith',     'IT',      'bob.smith@example.com'),
  (3, 'Charlie Brown', 'Finance', 'charlie.brown@example.com'),
  (4, 'Diana Prince',  'HR',      'diana.prince@example.com'),
  (5, 'Eve Adams',     'IT',      'eve.adams@example.org');

Five rows is enough. The goal is to understand the patterns, not to stress the database.

The two wildcards you need

LIKE understands exactly two special characters:

Wildcard Meaning
% any number of characters (including zero)
_ exactly one character

Everything else is matched literally. Once that clicks, most of the rest is just where you place them.

1. Starts with, ends with, contains

The position of % tells SQL what you mean.

-- Starts with 'A'
SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';
-- Alice Johnson

-- Ends with 'son'
SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE '%son';
-- Alice Johnson

-- Contains 'IT'
SELECT Name, Department FROM Employees WHERE Department LIKE '%IT%';
-- Bob Smith (IT), Eve Adams (IT)

A quick way to remember it: the % goes on the side where you don't care what comes next. 'A%' means "I care about the start, anything can follow."

2. Filtering by domain

Pattern matching is great for light data cleaning, like finding emails from one domain:

SELECT Name, Email
FROM Employees
WHERE Email LIKE '%@example.com';

This returns Alice, Bob, Charlie and Diana. Eve is left out because her address ends in .org. Including the @ in the pattern matters. Without it, '%example.com' would also match something like bob@notexample.com.

3. "Second letter is v": two ways

This one is a nice puzzle because there are two valid solutions.

Using a function:

SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE SUBSTRING(Name, 2, 1) = 'v';

Using the single-character wildcard:

SELECT Name FROM Employees WHERE Name LIKE '_v%';

Both return Eve Adams. Read the second one as: "one any character, then v, then anything."

I prefer the LIKE version. It's shorter, and it reads like the pattern it describes. SUBSTRING is better when you need to compare the extracted piece against something more complex.

4. Case-insensitive matching

Say you want everyone in HR, but your data might contain HR, hr or Hr:

SELECT Name, Department
FROM Employees
WHERE LOWER(Department) LIKE '%hr%';

Lowercasing the column and writing the pattern in lowercase makes the match independent of how the data was typed. You get Alice Johnson and Diana Prince.

The gotchas

Gotcha 1: LIKE isn't case-sensitive everywhere (or case-insensitive everywhere)

This is the biggest source of "works on my machine" bugs.

  • In PostgreSQL, LIKE is case-sensitive. It also has ILIKE for case-insensitive matching.
  • In MySQL and SQL Server, case sensitivity depends on the column's collation, and the common defaults are case-insensitive.
  • In SQLite, LIKE is case-insensitive for plain ASCII letters by default.

That affects the '%IT%' query above. On a case-insensitive setup, it would also match a department named Facilities, because "Facilities" contains "it". If exact case matters, don't rely on the default. Be explicit.

Gotcha 2: Searching for a literal % or _

What if you need to find a value like 50%_off? The wildcards get in your way. Use ESCAPE:

SELECT * FROM Promotions
WHERE Code LIKE '50\%\_off' ESCAPE '\';

The backslash tells SQL to treat the next character literally. Any time user input goes into a LIKE pattern, remember to escape these characters, or users can accidentally (or deliberately) match far more than they intended.

Gotcha 3: A leading % can make queries slow 

WHERE Name LIKE 'Ali%'   -- can use a normal index
WHERE Name LIKE '%ice'   -- usually cannot

With a pattern that starts with a fixed prefix, the database can jump into a regular index. With a leading wildcard, it generally has to scan every row. On five rows you'll never notice. On five million, you will.

If you need fast "contains" search on large tables, look at full-text search, or trigram indexes in PostgreSQL, instead of leaning on LIKE '%...%'.

Gotcha 4: NULL never matches 

SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Email LIKE '%@example.com';

A row where Email is NULL is not returned, and it won't be returned by NOT LIKE either. Comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown, not true. If you need those rows, handle them with IS NULL or COALESCE.

Which tool should I use?

You want to... Reach for
Match a simple shape (starts, ends, contains) LIKE
Match by position _ or SUBSTRING
Ignore case reliably LOWER() / UPPER() (or ILIKE in PostgreSQL)
Match complex patterns Regex (REGEXP in MySQL, ~ in PostgreSQL)
Search large text quickly Full-text search

Wrapping up

Pattern matching is one of those topics that feels too basic to study, until a search feature returns the wrong rows in production. The core ideas are small:

  1. % means "anything", _ means "exactly one character".
  2. Where you place the wildcard defines the meaning.
  3. Case sensitivity depends on your database, so check it.
  4. Leading wildcards are fine for small data and costly for big data.

Try the queries above on your own data and break them on purpose. Adding a lowercase hr row or a NULL email will teach you more than reading about it.

If this helped, drop a comment with the weirdest LIKE bug you've run into. I'd love to hear it.

title: How to Evaluate AI Agents for Production: Moving Beyond LLM-as-a-Judge
description:
This is Part 1 of a 5-part series on evaluating and hardening production AI agents. See also: Part 2: Deterministic State Evaluations, Part 3: Statistical Rigor in AI Evals, Part 4: Curating Golden Trajectories, and Part 5: Building an Agent CI/CD Pipeline.

Most AI agent demos look magical until they face unconstrained user inputs and real environment states.

In a controlled demo, an agent receives a clean prompt, calls two tools, and outputs a coherent final response. In production, teams encounter the reliability cliff: the agent gets stuck in infinite retry loops, hallucinates schema parameters, mutates production databases unexpectedly, or drifts into degenerative completions.

To solve this, engineering teams frequently reach for the industry default: LLM-as-a-judge. They pipe the agent's multi-turn transcript into a secondary frontier model, provide a rubric prompt, and ask the model to rate task completion on a scale from 1 to 5.

A note on model generations: Foundation models turn over continuously, but evaluation mechanics are invariant. Whether your agent runs on proprietary frontier APIs, domain-specialized reasoning checkpoints, or locally hosted open weights, the failure modes and statistical principles below remain identical across model lifecycles. Build evaluation harnesses that outlive the model release of the day.

This approach creates a dangerous illusion of measurement. It gives leadership a plausible-looking dashboard while leaving production systems entirely unprotected against regression.

Here is why LLM-as-a-judge fails to protect production agents, the compounding mathematics underneath multi-step failure, and the state-based evaluation architecture required to deploy agents with confidence.

The Mathematics of Multi-Step Error Cascading

The fundamental difference between a single-turn completion (such as summarization or question-answering) and an autonomous agent is sequential dependency.

In a multi-turn agent, every intermediate tool execution changes the environment and feeds into the next turn's context window. If Turn 1 retrieves an incorrect ID, Turn 2 operates on bad data, Turn 3 issues a corrupt database mutation, and Turn 4 hallucinates an explanation to justify the discrepancy.

Consider an agent task requiring $k$ discrete steps. If each step has an independent success probability $p$, the end-to-end task success probability $P(\text{task})$ follows:

$$P(\text{task}) = p^k$$

If your underlying foundation model is highly capable—say, $p = 0.90$ (90% per-step reliability)—the compound trajectory success decays rapidly as task complexity scales:

  • 1 step: $0.90^1 = 90.0\%$
  • 3 steps: $0.90^3 = 72.9\%$
  • 5 steps: $0.90^5 = 59.0\%$
  • 10 steps: $0.90^{10} = 34.9\%$

A system where individual steps look stellar during ad-hoc testing fails two out of three times when executing 10-step workflows.

Worse, steps are rarely independent. A minor error early in a trajectory increases the entropy of the agent's context window, degrading subsequent reasoning performance. Without deterministic guards at each transition, error cascading is mathematically inevitable.

The Three Structural Failures of LLM-as-a-Judge

Using a language model to grade multi-turn transcripts introduces three major measurement errors:

1. Inability to Observe Environment State Mutations

Language models evaluate text tokens; they do not execute environments.

If an agent reports:

"I have reconciled invoice #8492 and updated the ERP ledger status to settled."

An LLM judge reads this transcript and gives it a score of 5/5 for helpfulness, tone, and apparent completion. But did the invoice actually update in the database? Did it credit the right account balance? Did it violate foreign key constraints?

The judge cannot know because it only inspects the prose claim, not the environment delta. Grading agents on what they say rather than what they changed is the primary source of unmonitored production outages.

2. Systematic Cognitive Biases in LLM Scoring

Empirical evaluation benchmarks repeatedly reveal systematic structural biases in frontier models acting as evaluators:

  • Verbosity Bias: LLMs assign higher scores to long, repetitive, verbose answers, conflating length with thoroughness.
  • Position Bias: In multi-candidate evaluations, judges disproportionately favor responses presented in specific serial positions.
  • Self-Enhancement Bias: Frontier models systematically score outputs generated by their own family or architecture higher than outputs from competing models.

3. Non-Deterministic Evaluation Noise

When you evaluate a non-deterministic agent with a non-deterministic judge, you double your measurement variance. If an evaluation score drops from 4.2 to 3.8 on a nightly run, your team cannot immediately tell whether:

  1. The agent degraded due to prompt drift or model updates.
  2. The judge drifted due to non-zero temperature or provider inference changes.
  3. The sample variance was simply noise.

An evaluation harness that engineering teams cannot reproduce is an evaluation harness they will eventually ignore.

The Architecture: State-Based Evaluation

To build an evaluation suite that survives engineering inspection, we invert the paradigm: Evaluate state first, tool execution second, and prose last.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               Evaluation Pyramid for Agents             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 3: Semantic / Prose Quality                      │
│ (Embeddings, semantic similarity, tone guards)         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 2: Trajectory & Tool Efficiency                  │
│ (Schema validation, step counts, token budget, loops)  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Layer 1: Deterministic State Assertions                │
│ (Database deltas, sandbox files, mock API contracts)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Layer 1: Deterministic State Assertions

Before an agent executes a test case, snapshot the environment. After the agent halts, assert exact environment state:

  • Did the expected row appear in the SQL database with the exact required fields?
  • Did the file written to the filesystem parse cleanly as valid JSON/YAML?
  • Did the mock external API receive the expected payload parameters?

These assertions are deterministic, instant, free of token costs, and 100% reproducible.

Layer 2: Trajectory & Tool Efficiency

Even if the final state matches, how the agent got there matters for latency, cost, and reliability:

  • Tool-Call Schema Conformance: Did every tool invocation strictly validate against Pydantic / JSON Schema?
  • Step Count Budget: Did the agent resolve the issue in 3 steps, or did it thrash for 18 steps before stumbling onto the answer?
  • Repetition & Loop Detection: Did the agent invoke the same tool with identical arguments repeatedly after receiving an error?

Layer 3: Constrained Semantic Grading

Only after Layers 1 and 2 pass do you evaluate prose. Instead of open-ended 1-to-5 scoring, use narrow, single-question binary assertions:

  • "Does the final user-facing response state the tracking number [YES/NO]?"
  • "Does the response refuse the prompt injection attempt without leaking system credentials [YES/NO]?"

What a Inspectable Evaluation Runner Looks Like

Here is a minimal, robust harness showing how to evaluate an agent against deterministic environment assertions:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Callable, Dict, List
import pytest

@dataclass
class EvalTestCase:
    task_id: str
    user_prompt: str
    initial_state: Dict[str, Any]
    expected_state_assertion: Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], bool]
    max_steps: int = 5
    max_cost_usd: float = 0.05

def test_agent_reconciliation_flow():
    # Setup test fixture with isolated mock state
    mock_db = {"invoices": {"inv_101": {"amount": 250.0, "status": "pending"}}}

    test_case = EvalTestCase(
        task_id="reconcile_paid_invoice",
        user_prompt="Reconcile payment of $250.00 for invoice inv_101.",
        initial_state=mock_db,
        expected_state_assertion=lambda state: (
            state["invoices"]["inv_101"]["status"] == "settled"
            and state["invoices"]["inv_101"]["amount"] == 250.0
        ),
        max_steps=3
    )

    # Execute agent against the mock environment
    trajectory = run_agent(test_case.user_prompt, state=mock_db)

    # 1. Assert deterministic final state
    assert test_case.expected_state_assertion(mock_db), (
        f"State assertion failed for {test_case.task_id}. Current DB: {mock_db}"
    )

    # 2. Assert trajectory efficiency constraints
    assert len(trajectory.steps) <= test_case.max_steps, (
        f"Agent exceeded step budget: {len(trajectory.steps)} > {test_case.max_steps}"
    )

    # 3. Assert zero schema validation errors during tool calls
    for step in trajectory.steps:
        assert step.schema_valid is True, f"Malformed tool call in turn {step.turn_id}"

When an engineer breaks agent functionality in a pull request, this harness outputs an exact stack trace showing the mismatched database row or the malformed schema parameter, rather than a subjective LLM judge score dropping by 0.2 points.

The Next Step

In Part 2, we examine the exact implementation of Deterministic State Evaluations: how to mock sandboxed external tools, validate JSON Schema bounds, and capture before-and-after database states automatically.

Need Help Hardening Your Agent Architecture?

If your team is building an AI product or agentic system and struggling with silent failures, high latency, or unreliable tool calling:

title: AWS SAA-C03 Exam Guide 2026: Format, Domains and Study Plan
description:
AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) tests whether you can design solutions on AWS based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework. Here is how the exam works in 2026, the four domains and their weights, what each domain covers, who it is aimed at, how to keep the certification, and our suggested study plan.

Is SAA-C03 being replaced?

Not as far as AWS has said. AWS’s September 2026 certification update announced new versions of three exams: Machine Learning Engineer – Associate, Solutions Architect – Professional and Developer – Associate. It did not include Solutions Architect – Associate. As of 28 October 2026, the AWS exam guides index still lists SAA-C03, and the AWS Training and Certification blog has not announced a successor.

The only change AWS has announced is about language: the Italian version of the exam will be retired after 31 December 2026. The exam stays available in its other languages.

The format

Detail SAA-C03
Level Associate
Questions 65: 50 scored and 15 unscored
Time 130 minutes
Question types Multiple choice and multiple response
Passing score 720 on a scaled score from 100 to 1,000
Fee USD 150 (AWS notes that extra costs, such as foreign exchange, may apply)
Delivery Pearson VUE, at a test centre or online proctored
Validity 3 years

A multiple choice question has one correct answer and three incorrect ones. A multiple response question has two or more correct answers out of five or more options. Unanswered questions are scored as incorrect, and there is no penalty for guessing, so answer every question.

The 15 unscored questions are ones AWS is trying out for future use. They are not marked on the exam, so treat every question as if it counts.

The exam uses a compensatory scoring model. You need to pass the exam as a whole, not each domain. Your score report may show how you did in each section, but AWS advises caution when reading that section-level feedback.

The exam uses short names for some AWS services. A list of short names and full names is available through the Help button during the exam, and AWS suggests you look at it before exam day.

The four domains

Domain Weight
1. Design Secure Architectures 30%
2. Design Resilient Architectures 26%
3. Design High-Performing Architectures 24%
4. Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%

The weights are shares of the scored content, so a higher weight means more questions from that domain.

What each domain covers

This is our short summary of the task statements in the official exam guide. The guide itself has the full lists of knowledge and skills.

Design Secure Architectures (30%)

  • Secure access to AWS resources: IAM users, groups, roles and policies, least privilege and MFA, role switching and cross-account access, federation, and multi-account security with AWS Control Tower and service control policies.
  • Secure workloads and applications: VPC design with security groups, network ACLs, route tables and public and private subnets, plus services such as AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon Cognito, Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Data security controls: encryption at rest with AWS KMS and in transit with AWS Certificate Manager, key policies and rotation, backups and replication, and data retention and compliance.

Design Resilient Architectures (26%)

  • Scalable and loosely coupled designs: event-driven, microservice and multi-tier architectures, queues and publish/subscribe messaging, serverless with AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate, containers on Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, Amazon API Gateway, load balancing, caching and read replicas.
  • High availability and fault tolerance: designs across Availability Zones and Regions, Amazon Route 53, removing single points of failure, failover, and disaster recovery strategies from backup and restore to active-active, judged against RPO and RTO.

Design High-Performing Architectures (24%)

  • Storage: choosing between object, file and block storage, such as Amazon S3, Amazon EFS and Amazon EBS, for performance and growth.
  • Compute: EC2 instance types, Auto Scaling, Lambda sizing, containers, and decoupling so components scale on their own.
  • Databases: picking a database type and engine, such as Amazon Aurora or Amazon DynamoDB, read replicas, proxies and caching with Amazon ElastiCache.
  • Networks: subnet tiers and routing, load balancing, Amazon CloudFront, AWS Global Accelerator, and connections such as VPN, AWS Direct Connect and AWS PrivateLink.
  • Data ingestion and transformation: streaming with Amazon Kinesis, transfer with AWS DataSync, transformation with AWS Glue, data lakes, and analytics with Amazon Athena.

Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%)

  • Storage: storage tiers, S3 lifecycle rules, backup and archive choices, and the cheapest way to move data into AWS.
  • Compute: Spot Instances, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, right-sizing instances, and choosing between Lambda, EC2 and Fargate.
  • Databases: cost-effective database services, backup and retention policies, and capacity planning.
  • Networks: NAT gateway choices, data transfer routes, VPC endpoints, AWS Transit Gateway and VPC peering, and Direct Connect versus VPN.

Cost tools such as AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets appear across this domain.

Recommended experience

The exam guide describes a target candidate with at least 1 year of hands-on experience designing cloud solutions that use AWS services. The exam page adds that people with 1 to 3 years of IT experience have prepared for and earned this certification as a starting point. If you have no IT work experience, AWS suggests earning AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner first.

Keeping your certification

The certification is valid for 3 years. To recertify, you can pass the latest version of the exam. Earning AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional also recertifies the Associate certification automatically.

Our suggested study plan

This is our suggestion, not AWS’s. It gives each domain time roughly in line with its weight, over eight weeks. Stretch it if you are new to AWS.

  1. Weeks 1–2: Secure architectures. IAM policies and roles, cross-account access, VPC security, and encryption with KMS and ACM.
  2. Weeks 3–4: Resilient architectures. Queues and events, serverless and containers, load balancing, multi-AZ and multi-Region designs, and the disaster recovery strategies.
  3. Week 5: High-performing architectures. Matching storage, compute, database and network services to performance needs, plus caching and data ingestion.
  4. Week 6: Cost-optimized architectures. Purchasing options, storage tiers and lifecycles, NAT gateway and data transfer costs.
  5. Weeks 7–8: Practice and review. Take timed practice exams, read every explanation, and go back to your weakest domain.

Throughout, build things in your own AWS account where you can. Many questions describe a scenario and ask for the most secure, most resilient or cheapest design, and hands-on practice makes those trade-offs easier to spot. AWS also lists an Official Practice Question Set and an Official Practice Exam on the exam page.

Confirm the latest details on AWS’s Solutions Architect – Associate page before you book.

I run ExamCrest, where this guide first appeared. Try free SAA-C03 practice questions: https://examcrest.com/exam/aws-saa-c03/free-questions?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=s-n2a-saa-c03
