title: Waste Is an Output, Not a Subtraction: Modelling By-Products, Waste Streams and Licensed Collections in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

Most production software models a batch as inputs in, one product out. Whatever doesn't make it into the finished-goods line is "loss", a single number that nobody can explain. In a food factory that number is made of very different things: rejects, line purges, bran, whey, pomace, film offcuts, chemical containers and effluent. Some of it is sold as feed, some goes to a licensed collector, some is hazardous. If the system can't tell them apart, nobody can manage them.

This post walks through how we think about modelling waste and by-product streams in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Codex CXC 1-1969 (9.2.1): waste "should be collected, disposed of by trained personnel and, where appropriate, disposal records maintained"; containers "for waste, by-products and inedible or hazardous substances should be specifically identifiable". Source
  • EAS 39:2001 (10.8): skips emptied "at least once per week", factory waste containers "emptied daily" and not mistakable for food containers. Source
  • Kenya's Sustainable Waste Management Act, 2022: segregate "non-hazardous waste into organic and non-organic fractions" (s.12); a private sector entity's annual monitoring report specifies "the actual quantities of waste generated by the entity" (s.19); waste goes to "a person who is licensed to transport and dispose of the waste". Source

Translated into engineering terms: every production output has a type, every waste movement has a stream, a quantity and a destination, and every collection points at a counterparty whose licence has an expiry date.

Outputs are typed, not leftover

The first design choice is to stop calculating waste as input - output. Declare it.

RecipeOutput     (id, recipe_id, item_id, output_type, expected_pct)
                 output_type IN ('primary','co_product','byproduct','waste')
ProductionOutput (id, run_id, recipe_output_id, qty_kg, recorded_at, recorded_by)

A recipe that turns 1,000 kg of maize into flour, bran and screenings says so up front. When the run closes, each output is weighed and recorded against the run. "Unexplained loss" becomes the residual after declared outputs, which is the number you actually want to drive towards zero.

By-products are items. Bran or whey that leaves the gate as feed gets an item code, a lot, a stock location and a dispatch record, exactly like finished goods. If a raw-material lot is later found to have a problem, the by-product lot is in the same trace.

Waste never enters saleable stock. A waste output posts to a waste location (or no stock at all), so it can't be picked, sold or counted as inventory value.

Streams, movements and collections 

WasteStream      (id, name, category, hazardous, container_spec, removal_frequency, owner_id)
                 category IN ('organic','plastic','general_dry','hazardous','effluent')
WasteMovement    (id, stream_id, source_run_id NULL, source_area, qty_kg, moved_at, moved_by)
WasteCollection  (id, stream_id, collector_id, qty_kg, collected_at, destination, document_ref)
Collector        (id, name, licence_no, licence_expires_on)

A few rules make this useful:

Category is fixed on the stream. Segregation at source maps one-to-one to streams. If organic and plastic are mixed in one stream, the report can't separate them later.

Block expired collectors. A collection against a collector whose licence_expires_on is in the past should fail validation, or at least raise an exception for the EHS lead. That turns a filing-cabinet check into a system rule.

Schedules generate tasks. removal_frequency on the stream creates cleaning-schedule tasks (empty line bins every shift, skip weekly). A missed task is a hygiene finding, not a surprise at audit.

The queries that matter

Monthly totals by category, which is close to what an annual monitoring report asks for:

SELECT ws.category, date_trunc('month', wc.collected_at) AS month, SUM(wc.qty_kg) AS kg
FROM waste_collection wc
JOIN waste_stream ws ON ws.id = wc.stream_id
GROUP BY ws.category, month
ORDER BY month, ws.category;

And the one production managers care about, waste as a share of output per product and shift:

SELECT pr.product_id, pr.shift, 
       SUM(po.qty_kg) FILTER (WHERE ro.output_type = 'waste') /
       NULLIF(SUM(po.qty_kg), 0) AS waste_share
FROM production_output po
JOIN recipe_output ro ON ro.id = po.recipe_output_id
JOIN production_run pr ON pr.id = po.run_id
WHERE pr.started_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY pr.product_id, pr.shift
ORDER BY waste_share DESC;

When waste share on one shift starts climbing, it's usually a yield, equipment or training problem showing up early, long before it shows up in the month-end cost.

Takeaways

  • Declare outputs on the recipe: primary, co-product, by-product, waste.
  • Treat by-products as stock items with lots, not as negative waste.
  • Model waste streams with a fixed category so segregation is reportable.
  • Put licence expiry on collectors and validate against it.
  • Measure waste where it is made, per run, not by subtraction at month end.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Codex, EAS 39, Kenya's food hygiene regulations and the Sustainable Waste Management Act, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: My fix for the agent-edited test gate was wrong. The pin has to be older than the agent.
description:
Three weeks ago I published four fixes for a test gate that runs the tests in the tree the agent just edited. Fix 2 was this: do not run the tests in the agent's tree, run them in a pristine worktree off HEAD and copy in only the unprotected changes.

@howcani_howcani_77e786a89 took it back to a local repo, stopped at fix 2, and wrote: fix 2's precondition is the thing evasion 1 removes. Evasion 1 is the agent committing. After that, HEAD is the agent's commit, so "a commit you control" is a commit the agent controls, and a worktree off it is pristine only with respect to the uncommitted dilution.

He was right. I reproduced it before writing this. Baseline has one real test. The agent commits a weakened one. A clean worktree off HEAD, fresh checkout, nothing copied in from the working tree:

old fix 2 worktree tests/test_calc.py:
    assert True
old fix 2 verdict: PASS

The gate passes on a test that asserts nothing. Fix 2 moved the dilution from "uncommitted edits" to "a commit", and a commit is exactly the thing the agent can make.

The pin has to be older than the agent

The fix is not a better use of HEAD. It is to stop asking HEAD what the baseline is.

Before the agent runs, while the tree is known good, record the protected set as content: every path under tests/, conftest.py, the runner config, the CI file, each mapped to its blob hash.

37895b28ab864addfe1921d4bf035a1563ac0689 conftest.py
4b341e0595f8265e27ed7b7e6119711b672e0e17c tests/test_calc.py

At check time, recompute the same tree listing for those paths and compare. Three ways to differ, all fail: a path is missing, a path's hash changed, a path that was not in the pin appears. Then run the tests on a tree assembled from the pins for protected paths and from the agent's commit for everything else.

A blob hash is not a ref. An agent can rewrite history, orphan its commits, delete a branch. It cannot produce a different file with the same hash.

What I actually ran, four repos from one baseline, one shared pin:

A control src-only:                    added=0 changed=0 missing=0 -> PASS
B agent-committed weakened test:       added=0 changed=1 missing=0 -> FAIL
C delete + add inside tests/:          added=1 changed=0 missing=1 -> FAIL
D rewritten history (1 orphan commit): added=0 changed=1 missing=0 -> FAIL

Case C is the one that caught my own corrected check. Compare hashes of the paths you know about and the agent can leave every pinned path alone, delete them, and drop tests/test_zz.py with assert 1 == 1 in the same commit. The path set has to be compared, not just the hashes. Case D is a repo rewritten to a single orphan commit where the baseline is not an ancestor of anything. The pin does not care, because it never asks about ancestry.

What the pin does not fix

Where the pin lives.

If the harness writes the expected hashes into the worktree it is about to inspect, or reads them out of the repository it is checking, this whole method collapses into the class I hunt for a living: a check that decides on bytes it never reads. An agent that can write the pin can set it to whatever it just produced, and every check above passes.

So the pin is written by the step that owns the checkout, before the agent exists, and kept out of every path the agent's process can write. If you cannot name the component that owns the pin, you do not have this fix, you have a second copy of the problem.

The general shape

A gate is only as strong as the oldest copy of the expected value it holds. If the expected value is derived at check time from anything the checked party touched, then the gate's verdict is decided by the artifact, not by the check. The agent committing is just the most convenient way to make the artifact supply its own baseline.

Corrections: this one came from someone who ran my method instead of agreeing with it, which is worth more than a like and costs him an afternoon. The first piece is https://dev.to/mayailands/your-agents-test-gate-runs-the-tests-in-the-tree-the-agent-just-edited-574

If you ship the pinned version and want a third-party re-run of the check against your repo, with a control that must pass and a negative control that must fail, the receipt is $25 and the card is here: https://buy.stripe.com/fZu5kD1rN0laceh13n5kI02

The finding is free. That is why it is above and not behind a link.

title: TIL: GBase Database Installation — What the -i Flag Actually Skips
description:
The first time I encountered the -i flag in a database installation command, I assumed it meant "ignore all errors."

It doesn't.

In GBase Database(GBase 8a), the -i flag skips the operating system version check during installation. It does not disable every compatibility check, resolve missing dependencies, or guarantee that the database will start successfully.

Understanding this distinction can save a lot of unnecessary troubleshooting.

1. What Does the -i Flag Actually Do?

During installation, the GBase Database(GBase 8a) installer checks the operating system information against its expected compatibility list.

If the detected environment does not match the expected list, the installer may report an error similar to:

operating system is 'xxx', must be centos7

The installation process then exits.

You can use the -i flag to bypass this operating system version check:

cd gcinstall
./gcinstall.py --silent=demo.options -i

The script continues beyond that particular check.

However, there is an important distinction:

Skipping an OS check does not make an unsupported operating system officially supported.

The flag allows the installation process to proceed. It does not certify compatibility or guarantee runtime stability.

For a POC or temporary validation environment, this option can be useful when the target system is not listed in the standard compatibility checks.

For production deployment, you should still verify the operating system against the official GBase Database compatibility matrix.

If the flag is used as an exception, record that decision in the deployment handover documentation.

2. What the -i Flag Does NOT Fix: Missing Dependencies

Another common misunderstanding is assuming that -i bypasses all installation problems.

It does not.

The flag only affects the operating system version check. It does not install missing libraries or repair service startup failures.

For example, you may successfully pass the initial installation check but encounter an error later when adding cluster nodes.

The actual cause may be that GCware or GCluster cannot start because a required shared library is missing.

In this situation, the problem is no longer the operating system version check.

The troubleshooting approach should be different:

  • If installation stops at the initial OS validation stage, investigate the compatibility check.
  • If installation proceeds but a service fails to start, investigate environment variables and shared library dependencies.
  • If node addition fails, verify the relevant service status and dependencies on every affected node.

For GBase Database(GBase 8a), passing installation validation and having a fully operational cluster are two separate milestones.

Do not treat them as the same thing.

3. Terminal Escape Sequences Can Look Like Script Bugs

Another issue that can interrupt GBase Database installation is terminal configuration.

You may encounter an error similar to:

invalid literal for int()

The actual input may contain terminal escape sequences such as:

\x1b[?2004l

These characters are terminal control sequences rather than ordinary numeric input.

If they enter the installation script's input stream, a value that should have been parsed as an integer may become invalid.

This can make the problem look like a Python code defect when the terminal environment is actually interfering with input processing.

How to troubleshoot:

  • Try running the installation in a clean shell.
  • Check the terminal configuration and input behavior.
  • Avoid carrying over problematic terminal settings from remote sessions.
  • Reproduce the command in a standard terminal environment.

The key is to distinguish between invalid script input and an actual script logic error.

4. Python Interpreter Selection Matters

The Python interpreter is another environment-related issue worth checking.

Some GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation scripts have specific runtime expectations.

If both Python 2 and Python 3 are installed, the python command may point to a different interpreter than expected.

This can result in syntax errors or unexpected installation behavior.

Check the interpreter used by the current account:

which python
python --version

Do not assume that installing Python 2 automatically means the installation script will use it.

The important detail is which interpreter is actually invoked through the expected entry point.

Follow the invocation method documented for your specific GBase Database release. If the installer expects to be called through python, do not arbitrarily replace the entry point with python2 gcinstall.py.

Changing the interpreter command without understanding the installer's runtime expectations can introduce another problem instead of solving the original one.

5. Check Environment Variables Under Both Accounts

A final detail is often overlooked: root and the database installation user may have different environment configurations.

For example, the root account may have the correct Python path and system environment, while the gbase or dba account does not.

After switching users, the expected environment variables may not be loaded automatically in every situation.

Check the environment under each account separately and reload the appropriate profile when necessary.

This matters because the same installation script can behave differently depending on which user invokes it and which environment variables are available.

A Practical GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting Checklist

When the GBase Database installer fails, use this sequence before modifying scripts or reinstalling packages.

Check What to investigate
OS validation Is the detected OS version in the supported list?
-i flag Is the failure actually occurring during the OS check?
Dependencies Can GCware and GCluster locate their required libraries?
Terminal Are escape sequences interfering with script input?
Python Does python invoke the expected interpreter?
User environment Are environment variables correctly loaded under the current account?

The most useful first question is:

Did the installation script generate the error, or did the environment pass unexpected input to the script?

That distinction helps narrow down the root cause much faster.

Final Thoughts

The -i flag in GBase Database(GBase 8a) has a specific purpose: bypassing the operating system version check.

It is not a universal troubleshooting switch.

Missing dependencies, terminal escape sequences, Python interpreter mismatches, and incorrectly loaded environment variables are separate issues that require separate solutions.

When troubleshooting a GBase Database installation, investigate the environment layer before assuming the installer itself is defective.

And remember: bypassing a compatibility check is not the same as proving compatibility.

For exact flag behavior, Python runtime requirements, and supported operating systems, always consult the installation manual for your specific GBase Database version.

title: How to Learn SQL Joins (and Stop Mixing Up LEFT and INNER)
description:
For about two years I wrote SQL joins by trial and error. I'd type JOIN, run it, count the rows, feel uneasy, swap in LEFT JOIN, count again, and keep whichever number looked less wrong. It worked often enough that I never sat down and learned the thing properly.

Then a report I'd written quietly dropped every customer who hadn't placed an order. Nobody noticed for a month. That was the week I finally figured out joins, and the approach that stuck is pretty different from the Venn diagrams most tutorials open with.

Forget the Venn diagram for a minute

The circles are fine as a rough picture, but they hide the part that actually trips people up: joins don't combine sets of values, they match rows. One customer with three orders becomes three rows. A customer with zero orders becomes either zero rows or one row full of NULLs, depending on the join type.

So the question I ask now is always the same. For each row on the left, how many rows on the right match it, and what happens when the answer is zero?

That one question covers almost everything:

  • INNER JOIN keeps only rows with at least one match. Zero matches means the row disappears.
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. Zero matches means you get one row with NULLs on the right side.
  • RIGHT JOIN is the same thing mirrored. I almost never use it; I flip the table order and write a LEFT JOIN so I'm always reading in one direction.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.
  • CROSS JOIN matches every row with every row, which is what you get by accident when you forget the join condition in old comma-style syntax.

Build two tiny tables and break them

Reading about joins taught me very little. Running them on data small enough to check by eye taught me a lot. Open SQLite, DuckDB, or the free DB Fiddle and make this:

CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, customer_id INT, total INT);

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Asha'), (2, 'Ben'), (3, 'Chen');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1, 50), (11, 1, 20), (12, 2, 35), (13, 9, 99);

Asha has two orders, Ben has one, Chen has none, and order 13 points at a customer who doesn't exist. Before you run each query, write down how many rows you expect. Then run it.

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;   -- 3 rows, no Chen

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;    -- 4 rows, Chen with NULL

Guessing first is the important bit. When your guess is wrong, you've found the exact gap in your understanding, and that sticks far better than a correct answer you read off a page.

The two bugs worth memorizing

Most join bugs I've shipped or reviewed come down to two mistakes.

The first is filtering a LEFT JOIN in the WHERE clause:

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 30;

That looks like "all customers, plus their orders over 30." It isn't. Chen's row has o.total = NULL, NULL > 30 isn't true, so Chen gets filtered out and you've rebuilt an inner join without meaning to. If you want to keep every customer, move the condition into the ON:

LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 30

The second is row multiplication. Join customers to orders, then join to a table of support tickets, and a customer with 3 orders and 4 tickets turns into 12 rows. Run SUM(o.total) over that and the number is quietly four times too big. The fix is usually to aggregate each side in a subquery or CTE first and join the summaries.

Turn every "wait, why?" into a flashcard

Here's the habit that made it stick for me. Any time a query surprised me, I wrote a card with the situation on the front and the reason on the back.

I LEFT JOINed and then filtered on the right table in WHERE. Why did rows vanish?
NULL fails the comparison, so unmatched rows are dropped. Put the filter in ON.

My SUM doubled after adding a second join. Why?
One-to-many on two sides multiplies rows. Aggregate before joining.

How do I find customers with no orders?
LEFT JOIN orders, then WHERE o.id IS NULL.

I review them on a growing schedule: the next day, a few days later, a week, two weeks. That's spaced repetition, and it's the reason I can still write an anti-join from memory instead of searching for it. If you're curious how the intervals get calculated, I wrote up how to implement spaced repetition (SM-2) in JavaScript.

Keep the cards about situations you'll actually hit at work. "What is a semi-join?" is trivia. "How do I check if a customer has any order without duplicating rows?" (answer: EXISTS) is something you'll need on a Tuesday.

Don't lose the good explanations

Plenty of what finally made joins click came from videos and blog posts, and I used to watch one, nod, and forget it by the weekend. That's part of why I built Recl. You share a video, reel, podcast or article to it from your phone or the Chrome extension, and it summarizes the key points, files it under a topic like "SQL", and brings it back on a spaced schedule so you see it again before it fades.

Read execution plans once you're comfortable

When the row counts make sense, run EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres) on a join and look at whether it picked a hash join, a nested loop, or a merge join. You don't need to tune anything yet. Seeing that the database is literally looping over rows and looking up matches makes the "how many matches per row" model feel real.

I still check row counts on every non-trivial query. The difference is that now I know what number to expect before I hit run, and that report from a few years ago would have been caught in about ten seconds.

I build Recl, an AI learning app that saves your videos, reels, podcasts and articles, summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and uses spaced repetition so you remember what you learned.

title: Workflows that survive a closed tab: durable waits with checkpoints and chrome.alarms
description:
"Browser automation dies when you close the tab" is the standard objection to running workflows in an extension. For a while it was true for AWFlow too: a workflow with a "wait 3 days, then check again" step only worked if you left a tab open for three days.

This post is about how runs can now pause for up to 30 days, survive a closed tab, a browser restart or an extension update, and resume where they stopped. It's the same mechanism that lets a run pause for a human approval.


Flip it. Save the run, let the browser wake it.

The constraint: MV3 has no long-lived process

In Manifest V3 the background is a service worker, and Chrome suspends it when it's idle. setTimeout(resume, 3 * DAY) is useless there: the worker is gone long before the timer fires. The page that runs the engine (the extension's app tab) can be closed by the user at any time.


Memory is the problem. The wait has to live somewhere else.

So a long wait has to be two things:

  1. a serialized snapshot of the run, stored somewhere that survives restarts, and
  2. a wake-up call that the browser itself owns.

In an extension, those are chrome.storage.local and chrome.alarms. If you want the bigger picture of what a browser can and can't do compared with a server, browser vs server automation covers it.

How a run pauses

Let a node ask to pause

Normally a node's execute() returns output. A node that needs to wait returns a suspend request instead:

type SuspendRequest = {
  resumeKey: string;              // filled in by the engine
  kind: 'approval' | 'timer' | (string & {});
  prompt?: string;                // shown in the "waiting" row
  meta?: Record<string, unknown>; // e.g. { resumeAt: 1735689600000 }
};

The engine spots it and throws a SuspendSignal to unwind the work queue back to the place where the queue and visited sets are in scope. That's where the checkpoint gets written. (One subtlety: the node runner's own catch must re-throw this signal instead of turning it into a node failure.)

Write a checkpoint that's actually resumable

My first version stored "which node paused, plus its input". It broke immediately on real workflows. A useful checkpoint needs everything the scheduler would need to continue as if nothing happened.


Peel it apart: five layers, each one needed to carry on.

Here is the shape in code:

const checkpoint = {
  resumeKey, workflowId, pausedNodeId, kind, meta,
  pausedInput,
  queue: queue.map(n => n.id),     // what was about to run
  visited: [...visited],
  wasVisited: [...wasVisited],     // see below
  nodeOutputs,                     // so downstream $('Node') references still resolve
  runVariables: runVariables.snapshot(),
  nodeExecutionCtx,                // per-node scratchpads: loop cursors, batch offsets
  parentLink,                      // a paused sub-workflow must still resume its parent
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
};

Two bugs taught me the less obvious fields:

  • Loops. An iterating Loop node is moved out of visited on each pass. If you only save outputs of visited nodes, a pause inside a loop body resumes with the loop's current item gone. Save outputs from visited ∪ wasVisited.
  • Batch cursors. A "Split in Batches" node keeps its offset in a per-node scratchpad. Capture the scratchpad of every node, not just visited ones, because the loop node is exactly the one that's been un-marked when you pause.

Serialize defensively, fail loudly

Node outputs are user-controlled (a Code node can return anything), so a BigInt or a circular reference would crash the run at the moment it tries to pause. So the checkpoint goes through a few guards before it is stored.


Save it under the run's resume key.

If the checkpoint can't be saved, the run fails loudly at that node. A pause that silently didn't persist would be the worst outcome: the user thinks it's waiting and nothing ever resumes it.

How it wakes up

For a timer suspend, saving the checkpoint also arms a one-shot alarm named after the resume key:

if (cp.kind === 'timer' && typeof cp.meta?.resumeAt === 'number') {
  chrome.alarms.create(`resume:${cp.resumeKey}`, { when: cp.meta.resumeAt });
}

In practice the app page asks the service worker to do it, because the worker owns the alarms API and the onAlarm listener. Here is the full round, from pause to resume.


The run carries on. Queue, visited sets, outputs and variables are rebuilt, and the next node runs.

The run saves itself

The engine writes the checkpoint before anything else happens.

It asks for a wake-up call

The app page messages the service worker, which owns the alarms.

The browser holds the alarm

A one-shot alarm named resume:<key> is set for the deadline.

Days later, it fires

The worker's onAlarm sees the resume: prefix: this is a parked run, not a scheduled workflow.

The worker opens the app

The engine lives in the app page, so the worker finds or opens that tab and passes the resume key.

The page loads the checkpoint

Everything the scheduler needs is read back from storage.

The run carries on

Queue, visited sets, outputs and variables are rebuilt, and the next node runs.

Re-arm the alarms you lost

Alarms don't survive everything. An extension update, for example, can clear them. So on startup the worker reconciles: list the timer checkpoints, list the existing alarm names, and create the missing ones.

function computeMissingResumeAlarms(checkpoints, existingAlarmNames) {
  const existing = new Set(existingAlarmNames);
  return checkpoints
    .filter(cp => cp.kind === 'timer' && typeof cp.meta?.resumeAt === 'number')
    .filter(cp => !existing.has(`resume:${cp.resumeKey}`))
    .map(cp => ({ name: `resume:${cp.resumeKey}`, when: cp.meta.resumeAt }));
}

It's a pure function, so it's trivially unit-tested, and it's the piece that makes the design trustworthy rather than "usually works". A deadline already in the past fires right away, so a laptop that was asleep through the deadline resumes as soon as the browser is back.


Missing alarms come back. Past deadlines fire right away.

Where the thresholds come from

  • Under 1 minute stays in memory. chrome.alarms doesn't fire reliably below about a minute, and a 5-second wait isn't worth a storage round-trip. Short waits stay plain timers.
  • Up to 30 days. An upper bound, so nobody schedules an alarm for 2031 by typo.
  • One pause per input, not per item. A Wait node pauses once for the whole batch. Per-item pauses can't be checkpointed cleanly. If you want per-item waits, wrap the step in a Loop.


Thirty days, with the tab closed and the browser restarted.

One mechanism, many kinds

Once the plumbing existed, other kinds came almost for free:

  • approval pauses until a person clicks approve. Because it's waiting on a human, the extension signals it: a badge, a sound, and an OS notification when the app isn't focused. It can even render the approval card on the web page you're on.
  • "Poll until" resumes on a timer, checks a condition, and if it's not met yet, suspends again. A resume that is allowed to re-suspend turned out to be the key primitive.
  • Sub-workflows pause with a parentLink, so the parent run continues once the child finishes.

The approval kind is the easiest to see in a real workflow. This docs example fills a web form from saved values, but stops before touching the page until you approve:


Run it. Every step shows what it did.

If page watching is your use case rather than forms, monitoring competitor prices shows the other side: a trigger that reacts when a page changes.

The honest limit

This is durable, not always-on. The alarm fires when the browser is running. If your laptop is off at the deadline, the run resumes when you next open Chrome, not at 3:00:00 sharp.


But it needs the browser running. Laptop off means it resumes later.

For "every 30 seconds, 24/7" you still want a server. For "wait until Thursday, check the price, ask me before buying", it's enough, and there's nothing to host.


Call to action. Viewers scan the code, readers click the link.

Try it in AWFlow →

If you're building something similar in your own extension, here is the short version.


Never pretend to wait. A failed save fails the run.

AWFlow is free to install. I'm happy to answer questions, especially from anyone who's done this with IndexedDB instead of storage.local.

Interactive version with animations: https://awflow.io/blog/workflows-that-survive-a-closed-tab

Try it

Agentic Workflow (AWFlow) runs in your browser, on the model you choose, free and with no account needed to start. Install it from the Chrome Web Store here.

title: How to Fix 401 Unauthorized Errors in an LLM API
description:
The Problem

401 Unauthorized is one of the most common first-day errors in any LLM API project. It's also the one that eats the most time, because the body says the same thing whether your key is wrong or just badly copied:

openai.AuthenticationError: Error code: 401 - {'error': {...'invalid api key'...}}

The confusing part: 401 doesn't mean your key is wrong. It means the server refused to accept your credentials as presented. That gap covers several very different causes. Here's the checklist I run through, in order of likelihood.

Quick Definitions: 401 vs 403 vs 429

Code Meaning Usual cause
401 Server didn't accept your credentials Key missing, malformed, or invalid
403 Credentials accepted, but you're not allowed Account state, permissions, regional restrictions
429 Too many requests Rate limits — retry with backoff, see my next post

If you're getting 403, this isn't your article — but the table above saves you an hour of debugging the wrong thing.

The Checklist

1. Is the key actually being sent?

With an SDK, an empty or misnamed environment variable silently produces "no key":

import os
key = os.environ.get("HEFUAI_API_KEY")
if not key:
    raise SystemExit("HEFUAI_API_KEY is not set — check .env and load_dotenv()")

With raw HTTP, the header must include the scheme, exactly once:

Authorization: Bearer sk-...

Authorization: sk-... (no Bearer) and Bearer: sk-... (schemes swapped) both produce 401 on many gateways.

2. Is there invisible whitespace in the key?

The cause that wastes the most time. Copying a key out of a dashboard or a chat message drags along a trailing newline or space:

key = os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"]
print("leading/trailing whitespace:", key != key.strip())

Fix it at the source (your .env file), not with .strip() everywhere — but if the key comes from user input or a config system you don't control, strip it defensively.

3. Test the key independently of your app

Before you blame your framework, send one raw request. This isolates key validity from code:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  https://api.hefu.hk/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HEFUAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}]}'
  • 200 → your key is fine; the bug is in your app (wrong env var name, dotenv not loaded, per-directory .env)
  • 401 → the key itself is the problem; continue to #4

4. Was the key rotated, revoked, or never saved correctly?

Keys get invalidated more often than people admit:

  • Someone on the team rotated the key "for security" and your deploy didn't get the memo
  • You regenerated the key while debugging and are now running two versions
  • The key was never fully copied in the first place

Worth knowing how your provider stores keys. For example, HefuAI shows the plaintext once at creation and never again — so if you didn't save it, regeneration is the only path, not "view it again." If a key might be compromised, revoke and rotate in the console rather than hoping it blows over.

5. Are you hitting the right base URL with the right key?

A subtle one: if your base_url points at a different gateway or vendor than the one that issued your key, you'll get a 401 that has nothing to do with the key's validity. Same class of bug: dev keys against prod endpoints. Print both, every time, during setup:

print("base_url:", client.base_url)
print("key prefix:", os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"][:6] + "...")

Don't Retry a 401

A rookie mistake is wrapping everything in a retry loop. 401 is not transient — retrying the same credentials will fail the same way 100% of the time, and retrying can even trigger rate-limit lockouts. Handle it explicitly and fail fast:

from openai import OpenAI, AuthenticationError

try:
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v4-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}],
    )
except AuthenticationError:
    # stop the pipeline, alert a human, check the checklist above
    raise SystemExit("Auth failed — do NOT retry. Check key, header, base URL.")

Retry budgets belong to 429 and 5xx errors — that's the next post in this series.

Common Mistakes

  1. Debugging 403 problems as if they were 401 (see the table above — account state vs credentials).
  2. Hardcoding the key to "test quickly," then the hardcoded key rotates and prod breaks mysteriously.
  3. Sharing a screenshot of your terminal that contains the full key. Rotate immediately if this happens.
  4. Mixing two providers' keys and base URLs in the same .env file.

Next Steps

Once auth works, the next error you'll meet in production is 429 Too Many Requests. The next post covers rate limits, exponential backoff, and building retry logic that actually respects Retry-After headers.

Disclosure: this tutorial series uses HefuAI as its example gateway. All code patterns apply to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

title: SQL: WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT — Why Your Query May Return the Wrong Employees
description:
A SQL query can run successfully and still return the wrong result.

Imagine your manager asks you to find the three highest-paid employees in the IT department.

You write a query, execute it, and get three rows. Everything looks fine.

But are those really the three highest-paid employees?

Let's use a simple example to understand where things can go wrong.

Sample Data

Consider the following "employees" table:

CREATE TABLE employees (
emp_id INT,
name VARCHAR(30),
dept VARCHAR(30),
salary INT
);

emp_id| name| dept| salary
101| Amit| IT| 60000
102| Neha| HR| 75000
103| Rahul| IT| 85000
104| Priya| IT| 50000
105| Kiran| IT| 90000
106| Sneha| Finance| 95000
107| Raj| IT| NULL
108| Meera| IT| 70000

Our requirement:

Find the three highest-paid employees from the IT department. Employees with missing salaries should be excluded.

  1. Using LIMIT Without ORDER BY

Let's start with a query that looks reasonable:

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
LIMIT 3;

This query returns three employees from the IT department.

But there is a problem.

We haven't told SQL how to sort the employees.

The database is free to return qualifying rows in an order that does not represent salary ranking.

So, getting three employees does not mean getting the three highest-paid employees.

  1. Adding ORDER BY

Let's improve the query:

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3;

Now the records are sorted by salary, from highest to lowest.

However, there is one more detail worth understanding.

What happens when an employee's salary is NULL?

The position of NULL values in sorting depends on the database.

For example, MySQL and SQL Server generally place NULL values last with descending order, while PostgreSQL and Oracle generally place them first.

This means the result may differ between databases.

  1. The Correct Query

If the requirement says employees with NULL salaries must be excluded, don't depend on the database's default sorting behaviour.

Add an explicit condition:

SELECT emp_id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
AND salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3;

Expected Output

emp_id| name| salary
105| Kiran| 90000
103| Rahul| 85000
108| Meera| 70000

Now we get exactly what the manager asked for.

Here's what SQL does:

  1. "WHERE" filters employees belonging to the IT department.
  2. "salary IS NOT NULL" removes employees without a salary.
  3. "ORDER BY salary DESC" sorts employees from highest to lowest salary.
  4. "LIMIT 3" returns only the first three records.

Remember These Three Clauses

Clause| Purpose
WHERE| Filters records
ORDER BY| Sorts records
LIMIT| Restricts the number of returned rows

A small mistake in any of these clauses can change the result of a business report.

One more thing: "LIMIT" is supported by MySQL and PostgreSQL. Oracle and SQL Server use different row-limiting syntax.

Try This Yourself

What would happen if we removed this condition?

AND salary IS NOT NULL

Would the query return the same three employees in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server?

Think about how each database handles NULL values when sorting in descending order.

Share your answer in the comments.

Learn More

For more practical examples, SQL interview questions, and explanations of filtering and sorting, visit:

"Restricting and Sorting Data in SQL — Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/restricting-sorting-data-sql-faq.html)

title: How AI Is Changing Digital Marketing in 2026
description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the way businesses promote their products and services online. In 2026, AI has become an important part of digital marketing, helping businesses create content, understand customer behaviour, improve advertising campaigns, and deliver personalized experiences. From social media marketing to search engine optimization, AI-powered tools are changing how marketing strategies are planned and executed. Businesses can now use AI to save time, analyze information, and make better marketing decisions. Understanding how AI is changing digital marketing in 2026 is important for businesses that want to stay competitive and build a strong online presence. Working with the Best Freelance Digital Marketer in Perinthalmanna can also help businesses use modern digital marketing techniques effectively and achieve better results.

What Is AI in Digital Marketing?

AI in digital marketing refers to the use of artificial intelligence technologies to improve marketing activities and business performance. These technologies can analyze large amounts of information, identify patterns, generate content, and support marketing decisions. Instead of handling every task manually, marketers can use AI-powered tools to make their work faster and more efficient. For example, AI can help generate social media captions, suggest SEO keywords, analyze advertising performance, and create personalized email content. It can also help businesses understand what their customers are interested in and develop marketing strategies based on that information. In 2026, AI is becoming an important part of everyday marketing activities, but human creativity and decision-making remain essential.

How AI Is Changing Digital Marketing in 2026

AI is influencing almost every area of digital marketing. Businesses are using it to improve content creation, search visibility, social media engagement, paid advertising, customer communication, and data analysis. According to HubSpot's 2026 marketing research, marketers are increasingly using AI for content creation, media production, automation, and advertising optimization. This shows how AI is moving beyond simple experimentation and becoming part of regular marketing workflows. The main advantage is that businesses can complete certain tasks more efficiently while giving marketers more time to focus on strategy and creativity.

AI in Content Creation

Content creation is one of the biggest areas where AI is making a difference in digital marketing. Creating regular content for websites, blogs, social media platforms, and advertisements can take considerable time. AI-powered tools help marketers generate content ideas, prepare blog outlines, write captions, develop advertising headlines, and create different versions of marketing messages. Tools such as ChatGPT can support writing and brainstorming, while Canva AI can help with visual content creation. These tools make the content production process faster and provide new creative ideas. However, AI-generated content should always be reviewed and improved by a human. Adding personal experience, accurate information, brand identity, and a natural writing style helps make content more useful and engaging for the audience.

AI in Search Engine Optimization (SEO)

Artificial Intelligence is also changing how businesses approach Search Engine Optimization. Traditional SEO mainly focuses on keyword research, website optimization, quality content, and backlinks. These activities are still important, but AI-powered search experiences are changing how people discover information online. Users increasingly ask detailed questions through AI-powered search tools and expect direct, relevant answers. This means businesses need to create helpful, well-structured, and informative website content that clearly answers their audience's questions. AI tools can assist with keyword research, content planning, competitor analysis, website audits, and search intent analysis. Businesses should also pay attention to Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), which focuses on making content easier for AI-powered search and answer platforms to understand and reference. However, AI tools cannot guarantee better rankings. High-quality content, useful information, technical website performance, and a good user experience remain important parts of SEO.

AI in Social Media Marketing

Social media marketing is becoming more efficient with the support of artificial intelligence. Businesses need to publish regular content, communicate with followers, understand audience interests, and monitor performance across platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, and YouTube. AI tools can help marketers generate content ideas, write captions, prepare content calendars, suggest suitable posting times, and analyze audience engagement. They can also assist with creating images and short-form video concepts. This allows businesses to maintain a more consistent social media presence without spending too much time on repetitive tasks. However, successful social media marketing still requires creativity, original ideas, audience understanding, and genuine communication. Businesses should use AI as a supporting tool rather than depending on it for every post or interaction.

AI in Google Ads and Paid Advertising

AI is changing how businesses create, manage, and optimize paid advertising campaigns. Platforms such as Google Ads already use machine learning to support automated bidding, audience targeting, and campaign optimization. AI can help marketers analyze campaign data, identify performance patterns, test different advertising messages, and make adjustments based on available information. It can also support the creation of multiple headlines and descriptions for advertisements. These features help marketers manage campaigns more efficiently and understand which approaches may perform better. However, successful advertising still depends on choosing the right keywords, setting suitable budgets, creating relevant advertisements, and developing effective landing pages. Human monitoring is important to ensure that campaigns remain aligned with business goals and advertising budgets.

AI-Powered Personalization

Personalization is becoming an important part of modern digital marketing. Customers are more likely to engage with businesses when the content, offers, and messages match their interests and requirements. AI helps businesses analyze customer behaviour, preferences, previous interactions, and browsing patterns to create more relevant experiences. For example, an online shopping website can recommend products based on a customer's previous activity, while an email marketing campaign can send different messages to different audience groups. AI can also help businesses develop personalized advertisements and website experiences. This makes it easier to communicate with customers in a more relevant way. However, businesses must use customer information responsibly and respect privacy when applying personalization techniques.

AI Chatbots and Customer Support

AI chatbots are changing how businesses communicate with customers online. Instead of depending entirely on manual responses, businesses can use chatbots to answer common questions, provide service information, collect basic enquiry details, and guide visitors through their websites. These tools can help businesses respond to customers outside regular working hours and manage repeated enquiries more efficiently. For example, a cleaning service company can use a chatbot to answer questions about available services, collect customer contact details, and direct enquiries to its support team. AI chatbots can improve customer communication, but they should also provide a way for customers to contact a real person when they need personal assistance or have a more complicated issue.

AI in Data Analysis and Marketing Decisions

Understanding marketing performance is essential for business growth. AI-powered analytics tools can help marketers process large amounts of information, identify trends, and understand how customers interact with websites, advertisements, and social media content. Instead of reviewing every report manually, marketers can use AI-supported insights to identify areas that need improvement. For example, businesses can analyze website traffic, advertising conversions, customer engagement, and campaign performance to make more informed decisions. AI can also support predictive analysis by identifying patterns that may help businesses plan future marketing activities. However, marketers should verify the information and consider the business context before making important decisions based on AI-generated recommendations.

Popular AI Tools Used in Digital Marketing in 2026

Several AI-powered tools are helping marketers improve their daily activities. ChatGPT is useful for content ideas, blog outlines, marketing copy, and research assistance. Canva AI supports graphic design and visual content creation. Google Gemini can assist with research, writing, and brainstorming. Grammarly helps improve writing quality and clarity, while Semrush offers SEO research and website analysis features. Adobe Firefly provides AI-powered creative features for visual content. These tools can support different areas of digital marketing, but choosing the right tool depends on your business requirements, budget, and marketing objectives. Using too many tools without a clear strategy may create unnecessary work, so businesses should focus on tools that provide practical value.

Benefits of Using AI in Digital Marketing

AI offers several advantages for businesses and marketing professionals. It can reduce the time required for repetitive tasks, support faster content production, improve data analysis, and help businesses understand customer behaviour. It also makes it easier to test different marketing ideas and prepare personalized content for different audiences. Small businesses can benefit from AI because it provides access to tools that support activities such as content planning, customer communication, and advertising analysis. However, AI does not automatically guarantee business growth. Its effectiveness depends on how well businesses use the technology, the quality of the information provided, and the marketing strategy behind it.

Challenges of AI in Digital Marketing

Although AI provides many opportunities, businesses should also understand its limitations. AI-generated content can sometimes contain incorrect information, repetitive language, or ideas that lack originality. Depending too much on AI may also make a brand's communication feel less personal. Privacy and data protection are other important concerns, especially when businesses use customer information for personalization and advertising. In addition, AI tools cannot fully understand every business situation or replace human creativity, emotional intelligence, and strategic thinking. Marketers should review AI-generated content, verify important information, and ensure that all marketing activities follow relevant privacy and platform policies. A balanced approach that combines technology with human judgment is essential.

Will AI Replace Digital Marketers?

AI is changing the responsibilities of digital marketers, but it does not mean that human professionals are no longer needed. AI can support tasks such as content drafting, data analysis, keyword research, and campaign optimization. However, businesses still need professionals who understand customer behaviour, brand positioning, communication, creativity, and marketing strategy. A digital marketer must know how to select the right audience, develop effective campaigns, understand business goals, and evaluate results. In 2026, marketers who understand how to use AI tools effectively can improve their productivity and deliver more value to businesses. The future of digital marketing is likely to involve greater collaboration between human professionals and AI-powered technology.

Why Businesses Need an AI-Powered Digital Marketing Strategy

As digital platforms continue to evolve, businesses need marketing strategies that adapt to changing customer behaviour and technology. AI can support different marketing activities, but using tools without a clear plan may not produce meaningful results. Businesses should identify their target audience, understand their objectives, choose suitable platforms, and measure campaign performance regularly. Combining AI with SEO, social media marketing, Google Ads, and quality content can help businesses build a stronger online presence. If you are looking for the Best Freelance Digital Marketer in Perinthalmanna, working with a professional who understands both traditional digital marketing and modern AI-powered strategies can help you make better marketing decisions and improve your online visibility.

How AI Is Changing Digital Marketing in 2026: Final Thoughts

Artificial Intelligence is creating new opportunities for businesses to improve their digital marketing activities in 2026. From content creation and SEO to social media marketing, paid advertising, personalization, and customer support, AI is helping marketers work more efficiently and make informed decisions. However, technology alone cannot build a successful brand. Creativity, strategy, original content, customer understanding, and human involvement remain important for achieving meaningful results. Businesses that combine AI-powered tools with effective marketing strategies can improve their online presence and stay prepared for future changes in the digital world.

Looking to grow your business with modern digital marketing strategies? Connect with the Best Freelance Digital Marketer in Perinthalmanna to explore SEO, social media marketing, Google Ads, and AI-powered solutions for your business. Let's build a stronger brand, reach the right audience, and achieve better digital results.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

How is AI changing digital marketing in 2026?

AI is changing digital marketing by helping businesses create content, analyze customer behaviour, improve advertising campaigns, personalize customer experiences, and automate repetitive marketing tasks. It is also influencing how people discover information through AI-powered search platforms.

How can AI help small businesses with digital marketing?

AI can help small businesses generate content ideas, prepare social media captions, analyze marketing performance, improve customer communication, and support advertising activities. These tools can make marketing tasks more efficient and help businesses use their available resources effectively.

Will AI replace digital marketing jobs?

AI is more likely to change digital marketing roles than completely replace digital marketers. Professionals who combine marketing knowledge, creativity, strategic thinking, and AI skills can adapt to the changing industry.

Is AI-generated content good for SEO?

AI can help create and improve website content, but the quality and usefulness of the final content are what matter. Content should be accurate, original in value, relevant to the audience, and reviewed by a human before publishing.

What are the best AI tools for digital marketing in 2026?

Popular tools include ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Canva AI, Grammarly, Semrush, and Adobe Firefly. Each tool supports different marketing activities, so the best choice depends on your specific requirements.

Can AI improve Google Ads performance?

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: Bulkheads in Go: Isolating Failures Across Dependencies
description:
A service can have healthy code, reasonable timeouts, and a circuit breaker—and still suffer a cascading failure.

Imagine a Go API that serves portfolio data, market prices, and investment reports. It calls three external dependencies:

  • A market data provider
  • A portfolio database
  • A reporting service

The reporting service becomes slow. Requests begin waiting for it, goroutines remain occupied, and incoming traffic continues to grow. Eventually, requests that do not even need reports start failing because they compete for the same resources.

The original failure was isolated to one dependency. The application's resource usage was not.

This is the problem the bulkhead pattern is designed to address.

In this article, we'll build dependency-specific bulkheads in Go, explore admission and waiting policies, examine common implementation mistakes, and discuss how to verify that isolation actually works under load.

1. What is the bulkhead pattern?

The name comes from the watertight compartments inside a ship. If one compartment floods, the others should remain intact.

In software, a bulkhead creates a resource boundary around a particular dependency, workload, or tenant. When one boundary reaches capacity, work inside that boundary is limited without automatically consuming capacity reserved for others.

Consider a service with three downstream dependencies.

Without isolation:

                 ┌────────────────────┐
Incoming ───────►│   Shared Capacity  │
                 └─────────┬──────────┘
                           │
                ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                ▼          ▼          ▼
             Market     Portfolio   Reporting
             Data       Database    Service

If reporting requests become slow, they can consume the shared capacity needed by market data and portfolio requests.

With dependency-specific bulkheads:

                 ┌────────────────────┐
Incoming ───────►│    Go API          │
                 └─────────┬──────────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
          ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐
          │ Market │   │Portfolio│  │Report  │
          │ Limit  │   │ Limit   │  │ Limit  │
          └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘
              ▼            ▼            ▼
          Market API    Database     Report API

Each dependency receives its own concurrency budget.

If the reporting bulkhead is full, new reporting work can be rejected or briefly delayed according to policy. Market data and portfolio operations retain their own permits.

The important property is not that failures disappear. It is that one dependency cannot consume all the capacity reserved for unrelated work.

2. Bulkheads are not circuit breakers

Both patterns help prevent cascading failures, but they protect against different problems.

Pattern What it protects against
Timeout Waiting too long for an operation
Rate limiter Excessive request frequency
Load shedding Accepting more work than the service can safely handle
Circuit breaker Repeated calls to a dependency that is failing
Bulkhead One workload consuming resources needed by another

Suppose a reporting API has a 10-second response time.

A timeout limits how long a caller waits. A circuit breaker may stop future calls after repeated failures. Neither automatically prevents 100 concurrent reporting calls from consuming every available application slot.

A bulkhead limits that concurrency independently.

These patterns complement one another. A typical dependency call may use a bulkhead, a deadline, and a circuit breaker, with a carefully bounded retry policy where retries are safe.

3. Start with a bounded semaphore

Go's channel primitives provide a straightforward way to limit concurrent operations.

A buffered channel can represent available permits. Each operation acquires a permit before executing and releases it when finished.

For a dependency that should allow at most 10 concurrent calls:

var reportingSlots = make(chan struct{}, 10)

However, the acquisition policy matters.

If all permits are occupied, should a new call wait for capacity or fail immediately?

For an already-slow dependency, waiting indefinitely can simply move the queue into application memory. In many latency-sensitive paths, a non-blocking bulkhead is preferable.

Let's implement a reusable version.

4. Implementing a fail-fast bulkhead

The following implementation limits active operations and returns a recognizable error when capacity is exhausted.

package bulkhead

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var ErrFull = errors.New("bulkhead capacity exhausted")

type Bulkhead struct {
    slots chan struct{}
}

func New(maxConcurrent int) *Bulkhead {
    if maxConcurrent <= 0 {
        panic("maxConcurrent must be greater than zero")
    }

    return &Bulkhead{
        slots: make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrent),
    }
}

func (b *Bulkhead) Do(
    ctx context.Context,
    fn func(context.Context) error,
) error {
    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    select {
    case b.slots <- struct{}{}:
        // A permit has been acquired.
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    default:
        return ErrFull
    }

    defer func() {
        <-b.slots
    }()

    // Cancellation may race with permit acquisition.
    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return fn(ctx)
}

This implementation deliberately does not queue callers waiting for a permit.

If capacity is available, the operation proceeds. If every slot is occupied, the caller receives ErrFull immediately.

The second context check handles the case where cancellation races with permit acquisition. If the context is canceled by that point, the deferred release returns the permit.

The function passed to Do should honor its context and should not start detached work that outlives the operation without an independent lifecycle policy.

Using the bulkhead 

var reportBulkhead = bulkhead.New(10)

func GenerateReport(
    ctx context.Context,
    reporter Reporter,
) error {
    return reportBulkhead.Do(ctx, func(
        ctx context.Context,
    ) error {
        return reporter.Generate(ctx)
    })
}

Reporter is an application-defined interface in this example.

The reporting dependency now has an independent concurrency limit. If it becomes slow and all 10 permits are occupied, additional reporting calls fail fast rather than accumulating behind the dependency.

The limit is a policy choice, not a universal recommendation. Choose it based on load testing, downstream capacity, latency objectives, and the number of application instances.

5. Choose the right rejection behavior

A full bulkhead does not always need to produce an HTTP error directly. The appropriate response depends on the caller and the operation.

For example:

func handleReport(
    w http.ResponseWriter,
    r *http.Request,
) {
    err := GenerateReport(r.Context(), reporter)

    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, bulkhead.ErrFull):
        http.Error(
            w,
            "reporting capacity temporarily exhausted",
            http.StatusServiceUnavailable,
        )
        return

    case errors.Is(err, context.Canceled):
        // The client or upstream caller canceled the request.
        return

    case errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded):
        http.Error(
            w,
            "report generation timed out",
            http.StatusGatewayTimeout,
        )
        return

    case err != nil:
        http.Error(
            w,
            "report generation failed",
            http.StatusBadGateway,
        )
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

This is a simplified handler; the application would need to define reporter, imports, and its actual response contract.

The important distinction is between admission rejection, caller cancellation, deadline expiration, and dependency failure. They are different events and should not be collapsed into one generic error.

For public APIs, document the overload response and decide whether a 503 or another status is appropriate for the contract. Avoid encouraging immediate retries when the dependency is already saturated.

6. A bulkhead must protect the actual bottleneck

A semaphore limits how many operations enter a code path. It does not automatically isolate every resource used by that path.

Consider a Go service that calls three downstream APIs through a single http.Client.

The client uses a shared http.Transport, which manages connection pooling and other transport resources. Even if the application has separate concurrency semaphores, shared transport configuration or other shared resources may still create contention.

A useful design starts by identifying what is being protected:

  • Concurrent requests to a dependency
  • Connections to a database
  • Worker capacity for background jobs
  • CPU-intensive computation
  • Memory-intensive report generation
  • Per-tenant capacity
  • External provider quotas

Then enforce limits at the relevant resource boundary.

For outbound HTTP calls, use dedicated transports when separate connection-pool configuration or transport-level isolation is useful:

func newHTTPClient(maxConns int) *http.Client {
    transport := &http.Transport{
        MaxConnsPerHost:     maxConns,
        MaxIdleConns:        maxConns,
        MaxIdleConnsPerHost: maxConns,
    }

    return &http.Client{
        Transport: transport,
        Timeout:   2 * time.Second,
    }
}

var (
    marketClient = newHTTPClient(20)
    reportClient = newHTTPClient(5)
)

This snippet requires the net/http and time imports.

The clients have separate transports and different connection limits. The timeout is an example; production systems should choose deadlines based on their latency budgets and may prefer request contexts plus explicit transport settings.

Connection limits are not a replacement for application-level concurrency limits. A connection can be reused, and one operation can involve more than one resource. Use both controls when they protect distinct bottlenecks.

Also remember that a custom transport changes the default transport behavior. Configure TLS, proxy handling, connection lifetimes, idle timeouts, and other relevant settings according to your environment.

7. Waiting queues: useful, but not free

Fail-fast admission is not always the best policy.

Some operations can tolerate a short wait for capacity. In that case, a bounded waiting policy may improve utilization without allowing unbounded accumulation.

There are three common approaches:

  1. Fail fast: Reject immediately when no permit is available.
  2. Wait with a deadline: Wait for a permit, but only until the caller's context expires.
  3. Bound active work and queued work separately: Allow a defined number of operations to run and a small number to wait.

The third approach requires particular care. A semaphore that limits active calls does not limit the number of goroutines waiting to acquire it.

A context-aware waiting version can be implemented like this:

func (b *Bulkhead) DoWait(
    ctx context.Context,
    fn func(context.Context) error,
) error {
    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    select {
    case b.slots <- struct{}{}:
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }

    defer func() {
        <-b.slots
    }()

    if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return fn(ctx)
}

This method waits for a permit or cancellation. It does not bound the number of callers waiting in goroutines.

If the service can receive an unbounded number of waiting callers, use an explicit bounded admission queue, reject before creating excess work, or use a bounded worker pool.

The distinction is important: a concurrency limit without a queue bound can still leave the system with too many waiting goroutines.

8. Isolate workloads, not just services

Dependency-level bulkheads are useful, but some applications need additional boundaries.

Consider a service with the following operations:

  • Interactive portfolio queries
  • Historical analytics
  • Exporting large reports
  • Background notifications

These workloads may share dependencies while having very different resource profiles.

A report export can occupy database connections for much longer than a small portfolio query. If both share the same database pool and the same admission policy, the reporting workload may starve interactive traffic.

Possible isolation strategies include:

  • Separate concurrency limits by workload.
  • Dedicated worker pools for long-running jobs.
  • Bounded queues for background processing.
  • Database connection budgets for distinct workloads, where operationally feasible.
  • Reserved capacity for latency-sensitive operations.
  • Per-tenant limits to prevent one customer from dominating capacity.

Do not create a separate pool for every function by default. Each additional boundary introduces configuration, monitoring, and capacity-planning costs.

The goal is meaningful isolation around resources that have different failure modes or service-level requirements.

9. Beware of multiplicative concurrency

A local bulkhead limit is not necessarily a global limit.

Suppose a service runs 8 replicas, and each replica allows 20 concurrent calls to a reporting provider.

The potential aggregate concurrency is:

[
8 \times 20 = 160
]

If the provider can safely handle only 50 concurrent calls, the local configuration does not protect the global dependency.

This is one of the most common capacity-planning mistakes in distributed systems.

When choosing limits, account for:

  • The maximum number of replicas.
  • Autoscaling behavior.
  • Other applications calling the same dependency.
  • Provider-wide quotas.
  • Deployment overlap during rolling updates.
  • Traffic distribution and uneven load.

A local bulkhead is excellent for protecting each process. A global quota may require a shared admission mechanism, provider-side limits, a centralized dispatcher, or a different partitioning strategy.

Avoid introducing a distributed semaphore unless global coordination is genuinely needed. The coordination service can become another dependency whose failure must be handled.

10. Combining bulkheads with circuit breakers and retries

These patterns solve different parts of the same failure scenario.

Imagine a reporting provider starts timing out.

  1. The bulkhead limits how many reporting calls can be active.
  2. The deadline prevents each call from waiting indefinitely.
  3. The circuit breaker can stop repeated calls after a failure threshold is reached.
  4. A retry policy may retry selected transient failures, within a strict budget.
  5. Load shedding rejects additional work when admission capacity is exhausted.

Order and interaction matter.

If retries happen inside a bulkhead permit, the permit remains occupied across attempts and backoff periods. This can reduce pressure on the downstream service, but it also ties up local capacity while no useful work is being performed.

If retries happen outside the bulkhead, every attempt must reacquire capacity, which may make admission more responsive but can complicate retry scheduling.

Neither choice is universally correct. Define whether the permit represents a whole logical operation or one outbound attempt, then test the behavior under slow failures.

Never retry a bulkhead rejection immediately by default. The rejection indicates that local capacity is exhausted; an immediate retry simply competes for the same capacity again.

For operations with side effects, retries also require idempotency or another mechanism that makes repeated attempts safe.

11. Observability: prove that isolation works

A bulkhead without metrics is difficult to tune and nearly impossible to validate during an incident.

For each bulkhead, consider recording:

  • Active operations
  • Configured concurrency capacity
  • Rejected acquisitions
  • Wait duration, if waiting is allowed
  • Operation duration
  • Timeouts and cancellations
  • Downstream error rates
  • Circuit-breaker state, where applicable

Useful metric names might include:

dependency_bulkhead_active
dependency_bulkhead_capacity
dependency_bulkhead_rejected_total
dependency_request_duration_seconds
dependency_request_errors_total

Use bounded labels such as a dependency name or workload class. Avoid raw user IDs, request IDs, and other high-cardinality values.

Monitor the bulkheads independently. A global saturation metric can hide the fact that reporting is exhausted while market data remains healthy.

A useful operational question is not merely, “Is the service saturated?”

It is: Which resource boundary is saturated, how long has it been saturated, and are unrelated workloads still meeting their latency objectives?

12. Test the failure boundary

A bulkhead should be tested with a deliberately slow dependency.

For example, configure a dependency bulkhead with a capacity of two, start two operations that block on a test-controlled channel, and then submit a third operation.

The third operation should receive ErrFull without invoking its callback.

A simplified test:

func TestBulkheadRejectsWhenFull(t *testing.T) {
    b := bulkhead.New(2)

    release := make(chan struct{})
    started := make(chan struct{}, 2)

    operation := func(context.Context) error {
        started <- struct{}{}
        <-release
        return nil
    }

    var wg sync.WaitGroup

    for range 2 {
        wg.Add(1)

        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            _ = b.Do(context.Background(), operation)
        }()
    }

    // Wait until both permits are occupied.
    <-started
    <-started

    err := b.Do(
        context.Background(),
        func(context.Context) error {
            t.Fatal("operation should not have been admitted")
            return nil
        },
    )

    if !errors.Is(err, bulkhead.ErrFull) {
        t.Fatalf("got %v, want %v", err, bulkhead.ErrFull)
    }

    close(release)
    wg.Wait()
}

This test requires the usual testing, context, sync, and errors imports, and the bulkhead package import. It assumes the test is in a separate package where the bulkhead package can be referenced.

The test uses synchronization channels rather than arbitrary sleeps to establish that both permits are occupied.

Additional tests should cover:

  • Cancellation before acquisition.
  • Cancellation racing with acquisition.
  • Permit release after errors and panics.
  • Recovery after a dependency becomes healthy.
  • Waiting callers and bounded queues, if supported.
  • Isolation between two independent bulkheads.
  • Maximum aggregate concurrency across replicas.
  • Saturation of one dependency while unrelated operations remain responsive.

For a full integration test, make one fake dependency slow or unresponsive and verify that requests to other dependencies still meet their expected latency and success-rate objectives.

13. Common mistakes

Using one shared limiter for every dependency. This can recreate the very contention the bulkhead was intended to prevent.

Bounding concurrency but not waiting callers. A semaphore can limit active operations while allowing many goroutines to accumulate while waiting.

Assuming a local limit is a global quota. Per-replica capacity multiplies across replicas and deployments.

Holding permits during unnecessary work. Long retry backoffs, unrelated processing, or detached tasks can occupy capacity longer than intended.

Creating too many isolated pools. Excessive fragmentation can leave some pools idle while others reject work. Isolation should follow real workload and resource boundaries.

Ignoring shared infrastructure. Separate application semaphores do not automatically isolate database pools, HTTP transports, CPU, memory, or downstream quotas.

Measuring only errors. A bulkhead may be working correctly by rejecting excess work. You need rejection, saturation, latency, and dependency health metrics to interpret the behavior.

14. Production checklist

Before deploying a bulkhead, verify that:

  • The protected resource and isolation boundary are explicit.
  • Each materially different dependency or workload has an appropriate capacity budget.
  • Both active concurrency and queued work are bounded where necessary.
  • Context deadlines and cancellation are propagated.
  • Rejections are distinguishable from timeouts and dependency failures.
  • Permits are released on every exit path.
  • Retry policies do not amplify saturation.
  • Per-instance limits are compatible with global dependency quotas.
  • Metrics expose saturation and rejection per bulkhead.
  • Tests demonstrate that one slow dependency cannot starve unrelated workloads.

Final thoughts

Bulkheads do not make dependencies reliable. They make dependency failures more contained.

In Go, channels, semaphores, dedicated clients, bounded worker pools, and resource-specific limits can establish useful isolation boundaries. The hard part is not writing a semaphore. It is deciding what must be isolated, how much capacity each workload deserves, and what should happen when that capacity is exhausted.

A reliable system should not allow one slow dependency to determine the fate of every other operation.

The goal is not to eliminate every failure. It is to keep one failure from becoming everyone else's failure.
