title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Building a web studio's own site: Astro, one Cloudflare Worker route and a 199 KB homepage
description:
This month I started site-uri.ro, a small web studio in Romania that builds presentation sites and online stores for small businesses. Before showing anyone a portfolio, the studio's own site had to be the first proof: fast on a phone, easy to find, and boring to maintain.

Here is how it's built, with the parts of the code that matter.

Static output, one canonical URL per page

The whole site is Astro, built to plain HTML:

// astro.config.mjs
export default defineConfig({
  site: "https://site-uri.ro",
  trailingSlash: "never",
  build: { format: "file" },
  integrations: [sitemap({ filter: (p) => !p.endsWith("/404") })],
});

format: "file" writes /preturi.html, which is served at /preturi with no trailing slash. Every page has exactly one URL: the one in the sitemap, the canonical tag and the internal links. No redirect chains, nothing for Google to deduplicate.

No JavaScript framework ships to the browser. The pages carry three small inline scripts (the homepage animation, the mobile menu and the contact form) and zero .js files.

One Worker route, everything else is a file

The site runs on Cloudflare Workers with static assets. The Worker script only wakes up for one path:

// wrangler.jsonc
"main": "worker/index.js",
"assets": {
  "directory": "./dist",
  "binding": "ASSETS",
  "run_worker_first": ["/trimite"],
  "not_found_handling": "404-page"
}

/trimite is the quote form. Every other request is a static file served directly, without running any code.

A contact form with no database

The form posts JSON to the Worker, which sends it as an email through Cloudflare Email Routing (send_email binding) and stores nothing. Spam protection is two cheap traps instead of a CAPTCHA:

// From worker/index.js (comments translated)
// A hidden field a human never fills, and a form submitted less than
// 3 seconds after the page opened. Bots get a fake "ok" so they don't retry.
const openFor = Date.now() - Number(data.deschis ?? 0);
if (String(data.site_web ?? "") !== "" || !(openFor > 3000)) return reply(200, "ok");

The Worker also checks the Origin header, caps every field's length, and sets Reply-To to the visitor's email when they leave one, so answering a request is just pressing Reply.

Prices that can't go stale

Prices live in one TypeScript file. Pages never write a price by hand; they call a helper with the package name:

// Names translated from the Romanian original
export function price(s: Service, name: string): number {
  const p = s.packages.find((p) => p.name === name);
  if (!p) throw new Error(`Package "${name}" does not exist in ${s.slug}`);
  return p.price;
}

A typo in a package name, or a "from X" price that doesn't match any real package, stops the build. A title, a meta description or an FAQ answer can't keep advertising an old price after the price list changes.

The same idea applies to structured data: breadcrumbs (BreadcrumbList), the business (ProfessionalService) and the founder (Person, with sameAs links) are generated from the same data files the pages read.

The numbers

  • Homepage on a phone: 199 KB in total, including fonts and images (what a 375 px, 2x screen downloads).
  • 0 JavaScript files; 3 short inline scripts.
  • 0 accessibility errors from axe-core at the last check (27 October 2026).
  • Security headers (HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) in a _headers file.

The portfolio problem

A new studio has no clients, so the portfolio starts with six demonstration projects, each built end to end as if for a real client: a plumber, a dental clinic, a linen clothing shop, a guesthouse, a pottery studio and a real estate agency. For each one I first studied the top sites in that niche (what people search for, what information is missing, which structure works), then designed it with its own identity. They're clearly labelled as demos on the site.

You can see them at site-uri.ro/portofoliu.

Next up: the first real projects, and a write-up of how the real estate demo keeps its filters in the URL with about 2 KB of JavaScript.

If you build sites for small businesses: what do you ship by default, and what do you leave out?

title: VITI Special Report: Why NIST is the World's Best Cookbook (And Why Your IT Kitchen is Still on Fire)
description:
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) is the undisputed gold standard of IT frameworks. CISOs love it. Auditors worship it. But there is a massive, elephant-sized problem in the room: NIST is just a piece of paper. It tells you exactly what to do, but leaves the how completely up to you.

VITI sat down to explore how Erkki Laine’s Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF) takes the world’s most respected cyber frameworks and turns them from administrative Excel nightmares into ruthless, deterministic runtime code.

1. NIST CSF 2.0 and the "Govern" Trap

When NIST released the highly anticipated CSF 2.0, the biggest update was adding a new core function: Govern. The message was clear: cybersecurity risks must be managed as business risks.

The Reality: In most companies, adding "Govern" just meant setting up another steering committee and creating a new 106-row spreadsheet for auditors to check once a year.

The BIGF Solution: A framework taxonomy doesn't execute in production; code does. BIGF takes NIST’s "Target Profiles" and translates them into automated mathematical boundaries. It doesn't ask a committee for permission; it locks down the state machine.

2. NIST AI RMF: Asking Bots Nicely to Behave

NIST has also launched the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and an AI Agent Standards Initiative. They are trying to create global rules for how autonomous AI bots should operate safely.

The Reality: Text-based guidelines do not stop AI agents. Telling a hallucinating LLM to "be trustworthy and secure" is like telling a toddler not to touch a hot stove via an email memo.

The BIGF Solution: BIGF provides the missing mathematical shield. In Laine's architecture, every NIST AI control is tied to cold logic and cryptographic proof chains. The AI bot cannot break the NIST safety model because the BIGF state machine drops the runtime gates (a 403 Hard Halt) before the AI even has a chance to hallucinate a bad decision.

The Cookbook vs. The Kitchen

Think of NIST as the world's best, Michelin-star culinary cookbook. It has all the recipes for perfect security. But to get actual food, you need a kitchen and a chef.

Without automation, your chef is an exhausted IT manager filling out compliance forms. BIGF is the automated robotic kitchen that executes the NIST recipes flawlessly, in milliseconds, without human error.

Here is how BIGF translates NIST consultant-speak into runtime reality:

NIST CSF 2.0 Function What NIST Asks For (The Theory) How BIGF Executes It (The Reality)
GOVERN Define risk strategy, policies, and responsibilities. Hardcodes risk thresholds directly into the architecture's mathematical parameters (B*S*T).
IDENTIFY Map critical digital assets and risks. Generates a real-time State Vector from dynamic system dependencies.
PROTECT Prevent and limit cybersecurity threats. Acts as an unbreakable 403 Hard Halt gate, instantly blocking unverified state changes.
DETECT Discover anomalies as quickly as possible. Real-time deterministic monitoring: detects instantly if any data stream deviates from the canonical truth.
RESPOND React to incidents in a controlled manner. Automates decision-making via "Authority Over Truth" – no slow crisis meetings required.
RECOVER Restore normal operations. Automatically routes resources to what is mathematically proven to be most critical to the business (BIA).

Stop the Governance Theatre

NIST gives you an incredibly elegant list of things that should be in order. But without a deterministic engine like BIGF running underneath, all that elegance just leaks away into corporate Governance Theatre—endless audits, subjective guesses, and manual approvals.

If you are still managing your NIST compliance with spreadsheets and dropdown menus, your kitchen is already on fire. You just haven't looked at the thermometer yet.

title: The Save Button That Did Nothing
description:
Have you ever clicked Save on a long form and watched absolutely nothing happen?

No toast. No red text. No movement. Just a button that seems to be ignoring you.

That was our app. We build long forms: profile pages, multi-section settings, repeatable blocks like "contacts" or "addresses". Here's what kept happening:

  1. The user fills in the visible part of the form and clicks Save, which sits in a sticky header.
  2. Validation fails on a field far below the fold, or inside the third item of a repeatable list.
  3. Nothing visible happens. The user clicks Save again, then gives up or reports a bug.

The error was there all along, sitting politely at the bottom of the page where nobody could see it.

Server-side validation had the same problem. The form submits, the backend answers 400 with field errors, we map them into the form, and the screen still doesn't change.

We needed one consistent rule for every form: when validation fails, bring the first error into view.

What we were working with

  • React Hook Form (RHF) for form state, with Zod schemas through zodResolver.
  • MUI inputs, plus many composite controls: autocompletes, date pickers, chip selectors, custom list widgets.
  • React Router for navigation. Some forms are reused across tabs and routes.
  • A shared FormItem wrapper that renders the label, the control and the error message for every field.

"Doesn't RHF already do this?"

Sort of. RHF has shouldFocusError, and it's on by default. It focuses the first invalid field registered with a focusable ref.

It works well for plain inputs. But in our case:

  • Composite controls often don't expose a focusable ref, or they expose the wrong element.
  • Array-level errors (for example "add at least one contact") belong to no input, so there's nothing to focus.
  • Some fields are read-only displays of a value picked in a dialog. Focusing them is pointless.
  • Focus doesn't always scroll to a comfortable position. The field can land right under the sticky header.

So instead of chasing inputs, we decided to target the error message element.

The approach

Four small steps: mark, search, scroll, wait.

1. Mark: tag every error message with its field path

The shared FormItem already renders the error text. We add one attribute to it: the RHF field path.

{errorMessage && (
  <FormHelperText data-name={name}>
    {errorMessage}
  </FormHelperText>
)}

Why the error message and not the input?

  • It only exists when there's an error, so the selector never matches a valid field.
  • It works for any control type, including composites and custom widgets.
  • It works for errors with no input at all. A list-level error can render its own message with data-name="contacts".

Now every visible error has a predictable, framework-agnostic address in the DOM, like [data-name="contacts.2.email"].

2. Search: find the path of the first error

RHF errors mirror the shape of your form values:

// Plain field
{ title: { type: 'too_small', message: 'Required' } }

// Field array: sparse, only invalid items are present
{ contacts: [ , , { email: { message: 'Invalid email' } } ] }

// Array-level error
{ contacts: { type: 'too_small', message: 'Add a contact' } }

We need to turn each shape into a path that matches our data-name:

  • { title: {...} } → title
  • { contacts: [ , , { email: {...} } ] } → contacts.2.email
  • { contacts: { message: ... } } → contacts

The algorithm:

  1. Take the first key of the errors object. That's the first failing top-level field.
  2. Check whether its value has index keys ("0", "2", ...). If it does, it's a field array error.
  3. For a field array, take the first index present, then the first sub-field inside that item.
  4. Otherwise, use the top-level name as is.

How do you tell the two shapes apart? A plain FieldError has keys like type, message and ref. A field array error has "0", "2" and so on. One regex is enough:

const isIndex = (key: string) => /^\d+$/.test(key);

And "first index" really means the lowest one. JavaScript returns integer-like keys first, in ascending order, so Object.keys on a sparse error array always starts with the earliest invalid item.

3. Scroll: let the browser do it

Once we have a path, scrolling is a single DOM call:

document
  .querySelector(`[data-name="${path}"]`)
  ?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' });

block: 'center' matters. With a sticky header, start often hides the field right under it. Centering keeps the label, the control and the message all visible. If you'd rather use start, set scroll-margin-top in CSS to the header's height.

Two extra details in the final version:

  • Focus, not just scroll. Seeing the field isn't enough for keyboard and screen-reader users. After scrolling, we focus the first focusable element inside the same FormItem.
  • Reduced motion. If the user has prefers-reduced-motion enabled, we jump instead of animating.

4. Wait: let the page settle first

Our layout scrolls the page container to the top on every route change. When a form is submitted and the app navigates or re-renders a route, both scrolls race and neither works.

The quick fix is a setTimeout with a guess, say one second. But is one second enough? On a fast laptop it's too long. On a slow phone it might be too short.

Instead of guessing, we wait for the error message to settle. On every animation frame, we check two things:

  1. Does the element exist yet?
  2. Is it in the same place as in the previous frame?

When both are true, nothing is moving anymore, and it's safe to scroll. Here's the core of it, simplified:

const check = () => {
  const element = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(selector);
  const top = element?.getBoundingClientRect().top ?? null;

  if (element && top === lastTop) {
    callback(element);
    return;
  }

  lastTop = top;
  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);
};

This covers more than the route scroll. It also waits for content that renders late, like a list that loads its items or a section that expands with an animation. As a safety net, the loop stops after about a second (MAX_FRAMES) and scrolls to wherever the element is.

The helper returns a cancel function, and the hook returns it from the effect. A fast re-validation or an unmount never triggers a stale scroll. The effect also depends on location.pathname, so it runs again when the same form instance is shown on another route or tab.

A catch: isValid and server errors

A natural guard is to run the hook only when isValid is false. No errors, nothing to scroll to, right?

Not for server errors. setError doesn't touch isValid, because RHF derives it from schema validation only. When the client-side checks pass and the server returns a 400, isValid stays true, and a hook guarded by it would never scroll.

So the hook ignores isValid and reads the errors directly. If there's a path, it scrolls. submitCount is also in the dependencies, so submitting the same invalid form again scrolls again, even when the errors haven't changed.

Usage

Call the hook once per form:

const ProfileForm = () => {
  const form = useForm<ProfileFormValues>({
    resolver: zodResolver(profileSchema),
  });
  const { errors, submitCount } = form.formState;

  useScrollToFieldError({ errors, submitCount });

  return (
    <FormProvider {...form}>
      <FormItem name="title" label="Title">...</FormItem>
      <ContactsList name="contacts" />
    </FormProvider>
  );
};

Server errors work the same way. Map them into the form with setError, and the hook scrolls to the first one.

Trade-offs and limitations

  • "First" means first key, not first on screen. Top-level key order follows the order errors were added. That usually matches field order, but it isn't guaranteed. For a stricter version, collect all matching elements and pick the one with the smallest getBoundingClientRect().top.
  • One level of nesting. contacts.2.email works. sections.1.items.3.name doesn't. A recursive walk fixes that if you need it.
  • "Settled" is a heuristic. "Didn't move since the last frame" is a good signal, but it isn't an explicit "layout is ready" event. If your app has one, use it. MAX_FRAMES caps the wait either way.
  • Convention-based. It only works if every error message renders data-name. Putting that in one shared FormItem made it easy to enforce.

Conclusion

A small amount of code removed a whole class of "the Save button does nothing" reports. The ideas carry over to any form library:

  • Address errors, not inputs. Tag the error message with the field path. It exists only when needed and works for every kind of control.
  • Derive the path from the error tree. An "index keys" check tells plain fields from field arrays.
  • Let the browser scroll. scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' }) handles sticky headers well. Then move focus for accessibility.
  • Don't guess delays. Wait until the element stops moving, cancel on cleanup, and re-run on route change and re-submit.

Full code

waitForSettledElement.ts 

// Safety net if the layout never settles: ~1s at 60fps.
const MAX_FRAMES = 60;

// Calls `callback` once the element exists and hasn't moved
// since the previous frame. Returns a cancel function.
export function waitForSettledElement(
  selector: string,
  callback: (element: HTMLElement) => void,
) {
  let frameId = 0;
  let frames = 0;
  let lastTop: number | null = null;

  const check = () => {
    const element = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(selector);
    const top = element?.getBoundingClientRect().top ?? null;
    frames += 1;

    if (element && (top === lastTop || frames >= MAX_FRAMES)) {
      callback(element);
      return;
    }

    if (frames < MAX_FRAMES) {
      lastTop = top;
      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);
    }
  };

  frameId = requestAnimationFrame(check);

  return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
}

scrollToFieldError.ts 

import { waitForSettledElement } from './waitForSettledElement';

const FOCUSABLE = [
  'input:not([disabled])',
  'textarea:not([disabled])',
  'select:not([disabled])',
  'button:not([disabled])',
  '[tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])',
].join(', ');

function prefersReducedMotion() {
  return window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')
    .matches;
}

function reveal(message: HTMLElement) {
  message.scrollIntoView({
    behavior: prefersReducedMotion() ? 'auto' : 'smooth',
    block: 'center',
  });

  // Keyboard and screen-reader users need focus, not just scroll.
  message
    .closest('[data-form-item]')
    ?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(FOCUSABLE)
    ?.focus({ preventScroll: true });
}

// Returns a cancel function.
export function scrollToFieldError(path: string) {
  const selector = `[data-name="${CSS.escape(path)}"]`;

  return waitForSettledElement(selector, reveal);
}

getFirstErrorPath.ts 

import { type FieldErrors } from 'react-hook-form';

type ErrorNode = Record<string, unknown> | undefined;

const isIndex = (key: string) => /^\d+$/.test(key);

function hasIndexKeys(node: ErrorNode) {
  return node !== undefined && Object.keys(node).some(isIndex);
}

function getArrayFieldPath(name: string, node: ErrorNode) {
  // Integer-like keys come first, in ascending order.
  const index = Object.keys(node ?? {}).find(isIndex);
  if (index === undefined) {
    return '';
  }

  const item = node?.[index] as ErrorNode;
  const [subField] = Object.keys(item ?? {});

  return subField ? `${name}.${index}.${subField}` : '';
}

export function getFirstErrorPath(errors: FieldErrors) {
  const [name] = Object.keys(errors);
  if (!name) {
    return '';
  }

  const node = errors[name] as ErrorNode;

  return hasIndexKeys(node)
    ? getArrayFieldPath(name, node)
    : name;
}

useScrollToFieldError.ts 

import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { type FieldErrors, type FieldValues } from 'react-hook-form';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router';

import { getFirstErrorPath } from './getFirstErrorPath';
import { scrollToFieldError } from './scrollToFieldError';

type Config<T extends FieldValues> = Readonly<{
  errors: FieldErrors<T>;
  submitCount: number;
}>;

export const useScrollToFieldError = <T extends FieldValues>({
  errors,
  submitCount,
}: Config<T>) => {
  const { pathname } = useLocation();

  useEffect(() => {
    // Don't check isValid: setError() doesn't change it,
    // so server errors would be skipped.
    const path = getFirstErrorPath(errors);
    if (!path) {
      return;
    }

    return scrollToFieldError(path);
  }, [errors, submitCount, pathname]);
};

FormItem.tsx (simplified) 

import { type FC, type PropsWithChildren } from 'react';
import {
  FormControl,
  FormHelperText,
  FormLabel,
} from '@mui/material';
import { useFormState } from 'react-hook-form';
import { get } from 'lodash';

type Props = PropsWithChildren<Readonly<{
  name: string;
  label: string;
}>>;

export const FormItem: FC<Props> = ({ name, label, children }) => {
  const { errors } = useFormState({ name });
  const errorMessage = get(errors, name)?.message as
    | string
    | undefined;

  return (
    <FormControl
      data-form-item
      error={Boolean(errorMessage)}
      fullWidth
    >
      <FormLabel>{label}</FormLabel>
      {children}
      {errorMessage && (
        <FormHelperText data-name={name}>
          {errorMessage}
        </FormHelperText>
      )}
    </FormControl>
  );
};

Field array example 

import { useFieldArray, useFormContext } from 'react-hook-form';
import { FormHelperText, TextField } from '@mui/material';

type Props = Readonly<{ name: 'contacts' }>;

export const ContactsList = ({ name }: Props) => {
  const { control, register, formState } =
    useFormContext<ProfileFormValues>();
  const { fields } = useFieldArray({ control, name });

  const listError =
    formState.errors.contacts?.message ??
    formState.errors.contacts?.root?.message;

  return (
    <>
      {listError && (
        <FormHelperText error data-name={name}>
          {listError}
        </FormHelperText>
      )}

      {fields.map((field, index) => (
        <FormItem
          key={field.id}
          name={`${name}.${index}.email`}
          label="Email"
        >
          <TextField {...register(`${name}.${index}.email`)} />
        </FormItem>
      ))}
    </>
  );
};

title: How I got a thread dump from a timed-out GitHub Actions test
description:
A test hangs in CI, the job sits there for 30 minutes, and GitHub Actions cancels it. The log says the job exceeded its time limit and nothing about what the test was doing when it got stuck. Running it again locally rarely helps, because a timing problem that shows up on a 2-core runner can be close to impossible to reproduce on a laptop with 16.

What you want in that moment is a thread dump of the test JVM, taken while the test is still hung. I spent some time checking whether GitHub Actions leaves room for that, tried a few ways to get it, and ended up building an action around what I found. I built ThreadMine, the analyzer that action sends dumps to, but none of the collection methods below need it.

Is the JVM still running after a timeout?

That was the first thing to check, because if GitHub kills the test JVM right away there's nothing left to collect. I wrote a test that deadlocks on purpose and ran it on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest, with step-level and job-level timeouts. Every time, the forked test JVM was still alive after the timeout. jcmd could attach to it, and the dump showed both threads sitting on the locks they deadlocked on. It stays that way until the runner's final "Cleaning up orphan processes", which leaves a window to grab evidence.

The reason it works is in GitHub's cancellation docs. The runner sends SIGINT to the step's entry process, waits 7.5 seconds, sends SIGTERM, waits 2.5 more, and only then kills the whole process tree. For a run step the entry process is the shell, and bash exits on the first SIGINT, so the tree kill never happens and the JVMs it started are left running. If your step uses exec, or a script that traps those signals, you lose that, so I'd treat the window as something to confirm on your own setup.

Option 1: a watchdog next to the tests

Apache Kafka does it this way. Its thread-dump script starts in the background while Gradle runs the tests, sleeps until five minutes before the timeout, runs jstack on every GradleWorkerMain process, and the workflow saves the files as artifacts. It doesn't depend on the JVM surviving the cancellation, which suits Kafka, since their step wraps Gradle in the system timeout command.

The catch is picking the moment. Five minutes before the limit you might dump a test that's just slow and would have finished, and if you cut it closer you can miss the process altogether.

Option 2: let Surefire do it

With Maven, Surefire 3.6.0 and later can take a dump when a forked process hits its own timeout:

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.6.1</version>
  <configuration>
    <forkedProcessTimeoutInSeconds>600</forkedProcessTimeoutInSeconds>
    <forkedProcessTimeoutExtensionContext>
      <jstack.enabled>true</jstack.enabled>
    </forkedProcessTimeoutExtensionContext>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

Surefire writes a surefire-timeout-jstack-*.txt file before it kills the fork, and you upload it as an artifact. The Surefire timeout has to be shorter than the GitHub one, or GitHub stops the job before Surefire gets to it. It's Maven only.

Option 3: dump it in a later step

Since the JVM survives, a step after the tests with if: failure() || cancelled() can reach it. I ran this on ubuntu-latest with a step timeout and with a job timeout, and in both cases the step ran and found the Surefire fork still stuck in the deadlock. This is the approach the action is built on.

- run: ./mvnw -B verify
  timeout-minutes: 25

- name: Dump hung test JVMs
  if: failure() || cancelled()
  run: |
    mkdir -p thread-dumps
    for pid in $(jcmd -l | grep -E 'surefirebooter|GradleWorkerMain' | cut -d' ' -f1); do
      jcmd "$pid" Thread.print > "thread-dumps/$pid.txt"
    done

- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: failure() || cancelled()
  with:
    name: thread-dumps
    path: thread-dumps/

No guessing a time in advance, and the same step covers Surefire forks and Gradle test workers. jcmd comes from the JDK actions/setup-java installed. I'd leave a few minutes between the step timeout and the job timeout, so the dump and the upload have room to finish.

Reading the dump

A test JVM has a lot of threads that have nothing to do with your test: GC, JIT compiler, and whatever Surefire or Gradle use to talk to the build. A classic deadlock is the easy case. When two threads wait on each other's synchronized monitor or ReentrantLock, the dump ends with Found one Java-level deadlock and lists both threads and the locks.

Most hangs aren't a cycle, though. A CountDownLatch nobody counts down, a Future.get() without a timeout, or a pool with every worker blocked on the same call gets no special section in the dump. I'd start with the test thread (main under Surefire, Test worker under Gradle), see what it's parked on, and then look for the thread that was supposed to wake it up. Sometimes that takes one stack, sometimes forty.

Turning it into an action

I didn't want to paste that script into every repo, so it became threadmine-action:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write   # optional; needed for PR comments
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: 21 }
      - uses: maschiojv/threadmine-action@v1
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify

You put it before the test command. It's a JavaScript action, and the real work happens in its post step, which only runs when the job failed or was cancelled and, in every timeout I tested, ran before the orphan cleanup. It lists JVMs with jcmd -l and keeps the Surefire and Failsafe forks and the Gradle test workers. The Gradle daemon is skipped, since it's alive after every build and says nothing about which test is stuck. With forkCount=0 the tests run inside Maven itself, so in that case it dumps the Maven process. It also picks up the files Surefire writes on its own timeout.

The dumps always go to a workflow artifact. With analysis on, up to three of them go to ThreadMine, the result lands in the job summary, and with the pull-request permission there's one PR comment that later runs update instead of piling up new ones. On the action's own test, two threads called worker-A and worker-B each waiting on the other's lock, the comment named the deadlock, both threads and the lines in DeadlockTest.java where they stopped.

A plain assertion failure doesn't trigger any of this, because the test JVM has already exited when the post step runs. A run you cancel by hand in the middle of the tests does leave a live JVM, though, so the action only comments on the PR when the analysis actually finds a problem.

What gets sent

With analysis on, the dump goes to threadmine.dev. The repository name isn't sent, and reports made without an account expire after seven days. If thread dumps can't leave your environment, set analyze: false. You still get the dump at the right moment, in the artifact, and nothing is sent anywhere.

Without an account the limit is five analyses per hour and 20 per day per IP. GitHub-hosted runners share IPs, so on a busy day the summary says the analysis was skipped and the dump is still in the artifact. Windows runners aren't supported yet, and if the action itself breaks, you get a warning, not a second reason for the job to fail.

The action is MIT and the source is on GitHub. Even if you never use it, put a dump step after your tests. The next time a test hangs on CI, you'll have the stacks instead of a rerun and a hope that it hangs again.

title: A/B Testing for Data Analysts: How to Interpret Results Without Making Common Mistakes
description:
Imagine you're working as a data analyst for an ecommerce company. The product team has redesigned the checkout page and wants to know whether the new version performs better.

They run an A/B test, collect the results, and send you the data. The new checkout has a higher conversion rate, and the p-value is below 0.05.

So, should the company roll out the new checkout to everyone?

Not necessarily.

This is where A/B testing becomes more than comparing numbers. A good analyst needs to understand how the experiment was conducted, whether the observed difference is reliable, and what the results actually mean for the business.

Let's walk through a practical example.

1. Start With the Right Question

Before analysing an A/B test, you need to understand what the experiment is trying to achieve.

Suppose the existing checkout page is performing poorly. The team believes a simplified design could help more visitors complete their purchases.

The business question is:

Does simplifying the checkout process improve purchase conversion rates?

From here, we can define two hypotheses:

  • Null hypothesis (H₀): There is no difference in conversion rates between the existing and redesigned checkout.
  • Alternative hypothesis (H₁): The conversion rates are different.

This gives the experiment a clear objective. Without a predefined hypothesis, it's easy to look at the results and create an explanation that fits whatever numbers appear.

2. Choose Metrics That Actually Matter

One common mistake in A/B testing is tracking dozens of metrics without deciding which one determines success.

For our checkout experiment, we could use:

Metric Type Example Why It Matters
Primary Purchase conversion rate Measures whether more visitors complete purchases
Secondary Checkout completion time Helps explain how the experience changes
Guardrail Refund rate Checks for potential negative consequences

The primary metric answers the main business question. Secondary metrics provide supporting information, while guardrails help detect problems that might otherwise go unnoticed.

For example, a redesigned checkout could increase purchases but also increase refunds. Looking only at conversion rates would give an incomplete picture.

3. Understand the Experiment Before Trusting the Results

Let's say the experiment randomly assigns 10,000 eligible visitors between two checkout experiences.

Each group receives 5,000 visitors.

Before calculating significance, an analyst should confirm that the experiment was implemented correctly.

Were users randomly assigned? Was conversion tracking working? Did both groups follow the same eligibility rules? Was the experiment allowed to run for its planned duration?

These questions matter because even a statistically significant result can be misleading when the underlying experiment has problems.

A particularly useful check is sample ratio mismatch, which occurs when the observed traffic allocation differs unexpectedly from the planned split.

If the allocation is wrong, investigate why before interpreting the outcome.

4. A Practical A/B Testing Example

Here are the hypothetical results from our checkout experiment.

Metric Control (A) Treatment (B)
Visitors 5,000 5,000
Purchases 400 460
Conversion rate 8.0% 9.2%

The new checkout performs better in the observed data.

But how much better?

Absolute Uplift

9.2% − 8.0% = 1.2 percentage points

Relative Uplift

(9.2% − 8.0%) / 8.0% × 100 = 15%

This means the treatment group had a 15% higher observed conversion rate relative to the control.

Now comes the important question: Could this difference reasonably be explained by random variation?

For these independent binary outcomes, an approximate two-sided two-proportion test produces:

  • P-value: 0.032
  • 95% confidence interval: Approximately +0.1 to +2.3 percentage points for the absolute difference

At a predefined 5% significance level, the result is statistically significant.

However, statistical significance doesn't guarantee that the improvement will be equally large in future traffic, nor does it prove that launching the change is commercially worthwhile.

5. A/B Testing Cheat Sheet: What Every Analyst Should Check

A reliable A/B test follows a structured process, from defining the business question to interpreting the evidence and recommending an action.

Use this infographic as a quick reference when reviewing experiments or preparing for data analyst interviews.

6. Statistical Significance vs. Business Significance

Consider two possible experiments.

In the first experiment, a change produces a statistically significant improvement, but the actual uplift is extremely small. Implementing it might require substantial engineering effort.

In the second, a change shows a promising improvement, but the confidence interval is wide because the experiment has limited data.

Neither situation can be judged using the p-value alone.

A data analyst should consider three questions:

1. Is the experiment trustworthy?

Check randomisation, tracking, sample size and stopping rules.

2. How large and uncertain is the effect?

Report the absolute difference, relative uplift and confidence interval.

3. Does the outcome justify a business decision?

Consider implementation costs, user experience and guardrail metrics.

The goal is not simply to find a winning variant. It's to make a decision supported by reliable evidence.

7. Common A/B Testing Mistakes

A/B testing is a powerful technique, but several mistakes can lead to incorrect conclusions.

Stopping the Test Too Early

Checking results repeatedly and stopping as soon as the p-value falls below 0.05 can inflate false-positive risk under conventional fixed-horizon testing.

Changing the Success Metric After the Experiment

Selecting whichever metric looks most favourable makes the analysis less reliable. Define the primary metric in advance.

Ignoring Confidence Intervals

A p-value alone doesn't explain how large the effect might be or how uncertain the estimate is.

Confusing Correlation With Causation

Valid random assignment supports causal inference, but implementation, eligibility and tracking problems can undermine that interpretation.

Ignoring Guardrail Metrics

An improvement in one metric should not automatically justify rollout if important business or user-experience metrics deteriorate.

Recognising these issues is just as important as knowing how to calculate statistical significance.

8. How to Explain A/B Testing in a Data Analyst Interview

A/B testing is also a useful topic to prepare for when interviewing for analytics roles.

Rather than simply explaining what a p-value means, demonstrate how you'd approach a real business problem.

For example, if an interviewer asks how you would test a new checkout design, explain the experiment in this order:

  1. Define the business objective and hypotheses.
  2. Identify the primary success metric and guardrails.
  3. Explain randomisation, sample size and duration.
  4. Validate tracking and experiment allocation.
  5. Compare conversion rates and quantify the effect.
  6. Interpret statistical significance and uncertainty.
  7. Recommend whether to launch, continue testing or investigate further.

This approach shows that you can connect statistical analysis with business decisions, rather than just apply a formula.

Final Thoughts

A/B testing is not just about identifying which version performs better. It's about understanding what the experiment can reliably tell you and using that evidence to make a better decision.

For data analysts, developing this skill means learning how to design experiments, choose meaningful metrics, interpret uncertainty and communicate findings clearly.

The next time you review an A/B test, don't stop at the conversion rate or p-value. Ask whether the experiment was valid, whether the effect matters and what the business should do next.

title: The Dashboard Is a Story
description:
A recovery dashboard is read the way a headline is read: the first screen decides what the reader believes the month was. Lead with activity — attempts made, emails sent, texts fired — and the team learns to generate activity. Lead with outcomes — recovered, saved at the exit, ended honestly — and the same team learns to generate outcomes, which is a different and quieter discipline.

Order is argument. Outcome first, because that is what the revenue felt. Effort second, because it explains the outcome without impersonating it. Mix third — the decline families, the platforms, the timing — because that is where next month's decisions live. A dashboard that buries any of the three is not neutral; it is a story told in the wrong sequence, and merchants will act on the story they were given.

Swipe Again arranges its reporting like a narrative with the ending labeled first, inside a recovery flow whose every step is logged. The test we use: could a stranger retell the month accurately from the first screen alone? If not, the numbers may all be present — the story is still missing.
