title: AWS Marketplace now enables partners to list once and sell through multiple subsidiary accounts
description:
Today, AWS announces that AWS partners who operate multiple legal entities can publish a product listing once in their primary account and enable their local subsidiaries to sell it through direct private offers — eliminating the need to recreate and maintain duplicate listings across every account.

From the primary account, which retains ownership of the listing, partners authorize which products each subsidiary can sell and which buyer countries it can extend private offers to. Each subsidiary transacts under its own local tax identity, selects the local currencies it supports, and sets its own disbursement preferences and bank account. The AWS Marketplace insights report in the primary account provides a consolidated view of offers, agreements, and renewals across all connected subsidiary accounts. Partners can revoke a subsidiary authorization or a subsidiary connection at any time, which immediately stops that subsidiary from creating new offers — agreements and offers already extended to buyers remain unchanged.

This capability is available today at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace is available. To get started, see  Managing subsidiary account connections  and  Creating private offers as a subsidiary account .

title: Supabase vs Firebase for Startups: An Honest Comparison
description:
Supabase vs Firebase comes down to one question: do you want a relational Postgres database with SQL, or a document database that syncs to clients with almost no setup? For most SaaS products with users, teams, billing and reports, Supabase is the safer long-term default. Firebase still wins for real-time, mobile-first apps where you want Google to run everything and your data is shaped like documents.

I've shipped production work on Firebase (Timegram, a time-tracking SaaS I built, runs on it) and I regularly work on Supabase apps, many of them generated by AI builders like Lovable. Below is how the two compare on the things that actually hurt later: data model, security, pricing, lock-in and hiring.

What is the difference between Supabase and Firebase?

Both are "backend as a service" platforms. You get a database, authentication, file storage, server functions and real-time updates without running your own servers. The difference is what sits in the middle.

  • Supabase is built on Postgres. Its docs describe each project as a full Postgres database rather than an abstraction over one, and Auth, Storage, Realtime and Edge Functions all hang off that database. You write SQL, use foreign keys and joins, and can add Postgres extensions such as pgvector for AI embeddings, PostGIS for maps and pg_cron for scheduled jobs.
  • Firebase is built around Cloud Firestore, a NoSQL document database from Google. Data lives in collections of documents, clients read and write directly through the SDK, and access is controlled by Firebase Security Rules. It plugs into the rest of Google Cloud (Cloud Functions, Cloud Storage, Analytics, Crashlytics, Cloud Messaging).

Neither is "better" in general. They suit different shapes of data and different teams.

Supabase vs Firebase at a glance

Supabase Firebase
Database Postgres (relational, SQL) Firestore (NoSQL documents)
Queries Joins, aggregates, views, full SQL Simple queries per collection; joins done in app code
Access control Postgres Row Level Security policies Firebase Security Rules
Pricing model Plan fee plus usage (storage, egress, MAU) Pay per document read, write and delete
Free tier 2 active projects, paused after a week of inactivity Daily free quota on reads, writes and storage
Self-hosting Possible (open source) No
Best fit SaaS, dashboards, B2B, reporting, AI features Mobile apps, chat, live collaboration, quick prototypes

Supabase vs Firebase pricing: what will you actually pay?

I checked both pricing pages in October 2026. Prices change, so confirm before you budget.

Supabase pricing

Supabase uses plans with included usage:

  • Free: $0. 500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users, 5 GB egress, 1 GB file storage, 500,000 Edge Function invocations. You get two active projects, and free projects are paused after one week of inactivity.
  • Pro: from $25 a month. 8 GB database per project, 100,000 MAU, 250 GB egress, 100 GB file storage, 2 million Edge Function invocations, plus $10 of compute credits. Projects are never paused.
  • Overages on Pro: $0.125 per GB of database, $0.00325 per extra MAU, $0.09 per GB of egress, $0.0213 per GB of file storage.
  • Team: from $599 a month. Enterprise: custom.

A useful detail: the Pro plan has a spend cap switched on by default, so you won't get a surprise bill unless you turn the cap off.

Firebase (Firestore) pricing

Firestore charges per operation, not per plan. Google's Firestore pricing page lists a daily free quota of 1 GiB of stored data, 50,000 document reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes, plus 10 GiB of outbound transfer a month. Above that, in the Iowa (us-central1) location, you pay $0.03 per 100,000 reads, $0.09 per 100,000 writes and $0.01 per 100,000 deletes. Other regions are priced differently.

For sign-in, Google Cloud's Identity Platform pricing page lists email, phone, anonymous and social sign-ins as free up to 50,000 MAU, then $0.0055 per MAU up to 100,000. SAML and OpenID Connect (enterprise single sign-on) are free for only 50 MAU, then $0.015 per MAU. SMS for phone login is billed separately.

Which one is more affordable?

It depends on how your app reads data, not just how many users you have.

  • Firestore bills every document a query returns. A dashboard that loads 200 documents for every page view costs 200 reads each time. Listeners that re-run on every change add up fast. Badly structured Firestore apps are where surprise bills come from.
  • Supabase bills mostly for storage, egress and compute. A heavy SQL query costs CPU time, not per row returned, so read-heavy dashboards and reports are usually more predictable on a fixed plan.
  • For a small app with light traffic, both can stay free or close to it for a long time. Just remember the Supabase free plan pauses idle projects, which is fine for prototypes but not for a live product.

Is Supabase or Firebase better for a SaaS startup?

Ask what your data looks like six months from now.

A typical SaaS has organisations, users, roles, projects, invoices, subscriptions and audit logs, all linked to each other. That is relational data. In Postgres you model it with tables and foreign keys, and a report like "hours logged per client per month, grouped by team" is one SQL query. In Firestore you either duplicate data across documents so each screen can read it in one go, or you fetch several collections and join them in your code. Both work, but duplication means keeping copies in sync, and that is where bugs creep in.

Here is the same question asked both ways. In Supabase:

select c.name, sum(t.minutes) / 60.0 as hours
from time_entries t
join projects p on p.id = t.project_id
join clients c on c.id = p.client_id
where t.org_id = 'org_123'
  and t.started_at >= date_trunc('month', now())
group by c.name
order by hours desc;

In Firestore you would usually keep a running total on each client document and update it every time an entry is written, often from a Cloud Function:

// Illustrative: keep a per-client monthly total in sync on every new entry
export const onEntryCreated = onDocumentCreated(
  "orgs/{orgId}/entries/{entryId}",
  async (event) => {
    const entry = event.data?.data();
    if (!entry) return;
    const month = entry.startedAt.toDate().toISOString().slice(0, 7);
    const ref = db.doc(`orgs/${event.params.orgId}/clientTotals/${entry.clientId}_${month}`);
    await ref.set({ minutes: FieldValue.increment(entry.minutes) }, { merge: true });
  }
);

The Firestore version is fast and cheap to read, but you now have to handle edits, deletes and back-filling old data yourself. Every new report means another pre-computed total.

My rule of thumb:

  • Pick Supabase if your product is a B2B SaaS, has reporting or admin screens, needs complex permissions, or will add AI search with embeddings.
  • Pick Firebase if you're building a mobile-first or chat-style app, need offline sync on phones out of the box, already use Google Cloud, or your data really is a set of independent documents (user profiles, messages, feeds).

If you're still scoping your first version, this decision belongs in the planning stage of an MVP build, not halfway through development.

Supabase vs Firebase security: where do apps go wrong?

Both platforms let the browser or mobile app talk to the database directly. That's what makes them fast to build with, and it's also why security has to be done right on day one.

  • Supabase relies on Postgres Row Level Security (RLS). If a table is exposed and RLS is off, or the policies are too loose, anyone with your public anon key can read the data. This is the most common problem I find in apps built with Lovable and other AI tools. I wrote a full guide on it: Supabase RLS explained.
  • Firebase relies on Security Rules. The classic mistake is shipping with test-mode rules that allow all reads and writes, or rules that check a user is signed in but not that they own the document.

Check this before launch

Whichever you pick, test your access rules with a second, non-admin account. Try to read and change another user's data. If you can, so can anyone else.

Lock-in and switching later

Supabase is open source and the data sits in standard Postgres, so you can export it with normal Postgres tools or move to any Postgres host. That's a real advantage if investors or enterprise clients ask about vendor risk.

Firebase is a Google product with no self-hosted version. Moving away means rewriting data access code and reshaping documents into tables. Supabase publishes a migration path for this: community scripts that export each Firestore collection to JSON and import it as a Postgres table, flattening fields into text, numeric, boolean or jsonb columns. Nested arrays and objects need custom hooks or your own script to split into related tables, and each collection is migrated separately. It works, but plan time for the data modelling, not just the copy.

A quick decision checklist

  1. Write down your five main entities (users, orders, projects and so on) and how they link. Lots of links points to Supabase.
  2. List the reports and admin screens you'll need in year one. Cross-collection reports point to Supabase.
  3. Is it mostly a phone app that must work offline? That points to Firebase.
  4. Estimate reads per user per day. If a single screen loads hundreds of documents, model the Firestore cost before committing.
  5. Check if your team or future hires know SQL. Postgres skills are easy to find.
  6. Decide how much vendor lock-in you can accept.
  7. Whatever you choose, budget time to write and test RLS policies or Security Rules.

What this means for founders and app owners

If you're starting fresh, you can't really go wrong with either, as long as the data model fits the tool. The expensive mistakes come from forcing relational data into Firestore, or from launching a Supabase app with RLS switched off.

If you already have an app built with an AI tool and you're not sure whether the backend is set up safely or will scale, a production audit is the quickest way to find out what needs fixing before real customers arrive. And if you're planning a new product and want help choosing the stack, see how I approach MVP development.

Sources

  • Supabase pricing
  • Supabase docs: Database overview
  • Supabase docs: Migrate from Firestore to Supabase
  • Google Cloud: Firestore pricing
  • Google Cloud: Identity Platform pricing
  • Cover photo: Christopher Gower on Unsplash

Originally published on muhammadmoiz.dev. I'm Muhammad Moiz, a senior full-stack engineer building production apps with React, Next.js and Node.js. If you need a hand with your product, get in touch.

title: Confirming an English word with Enter sent the chat
description:
The chat sends on Enter. Shift+Enter inserts a newline. With a Chinese IME, Enter is how you keep an English word you typed in that mode, instead of a converted candidate. The field still receives a keydown whose key is Enter. The handler called send, and the word went out as a message.

This is the textarea (or input) event, not a component API. compositionstart, compositionend, blur, and keydown are on the element. A React prop with the same name is just that listener.

isComposing on the keydown is enough in Chromium. The keydown that confirms the composition still has it set, so the handler can return and let the IME write the string. Safari runs the events the other way. compositionend happens first, and the Enter keydown after it already has isComposing false. A check that only reads the event treats that keydown as a normal send.

Keep a flag, set true on compositionstart. On compositionend, clear it with setTimeout(0), not in the listener itself. The Enter keydown is still on the stack when the timeout is queued, so the flag is true and the handler returns. The timeout runs after that turn. The next Enter is a separate keypress, and that one sends.

Leave keyCode === 229 out of the check. During composition, 229 means the key belongs to the IME. Some Android keyboards also report 229 for a plain Enter, and then Enter would never send. isComposing and the flag are the two signals.

compositionend does not always arrive. Switch input method, or leave the field mid-composition, and the flag can stay true. Enter then stops sending until some later composition ends. blur sets the flag false.

Returning early also skips preventDefault, so the IME can still commit the string. A Send button never hits keydown. A click sends whatever is already in the field. Characters still in the preedit are not in that value yet. After the composition ends, Shift+Enter inserts a newline, same as before.

The listeners 

const composingRef = useRef(false);

<textarea
  onCompositionStart={() => {
    composingRef.current = true;
  }}
  onCompositionEnd={() => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      composingRef.current = false;
    }, 0);
  }}
  onBlur={() => {
    composingRef.current = false;
  }}
  onKeyDown={(e) => {
    if (e.nativeEvent.isComposing || composingRef.current) return;
    if (e.key === 'Enter' && !e.shiftKey) {
      e.preventDefault();
      send();
    }
  }}
/>

Without React, add the same four listeners with addEventListener. Read event.isComposing on the keydown. The flag is the piece Safari needs, because isComposing is already false by the time that Enter arrives.

I dispatched the events on a live textarea. Enter during compositionstart did not call preventDefault. Enter in the same turn as compositionend did not either. After the timeout, Enter did.

title: I wrote MobX from scratch in 150 lines. Here's every bug I hit
description:
I'm preparing for senior React Native interviews, and one kind of task keeps showing up: "write your own state manager". Redux is the usual target. I picked MobX instead, because I've used it for years and realized I couldn't explain what happens between store.count++ and the re-render.

The finished version is about 150 lines: observable, autorun, computed, action, and a React hook. Getting there took a lot more than 150 lines of wrong code. This post goes through the bugs in the order I made them. Every output below comes from running the code.

The core: track on read, trigger on write

MobX doesn't ask you to declare dependencies. A reaction runs once, MobX watches which fields it reads, and from then on it reruns only when one of those fields changes.

You need two pieces for that. A global variable that says which reaction is running right now, and a Proxy that records reads and announces writes:

type Reaction = (() => void) & { deps: Set<Set<Reaction>> }

let currentReaction: Reaction | null = null

export const observable = <T extends object>(object: T): T => {
  const reactionsByKey = new Map<string | symbol, Set<Reaction>>()

  const track = (key: string | symbol) => {
    if (!currentReaction) return
    let reactions = reactionsByKey.get(key)
    if (!reactions) {
      reactions = new Set()
      reactionsByKey.set(key, reactions)
    }
    reactions.add(currentReaction)
    currentReaction.deps.add(reactions)
  }

  const trigger = (key: string | symbol) => {
    const reactions = reactionsByKey.get(key)
    if (!reactions) return
    [...reactions].forEach((reaction) => reaction())
  }

  return new Proxy(object, {
    get(obj, key, receiver) {
      track(key)
      return Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver)
    },
    set(obj, key, value, receiver) {
      if (Object.is(Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver), value)) return true
      const result = Reflect.set(obj, key, value, receiver)
      if (result) trigger(key)
      return result
    },
  })
}

Every key has a Set of reactions that read it. autorun puts itself into currentReaction, calls your function, and every get along the way adds it to the right Sets.

A few Proxy details matter here. The set trap has to return true, because a falsy result throws a TypeError in strict mode. Reflect.set already returns a boolean, so passing it through is enough. Object.is skips writes that don't change anything, and unlike === it treats NaN as equal to NaN, so writing NaN over NaN doesn't wake anyone up. The receiver argument decides what this is inside getters and setters on the object. It confused me enough that it gets its own post.

Almost every line above was a bug fix at some point.

Bug 1: a reaction that listens to fields it stopped reading

My first autorun just set currentReaction, called the function and cleared it. Dependencies only ever got added. Here's what that does to a conditional read:

const s = observable({ show: true, name: 'Bogdan' })

autorun(() => console.log('render:', s.show ? s.name : 'hidden'))

s.show = false
s.name = 'Ivan'

render: Bogdan
render: hidden
render: hidden

After show became false, the function no longer read name. It still reran when name changed, because it was still sitting in the Set for name from the first run. In a React app this is a component that re-renders because of data it doesn't display.

Dependencies have to be rebuilt on every run. Before calling the function, remove the reaction from every Set it's in, and let the run add it back where it still belongs. That's why each reaction keeps deps, a Set of the Sets that contain it. Without the link back, there's no way to find those Sets:

const cleanup = () => {
  reaction.deps.forEach((set) => set.delete(reaction))
  reaction.deps.clear()
}

With cleanup the same code prints two lines.

Bug 2: the Set that never ends

Cleanup fixed bug 1 and broke something else. My trigger iterated the Set directly:

reactions.forEach((reaction) => reaction())

const s = observable({ count: 0 })
autorun(() => console.log('count:', s.count))
s.count = 1

count: 0
count: 1
count: 1
count: 1
count: 1
...

It never stopped. I had a guard that threw after a few runs, otherwise the tab would just hang.

Set.prototype.forEach visits entries that are added while it's iterating. If you delete an entry and add it back, it goes to the end of the Set and gets visited again. That's exactly what a reaction does: cleanup deletes it from the Set for count, then the function reads count and track adds it back. forEach sees a "new" entry and calls it, and the same thing happens again.

You can see it without any reactivity:

const set = new Set(['x'])
let visits = 0
set.forEach((v) => {
  if (++visits > 3) return
  set.delete(v)
  set.add(v)
})
visits // 4

The fix is to iterate over a copy, [...reactions]. Vue 3 copied the Set in triggerEffects in the same way, until 3.5 replaced Sets with linked lists. I hit this bug a second time later, when I wrote batching.

Bug 3: a nested autorun steals tracking from its parent

If an autorun creates another autorun, the inner one overwrites currentReaction. When it finishes and resets it to null, the outer one keeps running with no reaction to attach reads to:

const s = observable({ a: 1, c: 1 })

autorun(() => {
  autorun(() => console.log('inner a:', s.a))
  console.log('outer c:', s.c)
})

s.c = 2

Nothing happens on s.c = 2. The outer reaction read c while currentReaction was null, so it never subscribed.

The fix is a stack, but you don't need an array for it. Each run remembers the previous reaction and puts it back at the end, in finally so that an exception in the function doesn't leave the wrong reaction behind:

const previousReaction = currentReaction
try {
  currentReaction = reaction
  cleanup()
  fn()
} finally {
  currentReaction = previousReaction
}

After this change, s.c = 2 prints outer c: 2.

Bug 4: dispose that didn't dispose

autorun returns a function that stops it. It needs two things: cleanup() to remove the reaction from all Sets, and an isDisposed flag. The flag covers the case where trigger already copied the Set and the reaction is in that copy when it gets disposed. Without the flag, it would run one more time after you stopped it.

Later I moved the shared code into a helper and passed the flag as an argument:

const makeReaction = (isDisposed: boolean, fn: () => void) => {
  const reaction = () => {
    if (isDisposed) return
    // ...
  }
}

export const autorun = (fn: () => void) => {
  let isDisposed = false
  const reaction = makeReaction(isDisposed, fn)
  // ...
  return () => { isDisposed = true }
}

A boolean is passed by value. isDisposed = true in dispose changes the variable in autorun, and the helper still has its own false. The check has to read the variable through a closure, either by keeping it in the scope where the reaction is created or by passing a getter.

Hooking it up to React

The first hook was useState plus useEffect: run an autorun in an effect and push the selected value into state. Two things went wrong.

I wrote setState(value). When the selected value is a function, React calls it as an updater instead of storing it. The safe form is setState(() => value).

The selector you pass changes on every render, because it's usually an inline arrow. The autorun is created once, so it would keep calling the selector from the first render. The latest selector goes into a ref, updated in useLayoutEffect, and the autorun reads selector.current.

The second version uses useSyncExternalStore, which React 18 added for exactly this, and which avoids tearing in concurrent rendering:

export const useObserver = <T,>(fn: () => T) => {
  const selector = useRef(fn)

  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    selector.current = fn
  }, [fn])

  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onStoreChange: () => void) =>
      autorun(() => {
        selector.current()
        onStoreChange()
      }),
    []
  )

  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, fn)
}

subscribe has to be stable. If it's a new function on each render, React unsubscribes and subscribes again every time. The autorun calls selector.current() only to subscribe to whatever it reads, and onStoreChange tells React to call getSnapshot again.

There's a known trap I left unsolved. If the selector returns a new object or array, for example store.items.filter(...), getSnapshot returns a new reference on every call. React warns that the result of getSnapshot should be cached and then re-renders in a loop. A real implementation memoizes the snapshot.

computed: a cache that knows when it's stale

computed is a derived value that is lazy and cached:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)

total.get() // computes
total.get() // returns the cached value
cart.qty = 3 // marks it stale, doesn't recompute
total.get() // recomputes

It should recompute only when a field it actually read has changed. Its function also has to be pure. It can only depend on observable fields. If it reads a plain variable or Date.now(), nothing will ever tell it the value changed.

Bug 5: isDirty started as false

My first get() was if (isDirty) { value = fn(); isDirty = false } with isDirty initialized to false. The first call returned undefined, and nothing ever set the flag to true. That one's easy to find.

Bug 6: subscribing the function that computes

Then I needed something to set isDirty = true when a dependency changed. I reused the autorun machinery: a reaction that runs fn with tracking, and get() calls it when the value is stale.

The problem is which function ends up in the Sets. During tracking, currentReaction was the evaluator itself. So when cart.qty changed, trigger called the evaluator directly, bypassing get() and its isDirty check:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)
total.get()  // 200, evaluator calls: 1
cart.qty = 3 // evaluator calls: 2
total.get()  // 200

The value was recomputed eagerly when nobody asked for it. The result was thrown away, because trigger ignores return values. isDirty stayed false, so get() kept returning 200 from then on.

A computed needs two separate things. One is what trigger calls, and for a computed that function only marks it stale:

const markDirty = () => { isDirty = true }

The other is the tracked run of fn that happens inside get(), with markDirty as the current reaction. That way the fields subscribe markDirty, and fn runs only when someone reads the value.

Bug 7: two functions called fn

At this point autorun and computed had the same block: save the previous reaction, set the current one, clean up, run, restore in finally. I moved it into a shared createReaction:

const createReaction = (fn: () => void) => {
  const reaction = Object.assign(() => fn(), { deps: new Set() })
  const cleanup = () => { /* ... */ }
  const run = () => {
    const previousReaction = currentReaction
    try {
      currentReaction = reaction
      cleanup()
      return fn()
    } finally {
      currentReaction = previousReaction
    }
  }
  return { reaction, cleanup, run }
}

Inside createReaction, fn is the reaction callback: markDirty for a computed, and for an autorun a callback that calls run(). The user's function lives in a different scope with the same name. So the computed's run() executed markDirty and returned undefined, and the autorun did callback → run → callback → run until Maximum call stack size exceeded.

The function to run has to come in as an argument:

const run = <T,>(work: () => T): T => {
  const previousReaction = currentReaction
  try {
    currentReaction = reaction
    cleanup()
    return work()
  } finally {
    currentReaction = previousReaction
  }
}

The computed calls run(fn) with its formula, the autorun calls run(fn) with its body, and the parameter of createReaction gets a name that can't be confused with either, like onTrigger.

The autorun's callback calls run, which only exists after createReaction returns. This works:

const callback = () => {
  if (isDisposed) return
  run(fn)
}
const { reaction, cleanup, run } = createReaction(callback)
reaction()

A closure captures the variable, not its value. callback is created before run exists, but it isn't called until reaction() on the last line, and by then run is initialized. Calling callback() before the destructuring would throw "Cannot access 'run' before initialization".

action: five ways batching broke

Every write triggers reactions right away, so two writes run an autorun twice, and the first run sees a half-updated state:

autorun(() => console.log(cart.price, cart.qty))
cart.price = 200 // 200 2
cart.qty = 5     // 200 5

action should collect the writes and run each affected reaction once at the end. Values are still written immediately, so reading cart.price inside the action returns the new value. Only reactions wait.

Bug 8: a queue of Sets

My first version put the Set of reactions for each changed key into a queue. price and qty have separate Sets, and the same autorun is in both:

autorun: 100 2
autorun: 200 5
autorun: 200 5

The queue has to hold reactions. A Set<Reaction> deduplicates them on its own.

Bug 9: the queue was never cleared

The next action ran every reaction from the previous one again. clear() after the flush.

Bug 10: a nested action ended the batch early 

action(() => {
  action(() => { s.a = 2 })
  s.b = 2
})

The inner action set isBatching = false when it finished, so s.b = 2 ran reactions immediately. Each action has to remember the previous state of the flag, restore it, and flush only if it was the outermost one. MobX uses a counter, globalState.inBatch, and runs reactions when it drops back to zero. A saved boolean does the same job.

Bug 11: computed went stale inside an action 

const total = computed(() => s.price * s.qty)
total.get()

action(() => {
  s.qty = 3
  console.log(total.get())
})

total inside action: 200
total after action: 300

I had put the batching check into trigger: during an action, queue every reaction instead of calling it. That included markDirty. The computed didn't learn it was stale until the action ended, so get() inside the action returned the old value.

A computed doesn't need batching at all. Marking it stale is cheap and the recompute is lazy anyway. The question is where the decision belongs. You can teach trigger the difference between kinds of reactions, but then the Reaction type needs a flag. I moved the check into the autorun's callback instead, and trigger went back to calling everything:

const callback = () => {
  if (isDisposed) return
  if (isBatching) {
    batchingDelayedReactions.add(reaction)
    return
  }
  run(fn)
}

MobX is built the same way. When a value changes, it calls onBecomeStale_ on every observer. A computed reacts by propagating "maybe changed" to its own observers. A reaction calls schedule_(), which pushes it onto globalState.pendingReactions, and the list runs when the batch ends.

Bug 12: flushing while still batching

With the check inside the reaction, the next run of my tests printed nothing after the action. The flush loop called each queued reaction while isBatching was still true, and each one put itself back into the queue and returned. The flag has to be reset before the flush.

Bug 13: an exception left the flag on

If the function passed to action threw, the code after it never ran, isBatching stayed true, and from then on every write in the app was queued and never flushed. Restoring the flag and flushing go into finally. The flush runs over a copy of the queue, for the same reason as bug 2.

The final version:

let isBatching = false
const batchingDelayedReactions = new Set<Reaction>()

export const action = (fn: () => void) => {
  const previousBatching = isBatching
  isBatching = true

  try {
    fn()
  } finally {
    isBatching = previousBatching
    if (!previousBatching) {
      const reactions = [...batchingDelayedReactions]
      batchingDelayedReactions.clear()
      reactions.forEach((reaction) => reaction())
    }
  }
}

My tests cover four cases: two actions in a row, a nested action, a computed read inside an action, and an exception followed by a plain write. All four pass now. Before this version, each of them failed in a different way.

What's still missing

One gap is visible right away:

const total = computed(() => cart.price * cart.qty)
autorun(() => console.log('total:', total.get()))
cart.qty = 3

This prints total: 200 once, and nothing after qty changes. Inside get() the current reaction is markDirty, so the autorun never subscribes to price or qty, and the computed has no observers of its own. To fix it, a computed has to act as an observable: track whoever calls get(), and notify them when it becomes stale.

Even with that fixed, MobX does a lot more. Its graph avoids glitches: when two computeds depend on the same field and an autorun reads both, the autorun runs once and never sees one updated and one stale. A computed with no observers stops listening to its own dependencies. There are observable Map and Set, async actions with flow, comparers, onBecomeObserved hooks, trace and spy. That's why the production build of MobX 7.1.3 is around 14.7 KB gzipped, against my 150 lines.

What I got out of it is that I now know where all of that comes from. In an interview, "MobX tracks reads through Proxy" is the short answer. The cleanup, the copy before iterating, the restore in finally, and the batching check in the reaction are what the follow-up questions are about.

New posts go to my Telegram channel first: t.me/umaniuk_dev

Questions, or a senior mobile role you think I'd fit? Message me on Telegram: @umaniukbogdan

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. Keep host and guest kernels up to date, reduce the kernel attack surface via build and runtime configs, disable nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Why Empathy is a Mobile Developer's Greatest Tool
description:
Why Empathy is a Mobile Developer's Greatest Tool

As engineers, it is incredibly easy to get caught up in the technical details. We obsess over milliseconds of render time, the elegance of our state management, and achieving a 100% crash-free rate.

But sometimes, in our pursuit of technical perfection, we lose sight of the most important element: The User.

Designing for the Real World

A perfectly optimized app is useless if it frustrates the person using it. Empathy in mobile development means stepping out of the IDE and into the user's shoes.

Consider these scenarios:

  • The One-Handed User: Is your core navigation reachable with a thumb while holding a coffee?
  • The Low-Connectivity User: Does your app gracefully handle a sudden drop to 3G, or does it show an infinite loading spinner?
  • The Anxious User: When a payment fails, do you show an obscure HTTP 500\ error, or a calm, actionable message?

Bridging the Gap

Great engineers don't just write code; they solve human problems. By collaborating closely with UX designers and actively listening to user feedback, we can build products that aren't just fast, but feel genuinely delightful to use.

Next time you build a feature, ask yourself: How will this make the user feel? That simple shift in perspective is what separates good apps from unforgettable ones.

Originally published at uzairxdev.online

title: Google Considers 1,200 MW Data Center Campus on 1,000 Acres in Goochland, Virginia
description:
Google is weighing the purchase of a roughly 1,000-acre site in West Creek Business Park in Goochland County, Virginia, where it would build a 1,200-megawatt data center campus.

The company confirmed the plan following a news release from the county, marking the first time Google has been publicly linked to the proposed development. The project would further expand Google's data center footprint in Virginia, adding to its existing data center projects in the Richmond region and strengthening the state's position as a key market for US data center development. The proposed facility also reflects continued investment in US data center infrastructure as demand for AI and cloud computing capacity grows.

**Early Stage: Due Diligence, No Plans Filed
**Google is currently performing due diligence on the property. If it decides to proceed and buy the land, the next step would be site engineering to develop a site plan to submit to the county.
As of now, Google has submitted no plans, Goochland County Administrator Jeremy Raley said in an email Wednesday.

**By-Right Status Under the Technology Overlay District
**The site lies within the county's recently approved technology overlay district, known as the TOD, which means any data center project there would be a by-right use.
As a result, it would not need to go through the public hearing process.
The project site would bisect Route 288 north of Patterson Avenue. It is owned by an entity tied to Pruitt Associates and Riverstone Group, which control the bulk of the land in West Creek.
From Unnamed Filing to Named User
Wednesday's county release was the first time Google was associated with the proposal.
The project was first mentioned, without naming Google, in a State Corporation Commission regulatory filing dated July 14. That filing listed several potential data center campuses proposed by unnamed applicants for the eastern portion of Goochland.
Besides the 1,200-megawatt project now linked to Google, it included a 600-megawatt project that would rise on roughly 150 acres off Ashland Road and a 200-megawatt project east of Route 288 and north of Patterson Avenue.
All three developments are located in the TOD and an accompanying technology zone, which together span about 5 miles along Route 288, from Interstate 64 south to Patterson Avenue.
The TOD area is bordered to the west by Hockett Road and covers roughly 4,400 acres, about 3,500 of which are within West Creek and controlled by Pruitt Associates.
According to the July filing, the customer for the 1,200-megawatt campus had executed four ELOAs, or engineering letters of authorization, for the project.

Once an ELOA is issued, projects are placed in a project queue for Dominion Energy, where they can sit for years before a feasibility study is conducted on a site and a construction letter of authorization, or CLOA, is executed.

The filing did not identify the customer, but Google officials confirmed on Wednesday that the company was interested in that specific site.
County's Account of Its Contact with Google

The county's release laid out a timeline of its dealings with Google.
It begins with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership reaching out to the county in early 2024 to meet with a data center user and show them potential sites in Goochland County.

The county entered into a nondisclosure agreement with Google on Jan. 10, 2024, and county staff held one meeting with Google officials to discuss potential locations for a data center development on Jan. 30 of that year.
According to the release, after the meeting the VEDP told the county that Google was not interested and was not moving forward, and there was no further communication with Google at that time.

After last November's adoption of the TOD, however, Google re-engaged with the county and began due diligence on the West Creek site.
Because the county was already under the NDA from the earlier discussions, it did not enter into a new one, the release says.
In what the county described as an effort to provide transparency, it requested to be released from the NDA.
Both the county and Google agreed to the release on Tuesday, which prompted Wednesday's announcement of Google's involvement.

Neighboring Tuckahoe Tech Park Faces a Different Process
The potential Google site lies east of the proposed Tuckahoe Tech Park, which would rise within the county's TOD West area, a 900-acre tract where data centers require a conditional-use permit.

Denver, Colorado-based data center developer Tract is behind that project, which would need approvals through the public hearing process before it could move forward.

Lawsuit Over the TOD Awaits a Ruling
The announcement comes shortly after a recent hearing in a lawsuit that four Goochland residents have brought against the county.
The residents claim that supervisors and planning commissioners failed to clearly and lawfully explain their adoption of the TOD.

A hearing last Tuesday addressed the county's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, and that motion is under advisement by the judge in the case.

Building on Google's Chesterfield Presence
Google's efforts in Goochland would build on its existing data center plans in the Richmond region. The company has begun construction on a data center campus on a site of more than 300 acres at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road in eastern Chesterfield County, next to Meadowville Technology Park.
It also has several other data center facilities planned for the western end of Chesterfield County.

title: Building an AI Video App on Cloudflare Workers with TanStack Start
description:
I run a small AI video web app: users upload a character photo and a short motion clip, and a hosted video model renders the character performing those moves. The whole thing (UI, API, auth, payments, storage and the job pipeline) runs as one Cloudflare Worker. No servers, no containers, no separate queue service.

This post walks through the architecture and the handful of problems that turned out to be interesting. If you're considering Workers for anything that handles large files or long-running third-party jobs, most of this transfers.

The stack

  • TanStack Start + React 19 for SSR and file-based routing, built with Vite and the Cloudflare Vite plugin
  • A single Worker entry (src/server.ts) that hands requests to TanStack Start's handler
  • D1 (SQLite) through Drizzle ORM for users, credits and jobs
  • R2 for uploads and finished videos
  • KV as a cache
  • Workers AI for a vision-model safety check on uploaded photos
  • Better Auth for email/password and Google sign-in
  • Cloudflare Email for transactional mail, behind a small provider interface
  • GitHub Actions deploying with wrangler deploy on every push to main, plus per-PR preview URLs

TanStack Start's server functions (createServerFn with a Zod validator and middleware chain) replace a separate API layer. The client calls them like ordinary async functions, and they run inside the same Worker with direct access to the bindings.

Problem 1: large uploads without blowing up memory

Motion clips can be tens of megabytes. Buffering that in a Worker is a bad idea. Instead, the upload route takes the raw file as the request body and streams it straight into R2:

// simplified
const key = `uploads/${userId}/${crypto.randomUUID()}.mp4`;
await env.BUCKET.put(key, request.body, {
  httpMetadata: { contentType: request.headers.get('content-type') ?? '' },
});
return Response.json({ key });

The client then passes that key to the "start job" server function. Uploads are deleted as soon as a job has used them, and an R2 lifecycle rule removes anything older than a day as a safety net. That keeps storage costs flat and means user-provided material doesn't sit around.

Problem 2: pricing a video by length without downloading it

Pricing is per second of motion video, so the server needs the clip's duration before charging. Reading the entire file just to get one number defeats the point of streaming.

MP4 and MOV files store their duration in the mvhd box inside moov. So the server uses R2 range reads to walk the top-level box headers (8â€“16 bytes each), skips over mdat without reading it, fetches only the moov box, and parses timescale and duration from mvhd. Typically that's a few kilobytes read instead of the whole file. When the job is submitted, the video body goes to the model provider as a stream, again never held whole in memory.

Problem 3: jobs that outlive the request

Video rendering takes a few minutes, far longer than a request should stay open. Queues or Durable Objects would work, but a simpler pattern is enough:

  1. Start: one request validates input, runs the photo check, charges credits, submits to the provider and writes a row to an effect_job table with the provider's request ID.
  2. Advance on poll: the client polls a status server function. Each poll asks the provider for status and moves the job forward. When it's done, the result is copied into R2 under the user's files. When it fails, the credits are refunded.
  3. Notify: on completion, an email goes to the user ("your video is ready") so they can close the tab.

Because the status call is idempotent (it only moves a job forward from its stored state), duplicate polls from multiple tabs are harmless.

Problem 4: refunds that happen minutes later

The codebase has a withCredits helper that charges, runs a callback and refunds if the callback throws. That's perfect for synchronous AI calls but useless here: the job can fail five minutes after the request that charged for it has finished.

The fix was to store the spend on the job row. When a poll discovers a failure, it refunds exactly what that job cost and marks the row as refunded, so the refund can't happen twice. Treat the job row as the source of truth for money, not the call stack.

Problem 5: safety checks before charging

Every photo passes through a Workers AI vision model via the AI binding before any credits move. It flags sexual content and recognizable public figures (both always refused) and applies extra rules for photos that appear to include minors. If the check itself errors, the photo is refused rather than let through. Running it first means users are never charged for a request that would be rejected anyway.

Problem 6: private files, shareable thumbnails

Finished videos are private. They're served from a route that checks the owner's session. But generating a first-frame poster image uses Cloudflare Media Transformations, which needs to fetch the video by URL. The answer was short-lived signed links: the video route accepts either the owner's session or a valid signature, and the poster pipeline uses the latter, then stores the WebP through the Images binding.

Local development against remote resources

One opinionated choice: local dev and end-to-end tests connect to the remote D1, R2 and KV ("remote": true on each binding in wrangler.jsonc) rather than local emulators. That removes a whole class of "works locally" bugs around SQLite versions and R2 behaviour, at the cost of needing a dev database. For a solo project that trade has been worth it.

Would I do it again?

Yes. The single-Worker model keeps operations close to zero: one deploy, one log stream, costs that scale with usage, and no idle servers. Its constraints (no Node-only APIs, careful memory use, request time limits) pushed the design toward streaming and stateless polling, which ended up simpler than a queue-based design.

If you want to see the result, the app is live at MotionControlAI. It's an independent project, not affiliated with Kling AI or Kuaishou, even though it runs their motion control models. There's a plain-English guide to how Kling Motion Control works if you're curious about the model side.

description:
Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon Web Services (AWS)
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Exploring how cloud infrastructure works, how Amazon EC2 provides computing resources, and why businesses are adopting IaaS.
Written by: Ngombe Emmanuel Puwakeh
Cloud Computing | Academic Article

*Introduction
*Technology has changed the way individuals and organizations store information, develop applications, and manage their computing resources. In the past, businesses that wanted to operate their own digital systems often had to purchase physical servers, networking equipment, storage devices, and other hardware. They also needed dedicated spaces and technical personnel to install, maintain, and manage these resources.
Although this traditional approach provided organizations with control over their infrastructure, it also came with significant costs and maintenance responsibilities. As businesses expanded, managing these resources became increasingly difficult, especially when their computing requirements changed.
Cloud computing emerged as an alternative to this approach. Instead of purchasing and maintaining all their computing equipment, organizations can access computing resources through the internet whenever they need them.
One of the major service models that makes this possible is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
This article explores the meaning of IaaS, how it works, its major components, and its importance in modern computing. It also examines Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), as a practical example of how IaaS is implemented.

*1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
*Infrastructure as a Service, commonly known as IaaS, is a cloud computing model that provides users with access to computing resources such as virtual machines, storage, and networking over the internet.
Rather than buying physical servers and other infrastructure equipment, users rent these resources from a cloud service provider. The provider manages the physical infrastructure, while customers configure and manage the virtual resources required to run their applications.
In simple terms, IaaS allows an individual or organization to rent computing infrastructure instead of owning it.
For example, a company that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider, install the required software, and make its website accessible to users through the internet.
IaaS is particularly useful because it gives organizations flexibility. They can increase or decrease their computing resources depending on their needs without having to purchase additional physical equipment.

*2. How Does IaaS Work?
*IaaS works mainly through virtualization technology.
Virtualization allows a physical computer or server to be divided into multiple virtual computing environments. Each virtual environment operates independently and can have its own operating system, allocated memory, processing capacity, and storage.
Cloud service providers operate large data centers containing physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment. Through virtualization, they make these resources available to customers as services.
The process generally involves the following steps:

  1. A user selects a cloud service provider.
  2. The user chooses the computing resources required, such as CPU, RAM, storage, and networking.
  3. The provider allocates the requested resources through its cloud infrastructure.
  4. The user configures the virtual environment and installs the required operating system or software.
  5. The user deploys applications and manages the resources through an online interface or application programming interface (API).
  6. The provider maintains the underlying physical infrastructure. This arrangement allows users to concentrate on their applications without having to manage the physical servers on which those applications operate.

****3. Major Components of IaaS

Infrastructure as a Service consists of several important components that work together to provide computing resources.

**3.1 Computing Resources
**Computing resources provide the processing power required to execute applications and perform tasks. They include central processing units (CPU), random access memory (RAM), and virtual machines.
A virtual machine behaves like a physical computer but operates within a virtualized environment. Users can select different configurations depending on the type of workload they intend to run.

**3.2 Storage
**Storage allows users to save application files, databases, documents, backups, and other information.
IaaS providers offer different storage options depending on the purpose. These may include block storage, file storage, and object storage.
For example, a business hosting an online application may require storage for its application files and customer information.

**3.3 Networking
**Networking enables virtual machines and other cloud resources to communicate with one another and with external users.
It includes virtual networks, IP addresses, firewalls, routing, and other networking services.
Proper network configuration helps organizations control access to their resources and establish secure connections between applications.

**3.4 Virtualization
**Virtualization is one of the technologies that makes IaaS possible. It allows providers to allocate physical computing resources to multiple virtual environments.
Through virtualization, customers can access computing resources without directly owning or managing the physical machines.

***4. Difference Between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
*
**IaaS is one of the three commonly discussed cloud computing service models. The other two are Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS).
Although they all provide services through the cloud, they differ in the level of control and management offered to users.
Service model Description Example

  • IaaS Provides virtual computing infrastructure, including servers, storage, and networking. Amazon EC2 PaaS Provides a managed environment for developing and deploying applications. Google App Engine
  • SaaS Provides ready-to-use software over the internet. Gmail The major difference is the responsibility of the user. With IaaS, users have greater control over their virtual infrastructure and are responsible for managing their operating systems and applications. With PaaS, the provider manages more of the underlying environment, allowing developers to concentrate mainly on application development. With SaaS, users simply access and use an existing software application without managing its underlying infrastructure.

****5. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS)

**5.1 Introduction to AWS
**Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud computing platform operated by Amazon that provides a wide range of cloud-based services to individuals, businesses, and government organizations.
AWS offers services covering computing, storage, databases, networking, security, analytics, and other areas of information technology.
One of its major computing services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, commonly called Amazon EC2.
Amazon EC2 is a good example of Infrastructure as a Service because it allows customers to create and manage virtual servers in the AWS cloud without purchasing or maintaining physical server hardware.

**5.2 What Is Amazon EC2?
**Amazon EC2 is a cloud computing service that provides resizable computing capacity through virtual servers known as instances.
An EC2 instance functions much like a physical computer. Users can select the operating system, processing capacity, memory, and other configurations required for their applications.
For example, a developer building a web application can launch an EC2 instance, install a web server such as Apache or Nginx, upload the application files, and configure the server to receive internet traffic.
This makes it possible to host applications without setting up a physical server.

**5.3 Major Features of Amazon EC2
**Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for individuals and organizations.
Virtual Server Instances
EC2 allows users to launch virtual servers according to their computing requirements. Different instance types provide different combinations of CPU, memory, storage, and networking capacity.
Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
An Amazon Machine Image is a template used to launch EC2 instances. It contains the information required to create an instance, including an operating system and, optionally, additional software.
Storage
Amazon EC2 works with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent block storage volumes that can be attached to instances.
This allows users to store application data and other information separately from the temporary storage provided by certain instance types.
Networking
EC2 instances can operate within Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). This allows users to create logically isolated virtual networks and control how their cloud resources communicate.
Security Groups
Security groups act as virtual firewalls for EC2 instances. They allow users to specify which network traffic is permitted to reach their instances and which traffic can leave them.
Scalability
Users can increase or decrease computing capacity depending on their workload. EC2 can also be integrated with AWS Auto Scaling to adjust the number of instances according to defined conditions.

**5.4 How Amazon EC2 Works in a Real-World Situation
**Consider a small company that wants to launch an online shopping website.
Traditionally, the company might need to purchase a physical server, install an operating system, configure networking, and employ technical personnel to maintain the equipment.
With Amazon EC2, the process can be different.
First, the company creates an AWS account and accesses the EC2 service through the AWS Management Console.
Next, it selects an Amazon Machine Image containing a suitable operating system, such as Linux.
The company then chooses an instance type based on the expected workload and launches the virtual server.
After launching the instance, the company configures its network settings and security groups to control incoming and outgoing traffic.
It can then connect to the instance, install the necessary software, configure a web server, and deploy its shopping website.
Once the website is running, customers can access it through the internet.
If website traffic increases, the company can add more computing capacity using suitable AWS scaling services. When traffic decreases, it can reduce the resources being used.
This example demonstrates how IaaS makes computing infrastructure more flexible and accessible.

6. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution
Amazon EC2 provides several benefits to organizations that need flexible computing infrastructure.

**6.1 Reduced Initial Hardware Costs
**Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications. They can rent computing resources and avoid some of the initial costs associated with establishing a traditional data centre.

**6.2 Flexibility
**Users can choose the computing configurations that match their applications. They can also change their infrastructure as their requirements develop.

**6.3 Scalability
**EC2 allows organizations to adjust computing capacity as demand changes. This is useful for websites and applications that experience different levels of traffic at different times.

**6.4 Faster Deployment
**Creating a virtual server can be much faster than purchasing, installing, and configuring physical hardware. This helps developers and organizations deploy applications more quickly.

**6.5 Different Pricing Options
**AWS provides different purchasing options for EC2, including On-Demand Instances, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances.
These options allow customers to choose a pricing arrangement based on their expected usage and workload requirements.

**7. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

**Despite its benefits, IaaS also presents some challenges that organizations should consider before adopting it.

**7.1 Internet Dependency
**Cloud infrastructure is accessed through networks. Poor internet connectivity or network interruptions can affect users' ability to access their cloud resources.

7.2 Security Responsibilities
Although AWS manages the underlying physical infrastructure, customers are still responsible for securing important parts of their cloud environments.
For example, EC2 users must manage their operating system updates, application security, access permissions, and security group configurations.
Incorrect security configurations can expose applications and data to unauthorized access.

**7.3 Unexpected Costs
**IaaS can reduce the need for large hardware investments, but it does not mean that cloud computing is always inexpensive.
If organizations fail to monitor their usage, they may accumulate unnecessary charges from running instances, storage, data transfers, and other services.

**7.4 Technical Knowledge
**Managing an EC2 environment requires knowledge of operating systems, networking, security, and server administration.
Organizations without the necessary technical expertise may find it difficult to configure and maintain their cloud infrastructure properly.

**7.5 Dependence on a Cloud Provider
**Relying heavily on one cloud provider can make it difficult to move applications and data to another platform.
Differences in services, configurations, costs, and application architecture can make migration complicated.

8. Security and the AWS Shared Responsibility Model
Security is an important consideration when using Infrastructure as a Service.
AWS uses a Shared Responsibility Model to explain the security responsibilities of the cloud provider and its customers.
Under this model, AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, while customers are responsible for security in the cloud.
AWS manages the physical data centres, hardware, networking infrastructure, and virtualization layer.
Customers, on the other hand, are responsible for areas such as their guest operating systems, installed applications, data, access permissions, and security configurations.
For example, when a company launches an EC2 instance, AWS manages the underlying physical server, but the company must ensure that the operating system is updated and that its security groups are properly configured.
This arrangement is important because using a cloud provider does not automatically guarantee that every application and every piece of customer data is secure.

9. Practical Applications of IaaS
IaaS is used in different areas of information technology.
Some common applications include:
Website and Application Hosting: Organizations can use virtual servers to host websites, web applications, and backend services.
Software Development and Testing: Developers can create separate environments for testing applications without purchasing additional physical computers.
Data Storage and Backup: Businesses can use cloud storage services to store important files, application data, and backup copies.
Business Applications: Organizations can run internal systems, databases, and enterprise applications using cloud infrastructure.
Data Processing: Companies can rent computing resources to process large amounts of information and perform computational tasks.
These applications show that IaaS is not limited to large companies. Small businesses, developers, educational institutions, and individuals can also benefit from cloud infrastructure.

  1. Practical Application of IaaS

  1. Personal Observation: The Importance of IaaS to Small Businesses in Cameroon In my opinion, Infrastructure as a Service can be particularly useful to small businesses in Cameroon that want to expand their operations through technology. For example, a small business that sells clothes, electronics, or other products online may want to create an e-commerce website but may not have enough money to purchase and maintain its own physical server. Using a service such as Amazon EC2 would allow the business to rent computing resources instead of investing heavily in physical hardware. It could start with a small server configuration and increase its resources as the number of customers and website visitors grows. This would help the business manage its expenses while still having access to the computing infrastructure needed to operate online. Another advantage is that the business would not have to worry about maintaining the physical server equipment itself. AWS manages the underlying cloud infrastructure, while the business concentrates on managing its website, applications, and customer information. However, businesses must also consider challenges such as internet connectivity, electricity availability, security configuration, and the cost of cloud services. These factors are important when deciding whether cloud infrastructure is suitable for a particular business. Overall, I believe IaaS presents an opportunity for small businesses in Cameroon to access modern computing infrastructure without necessarily making large initial investments in physical equipment.

12. Conclusion
Infrastructure as a Service has become an important part of modern cloud computing because it provides individuals and organizations with access to computing resources without requiring them to own and maintain all the physical equipment.
The case study of Amazon Web Services, particularly Amazon EC2, demonstrates how this model works in practice. Through EC2, users can launch virtual servers, configure their computing environments, manage storage and networking, and adjust their resources according to their requirements.
However, adopting IaaS also requires proper planning. Organizations must understand their security responsibilities, monitor their cloud expenditure, and ensure that their infrastructure is configured correctly.
Overall, IaaS provides a flexible approach to managing computing infrastructure. As organizations continue to develop digital services and applications, cloud infrastructure remains an important option for meeting changing technology requirements.
