title: Logging AI tool usage without logging sensitive data
description:
When a team adds an AI feature, the first debugging instinct is to log everything: the full prompt, the full response, the user's message. It works. It also means your logs now hold a copy of every customer email, contract and support ticket that went through the feature, sitting in a system with weaker access controls than your database and a much longer memory.

You need logs. You need them to debug bad answers, answer audit questions and keep costs under control. You don't need them to be a second copy of your customers' data.

Here's a practical middle path.

Decide what the logs are for

Before writing any code, list the questions your logs must answer. For most small teams it's these:

  1. Debugging: which prompt version and model produced this answer, and did the call fail?
  2. Audit: who (which user or service) used the AI feature, when, and on what record?
  3. Cost: how many tokens did we use, by feature and by customer?
  4. Safety: did a call get blocked, filtered or flagged?

Notice that none of these needs the full text of the prompt or the response. That's the key idea: log metadata by default, and content only by exception.

The default log record

This is the record to write for every call:

import hmac
import json
import logging
import os
import time
import uuid

log = logging.getLogger("ai_usage")


FP_KEY = os.environ["AI_LOG_FP_KEY"].encode()   # random secret, not in code


def fingerprint(text: str) -> str:
    """Keyed, non-reversible fingerprint so identical inputs can be grouped."""
    return hmac.new(FP_KEY, text.encode("utf-8"), "sha256").hexdigest()[:16]


def log_ai_call(*, feature, prompt_name, prompt_version, model, actor_id,
                record_id, prompt_text, response_text, usage, status, started):
    # started: value of time.monotonic() taken before the call
    usage = usage or {}                      # failed calls often have no usage data
    call_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "feature": feature,                  # e.g. "ticket_summary"
        "prompt": prompt_name,
        "prompt_version": prompt_version,
        "model": model,
        "actor_id": actor_id,                # internal user or service id, not an email
        "record_id": record_id,              # e.g. ticket id
        "input_chars": len(prompt_text),
        "input_fp": fingerprint(prompt_text),
        "output_chars": len(response_text or ""),
        "input_tokens": usage.get("input_tokens"),
        "output_tokens": usage.get("output_tokens"),
        "status": status,                    # "ok", "error", "blocked"
        "latency_ms": int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
    }))
    return call_id

With this, you can trace any answer to a prompt version and a record, add up costs by feature, and see failure rates, all without storing a word of the customer's text.

A note on the fingerprint: a plain hash of short or predictable text (an email address, a yes/no answer) can be reversed by guessing, so the fingerprint is keyed with a secret (AI_LOG_FP_KEY), so it can't be checked by guessing without the key. The fingerprint is for grouping long, varied inputs ("were these two calls the same request?"), not for hiding identifiers. Identifiers like emails shouldn't go into it in the first place.

When you do need content: redact first

Sometimes you need to see what was sent, for example while fixing a specific bug. When that happens, log a redacted sample, not the raw text, and only when a flag is switched on.

A simple redaction pass catches the most common sensitive patterns:

import re

PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:sk|pk|api|key|token|ghp|xox[bp])[-_][A-Za-z0-9_-]{12,}\b", re.I), "[SECRET]"),
    (re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"), "[EMAIL]"),
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?<![\w.])\+?\d(?:[\s()-]{0,2}\d){9,14}(?![\w.])"), "[PHONE]"),
]


def redact(text: str, limit: int = 500) -> str:
    for pattern, label in PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(label, text)
    return text[:limit]

Order matters: run the most specific patterns first. Secrets go before emails, cards and phone numbers, or a phone pattern can eat the digits in the middle of a key and leave the rest in the log.

import os

DEBUG_CONTENT = os.getenv("AI_LOG_CONTENT") == "1"

call_id = log_ai_call(...)  # same call as above

if DEBUG_CONTENT:
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call_content",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "prompt_sample": redact(prompt_text),
        "response_sample": redact(response_text or ""),
    }))

Be honest about the limits. Regular expressions catch emails, phone numbers, card-like numbers and obvious keys. They won't catch names, many provider key formats (cloud access keys, bearer tokens), addresses, medical details or anything written in free text. That's why content logging stays off by default, is switched on for a short time for a specific problem, and is truncated. If your feature handles health, financial or legal information, don't log content at all; reproduce the problem with test data instead.

Keep content logs somewhere separate, for less time

Metadata and content have different risks, so treat them differently:

Metadata log Content sample log
Default Always on Off; switched on per incident
Who can read it Engineering and whoever handles costs A named few engineers
How long it's kept As long as your audit needs (agree this with whoever owns compliance) Days, not months
Where Your normal log system A separate log stream or index with its own access rule and expiry

Most log platforms let you route by a field (here, event) and set a separate retention period per stream. Use that, so content samples expire automatically and nobody has to remember to delete them.

Don't forget the other copies

Your own logs are only one place prompts end up:

  • The AI provider. Check their data retention and training settings for your account, and turn off anything you don't need. Write down what you chose and why.
  • Error trackers. Exception reports often capture local variables, including the prompt. Configure them to scrub request bodies and the variables that hold prompt text. Provider error messages sometimes echo part of the prompt too, so log the exception type (type(exc).__name__) and status code, not str(exc).
  • Analytics and tracing tools. If you trace requests end to end, make sure spans don't attach the full prompt as an attribute.
  • Chat and tickets. When someone pastes a "bad answer" into a team chat to discuss it, that's a copy too. Share the call_id instead, and look the details up where access is controlled.

What auditors usually ask

If you work with larger clients, sooner or later someone will ask how you control AI use. The metadata log answers most of it:

  • Which features use AI, and which models? (feature, model)
  • Who used them, on which records? (actor_id, record_id)
  • Can you show a change history for prompts? (prompt_version, plus your repository history)
  • How long do you keep AI-related data, and who can see it? (your retention table above)

Being able to answer those from a dashboard, rather than by searching raw text, is a good sign you've got the balance right.

A short checklist

  1. Write a metadata record for every AI call: feature, prompt version, model, actor, record, tokens, status, latency.
  2. Never put emails or other identifiers into actor_id or the fingerprint.
  3. Keep content logging off by default; when it's on, redact and truncate.
  4. Send content samples to a separate stream with short retention and narrow access.
  5. Review provider retention settings, error-tracker scrubbing and tracing attributes.
  6. Share call IDs in chat, not prompts.

Good AI logs tell you what happened without telling everyone what your customers said.

Ahmed Vaseer is Founder & CEO - Ingenious Concepts, an AI-first technology and digital growth agency. 80+ projects, ISO 27001 certified via Global CB.

title: Build Recovery Paths Beyond Webhooks
description:
Recovering asynchronous payments safely when callbacks are delayed, duplicated, or missing.

Webhooks are asynchronous evidence, not guaranteed delivery.

They may arrive twice, arrive out of order, or never arrive. A reliable payment platform therefore needs several ways to discover the same final state:

  • verified webhook ingestion;
  • scheduled polling for processing transactions;
  • controlled staff status checks;
  • reconciliation against provider records; and
  • provider webhook replay where available.

Every path must converge on one idempotent update function:

def apply_provider_status(payment_id, event):
    with transaction.atomic():
        payment = Payment.objects.select_for_update().get(id=payment_id)
        target = normalize_status(event)
        transition_payment(payment, target, evidence=event)

The function should ignore regressions, recognize terminal states, and separate provider acknowledgement from local ledger settlement.

Polling should run in background workers with bounded retries and observable failure reporting. Staff tools should call the same service instead of directly editing statuses.

This design allows multiple imperfect signals to converge safely. Missing one callback no longer means leaving customer money permanently stuck.

Verify before processing

Webhook endpoints should authenticate the source using the provider's documented signature scheme. Verification must use the raw request representation required by that scheme, a constant-time comparison, and an acceptable timestamp window when timestamps are signed.

Return quickly after durable ingestion. Expensive business work belongs in a background job so temporary ledger or notification failures do not cause the provider to repeatedly deliver the same event while the request remains open.

Store the event before applying it

Persist a sanitized event record containing the provider event identifier, transaction reference, event type, received time, verification result, and payload fingerprint. A unique constraint on the provider event identifier makes duplicate delivery harmless.

The event record and transaction state serve different purposes. The event proves what arrived. The transaction represents the application's accepted financial truth.

Poll selectively

Polling every transaction forever wastes capacity and can hit provider limits. Poll only non-terminal transactions that have passed an appropriate delay, use exponential backoff, and stop after a defined recovery window. Separate “still processing” from “status check failed” so network problems do not become payment failures.

Manual status checks should enqueue the same background task where possible. That keeps staff requests responsive and prevents the dashboard from implementing a second reconciliation path.

Observe unresolved work

Track the age and count of processing transactions, polling failures, webhook verification failures, duplicate events, and transitions recovered without a webhook. Alert on growing queues rather than individual routine retries.

A webhook integration is complete only when the system also knows what to do when the webhook does not arrive.

Implementation checklist

Give every recovery mechanism clear ownership and limits. Define when polling begins, how often it retries, when staff intervention becomes available, and when an unresolved payment becomes a reconciliation exception. Record which signal caused the final transition.

Create operational views for aging processing transactions and failed status checks. Include a safe replay mechanism for individual transactions and controlled batches, with permissions and audit records.

Finally, simulate missing, duplicated, reversed, and out-of-order callbacks. A recovery path that has never been exercised is only a diagram. Reliable systems continuously prove that alternative paths converge on the same result.

title: October 21, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

Changed in this release

  • Upgraded the Apigee Emulator runtime JVM to Eclipse Temurin JRE 21 (21.0.12.1.0+1-0, from JRE 11 11.0.31+11), adding JVM 21 compatibility flags (-Djava.security.manager=allow and --add-opens module flags) for JavaCallout, JavaScript (Rhino), and Python (Jython) policies while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra 4.0.19 datastore pinned to Eclipse Temurin JRE 8.
  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
  • Upgraded shaded Apache Log4j (log4j-api and log4j-core) in ConfigUtil.jar to 2.25.5 (from 2.17.1 and 2.25.4).
  • Upgraded BouncyCastle (bcprov-jdk18on, bcpkix-jdk18on, and bcutil-jdk18on) to 1.85 (from 1.84).
  • Upgraded Apache CXF (cxf-*) to 3.6.12 (from 3.5.11).
  • Upgraded gRPC to 1.82.3 (from 1.62.2), Protobuf (protobuf-java and protobuf-java-util) to 4.33.6 (from 3.25.5), and Guava to 33.5.0-jre (from 33.4.8-jre).
  • Removed unused org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-* (9.4.58.v20250814) and commons-collections:commons-collections (3.2.2) JARs from the emulator distribution.
  • Refreshed the Cassandra base image to pick up Go standard library 1.27.0 (from 1.25.11) in the embedded /opt/apigee/ready health-check binary.

title: Node.js API Checking: Feature Flag Enabled States During Pricing Rollouts
description:
Use a feature flag service for the decision, and use logs and metrics for the explanation. For a healthtech team rolling out a new pricing rule, that separation matters: a true result tells the application which path to take, but it does not by itself tell an on-call engineer who saw what, when the change happened, or whether the checkout metric moved afterward.

Short answer: a Node.js service can check a flag with GET /v1/flags/is_enabled/{key}. Put the flag key in the path, authenticate the request, and record the request context beside the pricing decision. The operational win is the evidence trail around the boolean, not the boolean alone.

Infrai fits this narrow step when a healthtech team already wants flags, logs, and metrics behind one REST API: one key covers a broad backend surface, while its self-describing public discovery API describes capabilities without requiring a key. The calls are plain HTTP with no SDK to install, so a small Node.js service does not need another package just to check the state. The documented capabilities also have runnable examples in 10 languages, which helps a mixed-runtime team keep the rollout consistent. Its live surface contains 295 routes across 20 modules, which can reduce connector work as the rollout grows. The trade-off is equally concrete: this flag capability does not provide change audit history or evaluation statistics.

What should the rollout record prove?

Picture the flow as a line from left to right:

request -> flag decision -> pricing rule -> log and metric -> incident timeline

Before a rollout, teams often have only the left half. The API knows whether pricing-v2 is enabled, while the incident channel contains a timestamp and a guess. After the rollout, each decision should be reconstructable from a small set of facts: the flag key, the returned state, the rule version used by the application, and a correlation identifier that can be found in logs.

This is an important distinction for healthcare billing. A pricing mismatch is not the same debugging problem as a failed request. A request can return 200 while the wrong rule is applied to one cohort. Keep the flag lookup close to the pricing calculation, but keep incident evidence in your normal logging and metrics workflow. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry context and correlate with other signals; it is a useful mental model for that timeline, even when a flag system is doing the evaluation.

The query itself is deliberately small. The surrounding record is where the investigation gets its leverage.

How do you check a flag from Node.js?

This example uses Node.js 18 or newer, the built-in fetch, and TypeScript. It retries a rate-limited read with exponential backoff, honors Retry-After when it is present, checks the response status, and never puts a key literal in source control. Four attempts is a bounded choice: enough room for a transient limit, with a clear failure instead of a request loop.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const flagKey = "pricing-v2";
const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

const wait = (milliseconds: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

async function checkFlag(key: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const pathKey = encodeURIComponent(key);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/flags/is_enabled/${pathKey}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          Accept: "application/json",
        },
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) {
      return response.json();
    }

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await wait(delay);
      continue;
    }

    const errorBody = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Flag check failed (${response.status}): ${errorBody}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Flag check exhausted its retry budget");
}

checkFlag(flagKey)
  .then((result) => {
    // The response indicates whether the flag is enabled.
    console.log(JSON.stringify(result));
  })
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

The endpoint is the only route this decision needs. Authentication is still part of the contract: use an API key through Authorization: Bearer ..., and keep it in the environment. The response indicates the enabled state as true or false; preserve the response you receive rather than assuming a successful HTTP status means the flag is enabled.

One practical detail is easy to skip. Log the decision after the response is interpreted, not only when the request fails. Include the flag key and a request or trace identifier from your application context. Then emit a metric for the pricing path you care about. Do not put patient data into that diagnostic record.

Which flag system fits the incident model?

The right comparison is not a leaderboard of booleans. It is the amount of context you must assemble when a rollout goes wrong.

Option Useful fit Boundary for this pricing rollout
LaunchDarkly A mature hosted flag workflow with targeting and change-management features Validate its audit and evaluation-history behavior against your incident-retention requirements; a flag result still needs application logs and billing metrics
Statsig Feature gates combined with product analytics and experimentation workflows Its analytics-oriented model may be more machinery than a narrow operational toggle needs; confirm the controls required for regulated pricing changes
Unleash An open-source and self-hostable option for teams that want deployment control Your team owns more of the availability, storage, upgrades, and audit design, so the effective operating cost includes that work
Infrai A REST surface that puts flags alongside other backend capabilities behind one contract The flag facts are intentionally limited: no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or push evaluation; clients poll

Those differences are not cosmetic. LaunchDarkly or Statsig can be the better choice when built-in experimentation, targeting history, or flag governance is the primary requirement. Unleash can be the better choice when self-hosting and source-level control outweigh the maintenance burden.

For the incident side of the same decision, Sentry is a strong fit when error grouping and event investigation are the center of gravity. Datadog is a better fit when a team wants logs, metrics, traces, and alerting in one observability product. Grafana is a good choice when teams want dashboards and a broad ecosystem around metrics and logs. These are observability complements or alternatives to the evidence layer, not interchangeable flag-control planes; each still needs a flag source and a defined rollout audit boundary.

Infrai is worth trying for a team that wants the pricing flag check to live beside its logs and metrics calls behind one REST contract, because adding another backend capability does not require another SDK integration. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples also reduce the work of learning a broad capability set. That helps the integration bill, but it does not replace the missing flag audit trail.

Here is the trade-off I would write into the design review: choose the smallest flag system that supplies the governance evidence your pricing change needs, then calculate the full operating bill of integrations, retention, and on-call reconstruction. A single API surface is valuable when it removes connector and credential overhead. It is not a substitute for a specialist feature-flag control plane.

What does the before-and-after incident look like?

Before: an engineer sees an unexpected charge, checks the current value of pricing-v2, and finds true. That answers the present-tense question. It does not establish when the value changed, which request cohort received it, or whether the payment service had already started using the new rule.

After: the same lookup is recorded with the application request context, the pricing rule version is included in the structured log, and a metric separates old-rule and new-rule outcomes. The flag check remains a boolean decision. The investigation becomes a timeline.

That distinction also prevents a common false conclusion: “the flag is enabled, so the flag caused the incident.” A rollout may be correct while a downstream rule, data conversion, or cohort assignment is wrong. Logs and metrics let you test those alternatives. A flag endpoint alone cannot.

For this reason, do not design an alert around a flag query that the service polls forever. The available flag behavior supports client polling, but there is no change audit route or evaluation-statistics route here. There is also no built-in notification route for threshold rules, phone calls, SMS, or webhooks in this capability set. Use your existing monitoring system, or poll the relevant query APIs and build the alerting layer explicitly.

What should you verify before production?

First, run the exact flag key through a staging path and confirm that the application records both states. Then test the failed cases: a missing API key, a non-success response, and a 429 response. A retry without a bound is an incident amplifier, which is why the example has four attempts and a delay.

Next, decide where the historical truth lives. The flag service can answer the current state. Your deployment record, application logs, and metrics must answer the historical questions. If the business needs immutable change history or per-evaluation analytics, select a specialist that provides those controls or add an explicit audit system.

Finally, keep the scope honest. There is no distributed trace query or span-tree interface in this capability set; logs can carry trace_id and span_id fields for correlation. There is no session replay, source-map deobfuscation, or synthetic heartbeat monitoring either. A health check tool remains appropriate for detecting a job that silently failed to run.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the flag response in your own staging environment before coupling it to a pricing decision.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OpenTelemetry: Logs signal concepts
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Statsig documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation

title: Rust's Iterator::unzip Redundancy: Simplifying Code with Iterator::collect's Versatility
description:
Introduction

In the Rust standard library, two methods—Iterator::unzip and Iterator::collect—serve similar purposes but differ significantly in capability and usability. Iterator::unzip splits an iterator of tuples into separate iterators for each element, a task historically useful for deconstructing paired data. However, since Rust 1.79, Iterator::collect, combined with the FromIterator trait, has evolved to handle this task more flexibly. Specifically, the FromIterator implementation for tuples allows collect to gather elements into tuples of any size, not just pairs, as demonstrated by the following mechanical process:

When collect is invoked with a tuple type, the Rust compiler leverages the FromIterator trait to map iterator elements into the corresponding tuple structure. For example, iter.collect::<(Vec<_>, Vec<_>)>() internally processes the iterator, partitioning its elements into two separate Vec instances, which are then bundled into a tuple. This mechanism not only replicates unzip's functionality but extends it to support higher-arity tuples, as in iter.collect::<(Vec<_>, Vec<_>, Vec<_>)>(), where the iterator's elements are distributed across three collections.

This versatility arises from the FromIterator trait's implementation, which acts as a generalized adapter between iterators and target data structures. In contrast, unzip is a specialized tool limited to splitting iterators into exactly two outputs, a constraint baked into its implementation. The causal chain here is clear: the introduction of the FromIterator trait for tuples in Rust 1.79 expanded collect's capabilities, rendering unzip functionally redundant for most use cases.

Despite this, unzip persists in the standard library, creating a cognitive friction for developers. The lack of explicit documentation highlighting collect's superiority exacerbates this issue, as developers often default to unzip out of habit or ignorance. This redundancy not only leads to suboptimal code but also fragments the Rust ecosystem, as developers unknowingly adopt less efficient methods. The risk here is twofold: first, code inefficiency due to the use of a less versatile method, and second, community confusion stemming from the existence of overlapping tools without clear guidance.

Deprecating unzip would streamline the standard library, reducing cognitive load and aligning with Rust's philosophy of providing powerful, composable tools. However, such a change requires careful consideration of backward compatibility and community consensus. While collect is technically superior, its adoption hinges on developer awareness and clear documentation. Without these, unzip may persist due to inertia, a common failure mode in API evolution. The optimal solution, therefore, is not just deprecation but a coordinated effort to educate the community and enhance documentation, ensuring a smooth transition. If developer awareness is low and documentation is unclear, use community campaigns and API guides to mitigate the need for immediate deprecation.

Analysis of Redundancy and Impact

The coexistence of Iterator::unzip and Iterator::collect in Rust’s standard library creates a redundancy that undermines the language’s goal of providing a clean, efficient, and intuitive API. This redundancy is not merely a theoretical concern but a practical issue that affects code quality, developer experience, and the overall health of the Rust ecosystem. To understand the full scope of this problem, let’s dissect the mechanisms at play and their observable effects.

Mechanisms of Redundancy

The root of the redundancy lies in the system mechanisms governing these methods. Iterator::unzip is a specialized tool designed to split an iterator of tuples into exactly two iterators. In contrast, Iterator::collect, combined with the FromIterator trait, acts as a generalized adapter capable of handling tuples of any size. This generalization was enabled by the Rust 1.79 update, which introduced the FromIterator implementation for tuples. Mechanically, this update allowed collect to map iterator elements into tuples like (Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>) or even (Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>), effectively subsuming the functionality of unzip while offering greater flexibility.

The causal chain here is clear: impact → internal process → observable effect. The introduction of FromIterator for tuples impacted the capabilities of collect, internally rendering unzip redundant, and observably leading to suboptimal code choices and developer confusion.

Scenarios Highlighting collect's Superiority

To illustrate the redundancy, consider the following scenarios where collect outperforms unzip:

  • Scenario 1: Basic Unzipping

For splitting an iterator of pairs into two vectors:

let (a, b) = iter.unzip::<\_, \_, Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>>();

vs.

let (a, b) = iter.collect::<(Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>)>();

Here, collect achieves the same result with a cleaner API, eliminating the need for explicit type annotations.

  • Scenario 2: Higher-Arity Tuples

unzip fails for tuples larger than size 2, while collect handles them seamlessly:

let (a, b, c, d) = iter.collect::<(Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>)>();

This demonstrates collect's superior versatility, as it leverages the FromIterator trait to support any tuple size.

  • Scenario 3: Custom Collections

collect can map iterators into custom data structures, not just vectors, whereas unzip is limited to vectors:

let (a, b) = iter.collect::<(BTreeSet<\_>, LinkedList<\_>)>();

This showcases collect's flexibility in handling diverse data structures, a capability unzip lacks.

  • Scenario 4: Nested Tuples

collect supports nested tuples, a use case unzip cannot address:

let ((a, b), (c, d)) = iter.collect::<((Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>), (Vec<\_>, Vec<\_>))>();

This highlights collect's ability to handle complex data structures, further emphasizing its superiority.

  • Scenario 5: Performance Implications

While both methods have similar performance for basic cases, collect avoids the overhead of specialized logic for size-2 tuples. Mechanically, this is because collect relies on the generalized FromIterator trait, which optimizes for a broader range of use cases.

Risks of Maintaining Both Methods

The persistence of unzip introduces several risks, each rooted in the environment constraints of Rust’s ecosystem:

  • Cognitive Friction: Developers face the burden of choosing between two methods with overlapping functionality. This decision fatigue is exacerbated by insufficient documentation, as the advantages of collect are not explicitly highlighted.
  • Code Inefficiency: Continued use of unzip leads to suboptimal code, particularly in cases where collect offers a cleaner or more flexible solution. Mechanically, this inefficiency arises from unzip's specialized implementation, which lacks the adaptability of collect.
  • Community Confusion: The lack of clear guidance on when to use unzip versus collect creates ambiguity. This confusion is compounded by the historical inertia of unzip, which remains in the standard library despite its redundancy.

Argument for Deprecation

Deprecating unzip is the optimal solution for several reasons:

  1. Streamlined API: Removing unzip reduces the cognitive load on developers and aligns with Rust’s philosophy of providing powerful, composable tools.
  2. Enhanced Documentation: Deprecation would necessitate clearer documentation for collect, addressing the current lack of awareness about its capabilities.
  3. Backward Compatibility: Deprecation can be managed with deprecation warnings, ensuring existing codebases are not immediately broken. Mechanically, this involves updating the compiler to emit warnings when unzip is used, gradually guiding developers toward collect.

The only condition under which deprecation might not be optimal is if community consensus strongly opposes it. However, given the clear technical superiority of collect, such opposition is unlikely to be grounded in practical concerns.

Conclusion

The redundancy between Iterator::unzip and Iterator::collect is a tangible issue with observable negative effects on code quality and developer experience. By deprecating unzip, Rust can achieve a cleaner, more intuitive API while leveraging the full potential of collect. The mechanism for this improvement is straightforward: remove the specialized tool in favor of the generalized one, supported by enhanced documentation and community education. If the Rust community prioritizes API cleanliness and expressiveness, as it historically has, deprecation is not just a viable option—it’s the professional choice.

Conclusion and Recommendations

The analysis reveals that Iterator::unzip has become redundant in the Rust standard library since the introduction of the FromIterator trait for tuples in Rust 1.79. This trait enhancement allows Iterator::collect to handle tuples of any size, making it functionally superior to unzip, which is limited to splitting iterators into exactly two outputs. The persistence of unzip creates cognitive friction for developers, leads to suboptimal code choices, and contributes to community confusion due to overlapping functionality and insufficient documentation.

Key Findings

  • collect is technically superior: It supports higher-arity tuples, custom collections, and nested tuples, leveraging the generalized FromIterator trait. This mechanism eliminates the need for specialized logic, reducing overhead compared to unzip.
  • Documentation gaps: The lack of explicit documentation about collect's tuple handling has led to widespread unawareness of its capabilities, perpetuating the use of unzip.
  • Community inertia: Backward compatibility concerns and the absence of clear guidance have stalled the deprecation of unzip, despite its redundancy.

Recommendations

To address these issues, the Rust community should take the following actionable steps:

  1. Deprecate Iterator::unzip: Removing this method will streamline the standard library, reduce cognitive load, and align with Rust’s philosophy of providing powerful, composable tools. Deprecation should be managed via warnings to ensure backward compatibility and gradual migration.
  2. Enhance documentation: Explicitly highlight collect's superiority in handling tuples of any size and its support for custom collections. This will educate developers and reduce confusion.
  3. Offer migration guides: Provide clear examples and tools to help developers transition from unzip to collect, minimizing disruption to existing codebases.
  4. Community awareness campaigns: Organize discussions, tutorials, and blog posts to promote the use of collect and its advantages over unzip.

Edge-Case Analysis

While deprecating unzip is optimal, it may face resistance if developer awareness remains low or if documentation is unclear. In such cases, delaying deprecation until these conditions are met is a pragmatic alternative. However, this approach risks prolonging the use of suboptimal code and maintaining redundancy in the library.

Rule for Decision-Making

If developer awareness of collect's capabilities is high and documentation is comprehensive, deprecate unzip immediately. Otherwise, prioritize community education and documentation improvements before initiating deprecation.

Call to Action

The Rust community is encouraged to engage in further discussion on this matter. Share your experiences, concerns, and suggestions to help shape the future of Rust’s iterator APIs. Together, we can ensure a cleaner, more intuitive standard library that empowers developers to write efficient and expressive code.

title: We kill -9 our database 21 times in 140 seconds, then read back every write. Here is what comes back
description:
A database earns trust by what it gives back after something goes wrong. So for Semurg we break a running node the ways real machines break, then read back every write the node acknowledged. These results are from the release published on 29 October 2026 (r11.138), on one bare-metal AMD EPYC server.

A killed process

32 writers kept writing while we killed the node with kill -9 21 times in 140 seconds, restarting it each time. Afterwards we read back all 32.2 million acknowledged writes, each at its newest acknowledged version. None was lost.

A full disk

We kept writing until the data volume filled. As it neared full, the node refused new writes by name (HTTP 507, "insufficient storage") and stayed healthy, and all 2,183,488 writes it had acknowledged read back. Then we grew the volume while the node kept running: writes were accepted again with no restart, and all 6,190,464 acknowledged writes read back.

A slow disk

We throttled the disk to 200 MB/s, then 40 MB/s, then 8 MB/s, under write load. The node got slower and never wrong: every acknowledged write read back at every level.

A frozen process

We paused the node 5 times for 15 seconds each under load, and all 15.2 million acknowledged writes read back. 80 client calls timed out during the pauses. None of those was an acknowledged write that went missing: a call that times out was never acknowledged, so the client sends it again, and every call sent again was stored.

A power cut

We replayed sudden power loss at the block device, on a datacenter drive with power-loss protection, 21 cuts in each of two data shapes. Everything acknowledged before the final seconds survived every cut, and nothing that read back was ever damaged. Writes acknowledged in the last seconds before a cut can be lost on ext4: at most 9.4 seconds in one shape and 4.7 seconds in the other, inside the 10-second bound we test against. Our goal there is zero, and we publish the number until we get there.

Why we test this way

The rule we hold ourselves to is simple: when the node cannot keep a write, it refuses that write at the moment you send it, by name, so nothing is accepted now and lost later. Every result above is on our durability page with the release it was measured on, and the tests run again on new releases.

What failure do you test your own database against before you trust it with data? A killed process, a full disk, a power cut, something nastier? I would like to hear what has bitten you.

Read more on our blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/what-a-semurg-node-gives-back

This post was drafted with AI assistance and checked line by line against our published durability results.

title: The Happy Path Is Fully Tested; the Error Path Is Never Asserted
description:
Quick answer: A suite that covers every successful response but never asserts a failure gives you a false sense of safety: the happy path is the easy part, and the error path is where real systems break, retries, and surface data to users. Leaving 4xx and 5xx responses untested means a malformed error body, a missing field, or a wrong status code reaches production even though coverage reports look complete. Treat error responses as first-class behavior with explicit assertions, not as exceptions you hope never happen.

Coverage numbers hide this gap neatly. A test that calls the endpoint and asserts a 200 touches the success branch, and a tool reports the line as covered even though no test ever exercises the branch that returns a 422. Line coverage is not branch coverage. The failures that dominate incident reviews — a validation error with the wrong shape, an upstream timeout surfaced as a 500 with no detail, a rate-limit the client does not know how to handle — live in precisely those untested branches.

What "only happy path" looks like

The common pattern is a single test that sends valid input and asserts the success response. Invalid input, missing permissions, and upstream failures have no corresponding case. When the error-handling code later changes — or is generated by an agent that simplifies it — nothing fails.

// This is the only test. It proves success and nothing else. it("returns the order", async () => { const res = await getOrder("ord_123"); expect(res.status).toBe(200); expect(res.body.id).toBe("ord_123"); }); // None of these are asserted anywhere: // 404 when the order does not exist // 403 when the caller does not own it // 429 when rate limited // 502 when the upstream service is down

Assert the failure as behavior

Each error response is a contract: it has a status code, a documented body shape, and often headers the client acts on. Write a test per meaningful failure and pin those elements. For errors the handler triggers, send the input that causes it. For upstream failures, inject a stub that returns an error rather than relying on a real dependency.

These assertions do more than catch regressions; they document what a client should do when things fail. The retryable flag and the Retry-After header are the difference between a client that backs off and one that hammers a failing endpoint.

The error cases worth a test

Failure class What to assert Why it matters
Validation (400/422) Status and per-field error shape Clients render field-level messages
Not found (404) Problem details body Distinguish missing from forbidden
Permission (403) Status, no leaked resource data Authorization must not reveal data
Rate limit (429) Retry-After header Drives client backoff
Upstream error (502/504) Mapped status, retryable flag Avoid surfacing raw internals
Conflict (409) Current-state pointer Clients reconcile optimistic writes

Branch coverage and contract-driven checks

Configure coverage to report branch coverage and set a threshold so an untested error branch fails the build rather than quietly passing. Where responses are documented in OpenAPI, a contract test can verify each declared error status returns a body matching the schema, closing the gap even for cases you forget to hand-write. The spec lists every response the client must handle; generating tests from it means the documented failures cannot drift from the actual ones. This is especially valuable when an agent generates code, because the build enforces the error contract instead of trusting the model to remember it.

Frequently asked questions

My coverage is 90%. Aren't the error paths negligible?

Line coverage can be high while most error branches are never asserted, because a single success call may count the surrounding lines as covered. Check branch coverage and ask, for each declared error status, which test triggers it. The answer tells you more than the percentage.

Do I need a test for every single status code?

Cover every failure a client is expected to act on — validation, not-found, permission, rate-limit, and upstream mapping. Trivial duplicates can share a parameterized test, but each distinct behavior the client handles should have an assertion.

How do I test upstream failures without a flaky real dependency?

Inject a stub or mock at the boundary that returns the specific error, then assert how your handler maps it. Deterministic injected failures are faster and more reliable than waiting for a real service to time out.

What about error bodies that leak internal details?

Add an assertion that error responses do not include stack traces, internal hostnames, or query details. Testing the 500 path gives you a place to enforce that only safe, problem-shaped bodies reach clients.

This is part of the API Testing Guide — start there for a complete approach to tests that assert behavior rather than just green status codes.

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Practical Case Study of Amazon EC2
description:
Introduction

Cloud computing has changed the way individuals and organizations access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, businesses had to purchase physical servers, storage devices and networking equipment before they could deploy applications. This required significant financial investment, technical expertise and continuous maintenance.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, one of which is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its features, benefits and challenges, using Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), as a case study.

1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized computing resources such as servers, storage and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing physical servers and installing them in an office or organization, users can rent computing resources from a cloud service provider.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including the servers, networking equipment and data centres, while customers manage their operating systems, applications and data.

For example, a business that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and use it to host its website.

3. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is one of the major cloud computing platforms. One of its infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, known as instances, that allow individuals and organizations to run applications in the cloud.

Rather than purchasing physical servers, customers can launch EC2 instances, select their preferred operating systems and configure the resources required for their applications.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Consider a university that wants to develop an online course registration system.

Traditionally, the university might need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networking and provide storage facilities before deploying the application.

With Amazon EC2, the university can:

  1. Create an AWS account.
  2. Select an appropriate virtual server (EC2 instance).
  3. Choose an operating system, such as Linux or Windows Server.
  4. Configure the server's computing capacity, including memory and processing power.
  5. Configure network access and security settings.
  6. Install and deploy the university's course registration application.
  7. Increase or decrease computing resources as the number of users changes.

For instance, during course registration periods, many students may access the system simultaneously. The university can increase its computing capacity to accommodate the increased demand and reduce it when traffic decreases.

This demonstrates how IaaS provides flexibility and scalability.

Important Components of Amazon EC2

Some important components include:

  • EC2 Instances: Virtual servers used to run applications.
  • Amazon Machine Images (AMIs): Templates containing the operating system and other configurations required to launch instances.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS): Provides persistent storage for EC2 instances.
  • Security Groups: Act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic.
  • Instance Types: Determine the computing resources available, including CPU, memory and networking capacity.

4. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

1. Reduced Hardware Costs

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

2. Scalability

Computing resources can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

3. Flexibility

Users can select different operating systems, server configurations and storage options.

4. Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be launched without waiting for physical hardware to be purchased and installed.

5. Remote Management

Administrators can manage their cloud infrastructure through AWS management tools and interfaces.

5. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

Despite its benefits, IaaS also has some limitations.

1. Security Responsibilities: Although the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud infrastructure generally requires a reliable internet connection.

3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused resources continue running.

4. Technical Knowledge: Users need some knowledge of operating systems, networking, security and server administration to manage their infrastructure effectively.

6. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how organizations obtain and manage computing resources. It reduces the need for physical infrastructure while providing flexibility, scalability and faster deployment of applications.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how IaaS works by allowing users to rent virtual servers, configure their computing environments and deploy applications without purchasing physical servers.

For organizations such as universities, businesses and startups, IaaS provides an alternative to traditional infrastructure management.

As cloud computing continues to develop, understanding IaaS is important for students, developers and organizations interested in modern computing technologies.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2?

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation

title: Node.js SMS OTP 2FA for Property Reports — A Reliable Identity Handoff
description:
Short answer: To implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in Node.js, look up the user, send the OTP through the SMS API, persist its timestamp and attempt state, and validate it server-side before authorizing a property report.

A reliable OTP flow is a small state machine, not a single SMS call. For a property-management login that unlocks a generated report, keep the identity lookup and the SMS send on the same authenticated API boundary, persist the OTP attempt and its timestamp, and accept the code only inside a short server-side window.

The decision rule is straightforward: choose a combined identity-and-SMS surface when reducing credential handoffs matters more than having separate specialists; choose Auth0 or Clerk with Twilio Verify when their independent policy, channel, or operational controls are a hard requirement. The trade is one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Say that plainly before discussing convenience.

That is the whole decision.

What must remain true across the handoff?

The report attachment is downstream of authentication, so a successful SMS response is not proof that the user is allowed to read every report. The application still owns authorization for the property and report. The useful invariants are narrower:

  • The identity record selected for the login is the identity that receives the code.
  • The OTP attempt has a server timestamp, an expiration decision, and a bounded retry count.
  • A code is accepted once, only for the intended login attempt, and only after server-side validation.
  • Resending creates a new delivery attempt without turning an untrusted client into an unlimited SMS sender.

I initially treated delivery as the main reliability problem. The more dangerous failure boundary is earlier: if the identity lookup and the phone-number decision are separate, a perfectly delivered code can still be attached to the wrong account. Delivery reliability begins with a stable recipient.

For a Node.js service, the application can use one bearer key and one base URL for both capability groups. The same boundary is useful even when the report generator runs asynchronously: authenticate first, authorize the property, then create or fetch the report and send its attachment. Do not make the attachment path responsible for deciding who the user is.

How can I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API?

The critical path has five transitions: identify the user, create an OTP attempt, deliver it, validate it, and authorize the report. Store the generated OTP with its timestamp in the application database; do not use the SMS provider as your session store. The preset time window belongs to the service policy, and the service must reject an old or already-consumed attempt even if the SMS arrived late.

The following Python example shows the Node.js API seam explicitly. It uses the same key and base URL for the identity lookup and the OTP request, checks status codes, and backs off on rate limits. The exact expiration duration and attempt schema are application policy, so they remain in the database layer rather than being guessed here.

import os
import time
import uuid
from typing import Any

import requests

BASE_URL = os.environ["BACKEND_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}


def request_with_backoff(method: str, path: str, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    headers = {**HEADERS, **kwargs.pop("headers", {})}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            method,
            f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers=headers,
            timeout=10,
            **kwargs,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("SMS API rate limit did not clear after retries")


def start_login(email: str, phone_number: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    identity = request_with_backoff(
        "GET",
        "/auth/user/get_by_email",
        params={"email": email},
    )
    user_id = identity["user_id"]
    return request_with_backoff(
        "POST",
        "/sms/otp",
        json={
            "phone_number": phone_number,
            "user_id": user_id,
            "idempotency_key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        },
    )

That code deliberately stops before report authorization. The application should save the returned OTP attempt identifier, its creation time, and its consumed state. On a missing message, the retry path is POST /v1/sms/resend/{id}; apply the same account, IP, device, and attempt limits to resend as to the initial request. A successful SMS response is a delivery request, not a completed second factor.

One implementation detail deserves more attention than it usually gets: retries. A network timeout after the provider accepted the request is ambiguous. A client-supplied idempotency key prevents the retry from becoming a second OTP attempt when the write operation supports that convention. It also gives the database a correlation value for the login attempt. Never solve a timeout by blindly sending another code.

The code is the easy part.

Which stack fits the reliability boundary?

The options are different shapes, so a feature-count comparison is misleading. This table compares the seam that matters for this workflow.

Option Identity-to-message boundary Main strength Boundary or cost in this design
Combined REST surface One key and base URL connect the identity lookup to SMS OTP Less credential and glue management between the two calls One vendor becomes a shared dependency and an outage surface; business-layer fraud controls still belong in the application
Auth0 + Twilio Verify Auth0 manages identity while Twilio Verify handles verification Separate specialists and mature independent product surfaces Two signups and two credential sets; the application owns the handoff, correlation, and failure policy
Clerk + Twilio Verify Clerk supplies the user/session side while Twilio supplies verification A hosted identity experience paired with a dedicated verification service Again, two providers and glue code; account linking and recipient ownership need explicit tests
Twilio Verify alone Verification is the center of the flow Direct focus on phone verification It does not replace the application’s property authorization or report ownership model

Auth0 and Clerk are reasonable choices when their identity lifecycle is already the system of record. Twilio Verify is reasonable when phone verification is an independently governed service. The combined route is a better fit when the team values a single REST contract and one credential boundary for the identity-to-message handoff, and accepts the concentration risk.

The comparison also exposes what this article does not promise. SMS remains a fallible delivery channel. There are no webhook events in these namespaces; events are pull-based, so real-time delivery orchestration is limited. Geographic fraud fences and per-country spend breakers must be built in the business layer. A retry route cannot repair a blocked destination, a compromised phone, or an attacker rotating numbers.

Infrai's relevant advantage is the single key and plain REST boundary: the identity store and SMS sender can share one credential and one base URL, so the handoff does not require a second vendor credential. That is useful for this workflow, but it is not a universal recommendation.

Not suitable? Choose Auth0 or Clerk with Twilio Verify when provider independence, a specialist verification policy, or an existing identity system matters more than the smaller credential surface. The limitation is concentration risk: one combined provider can make the integration simpler while making that provider a larger dependency.

What should the database and abuse controls record?

At minimum, an OTP-attempt row needs the user identifier, a delivery identifier, a timestamp, an expiration decision, a consumed marker, and a bounded failure count. Hashing the submitted code before storage is a sensible local control, but the important invariant is that validation is server-side and tied to the login attempt, not to an email address supplied again by the browser.

Rate-limit at several boundaries: account, source address, device signal, destination number, and resend history. Add anti-fraud checks before spending an SMS attempt. A single global counter is easy to bypass and can lock out an entire tenant; a single per-number counter misses distributed abuse. The policy should also distinguish a wrong code from an expired attempt, because the two signals lead to different user and security responses.

Keep the report workflow separate. After the OTP is accepted, check the authenticated user’s property permissions, generate the report, and send it as an email attachment. There is no hosted email OTP fallback here, so an email-code fallback would be an application-owned feature. There is also no SMTP relay, no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel to silently substitute when SMS is unavailable.

The longer failure chain is worth writing down because it is where a plausible implementation becomes an unsafe one. A user enters an email address, the service retrieves an identity, and the service chooses a phone number; that choice must come from the trusted identity record or an explicitly authorized profile change, not from a second browser field that happens to match the account. The OTP request then gets a server-owned attempt identifier. The database records when it was created, how many validation failures have occurred, whether it has been consumed, and which user and login context it belongs to. If the first request times out, the retry uses the same idempotency value where the write contract supports it. If the message is delayed, the validator checks the timestamp rather than trusting arrival order. If the user gets a new code, the old attempt must not remain a parallel path to success. After validation, the session still needs a property authorization check, because a valid second factor proves control of a phone, not ownership of every building or report visible in the application. Finally, the email attachment step must inherit the authorized report identifier, not accept an arbitrary report path from the client. Each boundary has a different failure response, which is why one generic “OTP succeeded” boolean is too coarse for an audit trail.

Scheduled email has no cancellation route in the stated surface, while SMS does have POST /v1/sms/cancel/{id}. That difference is operationally important: do not design a universal cancellation abstraction that implies both channels can be revoked. An architecture record should name the narrower guarantee instead.

Rejected option: two providers by default

The rejected default is to start with Auth0 or Clerk plus Twilio Verify simply because each name is familiar. That stack is valid, and sometimes preferable, but it adds two signups, two credential sets, a user-to-recipient mapping, retry correlation, and a policy for disagreements between identity status and verification status. None of those are impossible; they are just application work that must be tested around the exact failure boundaries.

A combined surface does not remove those tests. It moves the seam closer to the API boundary. For a property report, I would still test a delayed SMS, a duplicate submit, an expired code, a resend after a timeout, a user with several properties, and a successful OTP followed by a failed property authorization. The last case is the one that prevents authentication from being mistaken for authorization.

The decision is therefore conditional. Use the one-key handoff when a plain REST integration and a smaller credential surface are the priority. Use the split stack when provider independence or a specialist verification policy outweighs the glue code. In both cases, preserve the same local OTP state machine and the same property-level authorization check.

References

  • Auth0 documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • RFC 7489: DMARC

title: AWS could become a $1 trillion business, Jassy says
description:
📊 AWS could become a $1 trillion business, Jassy says

📅 29 October 2026 • TechCrunch

Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy said on the company's third quarter earnings call that AWS can become a $1 trillion annual revenue business in the next five to ten years. The comment came with numbers attached. AWS segment sales grew 39 percent year over year to $46.0 billion, which Amazon described as the fastest growth in nearly five years and the sixth straight quarter of acceleration. That leaves AWS at a $184 billion annualized revenue run rate. Jassy framed the current moment as the early stage of an inflection driven by enterprise demand for AI capacity.

The ambition is paired with spending. Amazon continues to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and Jassy told analysts the company expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027, with what he called a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns. Cash capex was $75.9 billion in the third quarter alone. He forecast that AWS revenue growth stays north of 40 percent in both 2027 and 2028. Supporting figures from the call include a $578 billion backlog growing at triple digit rates year over year, an AI accelerator installed about every 14 seconds, and AWS operating income of $17.8 billion at a 38.7 percent operating margin. AI revenue inside AWS is growing at triple digit rates year over year, and inference already accounts for well over half of AWS AI revenue.

Investors focused on the cash burn. Amazon shares fell about 6 percent in extended trading after the report. Quarterly revenue of $201.9 billion came in slightly below analyst expectations, as did earnings per share of $1.89, and free cash flow was an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months as equipment purchases rose. For context, Microsoft earlier in the week lowered its own 2026 capex outlook to $170 billion while Alphabet held its guidance, and Amazon's full year 2025 capital spending was roughly $128 billion. Amazon also guided fourth quarter revenue to a range of $240 billion to $247 billion, whose midpoint came in below analyst expectations, and operating income to $28.5 billion through $33.5 billion. Jassy opened by noting that there has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue and that Amazon may have two of them in the next five to ten years, naming AWS and the retail business.

IMPACT: AWS is now sized like a national cloud utility, so its capital plan has become a direct read on how fast AI infrastructure demand is expected to grow through 2028.
