title: Measuring a monitor's refresh rate with requestAnimationFrame (and why the average lies)
description:
"Is my 144 Hz monitor actually running at 144?" is a question people search for every day, and the browser can answer it reasonably well. requestAnimationFrame fires once per frame the browser presents, with a high-resolution timestamp. The gap between two callbacks is the frame time, and 1000 / frameTime is the refresh rate.

That's the whole idea. Making it give a trustworthy number took a few more decisions, which I made while building the refresh rate test on A2Z Tools.

The basic loop 

const WINDOW = 120;      // frames the rate is measured over
const AWAY_MS = 500;     // a gap this long is the tab being away, not a frame
let intervals = [], last = 0;

function frame(now) {
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  if (last) {
    const dt = now - last;
    if (dt > 0 && dt < AWAY_MS) {
      intervals.push(dt);
      if (intervals.length > WINDOW) intervals.shift();
    }
  }
  last = now;
}
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

A rolling window of 120 frames means the reading follows the display live instead of averaging over everything since page load.

Use the median, not the mean

One slow frame, from garbage collection or another tab waking up, drags an average well below the true rate. On a 60 Hz screen a single 50 ms hiccup in 120 frames pulls the mean down to about 59 Hz. The median ignores it:

function medianOf(values) {
  const s = values.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const m = s.length >> 1;
  return s.length % 2 ? s[m] : (s[m - 1] + s[m]) / 2;
}

const hz = 1000 / medianOf(intervals);

A refresh rate should be one of a handful of fixed numbers, so an outlier-resistant statistic is the right tool. I use the same idea for jitter: the median absolute deviation from the median frame time, not the standard deviation.

Snap to a known rate, but only when it's close

A 144 Hz panel measures as 143.9 or 144.1. Showing "143.9 Hz" makes people think something is wrong. So the big number snaps to a common rate, but only within a tolerance, and the raw value is always shown underneath:

const COMMON = [30, 48, 50, 60, 75, 90, 100, 120, 144, 165, 180, 240, 360];

function snap(rate) {
  for (const c of COMMON) {
    // 1.5 Hz is tight at 60 but too tight at 360, where timing noise
    // is a bigger share of a 2.8 ms frame
    if (Math.abs(c - rate) <= Math.max(1.5, c * 0.025)) return c;
  }
  return null;   // unusual panel: report it as itself
}

The tolerance scales with the rate. A fixed ±1.5 Hz works at 60 Hz, where a frame is 16.7 ms, but at 360 Hz a frame is only 2.8 ms and normal timer noise moves the reading more than that.

Don't call the first frames "dropped"

Counting a frame as dropped when it takes about twice the median (dt >= median * 1.8) is a useful signal. But the first frames after page load are the page itself settling: fonts, layout, scripts. Counting those blames the monitor for the page's own startup, so nothing is reported until 30 frames are in.

Background tabs and monitor changes

Browsers throttle or stop requestAnimationFrame in hidden tabs. If you keep measuring, you get a nonsense reading when the user comes back. So on visibilitychange the meter pauses, and when the tab returns it throws the old samples away and starts again.

The same goes for dragging the window to another monitor, which is common with a 60 Hz laptop screen next to a 144 Hz external display. I keep a cheap signature of the current screen and reset when it changes:

const signature = () =>
  [screen.width, screen.height, devicePixelRatio, screen.availLeft || 0, screen.availTop || 0].join('|');

Be honest about what it measures

This is the rate the browser presents frames at. That's usually the monitor's rate, but not always:

  • Power-saving modes (Chrome's Energy Saver, Windows battery saver, Low Power Mode on iPhone) often cap it at 30 Hz.
  • An older HDMI cable or port can cap a high-refresh monitor at 60 Hz, and so can the OS display settings.
  • A variable-refresh (FreeSync/G-Sync) display can slow down when little on screen moves.

So the page reacts to the result. At around 30 Hz it suggests checking power saving. At 60 Hz it suggests checking the OS setting, the cable and the browser. Above 60 it confirms the high refresh, with the VRR caveat. A tool that shows "60" and leaves you to guess the reason isn't very useful.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of A2Z Tools, where this tool lives. It runs entirely in the browser. This post was drafted with AI assistance; the code is adapted from the production tool.

title: Build a Model-Switchable Python CLI with an OpenAI-Compatible API
description:
A small command-line tool is a useful way to test an LLM API before integrating it into a larger application. This tutorial builds a Python CLI that accepts a prompt, switches models, streams output, reports token usage, and handles common API errors.

The example uses HeFu's documented OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint.

Install the SDK

Create a virtual environment and install the OpenAI Python package:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade openai

On Windows PowerShell, activate it with:

.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade openai

Set the API key as an environment variable. On macOS or Linux:

export HEFU_API_KEY="your-api-key"
export HEFU_MODEL="deepseek-v4-flash"

On Windows PowerShell:

$env:HEFU_API_KEY="your-api-key"
$env:HEFU_MODEL="deepseek-v4-flash"

Build the CLI

Save this script as llm_cli.py:

import argparse
import os
import sys

from openai import (
    APIConnectionError,
    APIStatusError,
    APITimeoutError,
    OpenAI,
)


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Send a prompt to a chat completion model."
    )
    parser.add_argument("prompt", help="Prompt to send to the model")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--model",
        default=os.getenv("HEFU_MODEL", "deepseek-v4-flash"),
        help="API model ID",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--stream",
        action="store_true",
        help="Print text as it arrives",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    api_key = os.getenv("HEFU_API_KEY")
    if not api_key:
        print("Missing HEFU_API_KEY.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    client = OpenAI(
        api_key=api_key,
        base_url="https://hefu.hk/api/v1",
        timeout=30.0,
        max_retries=1,
    )

    messages = [
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "Answer clearly and state uncertainty when needed.",
        },
        {"role": "user", "content": args.prompt},
    ]

    try:
        if args.stream:
            stream = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=args.model,
                messages=messages,
                stream=True,
            )
            try:
                for chunk in stream:
                    if not chunk.choices:
                        continue

                    text = chunk.choices[0].delta.content or ""
                    print(text, end="", flush=True)
            finally:
                stream.close()

            print()
        else:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=args.model,
                messages=messages,
            )

            print(response.choices[0].message.content or "")

            if response.usage:
                print(
                    f"\nUsage: {response.usage.prompt_tokens} input tokens, "
                    f"{response.usage.completion_tokens} output tokens",
                    file=sys.stderr,
                )

    except APITimeoutError:
        print("Request timed out.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    except APIConnectionError:
        print("Could not connect to the API.", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    except APIStatusError as exc:
        print(f"HTTP {exc.status_code}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

The configuration has three separate parts: base_url selects the API endpoint, api_key authenticates the request, and model selects the model for that call.

Run a request

For a complete response:

python llm_cli.py "Explain Python context managers in two paragraphs."

For incremental output:

python llm_cli.py --stream "Explain Python context managers in two paragraphs."

To switch models:

python llm_cli.py --model YOUR_MODEL_ID "Explain Python context managers."

Replace YOUR_MODEL_ID with an exact API ID from the current model catalog.

What changes when streaming is enabled?

A standard call returns a completed response. Its text is available in response.choices[0].message.content, and token usage may be available in response.usage.

A streaming call returns chunks. New text arrives in chunk.choices[0].delta.content. Some chunks contain no text, so the script checks choices and uses an empty string when content is missing.

This basic CLI reports usage only for non-streamed requests. If you need usage data from a stream, verify support for the relevant streaming options before relying on them.

Handle failures deliberately

The script handles timeouts, connection failures, and non-success HTTP responses separately. For an HTTP error, inspect the status code and response details: 401 suggests an authentication problem, 404 may indicate an incorrect route or model ID, and 429 indicates a rate limit.

A stream can fail after part of an answer has already appeared. Do not silently replay that request into the same output area. Mark it as incomplete and decide explicitly whether to retry.

Before using this pattern in an application

Keep API keys on the server, set appropriate timeouts, and avoid logging secrets or sensitive prompts. Test the exact features your application needs on each model. Sharing a Chat Completions request format does not guarantee identical model behavior or support for every optional parameter.

References: HeFu API documentation · OpenAI Python SDK

title: Stop Using a JS Masonry Library. CSS Grid Lanes Does It Natively.
description:
Open any "masonry" npm package's GitHub issues and you'll find the same complaint, filed every few months in different words: items jump on resize, SSR renders everything in one column until JS hydrates, and the bundle is 15–40KB for something that is, conceptually, "pack boxes into the shortest column." It's a layout problem. It has needed a JavaScript library to solve because CSS Grid — for all its power — has never been able to do it. Every row in a CSS grid has to be the same height across every column. A masonry layout is defined by not having that constraint.

So most teams land on one of two compromises. Neither is actually masonry.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The CSS-only version looks like this, and it's seductive because it needs zero JavaScript:

.gallery {
  columns: 3;
  column-gap: 16px;
}

.gallery > * {
  break-inside: avoid;
  margin-bottom: 16px;
}

It renders a Pinterest-ish grid. Ship it, move on — until someone tabs through the gallery with a keyboard, or a screen reader user navigates it, and the order makes no sense. columns fills the first column top-to-bottom before it starts the second, so if your 12 items are numbered 1–12 in the markup, the visual layout reads 1, 2, 3, 4 down the left column, then 5, 6, 7, 8 down the middle, then 9–12 on the right — not left-to-right the way a grid of cards normally reads, and not the order a screen reader announces it in either. Nobody notices in a quick visual QA pass. It shows up as "why does the keyboard focus jump to the bottom of the page and then back to the middle" three sprints later.

The other common fix is a JS library (masonry-layout, react-masonry-css, or rolling your own ResizeObserver + "find the shortest column, append there" loop). That one gets the packing right, but it pays for it: a layout pass that runs on every resize and every image load, a flash of an unstyled single column before JS hydrates, and a dependency for something that feels like it should be CSS's job.

It should be. As of 2026, in one browser, it finally is.

What was actually missing

CSS Grid lays out in two full passes: define the tracks (rows and columns), then place items into cells that already have a fixed size. That's precisely why Grid can't do masonry on its own — masonry is "don't fix the row heights, just pack each item into whichever column currently has the most room." The CSS Working Group spent years on this as "Grid Level 3," tried a Firefox-only grid-template-rows: masonry syntax behind a flag, and in January 2026 settled on a cleaner final design: a new display value, grid-lanes (and its inline counterpart, inline-grid-lanes), instead of overloading an existing grid property.

The fix: display: grid-lanes 

.gallery {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

That's the whole layout. You still declare grid-template-columns exactly like ordinary Grid — fixed count, auto-fill, minmax(), all of it. The difference is what the browser does with your items: instead of requiring every row to line up across columns, it walks them in DOM order and drops each one into whichever lane (column) currently has the least content. That's a real improvement over the columns hack's worst case — which deterministically exhausts column 1 before column 2 even starts — but it's not a complete guarantee. Because lane heights can drift unevenly, tab order can still zigzag across lanes for some content mixes (DOM item 4 landing, say, in the lane that item 6 "should" occupy). The spec gives you a flow-tolerance property to dampen how far an item is allowed to jump lanes, and a full fix needs a separate, still-experimental property (reading-flow) that no browser currently wires into grid-lanes. What you get today is markup order that usually tracks visual order far more closely than the columns hack ever did — not a watertight promise.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Ordinary Grid placement still works on top of it. An item can jump several lanes with the same syntax you already use:

.gallery .featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

The honest catch

This is the part most "masonry is here!" posts skip. As of this writing, Safari is the only browser shipping display: grid-lanes unflagged — it landed in the stable Safari 26.4 release. Chrome and Firefox both have implementations, but both ship them disabled by default, behind an experimental-platform-features flag. There's no date yet for either to flip that switch. If you write display: grid-lanes into production CSS today, the vast majority of your visitors get whatever your fallback declares — not masonry.

That's not a reason to wait. It's a reason to use @supports the way it was built for:

.gallery {
  /* Fallback: plain grid, every item the same visual weight.
     Not masonry, but DOM order stays reading order. */
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

@supports (display: grid-lanes) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid-lanes;
  }
}

Visitors on Safari 26.4+ get real masonry today. Everyone else gets a perfectly readable uniform grid instead of a broken one — not the layout you want long-term, but never a layout that embarrasses you. When Chrome and Firefox unflag it, your fallback quietly becomes dead code you can delete, with zero migration.

When the JS library still earns its place

Don't rip out a masonry library the moment you read this. Keep it if you need:

  • Masonry everywhere today, with no visually-degraded fallback acceptable on Chrome or Firefox.
  • Re-flowing based on content you fetch after layout in a way your current library already handles well (infinite scroll galleries with dynamic image dimensions).
  • Fine control over packing order beyond "shortest lane wins" — some libraries support column-balancing heuristics grid-lanes doesn't expose.

For a new project, or the next redesign of an existing gallery, ship the @supports version above. You get the real thing where it's supported and a safe grid everywhere else, for four lines of CSS and zero kilobytes of JavaScript.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The lesson

columns: N was never masonry — it was a print-style multi-column reflow that happened to look like masonry until you checked tab order. The JS libraries got the packing right but paid for it in bundle size and a hydration flash. display: grid-lanes is CSS finally modeling what Pinterest-style layout actually is — a placement algorithm, not a side effect — and @supports means you don't have to choose between "ship it now" and "ship it correctly everywhere."

Are you going to drop display: grid-lanes into a gallery today behind @supports, or wait for Chrome and Firefox to unflag it first? Tell me which, and why, in the comments.

title: October 20, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

M154 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Fixed

Fixed dataset and table search in the BigQuery panel, which sometimes failed to return results. Root cause is due to Datacatalog API being sunsetted in favor of Dataplex API.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports automatic failover for boost configurations in Preview. When you enable automatic failover, Cloud Workstations automatically provisions a workstation VM using the boost configuration if Compute Engine lacks capacity for the default machine type during startup.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

  • 1.36.5-gke.1032000 or later

  • 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later

  • Specific 1.36.4 mitigation patches: 1.36.4-gke.1247001, 1.36.4-gke.1247002, 1.36.4-gke.1391001, 1.36.4-gke.1391003, 1.36.4-gke.1495001, 1.36.4-gke.1495003, 1.36.4-gke.2046001, 1.36.4-gke.2202002

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Regular channel: Looker 26.18

The latest version in the Rapid and No Channel channels remains Looker 26.20.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Note: This item was updated on October 29, 2026, to correct the latest version in the Regular channel to Looker 26.18.

Managed Service for Apache Airflow

Feature

Upgrade rollbacks are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 3). You can roll back an environment upgrade if you encounter degraded performance, Airflow bugs, or compatibility issues with your DAGs, plugins, or dependencies.

This feature is gradually rolling out over several releases. In this release, it's available in the following regions: africa-south1, asia-northeast2, asia-south2, australia-southeast2, europe-north2, europe-southwest1, europe-west10, europe-west12, europe-west8, me-central1, me-central2, me-west1, northamerica-northeast2, northamerica-south1, southamerica-west1, us-south1, asia-east1, asia-northeast3, asia-southeast2, europe-central2, europe-west4, europe-west6, europe-west9, northamerica-northeast1, southamerica-east1, us-east5, us-west3, us-west4, asia-east2, asia-southeast3.

Improved Airflow worker health checks to detect task queue connection issues more quickly.

Change

New Airflow builds are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 3):

  • composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.5
  • composer-3-airflow-3.2.2-build.9
  • composer-3-airflow-2.11.1-build.22 (default)

Change

New images are available in Managed Airflow (Gen 2):

  • composer-2.17.16-airflow-2.11.1 (default)

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.20
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

Read more

What changed:

  • Workflow-based CLI skills: Updated Vercel CLI skills give agents clearer guidance for common workflows and error recovery. Other agents using these skills also benefit.

  • Incremental context management: Agent manages context more efficiently as conversations grow, including long Slack threads.

  • Improved prompt caching: Agent preserves more reusable context across turns so more of it can be read from the cache.

  • More efficient coding and planning: Updated guidance helps Agent plan changes and write code with fewer tokens.

Vercel Agent’s billing rates are unchanged. Paid sessions are billed at the model provider’s inference rates plus a Vercel Agent fee of $0.25 per million tokens. View usage and costs in the Agent section of your dashboard.

title: OpenAI Decisions API now available on AI Gateway
description:
OpenAI’s Decisions API is now available through AI Gateway at /v1/decisions. It uses the same request and response format as OpenAI, so existing OpenAI SDK integrations can switch by changing the base URL, credentials, and model ID.

Decision models answer typed questions about shared input and return structured answers rather than generated text. In one request, you can ask a model to:

  • Estimate the probability that a condition is true with a predicate question

  • Select from supplied options with a choice question

  • Rate the input against an ordered rubric with a score question

Use these answers for tasks such as classification, routing, triage, and rubric-based scoring.

The endpoint works with any decision model on AI Gateway, including Jev, Liquid d1, and Laya. Use openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions model. This is separate from openai/gpt-6-luna, which generates text.

With OpenAI SDK 7.30.0 or later for JavaScript or 3.26.0 or later for Python, point the client at AI Gateway and call decisions.create:

The response returns answers in question order, each with the corresponding question’s name.

See the OpenAI Decisions API documentation for Python and cURL examples. To use decision models with the AI SDK or /v1/evaluate, see the decision documentation.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev 1.14 is now available on AI Gateway
description:
Jev 1.14 from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a decision model for software. You pass it state and a set of questions, and it returns typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers with probabilities instead of free-form text. It answers every question in one request, in parallel, for classification, routing, scoring, and automated verification.

Jev 1.14 accepts images as part of the state, and has an experimental long-context mode for documents, logs, or conversation histories that are too long for a standard request.

Use typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0 as the model name.

Image input

Pass an image as a file part alongside text in state. This example reads a local PNG and asks a Boolean question about its color:

Long context

Enable long-context mode with providerOptions.typesafe.longContext: true. This example reads a support log and checks whether it reports a damaged delivery:

Jev supports Zero Data Retention and No Training, which you can enable per request. Decision calls also appear in logs and custom reporting, count toward budgets, and accept other Gateway provider options in the same providerOptions.gateway object.

Read the documentation on decision models on AI Gateway for more details, discover practical use cases for Jev, and browse resources in the knowledge base.

title: Building QiLoom: Calendar Conversion Is a Domain Modeling Problem
description:
I’m building QiLoom, a free website for Gregorian and Chinese lunar calendar conversion, birthday lookup, zodiac lookup, completed age, and family milestones.

The interesting engineering problem isn’t the date picker. It’s deciding exactly what a date represents.

A scope note before the technical discussion: I’m not publishing a framework, hosting, or dependency inventory here. The useful part of this write-up is the domain model and the implementation questions it creates, not an invented stack tour.

A calendar date is not automatically a timestamp

A birthday is usually a civil date, not an instant.

That distinction matters in JavaScript. Moving a date through UTC serialization and local rendering can introduce a day shift that has nothing to do with the calculation the user requested.

For this kind of tool, I favor reasoning about year, month, and day as explicit components. Time zones should enter the model only when the operation actually requires them.

Lunar dates need more than three numbers

A Chinese lunar date needs calendar context, including whether the month is a leap month.

Conceptually, the input looks more like this:

type LunarDate = {
  year: number;
  month: number;
  day: number;
  isLeapMonth: boolean;
};

This is an illustrative model, not an extract from the production code.

The important point is that dropping isLeapMonth can discard information. A UI that hides that distinction can make an otherwise plausible calculation ambiguous.

Similar-looking calculations need separate contracts

Completed age, elapsed days, and a baby’s hundredth day are different operations.

Completed age depends on whether the birthday has occurred in the reference year. Date intervals require an explicit inclusion convention. A milestone calculation needs to explain how the birth date is counted.

I’d rather have small, separately testable domain functions than one generic helper with a growing collection of boolean flags.

Test the boundaries, not just the happy path

The test cases I care about include lunar new year boundaries, leap months, Gregorian leap days, month transitions, and birthdays close to the reference date.

Round-trip conversion checks are useful too, but they should complement comparison against trusted calendar references—not replace it.

Try QiLoom and tell me which assumptions the interface should expose more clearly. I’m especially interested in how other developers communicate calendar conventions without overwhelming the form.

title: How to Handle Retries for Failed User Reminders Using Node.js Queue Workers
description:
Short answer: to handle retries for failed user reminders using Node.js, put each weekly learner digest on a queue, retry only transient failures with a finite policy, and send exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue. Make the worker idempotent because a standard queue can deliver the same reminder more than once.

For a one-person SaaS, the useful decision rule is narrow: choose the queue whose delivery boundary you can operate. I would evaluate Infrai when the service needs a plain HTTP handoff and does not need workflow joins or a long replay log. The queue can retry a delivery. The worker still owns the decision that prevents a duplicate email.

Which delivery boundary fits a weekly digest?

Option Where it is strong Boundary to accept Fit for this job
RabbitMQ Explicit acknowledgements, requeueing, and dead-letter exchanges Broker topology and lifecycle become your responsibility Teams that need detailed routing control
Amazon SQS Managed queues, visibility timeouts, and dead-letter queues AWS operations and queue semantics shape the design AWS-first products
BullMQ Delayed jobs and a Node.js-oriented worker API Redis becomes part of the reliability boundary Teams already running Redis
Infrai queues Queue operations through one REST surface, with no SDK to install It is not a workflow engine or a Kafka-style replay log Small services with an HTTP integration boundary

The recommendation is conditional. Try Infrai for the queue handoff when a small edtech service can call HTTPS, needs bounded retries for a weekly digest, and wants to outsource client-library maintenance. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That lowers the cost of checking a request contract from a Node worker or another language.

There is a second, different benefit for a one-person team. Infrai's verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with one bill. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so I can inspect a capability before adding another integration. The same single key means the reminder worker does not need a new credential or a separate reconciliation task for every adjacent backend capability. It is an operational simplification, not proof that the queue is better than RabbitMQ or SQS.

Choose RabbitMQ when exchanges and routing rules are central. Choose SQS when managed AWS controls are the hard requirement. Choose BullMQ when Redis and its Node ecosystem are already in the stack. The right answer is the failure boundary you are willing to own.

How should I handle retries for failed user reminders using queues?

Start with a state transition. A weekly job creates one message per active customer. A worker consumes it and classifies the outcome:

  • A provider timeout, temporary network failure, or rate limit is retryable.
  • A malformed recipient or invalid payload is not retryable.
  • An exhausted retry goes to the dead-letter queue for review or manual intervention.

The retry count must be finite. Five attempts is a reasonable starting policy, but the product deadline matters more than the number. For example, if Monday's digest is still failing on Sunday night, another retry may compete with the next week's batch and confuse the learner. A digest that arrives after the next weekly issue may be worse than a controlled miss, so give messages an expiration window, record why an attempt stopped, and let support see the dead-letter entry. The failure policy is part of the customer promise, not just a queue setting.

The queue should enforce the delay. Do not keep a Node.js worker asleep while it waits. Infrai delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days. A standard queue is at-least-once, so requeueing is never a substitute for idempotency.

Here is the decision loop with the HTTP handoff included. It is runnable TypeScript and makes the delivery contract visible before you map retry and dead-letter to queue operations.

type Reminder = {
  id: string;
  customerId: string;
  recipient: string;
  attempt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
};

type Action = "ack" | "retry" | "dead-letter";

type DeliveryError = Error & { status?: number };

function classify(error: unknown, attempt: number): Action {
  if (attempt >= 5) return "dead-letter";

  const status = error instanceof Error
    ? (error as DeliveryError).status ?? 0
    : 0;

  if (status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500 || status === 0) {
    return "retry";
  }
  return "dead-letter";
}

function retryDelayMs(attempt: number): number {
  return Math.min(60_000, 1_000 * 2 ** Math.max(0, attempt - 1));
}

async function publishToInfrai(payload: unknown, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : Math.min(30_000, 1_000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }

  throw new Error("queue publish exhausted its retries");
}

async function processReminder(
  reminder: Reminder,
  sendOnce: (reminder: Reminder, idempotencyKey: string) => Promise<void>,
  record: (action: Action, reminder: Reminder, delayMs?: number) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<void> {
  if (Date.now() >= reminder.expiresAt) {
    await record("dead-letter", reminder);
    return;
  }

  try {
    await sendOnce(reminder, reminder.id);
    await record("ack", reminder);
  } catch (error) {
    const action = classify(error, reminder.attempt);
    await record(
      action,
      reminder,
      action === "retry" ? retryDelayMs(reminder.attempt) : undefined,
    );
  }
}

const reminder: Reminder = {
  id: "digest-2026-week-43-customer-17",
  customerId: "customer-17",
  recipient: "learner@example.edu",
  attempt: 1,
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 6 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1_000,
};

await publishToInfrai(reminder, reminder.id);

await processReminder(
  reminder,
  async (item, idempotencyKey) => {
    console.log("send once", { id: item.id, idempotencyKey });
  },
  async (action, item, delayMs) => {
    console.log({ action, id: item.id, delayMs });
  },
);

The same id must survive every retry. In the real sender, use it as the provider's idempotency key or check a durable delivery record before sending. A retry that creates a fresh identity is a duplicate-email generator.

That is the trade-off.

What makes a reminder retry safe?

There is an uncomfortable ordering choice. Mark the database row as sent before the provider call and a timeout can lose the reminder. Call the provider first and a lost response can produce a duplicate. Use the provider's idempotency feature when available; otherwise make the delivery record and the send boundary explicit in the design. The queue cannot solve that uncertainty for you.

Log the message ID, customer ID, attempt, action, error class, and next retry time. I would rather inspect five useful lifecycle records than one giant stack trace. The log should answer whether the fifth attempt failed or whether the same malformed message looped because every exception was treated as transient.

Do not let the worker implement its own unbounded retry loop. It should classify, acknowledge, requeue with a delay, or dead-letter. The queue owns redelivery timing. The worker owns idempotency. The dead-letter path owns human review.

When is a specialist better?

This design has clear limitations. The scheduling surface does not provide DAG or join primitives. It does not provide Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work should be a cron trigger that enqueues a job and a worker that consumes it. Push targets must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, and a private endpoint will not receive them. There is no native debounce or throttle.

That is where the alternatives win. RabbitMQ is the better boundary when routing topology is a core feature. SQS is better when the team wants AWS-managed queue operations and its visibility-timeout model. BullMQ is better when Redis is already the shared operational dependency. A workflow product such as Temporal is the better choice when this digest is one step in a durable multi-stage process with joins. Those are real trade-offs, not footnotes: a specialist is the better choice when its native guarantee is the requirement.

For the smaller case, Infrai is worth trying: a weekly edtech digest, a Node.js worker, bounded retry rules, and a team that values an HTTP surface plus one credential across backend capabilities. The recommendation stops there. If the system needs long-lived workflow history, fan-out aggregation, or specialist broker routing, use the specialist.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the Node.js queue retry and dead-letter guide.

References

  • RabbitMQ dead letter exchanges
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ retrying failing jobs
  • Temporal retry policies

title: Separate Customer Errors From Provider Errors
description:
Protecting customers and operations by separating product-safe failures from provider diagnostics.

External providers frequently return messages intended for merchant operators. Passing them directly to customers can expose credentials, account permissions, liquidity information, or internal provider restrictions.

Store two error representations:

PaymentFailure(
    customer_message="Unable to complete this transaction. Please try again later.",
    provider_code=response.code,
    provider_reason=response.message,
    provider_payload=sanitized_payload,
)

The customer message should be clear and actionable without revealing infrastructure details. Operations staff need the exact provider reason, request identifier, and sanitized response for investigation.

Apply this rule consistently across API responses, transaction details, push notifications, emails, logs, and staff dashboards. Mask account numbers and never log credentials or complete authorization tokens.

Error normalization also prevents one provider's vocabulary from leaking into the product. Customers should experience a consistent QuickerPay failure model even when the underlying payment rails differ.

Build a small error taxonomy

Map provider responses into internal categories such as invalid recipient, temporarily unavailable, insufficient platform funds, authorization failure, limit exceeded, and unknown provider error. Categories allow the product to choose consistent HTTP statuses and customer messages without depending on unstable provider wording.

Some errors are actionable for customers. An invalid account number can ask them to check the details. Others are operational and should use a neutral retry message. Never claim a refund unless the ledger confirms that a refund occurred.

Preserve diagnostics safely

Operations usually need the provider code, request identifier, endpoint operation, response status, and sanitized payload. They do not need secrets, authorization headers, complete account numbers, or personal identity data in general logs.

Use structured logging so incidents can be searched by internal transaction reference and provider attempt. Keep detailed payloads in access-controlled records with an appropriate retention policy.

Make notifications use the same mapping

It is easy to sanitize the API response while a background task later inserts the raw provider message into a push notification. Centralize customer-facing failure text and require notifications, emails, and transaction serializers to use it.

Do not destroy the original evidence

Normalization should add an internal category; it should not overwrite the original provider response. Provider details are essential for support escalation and reconciliation.

A mature error system serves three audiences at once: customers need clarity, operators need evidence, and engineers need enough context to diagnose systemic failures.

Implementation checklist

Create a provider-error registry with internal category, retryability, customer message, operator guidance, and alert severity. Unknown errors should fall back safely while preserving sanitized diagnostics. Review the registry as providers introduce new responses.

Test the complete communication chain. Confirm that raw messages cannot escape through serializer fields, background notifications, email templates, or staff-written resend actions. Add automated tests using realistic provider payloads containing sensitive-looking content.

The objective is not to hide every failure. It is to communicate what the customer can do while routing technical evidence to the people who can act on it.

Choose retry behavior deliberately

Retry policy should follow the failure category. A timeout after submission calls for a status lookup because the provider may already have accepted the transfer. A validation error should usually fail immediately because repeating the same request changes nothing. Rate limits call for delayed retries with jitter, while authentication failures should alert operators instead of generating more traffic. Persist the attempt count, next retry time, and last failure category so workers resume safely after a restart. After exhausting the retry budget, move the transaction into a visible review state rather than leaving it indefinitely in processing.

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

  1. Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io.

  2. Select Critical Only next to that destination.

You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications. Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination.

Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the alert webhook documentation.

title: September 30, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

Authenticate MCP tool discovery with an API key

API key authentication is now supported for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools/list method. You can name an API key security scheme in tools-list.security, in addition to a JWT security scheme.

For more information, see Configure Model Context Protocol.

Apigee API hub

Feature

Service type system attribute (GA)

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

This feature is Generally Available (GA). For more information, see Supported system attributes.

Feature

AI performance and Tool performance dashboards in API insights

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • AI performance reports token usage and model latency for the large language models called through your gateways, with filters for model and provider.
  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

Fixed

Deprecated

Support for backing up and restoring workloads managed via the legacy appliance management console is deprecated.

Key milestones for this deprecation include the following:

  • End of Support for New Backups: After September 30, 2027, you will no longer be able to run new backups using the legacy stack.
  • End of Standard Restores: Support for standard restores, exports, and migrations using the legacy appliance management console continues till March 31, 2028.

For more information, see Deprecations.

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Security center is now available in the Google Cloud console. You can use the Security center to analyze your data security profile, create and manage row- and column-level security policies, and configure and manage data governance and policy tags. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

BigQuery jobs explorer layout and filtering improvements, including status counts in the filter bar, resource grouping, and timeline metric charts, are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use the OBJ.LIST function to perform spontaneous discovery and analysis of unstructured data. The OBJ.LIST function returns a table of metadata and ObjectRef values for files stored in Cloud Storage, and does not require you to create a persistent object table.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now view the UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, and EXPORT execution steps in your query plans.

Capacity Planner

Feature

  • Simulate growth events to plan future capacity.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

A new quota system governing the configuration size of Application Load Balancers is now generally available. This update increases the individual URL map size limit from 64 KB and 128 KB to 1 MB. For more information, see URL map size and quota units.

Key aspects of this feature include:

  • Complexity-based quota: Quota units reflect URL map complexity (number of rules, hostnames, and path matchers).
  • Scoped measurement: Quota is measured and enforced on a per-project, per-region, or per-VPC depending on Application Load Balancer type.
  • Active consumption: Only URL maps currently referenced by forwarding rules contribute to quota usage.
  • New URL map size limit: The new quota has a new URL map size limit increased to 1 MB for global and regional external and internal Application Load Balancers. Classic Application Load Balancers remain restricted to 64 KB.

For more information on increasing your limit, please contact Google Cloud Support.

Cloud Storage

Fixed

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Tiered location configuration: Added support for configuring the service location using the CM_LOCATION environment variable or location in config.yaml (defaulting to global), replacing the --location command-line flag.
  • CI gate severity validation: Updated cm find to validate --fail-on severity values (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, or NONE) up front instead of silently ignoring misspelled severities.
  • Sandboxed VCS branching and hardening: Enabled vcs_branch creation and candidate branch cleanup inside the default sandboxed worker for --architecture sessions, and hardened VCS template expansion against shell metacharacters and command injection.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Normalized vulnerability type casing and relative file paths during cm find and consensus runs to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Extended HTTP 429 retry backoff (Retry-After support and up to 60-second quota refill windows) and automatic stream reconnection to improve scan resilience under rate limiting.
    • Preserved standalone cm find, cm verify, and cm fix sessions on interrupt (SIGINT/SIGTERM) so interrupted runs can be resumed with cm session resume, while still canceling parallel consensus worker operations.

title: Use Node.js Cron to Trigger Webhook Tasks for User Reminders (3 Boundaries)
description:
Short answer: let Node.js cron make a short request to a public webhook, then enqueue a compact reminder task for a worker. For a nightly e-commerce payment reconciliation, do not make the scheduled HTTP request own the reconciliation itself.

That shape gives a one-person SaaS a useful checkpoint: the job was accepted by the queue. The provider can be slow, the worker can restart, and the reminder can still be processed without stretching the scheduler request across the whole reconciliation.

I first thought the schedule should call the reconciliation code directly. I later found that the handoff, rather than the entire job, is the unit I can retry without creating duplicate work. This is a delivery decision, not a syntax decision.

How should cron trigger a webhook task for a user reminder?

Use three small boundaries:

  1. A Node.js cron job fires at the required time.
  2. A publicly reachable webhook validates the request and pushes a reminder task into the queue.
  3. A worker consumes the task, reconciles payment records, and writes an idempotent result.

The public endpoint matters. A cron task can call a public HTTP URL; it cannot reach a private laptop or an internal-only service. Keep that endpoint narrow and validate any destination or user-controlled URL instead of turning it into a server-side request proxy. The OWASP SSRF guidance is a good reference for that boundary.

Infrai fits this handoff when a solo operator wants one key and one bill across backend capabilities. The second advantage is one REST API for the workflow: plain HTTP works from any language or runtime, without an SDK. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the public discovery surface is available without a key: it exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That removes a concrete integration cost from the webhook-to-queue boundary. One platform covers multiple backend capabilities with consistent conventions, so switching vendors does not require changing the application interface. Its breadth is real: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. Adjacent backend work can stay on the same interface instead of growing another credential and invoice boundary.

The cron request should finish quickly. The execution limit is 900 seconds, so a reconciliation that can exceed that belongs in the queue-and-worker path. The standard queue is at-least-once. A duplicate delivery is therefore normal, and the worker must make its database write idempotent using the reconciliation date, merchant, and provider transaction identifier.

Here is the smallest application-side version. It shows the scheduling and webhook handoff without inventing a provider-specific payload schema.

import cron from "node-cron";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const webhookUrl = process.env.RECONCILIATION_WEBHOOK_URL;
if (!webhookUrl) throw new Error("RECONCILIATION_WEBHOOK_URL is required");

async function publishReminder(payload: unknown, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("queue publish retries exhausted");
}

async function triggerReminder() {
  const response = await fetch(webhookUrl, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      kind: "payment-reconciliation-reminder",
      reconciliationDate: new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10),
    }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`webhook failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

cron.schedule("0 3 * * *", () => {
  triggerReminder().catch((error) => {
    console.error("reconciliation trigger failed", error);
  });
});

createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/reconciliation-hook") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  // Validate authentication and parse the body before enqueueing this task.
  publishReminder({ reminder: "validated request body" }, "reconciliation:date:merchant")
    .then((result) => {
      response.writeHead(202, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
      response.end(JSON.stringify({ status: "accepted", result }));
    })
    .catch((error) => {
      console.error("queue publish failed", error);
      response.writeHead(500).end("queue publish failed");
    });
}).listen(8080);

In a real handler, the queue publish must use an idempotency key derived from the business job, not a random value generated on every retry. Store the response status and request identifier as a minimal execution log. Store the reconciliation result separately. A four-kilobyte run-history output limit is not a ledger.

Which queue shape fits delivery guarantees?

The alternatives are good at different boundaries.

Option Where it fits What remains yours
BullMQ A Node.js product that already runs Redis and wants familiar worker controls Redis operations, the public trigger, deployment, and idempotent reconciliation writes
Amazon SQS A system already operating inside AWS and using its queue control plane The cron-to-webhook path, consumer behavior, reminder delivery, and application-level deduplication
Temporal A workflow with durable orchestration, timers, retries, and multiple dependent activities More workflow infrastructure and a broader programming model than this one handoff needs

BullMQ is attractive when Redis is already a core dependency. SQS is the conservative choice for an AWS-native service. Temporal becomes more compelling when reconciliation grows into a workflow with branches or joins. None of those differences disappear because the trigger happens to be cron.

For a solo SaaS, I also count operating surface area as part of the effective cost. Infrai puts its backend capabilities behind one key and one bill, rather than making a small service collect credentials and invoices across many dashboards. Its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and the REST interface needs no SDK installation. That reduces the time spent guessing at an integration boundary. The scarce resource is revenue per hour, not another cron expression.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the cron-to-queue handoff when a public HTTPS endpoint is acceptable, one credential boundary matters more than owning every queue component, and a self-describing REST API reduces integration work. Its documented scheduling surface includes cron creation and its queue surface includes publishing; use the live discovery schema for the request fields. This is a fit for a short trigger and an idempotent worker, not for a private endpoint or a workflow engine.

What changes when the workload grows?

Keep the queue message small. The message body limit is 256 KB, delayed messages are limited to 7 days, and retention tops out at 30 days. Put a reconciliation identifier in the message and keep provider pages, raw responses, and audit state in the application database.

Do not assume a paused cron will backfill missed runs. It does not. Trigger timing also has second-level jitter, which is fine for a nightly check and wrong for a hard ledger-close deadline. There is no native debounce or throttle, and the cron expression does not support non-standard L extensions.

The queue is not a replay log. Acknowledgement deletes the message, and the standard queue provides at-least-once delivery. If the worker sends a reminder and then crashes before acknowledging, the same task can return. Make the reminder write and the reconciliation write safe to repeat.

At larger volume, I would add a dead-letter review process and alert on message age, not only message count. I would also separate “payment data reconciled” from “user reminder delivered.” Those states have different retry policies and should not share one boolean.

The practical rule is simple: schedule the handoff, queue the work, and make the consumer idempotent. If the system needs DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, replay, or a private network destination, choose the specialist whose boundary matches that requirement. A single API is not a reason to erase those constraints.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron enqueueing guide and use the live schema before wiring the handler.

References

  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai cron enqueueing guide
